u2ue - the Unity to Unreal porting toolkit: Manual

Edition 2026-10-17. u2ue moves a Unity game to Unreal Engine 5 through one command-line facade. It reads the Unity project as text, converts what can be converted, measures in Unity whatever behaviour has to be matched exactly, proves every change before it ships, and reports - per effect, per system, per number - what draws as Unity draws it and what does not, always with the reason.

It was built while porting a commercial Unity 6 tactics game to Unreal Engine 5.7 (called the reference port throughout), and exercised on a second, unrelated game on Unity 2021.3.

About this manual

Who it is for. Three readers, each with a reading path below: a porter moving a Unity game to Unreal (a person, or an AI model working through the toolkit's skills); a reviewer judging how the port was done; and a developer extending the toolkit itself. It assumes you know Unity and Unreal as a user, Python well enough to run a script, and C# well enough to read a MonoBehaviour.

What it covers. Everything a port needs: installing the toolkit and describing your game, a tutorial that takes a game from its project file to its first report, the procedure for each part of a port (code, scenes, UI, audio, effects, measuring, verification, reports), the hard parts in depth, the Unity and Unreal tools the package ships, test-driven porting, the reference for every command, the architecture and its UML, troubleshooting, questions and answers, a worked example and a glossary.

How it is built. Its structure follows ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514 (the international standard for user documentation): front matter, the concept of operations, installation, a tutorial, procedures, reference, troubleshooting, and a glossary. Each part is arranged by the kind of reading it serves - learning, doing, looking up or understanding. The parts that describe the code (the command reference, the facade's requirements, the use cases, the class model, the switch, tool and selftest tables, the traceability) are generated from the code and the requirements model on every build, so the manual cannot describe a toolkit that has moved on.

Conventions

  • READ - a value taken from the Unity source (a file, a field) with where it came from.
  • MEASURED - a Unity behaviour observed in Unity itself by a probe, judged by a judge that refuses a planted wrong answer.
  • ABSENT - a value proven not to exist, or not readable, named with the reason. There is no fourth category: the toolkit never substitutes a plausible default, and a refusal is reported by name.
  • HAVE / NOT YET - whether the toolkit itself provides something today. NOT YET is always followed by the plan that delivers it.
  • Commands run from the toolkit's root folder: py -m u2ue .... Sample output is real; a project's name is written <game> and machine paths <work>/..., <unity project>, <unreal project>. Every command the manual shows is checked against the facade on every build: a verb or an option the facade does not have stops the build.
  • File references read path:line and were checked against the code on the edition date.
  • "Chapter N" and "Appendix X" are links in the one-page edition.

Related documents

The toolkit's own documents sit beside the code, and this manual holds their content: u2ue/README.md (the survey of every tool), u2ue/GUIDE.md (the route for a second game), u2ue/BASICS.md (the porting basics, topic by topic), u2ue/ARCHITECTURE.md (the reviewer's document), u2ue/CONCEPTS.md (the concept model), u2ue/USECASES.md (the problem story and the stakeholder requirements), u2ue/PACKAGE.md (the product plan) and the two skills. u2ue/manual/coverage_gate.py checks that every section of each of them is in this manual, or is named as out with the reason.

Building this manual

The Markdown files in u2ue/manual/ are the source. py u2ue/manual/build.py regenerates the parts that come from the code and the model, then writes manual.html, the single-page edition. It refuses to build when a page names a particular game, its folders or a machine path, or shows a command the facade does not have. py u2ue/manual/build.py --check exits 1 when any generated part is stale. py u2ue/manual/build.py --selftest proves both gates still refuse their plants.

Why u2ue

Port a Unity game to Unreal Engine 5, and prove it is still the same game.

u2ue is a porting toolkit with one command line. It reads the Unity project as text, with no editor running. It converts everything that is not game logic by itself: particle effects, scenes, UI, materials and audio. It measures in Unity any behaviour that has to be matched exactly. It holds the result to Unity on numbers, frame by frame and bit by bit. The game's logic is ported by an AI model following the toolkit's own skill, and a reviewer judges that port by reading a generated UML model instead of a diff.

The numbers below were measured on the reference port, a commercial Unity 6 tactics game moved to Unreal Engine 5.7. Each tile names the command that produced it. None of them is typed by hand.

The novel parts, and why they matter

Each of these began as an answer to a failure that cost real time on a real port. Each is in the package, has a selftest, and has its own chapter.

It reads Unity without Unity

Prefabs, nested prefabs, prefab variants, scenes, materials and ScriptableObjects are read straight from their YAML. Overrides are applied, removed components honoured, and fileIDs followed across nesting. The textures Unity actually samples (the imported mip chain, not the source file) are read from the project's Library/Artifacts. No editor has to be open, so nothing steals focus, waits on a license or blocks the person who is working. Chapter 7, Chapter 13.

Shuriken to Niagara, behaviour by behaviour, with evidence

The converter turns Unity's particle systems into Niagara systems. Every behaviour it ports is a route behind a switch. A route starts OFF, and is turned ON only after it has been measured, proven over every emitter, trialled, looked at, and given an evidence row in the flip table. The switch table in Chapter 20 lists each route with its evidence. When the converter cannot port something, it says what, and why, per emitter. Chapter 8, Chapter 13.

It measures Unity instead of guessing

When the port depends on how Unity behaves (a sub-emitter's birth frame, a scaling mode, a float format), the toolkit measures it in Unity. A probe case is data, not new editor code. A window runner starts only while the owner is idle and stops the moment they return. Each rule is stored with the Unity version it was measured on, and a project on another version sees it flagged as unverified. Chapter 9, Chapter 14.

Judges that can fail

Every check that decides "same as Unity" carries a planted fault that it must refuse. u2ue judge --prove runs every judge against its plant. A judge whose plant passes is reported as broken, because a gate that has only ever passed looks exactly like one that is switched off. Chapter 16.

Unity's own runtime, with no editor

The game's rules run on CoreCLR and on the target Unity version's own Mono runtime, headlessly, and are compared by float bits with the same rules running in Unreal (u2ue digest, u2ue parity). Each difference is named down to the row and the bits, and nothing is hidden behind a tolerance. Chapter 6, Chapter 16.

Data-first conformance

Unity's own particle state, read by one generic probe, is compared with Niagara's read-back for every emitter of every effect, paired by file id (u2ue conform). A miss is named: born late, the wrong count, or no partner. Pictures come last, and a capture artefact is labelled, never counted. Chapter 10, Chapter 13.

Headless Unity testing

Editor-folder NUnit tests run with no Unity Editor. C# is type-checked headlessly, and the Unity console is read as the headless test of whether the code actually ran: a watermark shows only what is new, and repeated spam collapses to one row. Chapter 14, Chapter 16.

Several agents, one machine

There are three ways to work with Unity, and the toolkit supports all of them: no editor at all, driving a live editor through its HTTP bridge, or a second editor instance on a clone with its own port. Each editor has one driver, the other agents work headless, and they coordinate through a file-backed mail channel. Chapter 14.

Unreal, headless and well behaved

The Unreal runner refuses to start in the conditions that measurably hang it, and runs one Unreal at a time. Audio is deterministic and never reaches the speakers. u2ue host makes the game's own Unreal project the way a customer would make one, and proves each step. Chapter 15.

A model to review, not a diff

The use cases, the facade's requirements, the class model and the traceability are all generated from the toolkit's code and documents, and gated. A diagram that names a class, a verb or a step that does not exist fails the build. A reviewer starts at the epic and follows each step into the command that proves it. Chapter 5, Chapter 18, Chapter 21, Appendix E.

Requirements nobody wrote

Chaining each use case step's precondition to the step before it exposes requirements that nobody wrote down. On the reference game, most of the requirements the chain inferred turned out to be real defects (see the tile above). Chapter 5.

The product checks itself

u2ue cycle checks every promise of the toolkit (its pillars) on every work cycle. A pillar with no check yet reads ABSENT, never PASS, and red stops the cycle. Chapter 16.

Built for an AI porter

Two skills tell an AI model how to work. One ports a game's logic into an engine-free model behind seams. The other ports an effect gap by the route protocol. Each step of each skill names the command that verifies it, so the model's work can be checked rather than trusted. Chapter 6, Chapter 8.

Never a silent default

Every value is READ (with where it came from), MEASURED (in Unity, by a judged probe) or ABSENT (named, with the reason). The toolkit never substitutes a plausible number, and a refusal names its cause. Chapter 1.

Porting to Unreal in a nutshell

The whole job on two screens: a quick start you can run today, and the five problems every Unity to Unreal port meets, each with the toolkit's answer and the chapter that has the details.

Quick start

You need Windows with native PowerShell, Python with PyYAML, the .NET SDK, Unreal Engine 5.7, and your Unity project saved as text (Force Text serialization). Chapter 3 has the full list.

py -m u2ue                                          # every verb the toolkit has
py -m u2ue find <words>                             # everything it holds about a subject, as path:line

Describe your game in one project file, u2ue/projects/<game>.json (Chapter 3 has a complete one). Then:

py -m u2ue --project <game> info                    # every path the file names, opened - fix the file until it exits 0
py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory --survey      # which folders are the game's own code; name them as code.roots
py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory               # the game's C#, type by type: Unity calls, pure rules, frame order
py -m u2ue --project <game> extract                 # the particle effects as the engine-neutral IR, every refusal named
py -m u2ue --project <game> check                   # the toolkit's selftests and your project's gates - red means stop
py -m u2ue --project <game> build --dry             # the plan and the Unreal host's state, before anything runs
py -m u2ue --project <game> build                   # the effects as Niagara systems (native PowerShell, one Unreal at a time)
py -m u2ue --project <game> report --out <game>.html
py -m u2ue --project <game> metrics                 # how identical it is, each number from a record

That is a first report. Chapter 4 walks the same steps with real output, then carries on through the game's code, scenes, UI and its own Unreal project. If an AI model is doing the port, start it with Chapter 17 and py -m u2ue --project <game> logic.

The five problems every port meets

1. Unity does not behave the way its documentation reads

A converter written from the documentation is wrong in the details that show: the frame a sub-emitter's child is born on, what a scaling mode really scales, how Mono prints a float. The toolkit measures Unity instead of reading about it. A probe case is data, run in the owner's editor only while the owner is idle, and judged by a judge that must refuse a planted wrong answer. Each rule is stored with the Unity version it was measured on, and on another version it is reported as unverified rather than trusted. Chapter 9, Chapter 14.

2. Shuriken and Niagara do not map one to one

Shuriken is a fixed set of modules; Niagara is an emitter stack of scripts. A Unity setting can need several Niagara modules, and some have no equivalent at all. The toolkit reads every effect into an engine-neutral IR, converts it in stages, and puts every behaviour behind a switch. A switch starts OFF and is turned ON only with an evidence row that a trial proved. What cannot be ported is named per emitter on the acceptance page, never dropped. Chapter 8, Chapter 13.

3. The game's rules are tangled into MonoBehaviours

The rules live inside Update methods, coroutines, inspector values and Unity types, in an execution order nobody wrote down. The toolkit moves them into an engine-free model behind seams. The engine fills the seams (view, input, camera, effects, platform); the model is driven in Unity's frame order and runs without either engine. Its answers are proven by float bits on .NET, on that Unity version's own Mono runtime, and in Unreal. Chapter 6, Chapter 16, and the logic skill.

4. Transforms do not compose the same way

The two engines differ in axes, units and rotation order. Worse, a non-uniform scale under a rotation makes Unity draw a shear that Unreal's transform cannot hold at all. The toolkit states one conversion, in one place, and finds every node Unreal cannot place as Unity does (py -m u2ue --project <game> shear), with the error in centimetres. Such a node is named for a decision, never averaged into something that looks close. Chapter 7.

5. "It looks right" is not proof

A photo of an effect is one draw of a random process. A metric alone can lie too: on the reference port, a render whose whole scene went black scored better, because dark geometry stopped hiding a bright backdrop. The toolkit proves the data first. It reads back every emitter frame by frame and holds it to Unity's own particle state (u2ue conform). It reports "identical" as a family of four numbers, never one. Pictures come last, with the capture's own artefacts labelled. Chapter 10, Chapter 11, Chapter 16.

The one rule under all five

Every value is READ from the source, with where it came from; or MEASURED in Unity, by a judge that can fail; or ABSENT, named with the reason. There is no fourth kind. A port that guesses looks finished long before it is. Chapter 1.

The short version

This part is the whole toolkit in one sitting: one screen per aspect of a port, each saying what happens, the command that does it, what it prints, and what it does not do yet. The chapters behind it go deeper: Part I gets you started (installation and the tutorial), Part III holds the procedure for each part of a port, Part IV the hard parts and the tools, Part V the reference, and the questions and answers take on the "why on earth did you do it that way" questions.

The output shown here is real, from a second Unity game the toolkit was not built on (Unity 2021.3, a different studio's project), with that game's name written <game> and machine paths written <work>/... and <unreal project>. Numbers from the game the toolkit was built on - a commercial Unity 6 tactics game ported to Unreal Engine 5.7 - are called the reference port.

S1. What u2ue is, in five lines

  1. A command-line facade, py -m u2ue, over the tools that move a Unity game to Unreal Engine 5.
  2. It reads the Unity project as text (YAML prefabs, scenes, materials, .meta files): no Unity editor runs to port anything.
  3. It converts what has a counterpart (particle effects, transforms, UI layout, lights, materials), and gives the game's own code a runtime and a method instead of pretending to translate it.
  4. Where Unity's behaviour is not written down, it measures Unity, once, in the owner's editor, and keeps the measurement.
  5. It proves every change before it ships and reports every difference by name, with a number and a reason.

It is not a button that makes a Unity game run in Unreal. Chapter 1 says exactly what it does and does not promise.

S3. Describe the game

What happens. One JSON file per game, u2ue/projects/<game>.json, names the Unity tree and version, the Unreal host, where the work goes and the game's folders. No field is defaulted: a missing one is an error, not a guess.

py -m u2ue --project <game> info
project <game> (u2ue/projects/<game>.json)
  unity.root           dir       <unity project>                     ok
  unity.assets         dir       <unity project>/Assets              ok
  work.effects         out-dir   <work>                              ok (exists)
  work.photos          out-dir   <work>/photos                       to be created (its parent exists)
  unreal.uproject      file      <unreal project>.uproject           ok
  unreal.content_root  game-path /Game/U2UE/<Game>                    ok (an Unreal content path)
  unity.editor         dir       <Unity 2021.3.21f1 install>         ok (its unity_builtin_extra exists)
  adapter: unity_project (spawn rules unity)

Every path is opened, not just printed. Limits: the project must be serialized as text (Unity's Force Text).

S4. The game's code

What happens. The toolkit does not translate MonoBehaviours into Actors. It tells you what every type touches, and gives you a method: move the rules into an engine-free model (plain C# that references no engine), let each engine run it through a thin host, and prove both engines get the same answers.

py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory
u2ue inventory <game>: 1987 files, 2453 types (plain 1384, MonoBehaviour 789, ScriptableObject 160, ...); 1148 pure rules
  serialized data                  473 types   1708 sites
  platform (log, files, prefs)     365 types   1525 sites
  spawn / destroy                  311 types   1049 sites
  coroutines / Invoke              273 types    997 sites
  transform                        222 types   1652 sites
  ...

The 1148 pure rules use no Unity API and move first. The inventory also lists every MonoBehaviour's script execution order with its lifecycle methods - the table Unity's frame is rebuilt from. Then:

need what the toolkit gives
inspector values, ScriptableObjects u2ue data: every serialized value, prefab overrides applied, references resolved to asset paths
Unity's frame, Time.deltaTime, coroutines the U2ue.Runtime .NET library: UnityFrame, UnityClock, Coroutines with Unity's rules, each held by tests
logging, files, PlayerPrefs, JSON, random six platform interfaces with Unity's exact semantics (Random.Range's bounds, JsonUtility's fields)
an Unreal host to start from the U2ue.Unreal templates: the frame actor, the pointer, the camera rig, the platform services
the model stays engine-free u2ue check --only model: an engine reference in the model fails
the answers agree u2ue parity: every runtime's digest compared float bit by float bit

Limits: the toolkit does not move the code or write the hosts. Chapter 6 is the method; the reference port is its proof (three scripted battles whose event logs are byte-identical between the Unity-free test run and the Unreal host).

S5. Transforms, hierarchies and scenes

What happens. Unity is metres, y up, left handed; Unreal is centimetres, z up, left handed. One module holds the conversion and its selftest pins every tool that converts to it:

Unity Unreal
position (x, y, z) (-x, z, y) x 100
rotation (qx, qy, qz, qw) (-qx, qz, qy, qw)
scale (sx, sy, sz) (sx, sz, sy)

The one thing that does not convert: a rotated child under a non-uniformly scaled parent is sheared in Unity, and Unreal's transform cannot hold a shear. u2ue shear finds every such node and says how far off it would land, in centimetres:

py -m u2ue --project <game> shear --from Assets/<Scene>.unity

On the reference port's first battle map, 46 nodes were sheared, two of them drawn, the worst 63 cm off at a mesh corner. Accepting, baking or fixing each is the owner's decision, made with the number.

Whole scenes go through u2ue scene: export to glTF in the owner's editor, import into a new Unreal level, read the saved level back, and scene check - a gate that grades hierarchy, materials, textures, lighting and placement against the scene's own measured baseline (the reference port's first map: 45 checks, PASS). Limits: the reference port ran steps of its own between import and readback (material parents, lighting, outline hulls) that are not verbs yet (Chapter 7).

S6. Prefabs, and reading Unity's YAML

What happens. Effects and data are read straight from the YAML: nested prefab instances expanded with their modifications, prefab variants, removed components, the material chain through m_Parent. A file the reader cannot handle is refused by name, never half-read:

py -m u2ue --project <game> extract
u2ue extract: 60 READ key(s): 56 IR file(s) with 189 emitter(s), 4 refused by name, 0 dropped, 0 foreign path(s)
  REFUSED unity.prefab.5ccd...: .../Winter Door.prefab: PrefabInstance 4843689442982340616: modification target 1211823196678298638 (m...

Limits: a prefab instance that removes one of its source's GameObjects is refused today (the reader that applies it is proven and lands with the next build); objects inside a nested model (FBX) are not read - FBX is binary - so a scene that modifies one is refused by name.

S7. Materials and lighting

What happens. Effect materials use custom shaders. The blend mode is read as a number from the material (_DstBlend == 1 is additive), never from the shader's name. Each shader family gets one Unreal parent material, authored once; every material of that family becomes an instance with its values read off its .mat.

Lit materials need Unity's lighting, not Unreal's. For Shader Graph materials the toolkit translates the HLSL Unity itself generated for the graph, and evaluates URP's own Lit lighting (its BRDF, its spherical-harmonics ambient, its reflection decode) from the scene's measured sun, ambient probe and reflection cube.

Point lights an effect carries become Unreal point lights by a mapping read from both engines' source: inverse-squared falloff, AttenuationRadius = 100 x range, intensity pi x I candelas, the colour's sRGB bytes. In Unity the mapping's source side was measured on lit pixels: nine cases fit URP's own formula at a ratio of 1.0000.

Limits: the lit route is behind a switch until its trial is looked at; a graph that moves vertices in object space, or that includes custom code, is refused by name; fog, shadows and ambient occlusion on these materials are named, not drawn.

S8. Particle effects

What happens. Every Shuriken ParticleSystem becomes a Niagara emitter, written through Unreal's own converter library, in twenty stages in the order Unity runs its modules. Each Unity behaviour the converter handles is a route; every route arrived behind a switch, default off, and was flipped on only with its evidence.

An emitter Unreal does not draw is a gap only if Unity draws it. The reference port, in numbers (2026-10-15, its acceptance rebuild part way through):

keys      674: BUILT 673, IR REFUSED 1; 673 drawn, 197 of them with a named gap
emitters  drawn 7810 | absent: gap 642 (Unity draws them, Unreal does not), 374 absent exactly as in Unity
coverage  92.4 % of the emitters Unity draws are drawn in Unreal (7810 / 8452)
measured  86.3 % of the drawn emitters carry no stand-in (6737 of 7810)

Limits: VFX Graph assets and particle systems authored directly in scenes are listed, not converted. TrailRenderers: Unity's law is measured and reproduced exactly by U2ue.Runtime.TrailLaw; drawing it in Unreal is next. Chapter 8 has the rest.

S9. UI

What happens. uGUI and UMG lay out differently, so the toolkit does not rebuild screens as UMG trees. A Unity Canvas is captured (every RectTransform, anchor and component, as Unity resolved it) and laid out in Unreal by a port of uGUI's own layout solver and TextMeshPro's glyph layout, the generic library U2ue.Ui:

py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test                                   # 398 pass, 9 skipped
py -m u2ue --project <game> ui convert <capture> --screen NAME --out DIR

The tests hold the library to Unity's own captures; a planted transform defect fails 264 of them. Limits: the capture runs in the game's Unity editor in Play mode and ships as the package's Editor assembly; which view model feeds which panel stays the game's.

S10. Audio

What happens. Authored clips (.wav, .ogg) import into Unreal as Sound Waves. Which sound plays, and how loud, should be a rule in the model, so both engines choose the same one. Sounds Unity generates at run time are rendered once to float PCM and played through a small bridge that hands the samples to Unreal's mixer unconverted. Limits: the bridge as a reusable plugin is on the roadmap.

S11. Measuring Unity

What happens. Much of what a port must match is not documented: the frame a sub-emitter's particle is born in, how a trail drops its points, what a Timeline does before its clip starts. The toolkit measures it:

  1. A judge (Python) states the rule and is selftested against planted wrong answers - before any measurement exists.
  2. A probe (an Editor C# script) is dropped into the owner's editor in a window: only after ten idle minutes, stopped the moment they return, compiled headless first, everything else's checksum compared before and after.
  3. The probe writes a bake; the judge reads the rule off it or refuses it with the numbers.
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only facts
  163 measured Unity bakes; this project is Unity 2021.3.21f1
       163 measured on Unity 6000.3.16f1    UNVERIFIED for Unity 2021.3 - re-measure where it matters

A rule measured on another Unity version is still used, but never reported as measured for this game.

S12. Proving every change

What happens. Four rules, each enforced by a gate rather than recommended:

  • Read it or name it absent - no plausible default stands in for a value.
  • A gate must be able to fail - every gate carries plants it must refuse.
  • Prove a change offline - the converter is replayed against a recording stub over every emitter of every effect: switched off, a new route must change nothing; switched on, exactly the emitters it names.
  • Verify with both - the data proves itself first; then the numbers and the pictures confirm it, each looked at.
py -m u2ue --project <game> check            # every selftest, the field gates, the measured rules' versions, the model gates
py vfxport/whole_trace.py REF.py WORK.py     # a converter change: identical engine calls, or exactly the predicted set

S13. Reports and numbers

What happens. Every number comes from a record on disk, with its denominator, its definition and its date; a number that cannot be computed prints ABSENT with the record it needs; an input older than the newest build prints STALE.

py -m u2ue --project <game> report --out <game>.html      # the acceptance page: every key, every gap, every owner decision
py -m u2ue --project <game> metrics                       # coverage, measured share, read-back, photos, machine hours, routes
py -m u2ue --project <game> tempo                         # each route's first code -> verified flip, read off git

Before anything is built, the page already lists every effect the game must account for.

S14. What it does not do

  • Animation (Animator state machines, Mecanim retargeting) and physics: not covered. The reference port had neither, so no tool is claimed until a game that has them is ported and measured. One animation case is handled: an Animator that drives an effect root's scale.
  • The game's code is moved by you, with the method, the runtime and the gates (S4).
  • Anything the toolkit cannot reproduce exactly is reported on the item, with the measured size of the difference.

1. Introduction

What u2ue is

u2ue is a set of tools behind one facade, py -m u2ue, for porting a Unity game to Unreal Engine 5. It was not designed in the abstract. Every tool in it was written to move one real game - the reference port, a Unity 6 tactics game - to Unreal 5.7, and each was kept only once it had run on that game and refused a deliberately broken input. A second, unrelated game (a different studio's project on Unity 2021.3) runs through the same facade to keep the toolkit honest about what is general and what was one game's.

A port with u2ue has two halves:

  • The game's code. The toolkit inventories the game's C# type by type, reads its serialized data, gives the moved code a runtime that keeps Unity's frame, time and coroutine rules, gates the result so it stays engine-free, and compares its answers across the runtimes it runs on (Chapter 6).
  • The game's content. Particle effects are converted end to end - read from the prefabs, converted to Niagara, built headless, read back frame by frame, photographed beside Unity's frames, and reported (Chapter 8). Transforms, scenes, UI and audio have their own tools and methods (Chapter 7).

For the effects, the job fits in one line: every Shuriken particle effect a Unity game fires becomes a Niagara system in Unreal that draws as Unity draws it - and every place it does not is named, on the emitter, with the reason.

What it does today

area today
Shuriken particle effects to Niagara HAVE - extract, check, build, read, photo, report, metrics (Chapter 8)
Effect materials (custom shader families) HAVE - one parent per family, every material an instance read off its .mat (Chapter 8)
Lit (Shader Graph / URP Lit) effect materials HAVE behind a switch - the graph's generated HLSL translated, URP's lighting evaluated; trial pending (Chapter 8)
Point lights on effects HAVE - read, mapped by both engines' source, spawned on the effect; the Unity side measured on lit pixels (Chapter 8)
Code inventory and frame order HAVE - u2ue inventory (Chapter 6)
Serialized data (inspector values, ScriptableObjects) HAVE - u2ue data (Chapter 6)
Unity's frame, time, coroutines, platform services HAVE - the U2ue.Runtime .NET library (Chapter 6)
Engine-free model gates HAVE - u2ue check --only model (Chapter 6)
Cross-runtime parity of the game's rules HAVE - u2ue parity (Chapter 6)
Unreal host templates (frame, pointer, camera, platform) HAVE - U2ue.Unreal, compiled against UnrealSharp; a headless smoke run is NOT YET (Chapter 6)
Transform conventions, shear HAVE - u2ue.transform, u2ue shear (Chapter 7)
UI layout (uGUI, TextMeshPro) HAVE - the U2ue.Ui library and u2ue ui convert; the capture as a package Editor assembly is NOT YET (Chapter 7)
Measuring a Unity behaviour HAVE - the probe / judge / window protocol (Chapter 9)
TrailRenderers HAVE the law (U2ue.Runtime.TrailLaw, exact against Unity); drawing it in Unreal is NOT YET (Appendix B)
Scene export / import / readback / fidelity HAVE - u2ue scene; the reference pipeline's middle steps (material parents, lighting) are NOT YET verbs (Chapter 7)
Audio as a plugin NOT YET - Appendix B; the method is in Chapter 7
Animation, physics ABSENT - no worked example yet (Appendix B)

Three principles

Every stage follows three rules. Each was earned by a failure, and the toolkit enforces them rather than recommending them.

  1. Read it, or name it absent. A value the port writes is read from the Unity source; one it cannot read is named absent with the reason. There are no defaults that stand in silently: a substituted value is a lie the acceptance report would repeat.
  2. Every rule is measured. How Unity behaves is read from its data, its source where it ships source (Unity's packages, Unreal's engine), or measured in Unity by a probe whose judge is written first and refuses a planted wrong answer. A rule measured on one Unity version is reported as unverified on another (Chapter 9).
  3. Every change is proven before it ships. A new converter route lands behind a switch, default off; the converter is replayed over every emitter of every effect and must show identical engine calls except exactly the predicted set; a trial is built, read, judged and photographed; only then does the default flip (Chapter 10).

In practice: a measured rule's bake is kept as a fact file (shared/conformance/*-facts.json) with the Unity version it was measured on, and a project on another version is told which rules are unverified for it (u2ue check --only facts). Documentation and intuition are where a rule is suspected, never where it comes from. The replay that proves a converter change is whole_trace.py: on the reference port it covers 9,560 emitters and 3.4 million engine calls in about 100 s (u2ue/ARCHITECTURE.md, 2026-10-15).

Who it is for

  • A porter - an engineer moving a Unity game to Unreal, who wants the game running the same and every difference named.
  • An AI agent - the toolkit ships with a playbook (u2ue/skill/u2ue-port/SKILL.md) so an agent can drive a port with the same discipline, and every output is text an agent can read.
  • A reviewer - a senior engineer judging how the port is done: Chapter 21 and u2ue/ARCHITECTURE.md are written for them.
  • The game's owner - who answers only the decisions that are theirs; the report lists them, each with its count.

Two systems support them: the owner's Unity editor, where a Unity behaviour is measured only while its owner is idle (Chapter 9), and the Unreal host, where one headless Unreal runs at a time (Chapter 3).

What it does not promise

u2ue does not make a Unity game run on Unreal by itself. The game's own code has to be moved into an engine-free model and given Unreal hosts - the toolkit gives the method, the runtime, the analysis and the gates, not a button. Where it cannot reproduce Unity exactly, it says so on the item, with the measured size of the difference.

The problem it solves

In one sentence: a studio engineer, helped by an AI agent, uses one package with a single entry point to port a whole Unity game to Unreal - its MonoBehaviour code, its transform chain and scenes, its effects and the rest - by implementing adapters or interfaces rather than making the game generic, with an architecture a senior engineer can grasp, and with the porting speed and the percent identical measured.

The problems that fall out of that sentence are the toolkit's shape:

problem where the toolkit answers it
knowing what the toolkit already holds py -m u2ue find (Chapter 2)
knowing what a game's code needs before porting it u2ue inventory (Chapter 6)
moving game code without making the game generic the engine-free model and its adapters (Chapters 6 and 12)
the transform chain u2ue.transform, u2ue shear (Chapter 7)
proving how identical the result is parity, read-back, photos and the metrics (Chapters 6, 10 and 11)
a review that holds the class model and the use cases (Chapter 21)

u2ue as a product

u2ue is built to ship as a Unity package installed in the source project, which an AI agent drives through the same command line a person uses (Appendix B has the package's layout and the release plan). Two of its promises are measured, not claimed: how fast a game is ported with it, and how identical the result is (Chapter 11). u2ue/README.md is the survey of every tool the reference port runs, by work package (Chapter 12 indexes it); u2ue/GUIDE.md is the route for a second game's effects.

What is reusable, in five layers

Of the 151 tools the reference port's live drivers called on 2026-10-14 (u2ue/PACKAGE.md), 32 bound nothing of that game's, 12 read their paths from a project file (the facade's U2UE_* variables), 107 still hard-wired one of its paths or names, and 48 carried their own selftest - which no driver ran until u2ue check existed. What they hold falls into five layers; the first three are the product, the last two the reference game's:

  • Unity readers, offline (no editor). The YAML prefab reader that writes the engine-neutral IR (u1e_ir, t1_guid_index; nested, variant and legacy prefabs; m_RemovedComponents); Unity's OWN imported textures read off Library/Artifacts, every mip it samples (unity_tex_artifact); the built-in resources (u1e_builtin_names, from unity_builtin_extra); alpha-source and alpha-fill derivations (u1e_alpha, u1e_alphadilate); a PSD inside a PNG (u1e_psdtex). Proven on two games and two Unity versions.
  • The engine-pair knowledge: Shuriken to Niagara. build_niagara and shuriken_size, every route flipped on with its evidence row in the flip table (patch_flip_defaults.TABLE) or named OFF with what it waits on (flip_audit); Chapter 20 counts them. Every rule in it was MEASURED in Unity (the probes' facts in shared/conformance/*.json) or READ in an engine's source. This is the asset a second game reuses for free.
  • The proof machinery. The read-back per frame (u1e_color_size_readback) and its sweep checks, a judge per route written BEFORE its trial with a plant that must fail, photo pairs against Unity's fixed-seed reference frames, sheets that LABEL the capture's own artefacts, the screen, the acceptance report, and u2ue metrics.
  • Asset-pack material ports. One hand-authored Unreal parent per Unity shader of the vendor effect packs the reference game uses (Chapter 12 lists them) - reusable by any game that uses those packs.
  • The reference game's own. Its engine-free model (the method of Chapter 6 is reusable; the code is not), its own effect maps, the chunking of its queues, its scenes.

2. Concepts

The project

A project is one JSON file, u2ue/projects/<name>.json, that names everything about one game: its Unity tree and version, its Unreal host, where the work goes, and the game-specific choices. Every field is named, never defaulted - a missing field is an error, not a guess. Chapter 3 lists the fields; py -m u2ue --project <name> info opens every path the file names.

The facade and its verbs

py -m u2ue is the only entry point. It answers verbs - find, info, inventory, data, shear, scene, parity, ui, extract, check, build, read, photo, report, metrics, tempo - listed in one registry (u2ue/verbs/__init__.py). Dispatch, the usage text and the search all read that registry, so a verb cannot exist in one place and be missing from another. A verb WRAPS the tools that do the work; it never rewrites them, so every tool still runs by hand with its own selftest.

py -m u2ue find <words> searches everything the toolkit holds - verbs, adapters, tools, every documentation section, measured rules, converter stages, verified routes - and needs no project:

py -m u2ue find coroutine
u2ue find coroutine: 19 hit(s)
  doc (19)
    2. Coroutines, WaitForSeconds, Inv u2ue/BASICS.md:49            - **Unity**: `StartCoroutine(IEnumerator)`, `yield return null` ...
    1. The lifecycle: Awake, Start, Up u2ue/BASICS.md:31            - **Unity**: Awake and OnEnable on load, Start before the first ...
    3. Give the model Unity's runtime  u2ue/manual/06-game-code.md  `u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime` (netstandard2.1 and net8.0, ...
    ... 16 more (--kind doc --top N)

Adapters: where a game plugs in

The toolkit holds no game's knowledge. The few questions whose answer depends on the game are ports (u2ue/adapters/__init__.py), answered by an adapter:

port the question the default (any Unity project) a game adapter (the reference port's)
effect_keys which prefabs are the game's effects every prefab holding a ParticleSystem the keys its battles actually fire, resolved as the game resolves them
spawn_rules what starts when the game spawns one Unity's: playOnAwake systems and their sub-emitters its effect pool's own rule
host_busy is the Unreal host free no Unreal is running and none of its own build queues is alive

Most games need none of their own: the project file says "adapter": "unity_project". A game whose effects are chosen by its code subclasses UnityProject and overrides one method (Chapter 12).

The project file names its adapter (u2ue/projects/<name>.json). extract refuses a resolve whose keys disagree with the adapter's spawn rule, because the IR reader picks the rule by the key. The default adapter was proven on the second game: 60 keys, 56 IR files, 189 emitters, 4 refused by name, 0 dropped - with no game code written.

Asset families: what ports itself

Everything except a game's logic ports with no AI in the loop. Each kind of asset is an asset family, and every family takes the same five steps: extract it from Unity, build it in Unreal, read back what Unreal built, judge that against Unity, and photograph it. A step no command does yet is ABSENT and says why. The table is generated from u2ue/assetfamily.py and checked against the facade, so it cannot name a command that does not exist:

family extract build read judge photo
effects extract build read conform diff photo
scene scene export scene import scene readback scene check ABSENT
ui ui capture ui convert ABSENT ui test ABSENT

Each command runs as py -m u2ue --project <name> <command>. Where a step is ABSENT:

  • scene photo: no verb photographs a level: the scene check judges data only (hierarchy, materials, textures, lighting, placement)
  • ui read: no separate read: the converted screen is laid out headless inside ui test, the same run that judges it
  • ui photo: no verb photographs a screen

The engine-neutral IR

Effects pass through an intermediate representation: one JSON file per effect, read off the Unity YAML by u1e_ir.py (nested prefab instances expanded, overrides applied, every node's frame composed). The IR is the seam between the engines: it is testable without either editor, diffable between runs, and a different Unity version changes only the reader.

The converter, its routes and switches

vfxport/build_niagara.py turns one IR emitter into Niagara stack writes, in twenty stages in the order Unity's own modules run. A route is one ported behaviour (a shape, a curve mode, a sub-emitter trigger). Each new route lands behind a switch (VFXPORT_<NAME>), default off, and is flipped on only after its proof (Chapter 10); the flip table (vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py) records each switch with its evidence. Chapter 20 lists them all.

Windows: measuring Unity

Where Unity's behaviour is not in its data, it is measured. A probe (a small Editor script) is dropped into the owner's Unity editor for one run inside a window - only when the owner has been idle ten minutes, stopped the moment they return - and writes a bake: raw numbers only. A judge (Python), written and selftested before the bake exists, decides what the numbers say and refuses a planted wrong answer. The bake is kept with the Unity version it was measured on (Chapter 9).

Records, reports and gates

Every build, read and photo writes a record. The acceptance page and the metrics are computed from records only, each number with its definition and age. Gates refuse what must not pass: field gates (an unread Unity field is a silent gap), model gates (the moved code must know no engine), the converter trace (a change must touch only what it predicts), parity (the rules must agree across runtimes).

The model architecture (the game's code)

The reference port did not translate MonoBehaviours into Actors one by one. It moved the rules into an engine-free model (plain C#) behind two kinds of seam - a platform seam (logging, files, preferences, JSON, random numbers) and view seams (what the presentation asks the engine to draw) - and wrote one thin host per engine. Unity and Unreal then run the same model, which is what makes parity provable at all. Chapter 6 is the method; u2ue/BASICS.md is the per-topic map.

The concept model: one class per idea

The toolkit's concepts are drawn as a class model first, and the code is moved under it piece by piece, each move proven output-identical: every idea a person needs to follow a port is ONE class, with a docstring that says what it is and where its evidence lives. The product in one sentence: a customer points an AI agent at a Unity game; the agent ports the game's LOGIC through the skill (Chapter 6), and every other asset family ports itself - each by Routes that follow measured Rules, held to Unity by Judges. py u2ue/survey/concepts_gate.py checks every concept the table below says exists, and counts how many do; a pillar of u2ue cycle requires that count never to go down. The concept diagram itself is generated from u2ue/CONCEPTS.md, never drawn by hand: Chapter 21, "The concept model".

Where each concept lives in the code

Every concept is a class today - the source table's status column reads EXISTS on every row - and the class column is the module and the class that holds it, which concepts_gate.py checks.

concept class where it lives, and what it does
Project u2ue/project.py:Project the project file and the environment it exports
Adapter u2ue/adapters/__init__.py:UnityProject the default; a game's own in u2ue/adapters/<game>.py
AssetFamily u2ue/assetfamily.py:AssetFamily effects, scene and ui, each with the facade command for its five steps or ABSENT with why, checked against the verbs and each verb's own usage lines (the generated table above)
Route u2ue/routes.py:Route the switch, the files that read it, its evidence rows, and its state read off the files; its judge still lives in the lane
Rule u2ue/facts.py:Rule one conformance bake (shared/conformance/*.json) and the Unity version it was measured on
ProbeCase u2ue/probecase.py:ProbeCase one case of the generic particle probe as data (a real prefab placed by the game's spawn, or a SYNTHETIC system set by name); a case run writes a run's cases file and its Unity window spec, and conform cases goes through it. Older probes are still their own .cs
Window u2ue/verbs/window.py:Window one runner; a window is a JSON spec (Chapter 9)
Capture u2ue/capture.py:Capture one photo run, judged by what it holds, never by its exit: its result record kept beside the frames; a system with an error, no background or no frame is NOT CAPTURED, and a frame asked for and not written by THIS run is SHORT. u2ue photo and a trial's photos step judge through it
Readback u2ue/readback.py:Readback one read of built systems and its capture summary; u2ue read and a trial's read step judge through it; systems() streams one system at a time, so a read larger than memory is judged with the same rows as a whole load
Judge u2ue/judge.py:Judge read off the trial specs' judge steps (no list kept by hand): each judge tool, the trials that run it, and its plant, proven by its own --selftest or declared by a trial (u2ue judge --prove)
Trial u2ue/verbs/trial.py:Trial one runner; a trial is a JSON spec
Run u2ue/run.py:Run pin() copies the code parts and marks each copy a snapshot of its commit, and points every tool's part at the copies; u2ue trial run pins first, so an edit to the live converter mid-queue cannot change what runs; the owner can stop it gracefully
Pillar u2ue/pillars.py:Pillar the product's pillars, checked by u2ue cycle
Check u2ue/pillars.py:Check one recurring check of a pillar: held, trending, or absent
LogicPort u2ue/logic.py:LogicPort each step of the logic skill judged by its DONE WHEN from the records (u2ue logic); the method is the skill
Seam u2ue/seam.py:Seam every interface the model declares, sorted by who implements it, read from the source: SEAM (an engine fills it), FACET (the model fills it), NONE (no implementer found by text - UNKNOWN, never absent); the socket list a host still lacks
Gate u2ue/gates.py:Gate check runs the field gates and the model gates as Gate objects; logic_diff.py and ue_publish_gate.py still run as their own tools
HostProject u2ue/hostproject.py:HostProject u2ue host: the game's own .uproject made from the host template, each step judged by its proof line (Chapter 3)
Release u2ue/release.py:Release u2ue release: the package assembled as a repository from the toolkit's own trees by one manifest (each part at <repo>/<part>, so U2UE_TOOLKIT_ROOT=<repo> resolves it), every exclusion named with its reason, a secret refusing the whole release, and the files that still name a game or a machine path counted as the public-readiness number

The table answers "where is X" without reading code; u2ue find answers it for everything else, and uml where <Name> for a class of the game's model.

How a concept becomes a class

A concept that is only functions or data (PARTIAL) moves to a class (EXISTS) in four moves: its class is drawn in the diagram first, with the members it needs and the concepts it talks to; the class is written, and the existing functions move under it as methods, one at a time; each move is proven output-identical (the tool's own selftest, whole_trace.py for the converter, the records it writes); and only then its row says EXISTS with the class path - the gate checks it, and the count rises.

3. Installation and the project file

Requirements

component version used what needs it
Windows 11 the Unreal runs are driven from native PowerShell
Python 3.13 every tool; the facade
PyYAML 6.0 with libyaml reading Unity YAML (libyaml is about 7x faster; measured equal output)
markdown (Python) 3.8 building this manual's HTML edition only
.NET SDK 8.0 or later (10.0 used) the runtime library and its tests; an UnrealSharp host
Unreal Engine 5.7 build, read, photo: Niagara, the CascadeToNiagaraConverter plugin (its FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary writes the Niagara stacks), the engine's Python scripting (UnrealEditor-Cmd -ExecutePythonScript)
UnrealSharp the host project's C# hosts for the game's model (Chapter 6)
Unity Editor the game's own only for measurement windows and reference photos, in the owner's editor; the toolkit never launches one

The Unity project must be serialized as text (Edit > Project Settings > Editor > Asset Serialization: Force Text): YAML .prefab, .unity, .mat, .asset and .meta.

Where the toolkit lives

The toolkit's folders are named once, in u2ue/tools.py (PARTS): the facade (u2ue), the converter (vfxport), the effect tools, the lanes, the Unity probes. Set U2UE_TOOLKIT_ROOT to move them as a whole. Run every command from the toolkit's root:

py -m u2ue                       # every verb
py -m u2ue find <words>          # search the toolkit

The project file

One file per game, u2ue/projects/<game>.json. A complete one, for a game whose effects are simply its particle prefabs:

{
  "name": "mygame",
  "adapter": "unity_project",
  "about": "free text, shown by info",
  "unity": {
    "root": "<unity project>",
    "assets": "<unity project>/Assets",
    "version": "2021.3.21f1",
    "editor": "<Unity 2021.3.21f1 install>"
  },
  "effects": {
    "key_source": {"kind": "particle_prefabs", "roots": ["Assets"]}
  },
  "unreal": {
    "uproject": "<unreal project>.uproject",
    "engine": "<Unreal Engine 5.7 install>",
    "content_root": "/Game/U2UE/MyGame"
  },
  "work": {
    "effects": "<work>",
    "ir": "<work>/ir",
    "guid_index": "<work>/guid_index.json",
    "resolve": "<work>/resolve.json",
    "records": "<work>/records",
    "photos": "<work>/photos",
    "inventory": "<work>/inventory"
  },
  "code": {
    "roots": ["Assets/Game", "Assets/GameShared"]
  }
}
field meaning
name the project's name
adapter unity_project (Unity's own rules) or a game adapter's name (u2ue/adapters/<name>.py, Chapter 12)
unity.root, unity.assets, unity.version the Unity project, its Assets folder, its version (measured rules are checked against it)
unity.editor (optional) that version's Editor install: its built-in shaders and materials are named off unity_builtin_extra
effects.key_source what the effects are: {"kind": "particle_prefabs", "roots": [...]}, or a game resolver through its adapter
unreal.uproject, unreal.engine, unreal.content_root the Unreal host, the engine, the content folder the systems are built under
work.* where the work goes: the IR, the guid index, the key list, the records, the photos, the code inventory
code.roots the game's OWN C# folders (u2ue inventory --survey lists every folder first; vendor packages live in Assets too)
model.root, model.layers, model.scan, model.hosting, model.unreal_links the engine-free model, once the game has one (Chapter 6)
parity.dir, parity.engines where the model's per-runtime digests are written (Chapter 6)

u2ue/projects/ holds two example projects: the reference port's (a game adapter, a model, parity) and the second game's (the default adapter, nothing else).

Check it:

py -m u2ue --project <game> info       # every path OPENED; exit 1 when an input is missing

The Unreal host

The verbs that run Unreal (build, read, photo, host) need a host project with the plugins above, and run one headless Unreal at a time from native PowerShell (Git Bash hands PowerShell a PATH without UnrealSharp's dotnet entry, and the verbs refuse that shell). A game builds under its own content_root (/Game/U2UE/<Game>).

u2ue host makes a game its OWN host, the way a customer would: name it in the project file's unreal.host block, then run the steps one at a time. Each step is judged by the line in its own log that proves it, never by an exit code.

py -m u2ue --project <game> host plan        # every step: its command and the line that proves it
py -m u2ue --project <game> host create      # the .uproject from the toolkit's host template, renamed
py -m u2ue --project <game> host install     # each plugin cloned at its pinned commit; the toolkit's own copied
py -m u2ue --project <game> host compile     # the editor target (UnrealSharp writes its C# glue on the way)
py -m u2ue --project <game> host generate    # UnrealSharp's own command makes the managed project - no editor dialog
py -m u2ue --project <game> host wire        # the model, the digest cases and the host templates into it
py -m u2ue --project <game> host publish     # to both folders the engine may load from
py -m u2ue --project <game> host run         # headless: the host answers the digest; then `parity --require Unreal`
py -m u2ue --project <game> host status      # each step: proven, not proven, or not run

Measured on the second test game: from nothing to parity --require Unreal exit 0 in 9 minutes, most of it the C++ compile.

Verifying the installation

Scope: the toolkit itself, on this machine. Precondition: the requirements above are installed and a project file exists. Minimal guarantee: a tool whose selftest fails is named. Success guarantee: every selftest passes, the runtime library's tests pass, and the manual matches the code. Trigger: the toolkit is installed or updated.

py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only selftests     # every tool's own selftest
dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests              # the runtime library
py u2ue/manual/build.py --check                          # this manual is current

The Unreal-run tools

ue_headless.ps1 is THE ONE PLACE an Unreal executable is launched: one at a time, with -DeterministicAudio, at below-normal priority. Every verb that runs Unreal reaches it. The effect build cuts the game's keys into chunks and builds each chunk in one headless run, reusing textures, parents and instances only when nothing they came from changed. "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest.

tool part what it does check
ue_headless.ps1 scene_tools the one launcher of an Unreal executable -
u1e_py.ps1 effects_tools runs ONE headless Python instrument of the effect tools inside Unreal (what u2ue read and u2ue photo run) -
u1e_build.py effects_tools builds one Niagara system per effect key, inside Unreal, through build_niagara.py -
fx17_build.ps1 effects_tools builds one chunk of effect keys with batched compiles (what u2ue build runs) -
fx17_chunks.py effects_tools cuts the keys into chunks by ESTIMATED build time, most-used effects first; the cost model is measured on a real chunk's per-phase timers -
fx18_chunks.py effects_tools the same for a whole-game rebuild, time-budgeted, so a series that is stopped has built what the game shows most -
u1e_resave.py effects_tools writes every effect system's non-edit compile, so no process compiles it again on load -
u1e_reuse.py effects_tools the build reuses a texture, a material parent or an instance only when nothing it was built from changed -
u1e_reuse_selftest.py effects_tools u1e_reuse.py driven with fakes of Unreal and the material author, outside Unreal yes
u1e_preflight.py effects_tools before ANY headless Unreal run, the script and every local module it imports (transitively) must parse and carry no undefined name; a failure refuses the run, so minutes of Unreal never start yes
u1e_py_introspect.py effects_tools what a few Unreal Python types actually expose - the names READ, not assumed -
u1e_compile_report.py effects_tools WHY a built system does not simulate, in the engine's own words -

u1e_preflight.py exists because two faults once reached Unreal that a two-second read finds: a truncated \u escape in a docstring (a syntax error at import, the run dead 30 s in) and a name written before it was bound. It refuses only what is a fault at run time - a syntax error and the undefined-name classes - and nothing about style.

A second game supplies its Unreal project and engine path (the .uproject, UE_SDKS_ROOT for a C++ build) and its content root.

Unattended queues and the pause protocol

The reference port ran its Unreal work as unattended chains: one queue rebuilt every key chunk by chunk, a second read and photographed after it, and a trial queue PAUSED the rebuild at a chunk boundary (a pause file the rebuild polls every 15 s), ran the whole trial chain on its own keys - build, material errors, resave, simulates, read, every check and its PLANT, photos - and then HELD for the flips. The pause protocol is the part to keep: a trial never shares the one Unreal slot with a running build, and nothing removes a pause but the hold's owner.

tool part what it does
queue_w.ps1 lane the acceptance rebuild: every key with an IR, chunk by chunk, one Unreal process at a time
queue_x.ps1 lane after the rebuild: the reads and the photos
queue_p04.ps1 lane a trial queue: the rebuild paused after a chunk for the next routes' trials, then a HOLD for their flips
hold_build.ps1 lane one key set through the whole trial chain, with switches set and the named checks and their plants; it refuses while the rebuild is NOT paused or another Unreal runs

These scripts are the reference port's job history - each trial's exact orchestration, kept so any result can be re-run - not the tool. A new project runs a trial as data with u2ue trial (py -m u2ue --project <game> trial run <spec.json>: build, resave, read, judge, photos; one Unreal at a time, stoppable), and supplies only its key lists and its work folders.

4. Tutorial: a first port, step by step

This chapter takes a game the toolkit was not built on - a different studio's project on Unity 2021.3 - through every step that runs without an Unreal host, with what each step printed on 2026-10-15. The game's name is written <game> and its folder names are shortened; the numbers are as printed.

Scope: one game, from its project file to its first report. Precondition: the toolkit is installed and verified (Chapter 3). Minimal guarantee: every path the project names is opened, and every key the game must account for is listed before anything is built. Success guarantee: the acceptance page and the numbers, each number read from a record or naming the record it waits for. Trigger: a game the toolkit was not built on is to be ported.

1. Describe the game and open every path

Write u2ue/projects/<game>.json (Chapter 3 has a complete one), then:

py -m u2ue --project <game> info
project <game> (u2ue/projects/<game>.json)
  unity.root           dir       <unity project>                     ok
  work.effects         out-dir   <work>                              ok (exists)
  work.photos          out-dir   <work>/photos                       to be created (its parent exists)
  unreal.uproject      file      <unreal project>.uproject           ok
  unreal.content_root  game-path /Game/U2UE/<Game>                    ok (an Unreal content path)
  adapter: unity_project (spawn rules unity)
  key source: {'kind': 'particle_prefabs', 'roots': ['Assets']}

Every path the file names is opened; an input that is missing exits 1.

2. Find the game's own code

Vendor packages live in Assets beside the game's code, so the toolkit never guesses which folders are the game's:

py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory --survey
  AssetStore     4226   + 917 in Editor folders
  GameCode       1907   + 55 in Editor folders
  GameShared       25
  ...

Name the game's folders as code.roots in the project file.

3. Inventory the code

py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory
u2ue inventory <game>: 1987 files, 2453 types (plain 1384, MonoBehaviour 789, ScriptableObject 160, base outside the scanned code 88,
EditorWindow 15, Editor 12, PropertyDrawer 5); 1148 pure rules; -> <work>/inventory
  serialized data                  473 types   1708 sites
  platform (log, files, prefs)     365 types   1525 sites
  spawn / destroy                  311 types   1049 sites
  lookups                          275 types    661 sites
  coroutines / Invoke              273 types    997 sites
  transform                        222 types   1652 sites
  UI                               134 types    373 sites
  time                             112 types    254 sites
  physics                           83 types    317 sites
  input                             75 types    236 sites
  animation / timeline              54 types    309 sites
  ...

<work>/inventory/inventory.md lists every type's Unity calls by family (each family points at its topic in u2ue/BASICS.md), the 1148 types that use no Unity API (what moves into an engine-free model first), and every MonoBehaviour's script execution order with its lifecycle methods - the table the frame driver is written from. Chapter 6 is what to do with it. Read the counts as a plan: this game has physics in 83 types and animation in 54, which the toolkit does not cover (Appendix B) - a porter knows that on day one.

4. Read the data the inspector holds

py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from Assets/<data folder>/<data asset>.asset --script <DataClass> --tsv data.tsv
u2ue data <game>: 1 component(s) in Assets/<data folder>/<data asset>.asset
  None  fileID 11400000  23 fields

Every serialized value as the file stores it (487 leaf values in the TSV for this game's ScriptableObject - a data asset and its class are written <data asset> and <DataClass>, as the game's own names are; the avatar-mask reference resolved to its asset path) - read, never retyped into the port.

5. Extract the effects

py -m u2ue --project <game> extract
    - Snow_Particles   active=True  depth 0 loop=True  dur 5  life (2.2, 2.2) size (0.15, 0.3) space World ...
        render Stretch  shape Box(enabled True)  rate 500.0 bursts []  modules ['colorOverLifetime', 'rotationOverLifetime', ...]
    material .../Snow_Particles.mat
        shader Legacy Shaders/Particles/Alpha Blended (None)  blend {'_SrcBlend': 1, '_DstBlend': 0, '_ZWrite': 1}
REFUSED BY KEY: 4 of 60 READ key(s), each named above
u2ue extract: 60 READ key(s): 56 IR file(s) with 189 emitter(s), 4 refused by name, 0 dropped, 0 foreign path(s)
  REFUSED unity.prefab.5ccd...: .../Winter Door.prefab: PrefabInstance 4843689442982340616: modification target 1211823196678298638 ...

The guid index (written to work.guid_index), the effect keys (every prefab holding a ParticleSystem, by the default adapter, written to work.resolve), one IR file per key (under work.ir), and for every emitter a one-line summary of what was read. Four keys are refused, each with the object the reader could not follow; nothing is dropped silently. What the effects path does not cover (VFX Graph assets, particle systems authored in scenes) is listed with counts.

6. Check before building

py -m u2ue --project <game> check
...
u2ue check: the measured rules' Unity versions against project <game>
  163 measured Unity bakes; this project is Unity 2021.3.21f1
       163 measured on Unity 6000.3.16f1    UNVERIFIED for Unity 2021.3 - re-measure where it matters
  163 of 163 rules this project's build uses were measured on another Unity: its report must not call them measured for it
u2ue check: PASS

Every tool's own selftest, the field gates over this project's IR (an unread Unity field fails here, not as a silent gap later), the measured rules' Unity versions against the project's (here every rule is reported unverified for this Unity - the build still runs, and the report says so), and the model gates (no model yet: said so).

7. Build, read, photograph (the Unreal host)

py -m u2ue --project <game> build --dry     # the plan and the host's state - always first
py -m u2ue --project <game> build
py -m u2ue --project <game> read --tag <TAG>
py -m u2ue --project <game> photo --tag <TAG>

Run from native PowerShell, one headless Unreal at a time. Appendix A has the reference port's numbers for these steps.

8. Report and measure

py -m u2ue --project <game> report --out <game>.html
py -m u2ue --project <game> metrics
u2ue metrics - <game> (every number from a record; definitions: u2ue/verbs/metrics.py)
  keys      60: NEVER BUILT 56, IR REFUSED 4; 0 drawn, 0 of them with a named gap; 0 from the acceptance rebuild
            the rules behind 'measured' were measured on Unity 6000.3.16f1; this project is Unity 2021.3.21f1 - UNVERIFIED for it
  machine   ABSENT: no per-key seconds in the chosen build records
  data      ABSENT: no <work>/records/checks_summary.json - the readback sweep has not run
  image     ABSENT: no sheets listing <work>/records/fx18_sheets.txt - the photo pass has not run

Before any build the page already lists every key the project must account for, and every number it cannot compute yet says which record it is waiting for. Chapter 11 defines every number.

Part two: the rest of the game

Part one brought the effects to a first report. A port also moves the game's code, its scenes, its UI and its Unreal project. The steps below are the same port continued, in the order that keeps each step's input ready for the next. Each step names its command and what that command proves. The chapter beside it holds the full procedure, the options and the traps.

9. Draw the class model of one slice

py -m u2ue --project <game> uml extract
py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus <TypeA> <TypeB>

extract reads the class model off the game's own code roots (and its engine-free model, once there is one). mermaid --focus draws one slice with every member a real one. A slice is a handful of types that hold one rule of the game. The diagram comes before any code moves, and a diagram that names a member the code lacks is refused. Chapter 6, and the u2ue-logic skill's step 2.

10. Make the engine-free model

py -m u2ue --project <game> scaffold --name <Model> --dir <DIR> --dry
py -m u2ue --project <game> scaffold --name <Model> --dir <DIR>

The first line shows what would be written, and the second writes it. You get a Core project that references only the toolkit's runtime library, a headless test project, and the project file's model block. Then the verb builds both and runs the model gates. Exit 0 means the model exists, compiles, and no engine reaches it. A second scaffold is refused, so this never overwrites. Chapter 6, step 6.

11. Move the slice and prove it on Unity's own runtime

Move the slice's rules into the Core, each with its test, then:

py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Class.Method> --cases <Cases.cs>
py -m u2ue --project <game> digest faithful
py -m u2ue --project <game> parity

digest run answers the rule's cases with no engine at all, on CoreCLR and on the project's Unity version's own Mono runtime. digest faithful proves that the no-editor Mono run gives the same rows as the Editor does. parity compares every runtime the rules run on by float bits, and names each row that differs. Chapter 6, step 7, and Chapter 16.

12. See where the logic port stands

py -m u2ue --project <game> logic

Each step of the u2ue-logic skill is judged by its own DONE WHEN, read from the project's records, and the verb names the step to take next. An AI model doing the port starts every session here instead of working out the state again. Chapter 6.

13. Find what Unreal cannot place as Unity does

py -m u2ue --project <game> shear --from Assets/<scene>.unity

This lists every node whose transform chain Unity can draw and Unreal's transform cannot hold (a non-uniform scale under a rotation shears), with the error in centimetres. Such a node is refused and named, never averaged. Chapter 7.

14. Bring a scene across

py -m u2ue --project <game> scene --dry
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene export
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene import
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene readback
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene check

--dry opens the scene's paths and shows the Unreal host's state. export runs in the game's own Unity Editor, in a window: the verb itself never touches an editor, and prints the trigger the window drops. import brings the glTF into a new Unreal level through the engine's own scene pipeline, and readback reads the saved level back headless. check is the fidelity gate: hierarchy, materials, textures, lighting and placement, held to Unity's files and to the scene's own measured baseline. Chapter 7.

15. Convert the UI

py -m u2ue --project <game> ui convert <capture dir> --screen <NAME>
py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test

convert turns one captured screen into a folder Unreal reads: the capture, its sprites, and each TextMeshPro font's TTF, proven by identical glyph indices. test runs the generic uGUI and TextMeshPro library's own tests headless. The capture itself runs in the game's Unity Editor in Play mode, so ui capture refuses by name until the package's Editor assembly is installed in the project. Chapter 7.

16. Make the game's own Unreal project

py -m u2ue --project <game> host plan
py -m u2ue --project <game> host create
py -m u2ue --project <game> host status

plan lists every step (create, install, compile, generate, wire, publish, run) with the command it runs and the log line that proves it. Run the steps one at a time, from native PowerShell, and status shows each one as proven, failed, or not run. The run step is proven only when the model's digest file is written after the run started. Chapter 15.

17. Hold the effects to Unity on numbers

py -m u2ue --project <game> conform cases --name <run>
py -m u2ue --project <game> conform diff --unity <particle-cases record> --unreal <readback record> --report <FILE>
py -m u2ue --project <game> conform latest --run <run>

cases writes one probe case per effect key, plus the Unity window and the Unreal read that measure them. After both have run, diff judges every emitter of every key on its live count and its first birth, paired by file id. latest prints the share that holds, from the newest stamped report. Chapter 10.

18. Check every pillar

py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle --dry
py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle

Every promise of the toolkit is checked: PASS, FAIL, HELD by a named decision, or ABSENT where no check exists yet. Red stops the cycle. Run it before any report. Chapter 16.

Where to go next

  • The game's code, in full: Chapter 6, and u2ue/BASICS.md topic by topic.
  • A behaviour that must match exactly: Chapter 9, and the tools that run it: Chapter 14.
  • An effect family the converter refuses: Chapter 8's route protocol, then Chapter 13.
  • Something went wrong: Chapter 22.

5. Use cases

This chapter is the toolkit's requirements model: what each kind of user does with it, step by step. It is generated, not written. The requirements engine reads the toolkit's own documents (the procedures of this manual, the two skills, the stakeholder requirements in u2ue/USECASES.md, and the pillars in u2ue/pillars.py), chains each procedure into a use case, and cites every step to the page it was read from. When a page changes, the model changes with it, and a step with no source is printed as INFERRED, a requirement nobody wrote.

How to read a use case

  • The level follows Cockburn: kite is a summary goal that spans many sittings (the epic), sea is one user goal achieved in one sitting (most cases), fish is a sub-function.
  • Fully dressed: each case states its primary actor, its trigger, its scope, the precondition that must hold before it starts, the minimal guarantee that holds even when it fails, and the success guarantee that holds when it succeeds.
  • The main success scenario is three to eleven steps. Each step's postcondition is the next step's precondition, so a step that needs what nothing before it guarantees shows a gap.
  • Extensions are where the chain breaks. Each is numbered by the step it branches from (3a branches from step 3; * from any step), and each one was read where its document says it starts. Chapter 22 is part of the model, not a page beside it.
  • Include and extend point opposite ways. An include runs from the base case to the case it includes (the epic includes the quick start). An extend runs from the extension to the base it extends.
  • Proven by names the command that checks a step. That command is the test, and it fails on a planted defect before it is trusted (Chapter 16).

Regenerating the model

py u2ue/survey/req_harvest.py --check      # what the harvest would read, procedure by procedure
py u2ue/survey/req_harvest.py --write      # the harvest files the requirements engine reads
py u2ue/manual/build.py                    # this chapter, from the engine's model

Between the last two, the requirements engine is run over the harvest: its trace, its epic builder, and its checker, which refuses a case without a dressed field, a scenario outside three to eleven steps, or a citation that does not resolve.

19 use cases - one summary-level epic and 18 user-goal cases - with 124 steps and 41 extensions, every step read from the page named beside it. The requirements engine's checker verifies the citation of every numbered row: 163 (the 2 extension(s) that branch from any step carry no row number). The model holds 1582 facts of this domain.

opus the AI model UC-12, UC-14, UC-17
owner whose product it is UC-07

field
Level kite (summary)
Primary actor porter - porting a game
Trigger a studio decides to move a Unity game to Unreal
Scope u2ue and the porter's two projects.
Precondition the Unity project is on disk serialized as text (YAML prefabs, .meta files); an Unreal project to build into.
Stakeholders the porter wants it to run and to look the same; the game owner wants every difference named and only their decisions asked; a reviewer wants the method to make sense (Q7).
Minimal guarantee everything not ported is NAMED with its reason - never dropped, never stood in for silently (Q11).
Success guarantee the game runs on Unreal from the same rules; the page says, per effect and per system, what draws as Unity draws it, and the numbers (identical, speed) come from records (Q4).

Main success scenario (each step's postcondition is the next step's precondition):

(Chapter 22)
  • 6a A measurement right after a recompile reproduces the old numbers - Entering Play while a compile is pending runs the old assembly. Wait until the editor assembly's timestamp is newer than the source and isCompiling reads false, then Play. (Chapter 22)

Extensions (where the chain breaks, numbered by the step they branch from):

  • 1a A rule does value-type maths (Vector3, Mathf, Color) - It does not move as written: where those types live in an engine-free model is the owner's decision, made once for the whole model, and the rule waits for it. (Chapter 6)
  • 7a Text built from floats differs between Unity and .NET - Unity's Mono rounds float text to seven significant digits first, rounds halves away from zero, and prints a value that rounds to zero without a sign. Any number a player reads, or a stream compared against Unity, goes through one formatter that reproduces Mono's rules. (Chapter 22)
  • 7b Float results differ by one ULP - Mono may keep a float expression at higher precision. u2ue parity names every such row; an allowance pins the exact row and bits, and the fix (explicit float locals) moves Unity's own value, so it is the owner's call. (Chapter 22)
  • 7c System.Text.Json writes {} for a Unity data class - Unity's JsonUtility serializes public fields; System.Text.Json ignores fields unless IncludeFields = true. (Chapter 22)

  8. Keep Unity's frame order: per-frame code the slice keeps (Update, LateUpdate, coroutines) registers with ONE UnityFrame in its script execution order (inventory's frame-order table, read from the .cs.meta files); coroutines run on U2ue.Runtime.Coroutines. (the u2ue-logic skill)
    • proven by py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory

The Unreal host: the game gets its OWN .uproject (the owner's decision for a second game), made by u2ue host the way a customer makes one: name it in the project file's unreal.host block (the template, each plugin with its source and pinned commit, the AutoSDK root, the digest's entry and cases), then run the steps in order from native PowerShell - each refuses while an Unreal runs and is judged by its proof line, (the u2ue-logic skill)
    • proven by py -m u2ue --project <game> host plan

    • proven by py -m u2ue --project <game> host status

    • proven by py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only model
