Extensions (where the chain breaks, numbered by the step they branch from):

  • 7a A headless Unreal never finishes and its log grows to hundreds of megabytes - UnrealSharp finds dotnet by the PATH entry Program Files\dotnet\ with the trailing backslash. Git Bash hands PowerShell a PATH without it, so UnrealSharp reports ".NET SDK can't be found" and, under -unattended, raises the dialog again forever (measured: a 634 MB log, nothing built). Run every Unreal verb from native PowerShell. The verbs refuse the Bash chain up front. (Chapter 22)
  • 5a An effect's blend mode is wrong - The blend mode is a number in the material (_DstBlend == 1 is additive), never the shader's name. (Chapter 22)
  • 7b A texture looks different in Unreal although the file is the same - Unity samples its imported texture (mip chain, alpha fill, size caps), not the source file. The import is in Library/Artifacts and can be read offline (_effects/tools/unity_tex_artifact.py); validate the match against the source, since the artifact index can point at a neighbouring asset. (Chapter 22)
  • 6a A gate reports a symbol ABSENT that you know exists - Check whether the port moved it (into the model, for example) before believing the gate. Widen the gate to follow the move, then re-run its plants. (Chapter 22)
  • 7c The photo of an effect differs from Unity's in a way the data does not - A photo is one draw of a random process, and a frame can catch a capture artefact. Labelled frames (RANDDRAW, GRIDTICK) are never counted. Compare several frames and the read-back data before calling a route wrong. (Chapter 22)
  • 8a u2ue metrics prints STALE - An input is older than the newest build. Re-run the step that writes it (the sweep, the photo pass); the number is never presented as current until then. (Chapter 22)
  • 7d A long build stops at exactly the shell tool's timeout, leaving the content half old and half new - Stopping a background task kills its children, including UnrealEditor-Cmd. Before a long launch, compare the tool's timeout with the script's own watchdog and give the tool the larger one. (Chapter 22)
  • 7e Two Unreal runs at once - One headless Unreal at a time. build, read and photo ask the adapter's host_busy and refuse while an Unreal (or the game's own queue) holds the host. build --dry shows the host's state. (Chapter 22)
  • 7f Niagara draws nothing in an editor script - -run=pythonscript asserts, and -ExecutePythonScript quits before the tick loop runs. The editor world never ticks actors, so Niagara simulates only inside Simulate or Play-In-Editor unless something advances it. The read-back advances each system itself: NiagaraSimCacheFunctionLibrary's immediate capture with bAdvanceSimulation (_effects/tools/u1e_color_size_readback.py, which u2ue read runs). (Chapter 22)
  • 7g A headless run plays sound through the user's speakers, or records silence - Pass -DeterministicAudio (the non-realtime renderer: nothing reaches a device, and each tick renders its own delta) and -ini:Engine:[Audio]:UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=1.0 (an unfocused application otherwise mixes at volume 0). (Chapter 22)
  • 7h An UnrealSharp editor wedges while files are being generated - With automatic hot reload on, the editor recompiles a managed file the instant it is written, mid-write, fails, and can stop responding. Set AutomaticHotReloading=Off in the host's DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini, or keep the editor closed while a tool writes managed C#. (Chapter 22)
  • 4a The reader refuses a scene with m_RemovedGameObjects - A prefab instance in a scene that deletes one of the prefab's objects is not handled yet (the reader that applies it is proven and lands with the next build; Appendix B). u2ue data --no-expand reads the scene's own components without expanding instances. (Chapter 22)
  • 5b A nested prefab's object cannot be found by its fileID - A nested object's id is the instance's id XOR the source object's id. (Chapter 22)
  • 5c A material's values look like its shader's defaults - A material variant stores only what it overrides; the rest comes through m_Parent. Read the chain. (Chapter 22)

6. Porting the game code

The particle effects are content; the game itself is code - MonoBehaviours, coroutines, inspector values, the transform chain. This chapter is the method the reference port used, with the toolkit's support at each step. u2ue/BASICS.md is the topic-by-topic map (seventeen topics: what Unity does, what Unreal offers, how the reference port did it, what the toolkit gives), and shared/PORTING_ANOTHER_PROJECT.md is the long form with the reasons. The same method as a playbook an AI model follows - a kickoff prompt, the concepts in plain analogies, every step with its command and the observable that ends it - is the u2ue-logic skill (u2ue/skill/u2ue-logic/SKILL.md); survey/skill_gate.py holds every command it names to the toolkit.

Scope: the game's code - its rules, its per-frame order, its data. Precondition: a project file names the game and its code folders. Minimal guarantee: what the toolkit cannot do for a rule is said, and the model's gates stop an engine reference. Success guarantee: one engine-free model both engines run, with the same answers by the bit. Trigger: the game's rules live in MonoBehaviours, which Unreal cannot run.

The decision everything follows from

Do not translate MonoBehaviours into Actors one by one. Move the game's rules into an engine-free model - plain C# that references no engine - and write one thin host per engine. Unity and Unreal then run the same model, and the only differences left are the hosts', which is what makes the port provable. The reference port's model is two assemblies: the rules (state and seed in, state out) and the presentation (the per-frame look: camera, popups, motion); the Unreal hosts are UnrealSharp C#.

flowchart LR
  subgraph model["engine-free model (plain C#)"]
    R["rules: state + seed -> state"] --> PR["presentation: what to show, frame by frame"]
  end
  PR -->|view seams| UH["Unity host: MonoBehaviours"]
  PR -->|view seams| EH["Unreal host: UnrealSharp actors"]
  PR -->|view seams| TH["headless test host"]
  RT["U2ue.Runtime: Unity's frame, clock, coroutines, platform"] --> model

The method, step by step

1. Inventory the code

py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory --survey     # every top folder under Assets with its .cs count: name the game's own as code.roots
py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory

Per type: MonoBehaviour / ScriptableObject / plain, its lifecycle methods, every Unity call by family, and the pure rules - types that use no Unity API, which move into the model first. Partial classes are merged across their files. The reader is lexical (comments and strings blanked, a brace stack per type): a call through an alias or reflection is not seen, so a miss is unknown, never "does not use". Unity's value types (Vector3, Mathf, Color) are a family of their own: a rule doing that maths is not pure as written, because its arithmetic is UnityEngine's. Chapter 4 shows a full run.

A rule does value-type maths (Vector3, Mathf, Color). It does not move as written: where those types live in an engine-free model is the owner's decision, made once for the whole model, and the rule waits for it. Branches from step 1.

Then draw the class model of the first slice before moving anything - the diagram is the plan a person reviews:

py -m u2ue --project <game> uml extract                        # the class model off the game's code roots (its own index)
py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus TypeA TypeB    # a slice's class diagram, every member a real one

2. Read the frame order

The same inventory lists every MonoBehaviour's script execution order (its .cs.meta executionOrder, from the file named after the class - the script Unity orders) with its lifecycle methods. Unity's frame is: Update in that order, then the coroutine phase (yield return null resumes after every Update), then LateUpdate. The order between scripts is behaviour: re-making it by hand across several engine ticks is how the reference port's first Unreal host drew things a frame late.

3. Give the model Unity's runtime rules

u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime (netstandard2.1 and net8.0, no engine reference):

type Unity's rule
UnityClock Time.deltaTime = the real step clamped to the project's Maximum Allowed Timestep, times timeScale; the unscaled step is not clamped. The maximum is the project's own: py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from ProjectSettings/TimeManager.asset --class 5 (the reference port: 0.33333334).
Coroutines Start runs to the first yield; a coroutine started during a frame resumes after the next frame's Updates; yield return <IEnumerator> runs nested and stops with its parent; yield return <Handle> waits and resumes the same frame its target ends; Wait.Scaled / Wait.Unscaled.
UnityFrame one frame in Unity's order: Update by execution order, the coroutine phase, LateUpdate. A host calls Tick once per engine frame.
Platform.* the six platform services (below) and SeededRandom.
FloatBits float bit patterns and ULP distance, for parity digests.
PlaybackQueue<TEvent> the model resolves an action at once and appends ordered events; the host shows one per frame, only when its presenter (IPresenter<TEvent>) is idle, and takes input only when IsCaughtUp. A history that shrinks is refused.
Digest one runtime's answers to the rule cases: digestVersion=N, then key=value rows in ordinal order, floats as bits - the file u2ue parity reads.
TrailLaw Unity's TrailRenderer as measured: the points it holds each frame (TrailLaw.Point) and the drawn vertices (TrailLaw.Vertex) with the fraction width, colour and U run on. Its test replays Unity's own play-mode bake.

What a host does with it - one frame object, the game's former MonoBehaviours registered by their execution order, one call per engine frame:

using System.Collections;
using U2ue.Runtime;

var clock = new UnityClock(0.33333334f);      // the project's Maximum Allowed Timestep, READ with `u2ue data` (above)
var coroutines = new Coroutines(clock);
var frame = new UnityFrame(clock);
frame.Add("CameraRig", -100, update: rig.Update, lateUpdate: rig.LateUpdate);   // -100: its .cs.meta executionOrder
frame.Add("HudPresenter", 0, update: hud.Update);
frame.AddCoroutines(coroutines);

IEnumerator Flash() { hud.Show(); yield return Wait.Scaled(0.5f); hud.Hide(); }
coroutines.Start(Flash());

// the host's tick, once per engine frame, with the real elapsed seconds:
frame.Tick(deltaSeconds);    // clock -> every Update by order -> coroutines -> every LateUpdate

Run with two frames of 0.3 s (the snippet compiled against the library as printed, with the rig and HUD writing a line each):

show            <- Start: the coroutine runs to its first yield at once
rig update      <- frame 1: every Update, by execution order
hud update
rig late        <- 0.3 s < 0.5 s: the coroutine waits; LateUpdate
rig update      <- frame 2
hud update
hide            <- 0.6 s >= 0.5 s: resumed in the coroutine phase, after every Update
rig late

dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests holds every rule and builds on any machine. dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.OriginTests runs a set of coroutine scripts on the reference port's own measured runner and on the library and requires identical step logs; it needs that port's code on disk, so it is a test project of its own.

4. Put the engine behind seams

  • The platform seam: six interfaces, one engine call per member - ILog (Debug.Log), ITextAssets (Resources.Load of text), IKeyValueStore (PlayerPrefs), IFileStore (the save file), IJsonCodec<T> (JsonUtility; on .NET, System.Text.Json needs IncludeFields = true or fields round-trip to {}), IRandomSource (Unity's bounds: int upper-exclusive, float both-inclusive).
  • View seams: what the presentation asks the engine to show. The reference port's are IEntityView, IHudView, ICameraDirector, IEffectPlayer and IInputSource. The model says what happened; the host decides how it looks.

5. Read the data, never retype it

py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from <scene|prefab|asset> --script <ClassName>    # or --class <id> for a built-in

Every serialized value of the matching components (nested prefab instances expanded, overrides applied, references resolved to asset paths), as JSON or a dotted TSV. "Unity serialization beats the C# initializer": the scene's value is what plays. On the reference port's camera rig this equals the hand-written reader it replaced on all 152 fields and 32 curve values.

6. Cut the model, then gate it

py -m u2ue --project <game> scaffold --name <Model> --dir <a folder outside Assets>
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only model

scaffold writes <Model>.Core (netstandard2.1 + net8.0, referencing only U2ue.Runtime) and <Model>.Core.Tests, adds the project file's model block, builds both and runs the gates on the empty model; it never overwrites.

layer_gate refuses an engine namespace in the model and any reference outside each layer's allowed set (model.layers, inner layer first); host_gate refuses a platform member declared anywhere but the hosting folder (model.hosting). Both run on the folders the project names (model.root, and the projects model.scan lists); layer_gate checks the model's Unreal-facing references only when model.unreal_links is set. A project with no model yet is told so.

7. Prove the rules agree across runtimes

Each runtime the model runs on (Unity on Mono, the Unreal host on CoreCLR, a headless test runner) writes a digest, <parity.dir>/logic-<Engine>.txt: a digestVersion=N line, then one key=value row per case with every float as its 8-hex-digit bit pattern. Unity's side needs no editor: u2ue digest run compiles the rule cases (a static method returning a Digest) twice - for CoreCLR (logic-Headless.txt) and with the project's Unity version's own Mono compiler and runtime (logic-UnityMono.txt):

py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Cases.Build> --cases <Cases.cs>
py -m u2ue --project <game> digest faithful      # standalone Mono vs a digest the Editor wrote: on Unity 6000.3, 383 of 383 rows equal

faithful reads the project's mono.faithful block: the Unity editor whose Mono it runs, the entry point and the case sources the Editor's own runner compiled, the assemblies they reference (mono.faithful.refs), and the digest that Editor wrote (reference).

Make the cases' inputs exact on every runtime (integer arithmetic, each input written to the sheet): a driver that makes its own inputs with float maths measures its own drift - on the second test game it produced 177 false differences where the rule had 2. Then:

py -m u2ue --project <game> parity
game-logic comparison - digest v1
  Headless    383 rows
  Unity       383 rows
  Unreal      383 rows
  per rule group (differing / total):
    damage_base                    27 /  144  <<<
    fpmode_fused                    8 /   36  <<<
    fpmode_stepped                  0 /   36
    ...
  DIFFERING ROWS (first 20):
    damage_base_009              Headless=40400001  Unity=40400000  Unreal=40400001
  ODD ONE OUT: Unity on 35 of 35 differing row(s)
  DIAGNOSIS: fpmode_fused differs and fpmode_stepped does NOT: an intermediate precision difference ...
  CHARACTERISED AND ALLOWED: 35 row(s), each pinned to its exact bits and to 1 ULP.
VERDICT: Headless / Unity / Unreal agree on all 383 rows except 35 characterised 1-ULP row(s), which are
         unchanged since they were measured.

That is the reference port's real output. Every row across every runtime is compared; a difference is red unless the characterised allowance pins that exact row to its exact bits and to one ULP. Here Unity's Mono is the odd one out on every differing row - it may keep float intermediates wider than float32, which ECMA-334 permits - and the two fpmode groups prove it: the same expression written with explicit float locals agrees everywhere. Applying that fix moves Unity's own values by one ULP, so it is the game owner's call.

8. Write the hosts

One thin host per engine implements the seams and drives the frame. The toolkit's Unreal templates (u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal, taken from the reference port's hosts with the game removed) are the starting point; copy them into the host's managed project:

template what it is
AU2ueFrameActor the actor that owns the frame: each tick hands the real step to UnityFrame (clamped by the project's own maximum step, which a subclass must supply - the default refuses). Summon it with -ExecCmds="summon /Script/UnrealSharp.<Name>_C"
UnrealPointer the cursor, its position in Unity's frame (origin bottom left), its world ray, and keys pressed or released this frame - polled before the frame runs
UnrealCameraRig one camera actor made the view target; the model's pose copied onto it, with Unity's vertical field of view converted to Unreal's horizontal one
UnrealPlatform.cs the six platform services on Unreal: the log, a manifest-backed text folder, a save-folder file store, PlayerPrefs as one file, System.Text.Json with fields, a random source with Unity's bounds

dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal compiles them against a real UnrealSharp install (set U2UE_UNREALSHARP to the host's Plugins/UnrealSharp), so a template that no longer matches the engine's bindings fails there.

What the toolkit does not do here

It does not move the code for you, decide the seams, or write the hosts. It tells you what each type touches, gives the moved code Unity's runtime rules, reads the data, gates the boundary and proves the answers agree - and the reference port is the worked example of all of it.

Topic by topic: the rest of a Unity game

The method above is the order of work. This section is the map by topic: for each part of a Unity game, what Unity does, what Unreal offers, how the reference port did it, and what the toolkit gives you today. NOT YET means the toolkit has nothing for it yet and the reference port's own route is the only worked example. shared/PORTING_ANOTHER_PROJECT.md is the long form with the reasons, and py -m u2ue find <words> searches it, the manual and the code together. The reference port's Unreal side is C# through UnrealSharp, with C++ only where UnrealSharp cannot reach.

The one decision everything else follows from

Do not translate MonoBehaviours into Actors one by one. Move the rules into an engine-free model (the reference port's is a rules assembly plus a presentation assembly for the per-frame look) and write one thin host per engine. The Unity build and the Unreal build then run the same model DLL, which is why parity can be proven at all: the same inputs go through the same code, and only the hosts differ.

  • Two gates keep it true: layer_gate.py (the model references no engine - not UnityEngine, not UnrealSharp) and host_gate.py (a host interface declares only questions the game asks; logging, files, JSON and random numbers go through the platform seam).
  • Toolkit: HAVE. py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only model runs both gates on the folders the project file names (model.root, model.layers, model.scan, model.hosting); a project with no model yet is told so.

The lifecycle: Awake, Start, Update, LateUpdate, OnDestroy

  • Unity: Awake and OnEnable on load, Start before the first Update, then every frame Update, the coroutines, LateUpdate, in script execution order; OnDisable and OnDestroy at teardown.
  • Unreal: an Actor's constructor, BeginPlay, Tick(deltaSeconds), EndPlay(reason). There is no LateUpdate and no coroutine phase; tick groups exist but do not mirror Unity's order.
  • The reference port: one actor owns the game screen and drives it. BeginPlay builds the world, Tick calls the model's presentation frame once per engine frame, EndPlay tears it down. That frame object IS Unity's frame order, written once where a headless test can hold it - the clock, each former MonoBehaviour's Update in its order, the coroutine pass, the camera, LateUpdate - and its header cites the executionOrder value each step stands for, read from the .cs.meta files.
  • Why not one actor per MonoBehaviour: the order between them is the behaviour. Re-making it by hand in separate actor ticks was tried on the reference port and drew things one tick late.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue inventory lists every MonoBehaviour's script execution order and lifecycle methods - the table a frame driver is written from - and U2ue.Runtime.UnityFrame is the driver itself (Update by execution order, the coroutine phase, LateUpdate), tested against that order.

Coroutines, WaitForSeconds, Invoke

  • Unity: StartCoroutine(IEnumerator), yield return null / WaitForSeconds, resumed after Update.
  • Unreal: latent actions, timers or async tasks. None of them resumes at Unity's point in the frame.
  • The reference port: the iterators are kept. A small runner steps them - Start, Stop, StopAll, and Resume (the yield-null pass) - with a scaled and an unscaled wait for WaitForSeconds and WaitForSecondsRealtime. The model never waits: a rule that waited in Unity becomes a step the host advances. Awaiting was rejected: the reference port had 833 coroutine sites, and an awaiting model inverts control into them.
  • ABSENT in the reference port, so there is no worked example: Invoke / InvokeRepeating, FixedUpdate.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. U2ue.Runtime.Coroutines runs C# iterators by Unity's rules (Wait.Scaled / Wait.Unscaled), stepped identically to the reference port's runner (dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.OriginTests); u2ue inventory counts every type that uses coroutines.

Time

  • Unity: Time.deltaTime (scaled, and clamped by the project's Maximum Allowed Timestep), unscaledDeltaTime, timeScale.
  • Unreal: Tick's deltaSeconds, and global time dilation.
  • The reference port: one clock for the whole frame takes the engine's unscaled seconds each frame and derives Unity's: DeltaTime = Min(unscaled, MaximumDeltaTime) * TimeScale, the maximum being Unity's default, 0.33333334.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. U2ue.Runtime.UnityClock takes the project's own maximum step (read it with u2ue data --from ProjectSettings/TimeManager.asset --class 5, field Maximum Allowed Timestep) and agrees with the reference port's clock frame for frame.

Random numbers

  • Unity: UnityEngine.Random, one global, unseeded stream.
  • Unreal: FMath::Rand, and random streams.
  • The reference port: the model asks IRandomSource. Unity's adapter keeps the global stream, so the sequence the player sees is unchanged; headless and parity runs use a seeded System.Random. A presentation-only noise (a UI sound's samples) draws from the host's own stream, never the rules' stream.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. U2ue.Runtime.Platform.IRandomSource and SeededRandom, with Unity's bounds (int upper-exclusive, float both-inclusive); u2ue parity compares the rules' answers across runtimes. For effects, a frame that differs because one engine drew one random sample is labelled RANDDRAW and never counted as a difference.

Floats across runtimes

  • Unity runs C# on Mono; the Unreal hosts and the headless runs use CoreCLR. The same float expression can round differently. Measured on the reference port: 35 rows, every one 1 ULP, all in one damage formula, and in every row Mono is the one that differs while the two CoreCLR runs agree (the header of logic_diff.py records it, correcting an earlier note that blamed CoreCLR). An explicit float local per step makes them agree; doing so moves the Unity build's values by 1 ULP, which is the game owner's call.
  • Compare floats by bit pattern, never by printed text: Mono prints 9 digits and .NET prints the shortest (FloatBits.Hex; the text difference alone once produced 230 false mismatches).
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue parity (wrapping logic_diff.py) compares every runtime's digest by float bits, with a characterised allowance that stays red on any new or wider gap; U2ue.Runtime.FloatBits writes and measures bit patterns.
  • Unity's side with no Editor: u2ue digest run compiles a game's rule cases twice - for CoreCLR and for the project's Unity version's own Mono (<editor>/Editor/Data/MonoBleedingEdge: its csc.exe and mono-bdwgc.exe) - and writes both digests. MEASURED 2026-10-16 (u2ue digest faithful): on Unity 6000.3.16f1 the reference digest computed that way equals the one the Editor wrote, 383 of 383 rows, including the 35 rows where Mono and CoreCLR differ. Another Unity version is UNMEASURED until its own Editor-recorded digest is compared. The second game's first slice: its PID formula differs by 1 ULP on 2 of 640 rows, and an explicit-local copy agrees on both runtimes - the same cause.
  • Unity's value types in a model (Vector3, Mathf, Color; u2ue inventory counts them as their own family): the reference port substitutes them member by member into its own rules, each copied from a measured shim (UnityCompat.Core, which declares only value types and is bit-exact on 101 of 105 members). Whether a ported game's model may reference such a shim instead is an open decision of the toolkit's owner; until it is made, port the float-only rules first.

Spawning and destroying: Instantiate, Destroy

  • Unity: Instantiate(prefab), Destroy(go).
  • Unreal: SpawnActor, DestroyActor; Niagara systems through UNiagaraFunctionLibrary.
  • The reference port: the model never spawns. It states what happened (an event stream, below) and the view adapter makes or removes the engine objects: AActor.Spawn for an entity, SpawnSystemAtLocation for an effect, DestroyActor to remove one - and it asks the engine whether an actor is still alive, because the managed wrapper outlives DestroyActor.
  • Toolkit: effects HAVE (the converter builds the systems the player spawns). Actors: a TEMPLATE, AU2ueFrameActor in u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal, compiled against UnrealSharp; a headless smoke run is NOT YET (Appendix B).

Finding things: GetComponent, FindObjectOfType, singletons

  • Unity: components found at run time, often through a static Instance.
  • Unreal: components and subsystems; GetActorOfClass.
  • The reference port: the model is handed what it needs through host interfaces (a roster interface and the other I*Host interfaces of its rules), so nothing searches a scene. The hosts hold their references directly.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue inventory lists, type by type, every Unity call by family (lookups among them) and the pure-rule types that use none - what moves into the model first (Chapter 4 shows the second game's run).

The transform: axes, units, rotation

  • Unity: metres; x right, y up, z forward; left-handed. Euler angles apply Z, then X, then Y.
  • Unreal: centimetres; x forward, y right, z up; also left-handed.
  • The conversion, one line each way: ue.X = -x*100, ue.Y = z*100, ue.Z = y*100, with its exact inverse. Directions: u2ue_dir(v) = (-x, z, y); rotations: u2ue_quat(q) = (-qx, qz, qy, qw) (both functions in vfxport/build_niagara.py). The ZXY Euler order was MEASURED on Unity 6000.3, not assumed.
  • A trap: a scene imported through glTF arrives in a frame the pipeline chose (Chapter 7), so a level and a hand-placed actor need not share a frame. Measure the imported level's frame once and convert every hand-placed actor through it.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue/transform.py holds every convention above in one place, held by its selftest to the converter's own functions; its Unreal composition is READ from the engine (TransformVectorized.cpp:295-323).

The transform chain: hierarchy, scale, shear

  • Unity: a Transform composes as a 4x4 matrix, so a rotated child under a non-uniformly scaled parent is sheared.
  • Unreal: a SceneComponent holds translation, quaternion and scale. It cannot hold a shear.
  • The reference port: measured, not averaged. Every node was composed both ways and each drawn mesh's corners pushed through both (Chapter 7 has the numbers); the error was accepted with its number and pinned by a gate, not baked. The effect converter refuses a sheared particle node and names it.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue shear --gltf <export> (or --from <scene>) lists every sheared node, whether it draws, and the error in cm under Unreal's own composition rule; on the reference port's first battle map it finds the same 46 nodes the scene work measured by hand. Effects: refused and named by the converter. (--from on a scene whose prefab instances remove GameObjects waits on the nested reader, Chapter 7.)

Scenes and prefabs

  • Unity: .unity and .prefab YAML, .meta GUIDs, nested prefabs and overrides.
  • Unreal: levels (.umap) and Blueprint or C# actor classes.
  • The reference port: geometry, materials and textures go through the standard pipeline - exported from Unity with glTFast, imported with Interchange. Inactive subtrees are skipped and listed; every value not carried is named ABSENT. scene_fidelity_gate.py re-measures hierarchy, materials, textures and placement against Unity's own files without opening either editor.
  • Toolkit: HAVE - u2ue scene (Chapter 7). The notes on reading prefab YAML (nested instances, variants, legacy prefab records) apply to any scene reader.

Inspector values, ScriptableObjects, data files

  • Unity: serialized fields on MonoBehaviours and ScriptableObjects, Resources.Load, JsonUtility.
  • Unreal: UPROPERTY defaults, data assets, data tables.
  • The reference port: the values are read, never retyped. A tool reads the scene YAML into a small TSV the model parses (the camera rig, the canvas scaler); a ScriptableObject is written out by a test. JSON goes through IJsonCodec<T>; on Unreal that is System.Text.Json with IncludeFields = true, without which public fields serialise as nothing. Text assets go through ITextAssets.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue data --from <scene|prefab|asset> --script <Class> (or --class <id>) writes any component's or ScriptableObject's serialized values as JSON or TSV, nested prefab overrides applied; on the reference port's camera rig it equals the hand-written reader on all 152 fields and 32 curve values.

Input

  • Unity: Input.GetKeyDown, the mouse position, Camera.ScreenPointToRay.
  • Unreal: Enhanced Input, or polling the player controller.
  • The reference port: polled. Its IInputSource implementation uses APlayerController.WasInputKeyJustPressed and UGameplayStatics.DeprojectScreenToWorld; the pick itself is a rule of the model, not an engine trace, so both engines pick the same cell. Enhanced Input is not used.
  • Toolkit: a TEMPLATE - UnrealPointer in u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal: the cursor, its position in Unity's frame and its world ray, and the keys pressed this frame, polled before the frame runs (compiled against UnrealSharp; the smoke run is NOT YET).

Logging, files, preferences: the platform seam

Six interfaces, one engine call per member: ILog (Debug.Log), ITextAssets (Resources.Load of a TextAsset), IKeyValueStore (PlayerPrefs), IFileStore (the save file), IJsonCodec<T> (JsonUtility), IRandomSource (above). A second game implements the same six. Toolkit: HAVE - the same six in U2ue.Runtime.Platform, their Unreal implementations as a template (UnrealPlatform.cs in u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal), and u2ue check --only model refuses a platform member declared outside the hosting folder.

Camera

  • Unity: a Camera component, often driven by a controller script; Cinemachine.
  • Unreal: a CameraActor or CameraComponent made the view target.
  • The reference port: the camera's rules are the model's, fed the rig's serialized values (read as data, above). Unreal places a camera actor and makes it the view target with SetViewTargetWithBlend; a director class on the host carries the shots.
  • Toolkit: a TEMPLATE - UnrealCameraRig in u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal: spawn, view target, pose, and Unity's vertical field of view converted to Unreal's horizontal one (compiled against UnrealSharp; the smoke run is NOT YET).

UI

  • Unity: a uGUI Canvas, RectTransforms, layout groups, TextMeshPro.
  • Unreal: UMG widgets, or Slate.
  • The reference port: not a UMG tree. The Unity Canvas is captured and laid out by a port of uGUI's own solver, then painted in one UUserWidget.OnPaint - because UnrealSharp's UWidgetTree.RootWidget is read-only, a UMG tree cannot be assembled from C#. Only panels with a view model and a binding are drawn.
  • Toolkit: HAVE the layout side - U2ue.Ui, the generic uGUI / TextMeshPro library with its own tests (u2ue ui test), and u2ue ui convert. The capture needs the package's Editor assembly (Appendix B). Chapter 7 has the whole route.

Audio

  • Unity: AudioSource pools, procedural clips through AudioClip.SetData.
  • Unreal: Sound Waves, Sound Cues, MetaSounds.
  • The reference port: a presentation rule picks the voice and the gain as Unity's audio manager did; Unity's procedural clips are rendered to float PCM once and played through a small C++ bridge that hands the samples to the mixer unconverted, as a 2D one-shot.
  • Toolkit: NOT YET as a shipped plugin (Appendix B). A plugin template, u2ue/templates/unreal/Plugins/U2ueAudio, holds the bridge and a judge for its selftest's rendered tone; whether that selftest has passed in a host is not recorded in this manual.

Animation and physics

The reference port's units are painted cards whose motion is a rule of the model, so it has no worked example for an Animator, Animation Blueprints, Sequencer, or physics simulation. ABSENT, said here so nobody reads silence as a recipe (Appendix B).

What none of this proves

A host that compiles is not a port. The reference port proves its hosts with the same model run on both engines and compared (logic_diff.py: 383 rows, identical except the 35 characterised 1-ULP rows above), and with pixels for the look. For another game the same comparison is py -m u2ue --project <name> parity: each runtime writes its digest, and every row is compared by float bits against a characterised allowance.

The logic playbook: the u2ue-logic skill in full

Everything that is not logic ports itself: the effects through the u2ue-port skill, scenes through u2ue scene, screens through u2ue ui, data through u2ue data. Logic is the one part a person or an AI model ports by hand, and this is the method as a playbook: the reference port's route (shared/PORTING_ANOTHER_PROJECT.md) made into steps, each with the command that runs it and the observable that says it is done. The skill file itself is u2ue/skill/u2ue-logic/SKILL.md; this section is its content.

The acceptance test: the game's rules run in ONE engine-free model; Unity, the Unreal host and a headless runner give the same bits for every case (u2ue parity exits 0); and the game as the owner plays it still works.

Scope: a Unity game's C# - its MonoBehaviours, coroutines and frame order - and the engine-free model it moves into. Precondition: the game's Unity project is on disk serialized as text, and a project file names it. Stakeholders: the porter wants the game running on Unreal, the same; the owner wants only their decisions asked; a reviewer wants the design reviewable from its class model, not line by line. Minimal guarantee: nothing is invented - a rule that cannot move is named with its reason, and a red gate stops the step. Success guarantee: the rules run in one model, Unity's runtime and the Unreal host give the same bits, and the game still plays.

Kickoff prompt

The owner pastes this to an agent, with the two names filled in:

Port the logic of the Unity game at <UNITY PROJECT ROOT> with u2ue, project name <name>. Follow the u2ue-logic skill step by step. One slice at a time, smallest first. Do every step's RUN, and do not start the next step until its DONE WHEN is true. Draw the class model before moving code. Ask me only for the decisions the skill names as the owner's.

The bones: each concept one thing

The analogy is the handle; the class is the truth.

  • Project (u2ue/projects/<name>.json) - the game's address book: every path, named once.
  • Inventory (u2ue inventory) - the survey of the house before the move: every type, what it touches in Unity, which are already furniture that moves as it is (pure rules), and the order the rooms are walked in each frame.
  • Core (<Model>.Core, made by u2ue scaffold) - the rulebook: what happens, never how it looks. No engine in it.
  • Aggregate - ONE class per entity holds its state (a unit, a card, a board); the engine's object HOLDS one and forwards to it. Never forty little interfaces over one MonoBehaviour: the reference port measured that shape and is undoing it.
  • Seam - the plug sockets: the platform seam (logging, files, preferences, JSON, random numbers - U2ue.Runtime.Platform), the view seam (what draws), the capability seam (what the game asks an engine to do). An engine implements a seam; the Core declares it.
  • Event stream - the referee's call sheet: rules resolve a whole action INSTANTLY and append ordered events. The model never waits.
  • PlaybackQueue (U2ue.Runtime.PlaybackQueue<TEvent>) - the replay operator: one event per frame, only when the view is idle; input waits for IsCaughtUp.
  • UnityFrame (U2ue.Runtime.UnityFrame with Coroutines and UnityClock) - Unity's frame order (Update by execution order, the coroutine phase, LateUpdate) as one object an engine ticks once per frame.
  • Digest (U2ue.Runtime.Digest) - one engine's answer sheet; parity (u2ue parity) marks the sheets against each other, bit for bit.
  • Host - the engine's side: a Unity MonoBehaviour or an Unreal actor that holds the aggregate, feeds input and presents events.

The law of the playbook

It overrides speed and tidiness:

  • READ or ABSENT - a value in the model comes from the game's code or data, with where it came from; never a plausible constant.
  • No fallbacks - a rule that cannot resolve throws and names what is missing; catch {} and a default are the same lie.
  • Move, do not rewrite - the rule's code moves into the Core as it is; a behaviour change is a separate, named decision.
  • The model knows no engine - u2ue check --only model after every move; a red gate stops the move.
  • A check that has only passed proves nothing - every gate here has a plant it must fail (--selftest); run it once.
  • The owner's editors are the owner's - never the Unity Test Runner; Unity runs only in a window the owner allows; one headless Unreal at a time; never a modal answered for them.

The playbook's steps

Each step has a DO (what to do), a RUN (the command; every one exists and runs, and skill_gate.py checks that) and a DONE WHEN (the observable that ends it). py -m u2ue --project <name> logic judges each step's DONE WHEN from the records and says where a port stands.

Before you start: name the project

  • Do: copy the second game's example project file in u2ue/projects/ to u2ue/projects/<name>.json and fill in the Unity root, its version and the work folders. For a port already under way, ask where it stands first and resume at the step it names next - never re-derive the state from the files.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> info, then py -m u2ue --project <name> logic.
  • Done when: info exits 0 - every path it names opened.

Step 1. Read the game before touching it

  • Do: survey the Assets folders, name the game's OWN code folders as code.roots (vendor packages live in Assets too - never guess which are the game's), then inventory them. Read inventory.md: the pure-rule types, each MonoBehaviour's Unity families, the frame-order table.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> inventory --survey, then py -m u2ue --project <name> inventory.
  • Done when: inventory.json lists every type with its kind, and you can name the ten purest types and the five heaviest Unity users.
  • Trap: the reader is lexical - a call through reflection or a helper is not seen; a miss is UNKNOWN, never "does not use".
  • Trap: "pure" means no Unity API AND no Unity value type (Vector, Mathf, Color are a family of their own; before they were, a Vector3 rule was listed as pure and could not move as written).

Step 2. Draw the class model of ONE slice before moving anything

  • Do: pick the first slice - one feature whose rules use the fewest Unity families (a damage formula, a scoring rule, an inventory stack). Extract the class model over the game's code roots, draw the slice's types, and write the TARGET diagram: which types become the aggregate, which stay hosts, which seams appear. The diagram is the plan a person reviews; the code follows it.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> uml extract, then py -m u2ue --project <name> uml mermaid --focus <TypeA> <TypeB>.
  • Done when: the slice's current and target diagrams exist, and every name in them resolves (uml where <Name>).

Step 3. Sort the slice's types and members

  • Do: give every type in the slice ONE destination - CORE (a pure rule: it moves as it is), AGGREGATE (the state and rules inside a MonoBehaviour: they move into one Core class the MonoBehaviour then holds), HOST (what only an engine can do: draw, play, read input) or SEAM (a platform chore). Label each member the host keeps by its kind: PUNCTUAL ("a thing happened" - one keyed registry per engine), ONGOING ("a value is now X" - the view polls it), MUTATION (the model asking the engine to change state it owns - it goes away with the aggregate), ANSWER (returns a value - real per-engine work), CONTROL (menus, the AI's turn, the camera).
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> inventory.
  • Done when: the target diagram carries every type's destination and every kept host member's kind.
  • Absent: a host-kind census for any game's model (the reference port's host_census.py reads only its own). Label by hand by the rule above: a non-void member is an ANSWER.

Step 4. Cut the Core

  • Do: create the engine-free model OUTSIDE the Unity Assets tree, declared in the project file.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> scaffold --name <Model> --dir <folder>.
  • Done when: scaffold exits 0 - both projects build and the model gates PASS on the empty Core.

Step 5. Put the platform seam in first

  • Do: every log line, file read, preference, JSON document and random draw the slice makes goes through U2ue.Runtime.Platform (ILog, ITextAssets, IKeyValueStore, IFileStore, IJsonCodec<T>, IRandomSource / SeededRandom) - never re-declared on a rule's host. The reference port found a log line declared on five hosts and a random draw on seven before it did this.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only model, then dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests.
  • Done when: host_gate PASSES and no rule in the slice calls Debug.Log, Random, PlayerPrefs, File or JsonUtility directly.

Step 6. Move the slice's rules into the Core

  • Do: move the code (do not rewrite it) into the aggregate; the MonoBehaviour now holds one aggregate and forwards its properties to it, so state has one home. A rule that waited (a coroutine, WaitForSeconds) becomes a step the host advances - the model never awaits. A rule doing Unity value-type maths (Vector3, Mathf) waits for the owner's decision on where those types live in a model (the reference port substituted them member by member; a measured shim is the other answer) - take the float-only rules first. Write one test per moved rule in <Model>.Core.Tests, with the value the Unity build gives.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only model, then dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests.
  • Done when: both gates PASS, the slice's tests pass, and the Unity project still compiles with the MonoBehaviour holding the aggregate.

Step 7. Emit events; replay them

  • Do: each rule that changes what the player sees appends an event to an ordered, append-only list instead of calling the view. The host replays the list through PlaybackQueue<TEvent> with a presenter that is idle when its animation ends; input is taken only when IsCaughtUp.
  • Run: dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests, then dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests.
  • Done when: a test runs the slice's action headlessly and asserts the event list, in order.

Step 8. Keep Unity's frame order

  • Do: per-frame code the slice keeps (Update, LateUpdate, coroutines) registers with ONE UnityFrame in its script execution order (the inventory's frame-order table, read from the .cs.meta files); coroutines run on U2ue.Runtime.Coroutines. Never one engine tick per former MonoBehaviour - the order between them IS the behaviour.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> inventory, then dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests.
  • Done when: every kept per-frame method is registered with the order the inventory lists for its type.

Step 9. Prove it: the same answers, by the bit

  • Do: write the slice's cases ONCE, as a static method returning a Digest (no NUnit in that file), driving the moved rules the way the game drives them (its own constants, READ with file and line). u2ue digest run compiles them twice - for CoreCLR (Headless: what an Unreal host runs) and for the project's Unity version's OWN Mono (UnityMono: no Editor opens) - and writes both sheets into parity.dir. Bump the digest's version whenever the case set changes.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> digest run --entry <Ns.Cases.Build> --cases <Cases.cs>, then py -m u2ue --project <name> parity.
  • Done when: parity exits 0 across Headless and UnityMono, and any characterised row (parity --characterise) carries its measured cause.
  • Trap: the cases' INPUTS must be exact on every runtime - make them by integer arithmetic and write each one to the sheet (_in rows). Measured on the second game's first slice: a driver that made its own target angles with float maths produced 177 false differences in 321 rows; with exact inputs the rule's true difference was 2 rows.
  • Trap: UnityMono is Unity's runtime, not the Editor. u2ue digest faithful measures one against the other on an Editor-recorded digest (Unity 6000.3: 383 of 383 rows identical); a Unity version without that measurement is labelled UNMEASURED in the provenance, and its Mono answer is not called the Editor's.

Step 10. The Unreal host

  • Do: the game gets its OWN .uproject (the owner's decision for a second game), made by u2ue host the way a customer makes one: name it in the project file's unreal.host block (the template, each plugin with its source and pinned commit, the AutoSDK root, the digest's entry and cases), then run the steps in order from native PowerShell - each refuses while an Unreal runs, and each is judged by its proof line, never by an exit code. wire references <Model>.Core, compiles the digest cases in, COPIES the toolkit's Unreal templates into the managed project (u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal: AU2ueFrameActor ticks UnityFrame with the project's own maximum step, UnrealPointer, UnrealCameraRig, and UnrealPlatform.cs - the six platform services) and writes the module that answers the digest; run starts the host headless, and it writes logic-Unreal.txt from the same cases. Grow the host from there: it holds the aggregate and presents events through PlaybackQueue.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> host plan; py -m u2ue --project <name> host create (then install, compile, generate, wire, publish, run, one at a time); py -m u2ue --project <name> host status; dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal.
  • Run: py -m u2ue.seam --project <name> --list names every seam the model declares that no model type fills and the Unreal host does not fill yet (the project's model.hosts says where each engine's host code is) - each a socket to implement, or one the host says it leaves out, and why.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> parity --require Unreal.
  • Done when: parity exits 0 across Headless, Unity and Unreal.
  • Measured: the second game's host was made this way from nothing in 9 minutes (the compile 255 s), and its digest equalled the headless CoreCLR one byte for byte. Absent: a generic publish proof by the loaded assembly's MVID (the reference port's ue_publish_gate.py does it for its own host); until it lands, run proves the host ran THIS publish only by the digest it wrote after the start.

Step 11. Record the slice and take the next one

  • Do: write the slice's record to <work.effects>/slices/slice-<N>.json (logic reads it there) - the slice, its first commit and its parity commit (the tempo), and the gates' output - and take the next slice, bigger. Each slice's diagram joins the game's model.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only model.
  • Done when: the record names both commits and the parity verdict, and the next slice is chosen.

When to stop and ask the owner

A behaviour change a rule would need (a bug the port would fix), where Unity's value types live for the Core, the second game's Unreal host, anything that would run in the owner's live editor, and anything outward-facing. Ask one precise question, and take the next slice meanwhile.

The model in depth: what a second game implements

This section is the reference port's architecture as a recipe for another game, folded in from shared/PORTING_ANOTHER_PROJECT.md. Every interface and member it names was read off disk by the port's own final gate on 2026-09-30; where something a plan called for does not exist, it says so. The claim it supports is that implementing the adapters is what a second game does - not that any port is finished: a person still has to PLAY the Unreal build, attended.

Three things to read before the rest:

  • Read the gates (below) before the recipe. On the reference port, three of seven gates were red on the morning they were first run together, and all seven green that night; a green summary that was not measured is the exact failure the gates exist to catch. The reference port runs all of them in dependency order, healing only what is mechanically stale, with one command, py port_heal.py from the toolkit root (--check heals nothing); its run under GC pressure fails on an engine ensure in the log.
  • The event stream is half the seam. The interfaces say what an engine must implement; the stream says what the model must tell it. Most of what went wrong on the reference port's first full day was the model leaving something unsaid, or saying it twice, while every interface was implemented correctly and the picture was still wrong.
  • The shim is not the architecture. Emulating namespace UnityEngine (the reference port's UnityCompat.Core and UnityCompat.Engine) lets Unity-shaped code compile anywhere, and it remains a parity oracle, but the reference port took it off the Unreal model path: the Unreal assembly references neither any more, and the SetBackend calls that installed it are deleted. A second game should not implement it (the last sub-section says why). Byte-identical artifacts are compared with cmp, and the exit code is what is quoted.

The layers, as they are on disk

  • The Core is the engine-free model. Its project file has ZERO Reference, ProjectReference or PackageReference items, and that emptiness is the whole design: there is nothing for an engine to arrive through. It is multi-targeted (netstandard2.1;net8.0;net10.0 on the reference port) so one assembly serves Unity as a managed plugin, the headless suites and UnrealSharp, and Deterministic is on. The model is (state, seed) -> state. It never waits: a grep for yield return or yield break over its sources counts 0, and an IEnumerator mention is prose. Check that with ls and a search, not memory.
  • The platform seam is one file of six interfaces. A domain host may declare only domain callbacks; anything a second game would implement the same way whatever the game is (a log line, a text asset, a preference, a file, a JSON document, a random draw) is declared there exactly once, and py host_gate.py refuses a new declaration of one of those member names anywhere else.
  • The presentation layer is the view seam: the view interfaces plus the reference port's PresentationHost, PlaybackQueue, ShownState and ViewCallFormat. It references the Core and never the reverse. Every method is a GAME VERB (Place(id, cell)), never an engine primitive.
  • The engine adapters, one set per engine: the entity view, camera director, effect player and input source, and on Unreal the platform hosts (UnrealPlatformServices.cs for five services, UnrealJsonCodec.cs for the sixth).

The interface set

The BASE set a second game implements is five view interfaces (the four a board needs, plus IHudView) and six platform services. On top sits the optional capability seam: interfaces an engine implements when it draws more of the game than the base calls say. Every other interface in the reference port's Core (152 in all) is a domain host or a facet of that game's rules, and a second game declares its own instead, because they are its rules.

The view seam

The reference port's view interfaces are the worked example; the rules they follow are what transfers.

  • IEntityView draws the world. Every call is a statement about what the player should now see, never a question: spawn, place (no travel), move (the view owns the duration and the path's shape), show a health change with the HP remaining, kill, despawn (removal with no death), and an IsIdle. There is deliberately no IUnitView and no ITileView: Unity spawns a GameObject per entity while Unreal can draw tiles as instanced meshes, both satisfy one interface, and the model never learns which. If a new entity kind forces a new method, the abstraction has drifted and the fix belongs in this interface, not in another.
  • ICameraDirector frames the action: play a beat on a focus entity, and an IsIdle. The model NEVER mentions a beat: the presentation derives beats from the event stream, which is what frees Unreal to use Sequencer and look nothing like Unity.
  • IEffectPlayer is effects and sound together, because an impact is a flash AND a thud, and splitting them makes every caller coordinate two things that always fire together. Its effectKey names the effect in the GAME's vocabulary, never an engine asset path; the adapter maps it to a Shuriken system or a Niagara asset, and that mapping is the one place the two engines may disagree about what an effect looks like.
  • IInputSource is the only way anything reaches the model, and it is pull-based on purpose: a push callback would run the model from inside an engine's input handler, the inversion the event stream exists to avoid. Its commands are GAME verbs, and the command type lives in the Core, because a command the model consumes cannot live above the model. (The reference port's first version had verbs like "select cell" and "confirm", which described a mouse rather than the game.)
  • PresentationHost is the one object an adapter hands over: the entities, camera, effects and input views, an optional HUD (none for a headless run), and an IsIdle that ANDs the idling views. One object beats five constructor parameters threaded everywhere.
  • IHudView draws the HUD from the board AS SHOWN (ShownState), and is handed nothing else. PlaybackQueue calls it after the initial board and after every event it shows, at the pace of the view calls, so the HUD is never ahead of the animation. It cannot show the verdict while the killing blow is still in flight - which is exactly what a HUD bound to the model would do, because the model resolves a whole turn instantly. The HUD is not part of IsIdle: it owes no animation, so the queue never waits on it.
  • One recorder both engines and the headless suite use: a view double that writes one line per view call. Beats are derived in PlaybackQueue itself; there is no separate beat-policy interface.

The capability seam

The base calls say WHAT happened; they cannot say how Unity paces and frames it (a settle before an effect, a zoom on a target, a cutscene's flight, a banner's wait). Porting those rules engine-free leaves three decisions, each held by tests on the reference port:

  • PlaybackQueue stays ONE switch. It never forks per engine. For each optional surface it tests the host's view with is against that surface's interface; a view that is not one gets the BASE call instead (a PlayBeat, a Play), exactly what it got before the capability existed.
  • The recorder (the reference port's RecordingView) records "the base call it replaces, or nothing". Alone (the headless suite) it answers as a view WITHOUT the capability; wrapped around a drawing view it forwards, and a drawing view that LACKS a capability makes it THROW - never a silent skip. So a run shown through the capability path records line for line what the base path records, and no recorded stream moves when a capability lands.
  • One frame object owns the one-tick order and ONE clock (popups, the bodies' Update, the show step, coroutines, the camera, LateUpdate - Unity's frame), so an adapter is a per-tick COPIER of engine-free state plus a click source.

The reference port's capabilities extend its entity view, its camera director, its effect player and its IHudView, each recording what its base call records. A new surface gets its own READ record (one data file per surface), never new lines in an existing slice, so a recording made before the surface existed stays valid.

The platform seam

These six are what a second game implements the SAME WAY whatever the game is; that is the test for belonging here. The toolkit ships them as U2ue.Runtime.Platform:

interface members the rule its reference implementations taught
ILog void Info(string), void Warn(string), void Error(string) a three-level log is the smallest complete logging seam, even before anything calls ILog.Error
ITextAssets string LoadText(string resourcePath) NULL is the ABSENT signal and the only one; an existing but empty asset returns "" and parses as zero rows. On Unreal, resolve a carried text through the copy's manifest, never by guessing an extension
IKeyValueStore int GetInt(string,int), void SetInt(string,int), string GetString(string,string), void SetString(string,string), void DeleteKey(string), void Save() PlayerPrefs' own flush semantics: Set changes memory, Save writes the file
IFileStore string RootPath { get; }, bool DirectoryExists(string), void CreateDirectory(string), bool FileExists(string), string ReadAllText(string), void WriteAllText(string,string) RootPath was once named after a Unity folder (StreamingAssetsPath) and was renamed on purpose: a platform seam must not name a Unity folder. Shipped data and save data are two stores, because one root cannot be both
IJsonCodec<T> string ToJson(T), T FromJson(string) on Unreal, System.Text.Json with IncludeFields = true - that option is the whole implementation: without it the reference port's game data serialised to {}, 2 characters
IRandomSource float Value(), int Range(int minInclusive, int maxExclusive), float Range(float minInclusive, float maxInclusive) the two Range overloads have DIFFERENT bounds, as Unity's do (int upper-exclusive, float both-inclusive), and getting that wrong compiles perfectly

Three more rules from the random source:

  • A seeded System.Random was measured bit-identical across Mono 6.13, .NET 8.0.22 and .NET 10.0.12 (the reference port, 2026-09-27), which is why one seed is one game on all three runtimes.
  • On Unreal, keep the game rules' stream private to the model's own SeededRandom, and give the host's random service only to what is NOT the rules; handing the rules a host stream would end the byte-identical event log. A Value() meant to reach the float overload's inclusive maximum cannot be built on NextDouble(), which is [0, 1); the reference port built it as Next(0, 1 << 24) / (1 << 24) - 1. Unreal's own FMath::Rand is not in UnrealSharp's managed glue, so System.Random is the runtime's own there.
  • IRandomSource is the member that proves the seam is worth having: before the seam, the reference port declared the same draw on five different domain hosts under five names. host_gate.py now refuses every one of those names outside the hosting folder, so the leak cannot come back under a sixth spelling.

The event stream contract: what the model must SAY

The view interfaces are the engine's half of the seam. The other half is the model's event list: ordered, append-only, written through one sink, read by PlaybackQueue, which turns it into view calls at the view's pace. An engine draws ONLY what the stream says, so everything a player must see has to be said, once, with what a view needs to draw it. On the reference port a headless suite that plays every authored action on a test board went looking for violations and found eleven classes of them - every one the model's, not an adapter's. These rules fixed them, and a second game's model should be held to them from its first event:

  • Every HP change is announced, with the HP LEFT - the delta and the remainder, because a health bar needs both. Silent writes are the trap (damage over time, reflected damage, an aura's victims, an action's own HP price). The check: every step's HP difference must be the stream's last word on it.
  • A status's tick is ONE announcement, its only HP event; the damage inside it says nothing more, or the same HP drops twice. A tick that moved no HP shows no number.
  • Every effect event names the square its effect plays on. An event left at the default cell asks for its effect at the board's origin and nothing else fails, so it is invisible until someone looks. That happened four separate times.
  • What a HUD shows is announced, not inferred: an action-point change with its delta and total, from ONE sweep in the flow, not from each place that writes it; a status leaving, one event per entry, from the one method entries leave through.
  • A unit an action moves is announced like a walk. A move the stream never states leaves the unit's view on the wrong square until its next walk.
  • Say each fact in ONE layer, and choose that layer on day one. The reference port inherited three facts said twice, and its presenter has to tell them apart; a second game should not need dedupe rules.
  • Durations are what the entry was GIVEN after every rule that touched it, not the authored number.
  • An end-of-turn tick of an action is its own event, and names the action. Whether a tick SHOWS anything is the presentation's decision, never the model's.

What it costs to check: the suite turns each rule into an expectation over every case, and each is proven able to fail by a planted fault. One was VACUOUS until a case existed that moves a unit - a gate that has only ever passed cannot be told from one switched off. Copy the suite's shape, not just the rules.

The recipe a second game follows

Step 1 - write the Core. An engine-free project with NO references at all, multi-targeted for every host you need: model state and rules only. Do not let a single using UnityEngine or using UnrealSharp in, and do not trust yourself about it: run layer_gate.py, which reads the banned namespace list, checks the model's projects, and checks that no engine build source-links .cs files out of another engine's tree. Run its --selftest and watch it FAIL on a planted using and on a planted <Compile Include> before you believe a PASS.

Step 2 - cut the platform seam FIRST, not last. The measured cost of not doing so, on the reference port: a log line declared on five domain hosts and a random draw on seven (its PlatformServices.cs header records it), every one of them surface a second game would have had to implement. Give host_gate.py your member names.

Step 3 - the engine class PRESENTS events; it never sequences a turn. This is the step that most looks like the old code and most must not be. The flow is INSTANT: it takes state and a seed, runs the whole action, and appends an ordered, immutable event list. The ENGINE ADAPTER owns a PlaybackQueue: the queue accepts the list (Accept), shows one event per frame into the views (Tick()), and exposes its Backlog and IsCaughtUp. Input is GATED on IsCaughtUp, so a player cannot act into an animation they have not seen; the adapter's IInputSource builds the commands, and the queue asks for one only once the views are idle. Three measured reasons this is not negotiable: a (state, seed) -> state model is why the reference port's Unreal side ran a whole game with no world at all; awaiting inverts control into coroutines (833 sites were already blocking that port); and different effect lengths per engine would otherwise take different code paths per engine.

Step 4 - write ONE adapter and prove it headlessly before writing a second. The reference doubles print one line per view call; that printed slice is the artifact everything else diffs against, so write it before any engine is involved.

Step 5 - write the second adapter and diff the slices byte for byte. Not "looks the same": cmp exit 0.

Step 6 - keep the model as a compiled artifact both engines LOAD, and prove the artifact is the one they loaded. This catches the failure nobody sees: an engine fighting a two-day-old model and producing a beautiful, stale, byte-identical artifact. It happened to both engines on the reference port on one day - Unity's plugin DLLs stale with nothing saying so until plugin_sync_gate.py was run by hand, and Unreal's stale minutes after a clean publish because another worker edited the model. staleness_check.py (run at session start) now warns when any model source is newer than the DLL an engine loads.

Step 7 - know what your reference checksum does NOT cover. A byte-identical reference run proves the MODEL on every engine. It does not exercise the engine's own game object at all if that object is not what the reference run plays on - and on the reference port it was not: every engine's reference run used the model's aggregate, while the game as played ran Unity's own Unit MonoBehaviour. A refactor of the engine object therefore needs the engine's OWN game played as its gate (battle_smoke.py: a real game driven in Play, every exception attributed), before and after, beside the checksum.

What a second game writes

  • Its own Core, all of it. The reference port's interfaces are its own rules (a damage formula, a type chart, and so on); a second game declares its own. Nothing here is a framework to inherit from. What transfers is the SHAPE: domain hosts for "a question the model needs answered, or an announcement only the game can render", and nothing else on them.
  • One engine-free aggregate per entity - not a header interface split into facets. Measured on the reference port: Unity's unit MonoBehaviour implemented 40 facets through 144 explicit pass-through members, one property was declared by seven of them, and exactly one production type implemented all 40, so nothing was segregated where it ships. Give the rules one aggregate per entity, let the engine's object HOLD one and forward its properties, and cut an interface only where a second implementor supplies it differently.
  • The host seam sorted into five kinds before it is ported, because they cost a second engine very different amounts:
kind what it says what it costs an engine
PUNCTUAL "a thing happened" one KEY-ADDRESSED registry per engine, not one implementation per member
ONGOING "a value is now X" one polling loop: the view reads the value each frame
MUTATION the model asking the engine to change state it owns nothing, eventually: it is model state living in the engine object, and it goes away with the aggregate
ANSWER returns a value real work per engine while the value lives outside the model
CONTROL menus, the AI's turn, the camera real work per engine, and honest

The reference port's 435 host members split 205 / 40 / 49 / 121 / 20 (its host_census.py, which reads only its own model). Only the last two are irreducible, and most ANSWERs existed only because unit state lived in the MonoBehaviour. - Art addressed by a KEY the model owns and a TABLE each engine owns. The model's own resolver turns an entity into a file name, a test runs it over the disk to write a table (READ or ABSENT per row, never a guess), and each engine resolves the same key to its own imported asset and FAILS LOUDLY, naming the path, when it is missing. Effects already work this way (IEffectPlayer takes a string key). A placeholder primitive in a missing asset's place is refused by no_toys_gate.py: a plausible frame with the wrong geometry is the failure that hides longest. - Six platform service implementations - roughly one afternoon per engine; every member is one engine call. - The view adapters per engine - the real work, and bounded: on the reference port, 16 methods and 4 properties in all. - Nothing else. No serialisation format, no message bus, no scripting layer. A JSON bridge between the engines was considered and rejected in favour of event-log replay, because a bridge makes every value cross a wire and a replay makes every value a diff.

The model's gates, G1 to G7

Copy these. Each exists because something passed every other instrument while broken. The reference port's runs of them, with their numbers, are in shared/PORTING_ANOTHER_PROJECT.md; what transfers is what each checks and the trap that made it.

  • G1 the layer boundary - py layer_gate.py, and its --selftest. No banned namespace in the model's projects, no unaccounted source link out of another engine's tree, and the accounted links kept on a ratchet file that must empty. Its selftest plants a <Compile Include> under the Unity tree and must report FAIL before a PASS means anything.
  • G2 the model's own suite - dotnet test of the model's tests, no engine in the process. Keep in it the tests that assert the cross-engine claim (the Unity build's native run equals the headless reference): they go red after every model change until the Unity side is re-recorded against the new model, as they should. The cure is the plugin sync (G4) and a re-record, never an edit to the test. Beside it, a second suite that plays every authored action headlessly, every expectation READ from the game's data with its provenance or ABSENT with the reason.
  • G3 it compiles on every host - py typecheck.py (the Unity side, headless Roslyn, no editor) and dotnet build of the engine's managed project.
  • G4 the artifact both engines load is the current source - py plugin_sync_gate.py hashes every plugin DLL against what the source builds now; --sync copies them. The order after a sync is: recompile, wait for the domain reload to SETTLE (not compiling, three times running), console_check, then the native re-run. A fresh recording timestamp is NOT proof of a fresh assembly: an editor whose compile fails keeps the old one and records against it happily. The lesson for a second game is the ordering: run this gate BEFORE any cross-engine diff, never after, because a stale plugin makes every later comparison one of two different games, and nothing in a diff says which side is stale.
  • G5 the slice is byte-identical across engines - cmp, exit 0, on the printed view-call slice and on the event log, and the exit code quoted; not a diff summary, not an md5 quoted in prose. A slice of 31 lines against one of 55 is a DIFFERENT GAME, not a near miss, and the entity ids give it away. An exit 2 (no such file) is the honest row: that side was never produced.
  • G6 the publish proof - before believing ANY artifact an engine produced: sha256sum every DLL in the engine's managed output; read the MVID from the #GUID heap of the CLI metadata of the model DLL there and of the one the current source just built; compare them; and compare each artifact's mtime against the DLL's. A mismatch, or an artifact OLDER than the DLL, means the engine ran a stale model and every artifact since the last publish is not proven. Reading the MVID is about 40 lines of Python, and it is the only thing that tells a fresh byte-identical run from a stale one. The reference port's gate is py ue_publish_gate.py, and the run writes its own run-manifest.txt naming the assembly it bound (by a type's assembly, not by searching for a name), written on arming so a crashed run still leaves one. The publish recipe, each part a trap met:
  • RunUAT.bat BuildUserSolution -ScriptsForProject=<uproject> -Project=<uproject> -OutputPath=<dir> ONCE PER PATH (Binaries/Managed and Binaries/Managed/net10.0), in Release. Unreal 5.7's success line is AutomationTool exiting with ExitCode=0 (Success); older notes grep for Result: Succeeded, which 5.7 does not print.
  • The proof run goes through the one launcher (ue_headless.ps1, as -game -RenderOffScreen -unattended), with the run's trigger file dropped FIRST; without it the module's startup digest does not run, and a stale logic-Unreal.txt is refused as older than the DLLs.
  • Launch from native PowerShell: UnrealSharp finds dotnet by the literal Program Files\dotnet\ on the PATH.
  • A publish does NOT need the editor closed, because UnrealSharp hot-reloads the DLLs. What must not happen while the owner's editor is open is WRITING the model's sources: a hot reload that lands mid-write fails to compile and can wedge the editor (Chapter 22).
  • Removing a reference does not remove the DLL. A runtime that probes a directory can still bind what the build no longer names; the publish gate fails if an old DLL comes back, and its selftest plants one to prove it.
  • G7 the game actually plays - enter play on the real scene, drive it to a verdict, and capture BOTH a JSON outcome and a PNG; then read the PNG. A gate that reads only the JSON cannot tell a played game from a black screen (Chapter 10 has the measured case). Its second half is easy to skip: console_check with --reset BEFORE the run and again after, and the count of new console errors (consoleNewErrors) is part of the verdict - one new error is RED, not "passed with a note". Three traps in how a result reads on disk: a JSON that exists is not a run, and ok:true is about the HTTP call, not the game (one such file said "ok":true with "turnsTaken":0: it had held a menu and never played); a run that hits a turn cap (TURN_CAP) proves the loop keeps running, not that the rules can end a game; only a real verdict row ("outcome":"DEFEAT", or a win) proves that. And a Unity run driven by a script writes to a scratch folder (deploy_record_run.py --out <scratch>), never to the default --out, which is the reference directory.

The headless UI capture trap. On Unreal, HighResShot does NOT capture UMG or Slate: a magenta rect painted at FLinearColor(1,0,1,1) over 30720 known pixels read rgb(12,4,1) in a HighResShot frame, identical to a control frame with no widget at all, while the engine's own screenshot showui captured it exactly, 30720 of 30720 pixels at rgb(255,0,255) (the reference port, 2026-09-29). Every HUD capture uses screenshot showui. Finding that before writing a HUD is the point of a probe.

What stays engine-specific, and why

The reference port's honest list, measured 2026-09-30; none of it was hidden behind a green gate. What a second game should take from each item:

  • Find a moved file's closure with the compiler, in passes. When the Unreal project stopped source-linking game files out of the Unity tree, most links turned out to be needed only by other linked files; the compiler named the rest, and they MOVED into the model byte for byte, keeping their global namespace so no Unity call site needed a using. It takes several builds: a CS0246 on one type stops the binder from naming what the next expression would have needed. The links that remain are deliberate: the measurement pair (float bits, the digest writer) compiled identically into every host, source-linked so there is ONE spelling.
  • Every platform service exercised on real data at start-up. The reference port's Unreal side runs all six on real data each time it arms and writes platform-Unreal.txt beside the run's artifacts, because a host that compiles and answers null for everything cannot be told from a game that ships no data.
  • A behaviour with no equivalent is REFUSED with its reason, not faked. The reference port's conformance oracle (conformance_diff --require Unity Unreal) records one failure - forward after a 90-degree yaw read (2.220446E-16, 1, 0) where (1, 0, 0) was expected, an axis convention, not rounding - and two skips: Unity's 32 named layers (Unreal uses collision channels and traces) and the screen size (a rendering concern out of parity scope; inventing 1920x1080 would be a fabricated value). A SKIP is an honest gap, recorded apart from a PASS.
  • The float difference is characterised, not waved through. Every differing row is pinned in logic-allowance.json to its exact bits AND to 1 ULP, so a new row, a moved value or a wider gap is still red; an allowance that said "floats differ, carry on" would be a fallback wearing a gate's clothes. RyuJIT does not contract a*b+c and .NET has no fast-math mode, while Mono's wider float intermediates are a divergence ECMA-334 permits (logic_diff.py's header holds the correction). It is latent in a game's own arithmetic, not caused by the port, and a second game meets it the moment it runs the same code on two runtimes.
  • Count the seam honestly; do not go looking for a kernel. The reference port's seam is what the interface set above lists, plus 56 distinct domain-host interfaces of its own; a single board interface and a kernel package were plans that did not land. Its HUD contract (IHudView, drawn from ShownState) is the one to copy: a second game's HUD draws from the board as shown, and does not invent a contract of its own.
  • Expect the ported-to engine to be the tidier side. The reference port's Unreal side implements all six platform services in one file plus one; its Unity side has two random sources nested privately in game files, some services only through composed domain hosts, and no JSON codec at all, because JsonUtility is still called directly. That is the normal shape of this work.
  • A logic gate's captures are greybox, and a capture manifest must be able to fail. The reference port's beat captures are conformance-harness renders (cubes and grey tiles), right for a logic gate and not to be read as the game; its Unity manifest records an md5 and a byte size per frame, while the Unreal one recorded only a label, which cannot detect the repeated frame the Unity one was built to catch. Its one Unity effect capture caught a loading screen at 0 percent instead of the effect - which is why a capture gate opens the PNG.
  • A test that re-implements the rule it tests passes when the product is wrong. The reference port's Unity-side test suite declared simulation types in 48 files, and at least fourteen of them were static classes holding a SECOND copy of a game rule; they are why a green suite is not by itself evidence about the model.
  • An instrument that answers anyway is worse than one that will not answer. Two of the reference port's instruments refuse when their input is stale - py port_holes.py exits 2 when its coverage report is older than the source it describes (a stale report once said 15 of 100 files at 18.3 percent where a fresh one said 90 of 101 at 74.1 percent: the opposite conclusion), and py port_todo.py --check exits 1 on a changed tree. Neither is a failure of the port.
  • Rendering parity was ruled out of the logic port's scope by its owner; logic parity is in. Nothing above is a rendering complaint.

Traps the model work met

Each was met on the reference port and still bites:

  • A blend mode is a NUMBER in the Unity material, never the shader name: DstBlend==1 means additive (Chapter 8).
  • A configured-but-not-running MCP server still lists its tool names. "Listed" never means "available": prove a server is up before planning around it.
  • Read every engine member from metadata, never from memory.
