UnrealLogger.Log(logName, message, verbosity) takes the CATEGORY first and the message second; both are strings, so the wrong order compiles perfectly and logs nonsense. The reference port keeps a seam map (unreal_seam_map.md) re-verified on every run, with an impossible sentinel row that must report STALE so the verdicts cannot be assumed.
  • UnrealSharp conventions the compiler is the right oracle for: [UClass] types must be partial (its source generator writes the other half), and AActor.BeginPlay is public virtual, not protected.
  • AStaticMeshActor's root is Static, and a Static component refuses every move in a game world. Set Mobility to Movable and READ IT BACK at spawn, and use the move FUNCTIONS rather than the RelativeLocation UPROPERTY, which never updates ComponentToWorld.
  • AActor.GetAttachedActors returns children REVERSED. Record the order SetParent was asked for and cross-check the count with the engine's.
  • The Unreal editor world never ticks actors outside Simulate or PIE: -run=pythonscript asserts and -ExecutePythonScript quits before the tick loop runs. A host that must tick has to be IN a world; run it headless as UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe <uproject> <Map> -game -nullrhi -unattended -nosplash.
  • A configured value says so where it is declared. The reference port's engine backend has two: FrameCount is its own tick count (Unreal exposes no frame counter to managed code) and FixedDeltaTime is Unity's 0.02 default (Unreal has no fixed timestep). Naming the provenance is the difference between a configured constant and a fabricated one.
  • A managed reference does not keep an Unreal asset alive. Unreal's garbage collector sees only what the ENGINE holds (UPROPERTYs, the root set, strong pointers); a C# field, a Dictionary cache or a plain C# property on a managed [UClass] is invisible to it. A cache of StaticLoadObject textures handed back a texture the collector was purging (it purges over several frames, and UnrealSharp zeroes the managed wrapper only at the final free, so IsValid does not save you in between): the renderer died with Texture not valid! UE-23902! and then an access violation, six minutes into a long run. Root every asset a cache keeps with UnrealSharp's TStrongObjectPtr<T>, and assert liveness on every cache hit. Make a GC bug deterministic before fixing it: -ExecCmds="gc.TimeBetweenPurgingPendingKillObjects 0.5" (a collection every half second) turned the six-minute crash into one in 32 seconds, every time; the reference port's long runs now run under that pressure, and fail if a log shows the default rate.
  • Move a rule into the model without touching a single call site. When the game's scripts live in the global namespace, C# resolves a global type before one a using imports, so a rule can be added to the model while the Unity copy still exists, the plugin synced, and only THEN the Unity copy deleted: every call site resolves to the model's copy unchanged. Two traps on the way: an alias such as using X = Rule.Nested; cannot see the file's other using lines, so spell its namespace out; and every test project that linked the old file must stop linking it in the same step.
  • A second implementation of an engine type silently wins. On the reference port a private UnityShim.cs shadowed the shim's bit-verified Mathf (UnityCompat.Core), and thousands of tests ran against the unverified copy with nothing in the build to say so. shim_dupes.py --project <path> refuses it.

The shim route, and why a new port should not take it

The reference port's shim declares Unity's value types in namespace UnityEngine (UnityCompat.Core, differentially tested against the real UnityEngine at float32 BIT equality) and an engine backend seam (UnityCompat.Engine: the IEngineBackend seam, a static facade, a LifecycleScheduler, a FakeBackend). A project's existing call sites then compile untouched; in a Unity build the real UnityEngine wins and the shim is not referenced. It is not part of this toolkit's package.

It was the right first move: it is how the reference port's Unreal side ran a game byte-identically before any adapter existed, and it remains the PARITY ORACLE during a migration (UnityCompat.Engine.Tests is 38 scenarios any backend must pass, and conformance_diff.py turns three backends into one verdict; what is left of it for that job, UnityCompat.Abstractions and UnityCompat.Conformance, declares nothing in namespace UnityEngine). But it keeps a game Unity-shaped for as long as it is load-bearing. A second game starting today writes its Core engine-free from the beginning and never grows a shim. Reach for one only to get an EXISTING Unity codebase moving before the extraction is done, and treat every day it survives after that as debt.

The shim tooling, if you need it:

  • shim_gap (a folder of the toolkit root) compiles a project's scripts against the shim and ranks what is missing. It is SUPPOSED to fail; the ranked list is the worklist, ordered by errors cleared.
  • port_surface.py sizes the Unity API surface by call sites. On the reference port Vector2 alone was 15.9 percent of call sites, the top 5 symbols 48.3 percent and the top 30 83.4 percent, so the small-interface argument is a measurement, not a preference.
  • port_oracle (a folder of the toolkit root) says which UnityEngine members are callable headlessly at all.
  • UnityCompat.Core.Diff proves the value types match the real UnityEngine bit for bit, and a wrong -p:UnityManaged= path FAILS the build rather than testing nothing.

The model's tools

The gameplay rules as an engine-free model both engines LOAD, behind a platform seam and a view seam, with the event stream as the contract: this chapter is the method, and these are the tools the reference port built around it. One command runs every gate in dependency order, healing only what is mechanically stale (an artifact older than what it was made from), each cure at most once a run with the gate re-run after it; anything else red is REAL and stops the run with its evidence:

py port_heal.py            # every gate in dependency order, healing what is only STALE; exit 0 = all green
py port_heal.py --check    # the same, healing nothing

The tools sit at the toolkit root unless the part says otherwise; "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest.

Game integration: the effect ledger

The ledger the Unreal adapter reads - effect key to built system, one row per key, joined from the three stages' own outputs (the key's verdict, its IR timing with provenance, what was built) and CHECKED against the disk, so the ledger and the assets cannot disagree - and the reference run played headless on Unreal, to prove the game fires what was built.

tool part what it does

7. Transforms, scenes, UI, audio

The conventions, in one place

u2ue/transform.py holds every transform convention the port uses; its selftest holds it to the effect converter's own functions (200 random cases) and to the reference port's game-model map, so the three cannot drift apart.

Unity Unreal
units metres centimetres
axes x right, y up, z forward x forward, y right, z up
handedness left left
position (x, y, z) (-x, z, y) x 100 - transform.position
direction (x, y, z) (-x, z, y) - transform.direction
rotation quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw) (-qx, qz, qy, qw) - transform.rotation
scale (sx, sy, sz) (sx, sz, sy) - transform.scale
Euler angles Quaternion.Euler(x, y, z) turns Z, then X, then Y, about the fixed axes (MEASURED, Unity 6000.3) -

From Python:

>>> from u2ue import transform as T
>>> T.position((1.0, 2.0, 3.0))                      # Unity metres -> Unreal centimetres
(-100.0, 300.0, 200.0)
>>> T.rotation((0.0, 0.7071068, 0.0, 0.7071068))     # Unity's 90 degrees about y (up) -> Unreal's 90 degrees about z (up)
(-0.0, 0.0, 0.7071068, 0.7071068)

How each engine composes a hierarchy

  • Unity composes a Transform chain as matrices: each level's rotation times scale applies to everything below it. A rotated child under a non-uniformly scaled parent is therefore sheared.
  • Unreal stores a component's world transform as rotation, scale and translation, and composes a child with its parent by the rule READ from the engine (Engine/Source/Runtime/Core/Private/Math/TransformVectorized.cpp:295-323): with no negative scale on either side, rotations multiply, scales multiply componentwise, and the child's offset is turned and scaled by the parent; with a negative scale, it multiplies the full matrices, normalises the axes and re-applies the signs (TransformVectorized.h:1552-1587). No shear survives either branch.

transform.compose_matrix and transform.compose_trs reproduce both; transform.shear_of and the corner errors measure the gap.

Finding the nodes Unreal cannot place: u2ue shear

py -m u2ue --project <game> shear --gltf <scene export>.gltf --json shear.json
py -m u2ue --project <game> shear --from Assets/<Scene>.unity

Every node composed both ways; for each sheared node: its axes' worst non-orthogonality, how far the corners (+-1, +-1, +-1) land apart (unitCornerCm), whether it draws, and for a drawn glTF mesh its bounds' corner error. On the reference port's first battle map: 46 sheared nodes, 2 of them drawing (a rope bridge's meshes, 63.46 and 55.89 cm at their box corners). A sheared node that draws nothing still moves its children. Whether such an error is accepted, baked into the mesh, or fixed in the Unity scene is the owner's decision, made with the number - the reference port accepted the rope bridge's and pinned the decision with a gate, so a later change that makes it worse fails.

Scenes: u2ue scene

Scope: one Unity scene, imported into Unreal as a new level. Precondition: the project file names the scene and its work folder, and the scene's own fidelity baseline exists. Minimal guarantee: a scene with no baseline is refused, never graded against another scene's numbers, and a sheared node's error is a number the owner decides on. Success guarantee: the imported level passes the scene's fidelity gate, every leg at or better than its baseline. Trigger: one of the game's scenes is to run in Unreal.

py -m u2ue --project <game> scene --dry          # the scene's paths, opened; the host's state
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene export         # REFUSED here: runs in the owner's editor, in a window - prints the trigger
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene import         # the glTF into a NEW level through Interchange (Unreal, headless)
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene readback       # the saved level read back (Unreal, headless)
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene check          # the fidelity gate against the scene's own baseline (no editor)

The project names its scene - "scene": {"unity": "Assets/<Scene>.unity", "name": "<Name>", "dir": "<scene work folder>", "content": "/Game/.../<Name>"} - and the gate grades it against that scene's own measured baseline, <scene dir>/fidelity-baseline.json (scene.dir is the scene's work folder): the counts and residuals every leg holds, and the materials and actors the scene expects by name. A scene with no baseline is refused, never graded against another scene's numbers. On the reference port's first battle map:

py -m u2ue --project <game> scene check
SCENE FIDELITY GATE - <Name>, Unity scene against the imported Unreal level
...
  PASS world AABB residual has not regressed     1037 row(s) (baseline 1037) worst centre 1.431278 / extents 1.453828
CHECKS 45, FAIL 0
VERDICT PASS

The reference port's pipeline is what the verbs wrap; between import and readback it ran further steps of its own (textures, material parents, lighting, outline hulls, effect actors) that are not verbs yet, so the gate grades the finished level:

  1. Export from Unity with glTFast (an Editor script in the game's project): meshes, materials and textures one to one; inactive subtrees skipped and listed; every value not carried named ABSENT; the terrain baked from its TerrainData (heights, the splat layers' albedo).
  2. Import into Unreal with Interchange (an editor Python script in the host).
  3. Check with scene_fidelity_gate.py: hierarchy, materials (slot by slot against the .mat), textures, lighting and placement against Unity's own files, through a headless readback of the saved level; it exits 1 the moment one moves.

A trap the pipeline taught: a scene imported through glTF arrives in a frame the pipeline chose (glTFast negates x; Unreal's importer takes glTF's y-up as z-up), so a level and a hand-placed actor need not share a frame. Measure the imported level's frame once (the reference port keeps it as one small class) and convert every hand-placed actor through it.

Prefab YAML: what a reader must handle

The effect reader (u1e_ir.py with u1e_nested.py) handles nested prefab instances with their modifications (a nested object's id is the instance's id XOR the source object's), prefab variants, legacy prefab records, m_RemovedComponents, and nested MODEL instances (left out and named). m_RemovedGameObjects (a prefab instance that deletes one of its source's objects) is refused by name today; the reader change that applies it is proven - every effect's IR identical except exactly the two files it was meant to change - and lands with the next build. Unity's YAML writes booleans as 0 and 1, so the loader keeps the words On, Off, Yes, No as strings.

UI

Unity's uGUI (Canvas, RectTransforms, layout groups, TextMeshPro) has no one-to-one Unreal counterpart: UMG and Slate lay out differently. The reference port does not rebuild its screens as a UMG tree. The Unity Canvas is captured (every RectTransform, its anchors and its components, as Unity resolved them in Play mode) and laid out in Unreal by a port of uGUI's own solver, then painted in one UUserWidget.OnPaint. OnPaint because UnrealSharp's UWidgetTree.RootWidget is read-only, so a UMG tree cannot be assembled from C#. Only panels with a view model and a binding are drawn, and each captured state is held to Unity's own pixels.

The generic part ships as the library U2ue.Ui (u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Ui): uGUI's layout, meshes, raycast and selectables, and TextMeshPro's layout, with no game reference, held to Unity's captures by its own tests:

py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test
Passed!  - Failed:     0, Passed:   398, Skipped:     9, Total:   407, Duration: 3 m 28 s - U2ue.Ui.Tests.dll (net10.0)

A planted transform defect fails 264 of them. A capture is turned into a folder Unreal reads with:

py -m u2ue --project <game> ui convert <capture dir> --screen NAME --out DIR

which locates each TextMeshPro font's TTF by the GUID its font asset recorded and refuses one whose glyph indices differ. The capture itself runs in the game's own Unity Editor in Play mode and ships as the package's Editor assembly (Appendix B). The bindings - which view model feeds which panel - stay the game's.

Scope: one game's uGUI screens, laid out in Unreal by a port of uGUI's own solver. Precondition: each screen can be reached in Play mode in the game's own editor. Minimal guarantee: a font whose glyph indices differ is refused, and a panel with no view model and binding is not drawn. Success guarantee: each captured screen is laid out in Unreal as Unity resolved it. Trigger: a screen of the game is to run in Unreal.

The UI port, in order:

  1. Capture the Canvas in the game's own Unity Editor in Play mode: every RectTransform, its anchors and its components, as Unity resolved them (the package's Editor assembly, Appendix B).
  2. Hold the library to Unity: py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test runs U2ue.Ui's tests against Unity's captures.
  3. Convert each capture into a folder Unreal reads: py -m u2ue --project <game> ui convert <capture dir> --screen NAME --out DIR.
  4. Bind each panel to its view model in the game's own host; only a panel with a view model and a binding is drawn.
  5. Paint the bound panels in one UUserWidget.OnPaint, laid out by the solver from the converted folder.

Audio

Authored clips (.wav, .ogg) import into Unreal as Sound Waves directly. Which sound plays and how loud should be a rule in the model (the reference port's is one presentation class), so both engines pick the same sound. Clips Unity generates at run time are rendered once to float PCM and played through a small C++ bridge that hands the samples to Unreal's mixer unconverted, as a 2D one-shot. Headless runs pass -DeterministicAudio so nothing reaches a device (Chapter 22). The bridge as a reusable plugin is on the roadmap.

Animation and physics

Not covered. The reference port's units are painted cards whose motion is a rule in the model; it has no Animator controllers, no Mecanim retargeting and no physics simulation, so the toolkit has no worked example and claims no tool. What a port of either needs, and what to measure in Unity first, is in Appendix B. The effects path does port one animation case: an Animator on an effect's root that drives its scale (Chapter 8).

What the UI capture measured

The working answer to "rebuild the UI the same rather than reinvent it" is a converter: CAPTURE the live uGUI subtree in Play (the reference port's Editor capture script, served on its editor bridge as /ui/capture: RectTransforms AND their resolved rects, layout components and LayoutUtility's answers, sprites with their pixels, mesh effects, selectables, and TextMeshPro's own per-glyph layout), CONVERT it (each font found by its TMP asset's source GUID and proven by identical glyph indices), and REBUILD it on Unreal by ports of uGUI's layout and mesh code and of TextMeshPro's layout, each held to the capture by tests. What that surfaced, all measured on the reference port:

  • The look is not in Image.color. uGUI's Outline draws FOUR offset copies behind the graphic, with alpha = the effect's alpha x the vertex alpha / 255, in bytes; under a translucent fill they tint the whole interior. A panel authored navy was teal on screen because of it.
  • Unity (linear colour space) blends in LINEAR space; Slate blends in GAMMA space. The same layers came out (55,147,165) in Unity and (41,99,117) on Slate. It is exact where the UI covers itself: composite the layers under each translucent graphic in linear, then solve its colour for the gamma blender (U2ue.Ui's UiMesh.SolveForGammaBlending). Glyph edges keep a residual (text about 0.85 of the ink).
  • Unity evaluates TextMeshPro's float maths in double, rounding only on a store: a float32 port missed 10 preferred sizes by exactly 0.01. The port matches at float32 bit equality once it does the same (TmpF32 in U2ue.Ui).
  • uGUI's layout is a rebuild of ROOTS in depth order, four passes each (horizontal sizes bottom-up, horizontal control top-down, then the same vertically). An Image's preferred size is its sprite's MIN size when sliced - a "shadow" child laid out as an 18 px bar is a real Unity behaviour the rebuild must reproduce.
  • HighResShot never captures UMG or Slate; screenshot showui does. A UI frame taken with the former shows the level and no UI while the log says the widget painted (Chapter 6 has the measurement).
  • Slate pixel-snaps DrawBox and DrawText vertices (there is no NoPixelSnapping through UMG's paint helpers) and puts a text baseline at the draw position + round(face height x ppem / upem) + round(descender x ppem / upem). Place glyphs ONE BY ONE at Unity's origins: a string drawn by Slate drifts (1.7 px over 12 characters), because its hinted advances are not TextMeshPro's.
  • Putting the owner's editor into Play steals focus, so a capture runs only while the editor is free (Chapter 9's window rules).

The column "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest (Chapter 20 lists them all).

The scene tools

The reference port's first battle level was ported step by step, each step a script with its own log: the glTF level import and the logical board on its tiles, the level build and its shader subgraphs, the lighting and the sky, the scene's own particle systems, the lights and the camera's aim, render parity shots, and the proof that starting a fight runs a game. Maps are DATA, not tools. u2ue scene (above) wraps the generic legs; these are the steps that are not verbs yet.

The UI part has its own README in its folder. The HUD's gate, hud_check.py, is with the model's tools in Chapter 6.

8. Effects

Shuriken particle effects are converted end to end. u2ue/GUIDE.md is the route in full, with the traps; this chapter is the shape.

The pipeline

flowchart TB
  U["Unity project: prefabs, materials, .meta"] -->|extract| IR[("IR: one JSON per effect")]
  IR -->|check| G{"selftests + field gates"}
  G -->|build| N["Niagara systems + build record"]
  N -->|read| R[("particles per frame")]
  N -->|photo| P["Unreal frames beside Unity's"]
  R -->|judge| J{"read-back checks, each with a plant"}
  J --> REP["acceptance page"]
  P -->|LOOK| REP
  REP --> M["metrics + tempo"]
step runs in tool what proves it
extract no editor u1e_ir.py over shuriken_ir.py every key an IR file or a named refusal; every path it names exists
check no editor u2ue check every tool's own selftest; every IR field read or excused with its values
build Unreal, headless u1e_build.py running build_niagara.py the build record: per key its verdict, every module written, every absent emitter with its reason
read Unreal, headless u1e_color_size_readback.py read-back checks per 1/60 s frame, each refusing its plant
photo Unreal, headless u1e_fx_photo.py, u1e_photo_sheet.py the pair sheets, LOOKED at; capture artefacts labelled, never counted
report no editor report_build.py every number from a record, with its denominator and its age

The IR

One JSON file per effect key, read off the Unity YAML. Every value carries how it was read, so a reader of the IR can tell a constant from a curve from a range, and a value that was not read from one that was zero. An excerpt (a snow emitter, from the second game):

{
 "key": "unity.prefab.4ca04dc9501451e498e3f029e625ccaf",
 "lifetimeSeconds": null,
 "naturalLengthWhy": "LOOPING emitter(s) Snow_Particles: no natural end",
 "emitters": [{
   "name": "Snow_Particles", "duration": 5, "looping": true, "simulationSpace": "World", "maxParticles": 900,
   "startLifetime": {"mode": "constant", "scalar": 2.2, "value": 2.2, "readAs": "scalar (minMaxState 0)"},
   "startSize": {"mode": "randomConstants", "scalar": 0.3, "min": 0.15, "max": 0.3,
                 "readAs": "minScalar..scalar (minMaxState 3, serializedVersion 2)"},
   "emission": {"enabled": true, "rateOverTime": {"mode": "constant", "scalar": 500, "value": 500, "readAs": "scalar (minMaxState 0)"},
                "bursts": []},
   "shape": {"enabled": true, "type": "Box", "scale": {"x": 30, "y": 1, "z": 30}, "...": "48 fields in all"}
 }]
}

lifetimeSeconds is null, not a number: a looping emitter has no natural end, and what ends a spawn of it is the game's code, so the IR says so instead of inventing a length.

The converter

vfxport/build_niagara.py writes Niagara stacks through Unreal's FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary. build_emitter is a loop over twenty stages in the order Unity's own modules run: setup, emitter state, spawning, particle spawn, shape, start speed, update, colour / size / rotation over lifetime, gravity, force, noise, velocity over lifetime, collision, renderer, flipbook, sub-emitter roles and trails, inherit velocity, and the modules not ported (named per emitter). A rule measured in Unity is re-derived from its bake at build time by its judge: a rule that stops holding stops the build instead of drawing wrongly.

What a gap is, and what it is not

An absent emitter is a GAP only when Unity draws it. The report counts apart, each by a measured or read rule, what Unity does not draw either: a sub-emitter Unity never fires, one the game never starts, one whose renderer draws nothing, one Unity measured at zero particles. On the reference port these were 348 emitters the first acceptance pages had counted as gaps.

The reverse is a gap too: an emitter the port DRAWS where Unity never does. Coverage counts it as drawn, so nothing flags it unless a probe looks. The reference port had one: a "spawner" particle living a ten-thousandth of a second, whose three Birth children Unity never fired, while the port drew them for a few frames. When a probe measures zero particles over every moment a parent could fire a child, that fact goes in a list derived from the probe record (never typed), the converter refuses the child by name, and the report counts it absent as in Unity. That is data for one effect, not a rule taken from one case.

The worst gap is a silent one

A reader that reduces a value it cannot port - a curve to its first key, two curves to one - and writes no note makes a gap the report cannot see: the emitter counts as drawn. The reference port found this class twice in one evening, the second time by auditing for it after the first:

  • an emission rate authored as a curve was built as its first key: a constant rate, or no spawn at all where the curve starts at 0 (52 emitters, not one named);
  • start size, start speed, start lifetime and gravity authored as curves read the same way (46 emitters).

The rule since: every reader of a min-max value either ports its mode or writes a SUBSTITUTED note, which the report counts as a stand-in. When one silent reader is found, audit every reader of the same kind of value before calling it fixed.

What the measurements say: a rate curve is the scalar times the curve at the LOOP's normalized time, the k-th particle born where its integral reaches k. A start size or lifetime (one curve or two) reads the curve at the END OF THE STEP that emitted the particle; a start speed reads it at the particle's own emission time inside that step. Gravity reads its curve at the emitter's normalized time on every step, and with two curves each particle keeps one fixed fraction between them. All of them run on the EMITTER's clock, which starts after its start delay and wraps when the system loops.

Which instant Niagara gives you. With interpolated spawning on (the default template's), the spawn script reads every float emitter parameter LERPED between last frame's value and this frame's by the particle's own spawn fraction: Emitter.Age read there is the particle's emission instant, not the frame's end (the engine's HLSL translator lerps everything but a short list of system constants: delta time, spawn rate, counts, seeds). So a start value Unity reads at the emission instant (speed) gets it for free, and one Unity reads at the end of the step (size, lifetime) needs the rest of the frame added back from values that are never lerped. Read the engine before you trust a parameter's name: "the emitter's age" means two different instants depending on the script that reads it.

How that was found is the lesson: the first probe recorded only each particle's age, and a size read one step late looked like a rule that held for 4 particles in 19. The second probe recorded the step each particle first appeared on, and the same data then fitted one rule exactly. When a rule fits most of the data but not all of it, record the variable you are missing before modelling around the gap.

A companion emitter needs its parent's lifecycle rule. A ribbon trail runs as its own emitter on its own loop. A sub-emitter child's emitter already lived until its parents' last trigger, but its trail's loop was timed from the system's start: the trail closed while the fired particles were still alive, and in an emitter whose time was rescaled it closed sooner still. When an emitter gains a lifecycle rule, every emitter that exists only to follow it needs the same rule.

Porting a gap: the route protocol

  1. Find the root: the report lists absent emitters by root - what porting each root would bring back.
  2. Read or measure the Unity behaviour (Chapter 9) - a judge first, its plant, then the bake.
  3. Write the route behind a VFXPORT_<NAME> switch, default off.
  4. Prove it offline: vfxport/whole_trace.py REF.py WORK.py (off: identical engine calls on every emitter; on: changes exactly the predicted set - --expect-only names it).
  5. Trial: build the affected keys with the switch on - in a content root of its own, so the trial cannot touch the accepted build - then read, judge (with the plant), photograph, LOOK.
  6. Flip with its evidence row in patch_flip_defaults.py.

A change to a tool a running build loads is written as a patch script with its proof (--prove on a copy) and applied (--land) after the build: a build that changes behaviour half way through is two builds, and neither is the one that was proven.

Materials

Unity effect materials use custom shaders. The blend mode is a NUMBER in the material (_DstBlend == 1 means additive), never the shader's name; each distinct shader family needs one hand-authored Unreal parent material, after which every material of that family is an instance with its values read off the .mat (a material variant's values come through its parent, m_Parent). Built-in shaders and materials are named off the Editor's unity_builtin_extra (set unity.editor). A family with no parent yet is refused by name.

Lit materials

A lit (URP Lit or Shader Graph) material cannot use Unreal's lighting and look the same: the BRDF, the ambient and the reflection decode differ. The toolkit evaluates URP's own lighting inside the Unreal material:

  1. The surface comes from the HLSL Unity generated for the Shader Graph (the translator u1e_sgport.py): texture samples with their tiling, keywords as scalars, Unity's frame for positions and normals. A graph that moves vertices in object space, or that includes custom HLSL, is refused by name.
  2. The lighting is URP 17's Lit, transcribed from its source (u1e_urplit.py): the metallic and specular workflows, the main light, per-pixel spherical-harmonics ambient, the reflection probe's mip and decode, emission added raw.
  3. The inputs are measured, not assumed: one window reads the scene's sun (colour, intensity, direction), its 27 ambient coefficients and its default reflection cube (every face of every mip), which are baked into the parent material.

The route is behind VFXPORT_URPLIT until its trial's photos are looked at against Unity's frames taken under the same lighting (the photo probe's lit option opens the scene and copies its sun). Named, not drawn: fog, shadows, screen-space ambient occlusion, and lighting that changes at run time.

Lights on effects

Point lights an effect prefab carries are read with the rule that turns each on (on at every play; on when a pooled instance is reused; never) and spawned on the played effect as Unreal point lights, attached so they follow it. The mapping, READ from both engines' source:

Unity (URP) Unreal
1 / d^2 x saturate(1 - (d^2 / r^2)^2)^2 inverse-squared falloff, AttenuationRadius = 100 x r (the same window)
intensity I, diffuse with no 1 / pi pi x I candelas (Unreal's Lambert divides by pi)
color.linear x I the colour's sRGB bytes, through the engine's own sRGB round trip
shadows off (the game's pool turns them off) CastShadows = false, the light made movable

The Unity side was measured on lit pixels: a probe renders each light on a lit plane, light on and off, and a judge holds the difference to URP's formula; nine cases fit at a ratio of 1.0000. The named residuals: URP's diffuse carries a 0.96 that Unreal's does not, and Unreal's distance term is 1 / (d^2 + 1 cm^2).

Beyond particles

Effect prefabs carry more than ParticleSystems. The toolkit inventories them and treats each as its own class:

what today
an Animator on the effect's root driving its scale ported
point lights ported (above)
a Timeline (PlayableDirector) starting groups at their clip times the law measured (Chapter 9); the route proven offline, landing with its trial
TrailRenderers the law measured and reproduced exactly by U2ue.Runtime.TrailLaw (72 of 72 frames, 15 of 15 meshes); the Unreal draw is next
audio sources listed

Appendix B says what lands next.

9. Measuring Unity

Unity's documentation does not state most of the rules a port has to reproduce exactly: the frame a sub-emitter's particle is born in, how a TrailRenderer drops its points, what a Timeline does to a ParticleSystem before its clip starts. A port that guesses at them looks right in a screenshot and wrong in the game. The toolkit's rule is that every value is either READ (from a file, with where it came from) or MEASURED (from Unity itself, with the run that measured it), and that a value it could do neither for is named ABSENT. It never substitutes a plausible number.

This chapter covers how a rule is measured: a probe, a judge, a bake, and a window in the owner's editor.

The parts

part what it is where
probe an Editor C# script that sets up a case in Unity, steps it, and writes every value it observed to a JSON fact file. It is triggered by a file, so nothing has to click vfxport/unity_probe/*.cs
judge a Python script that states the rule a port will rely on, and READS it off a fact file or REFUSES it with the numbers. Written and selftested before the bake vfxport/unity_probe/*_judge.py, *_check.py
fact file the bake: what Unity did, with the Unity version it ran on shared/conformance/*.json
window a short, guarded session in the owner's editor that puts a probe in, runs it, and takes it out again the worked example: _effects/lane/fin9xrl/run_window_*.sh

Write the judge first

A judge names the rule in terms a port can use ("a point is dropped once its age on Time.time passes time"), and the evidence it needs to READ it ("every removed point was still present at its last age at or below time plus one frame, and gone at its first age above it, with at least 10 removals seen"). Its --selftest builds synthetic facts that obey the rule, and planted defects that each break it one way; the judge must accept the first and refuse every plant. Only then is the probe run.

The order matters. A judge written after the bake is fitted to the bake, and passes whatever Unity happened to do. A judge written first can be wrong - then the bake refuses it, the numbers say why, and the rule is restated and re-planted. Where the judge's author does not know the answer, the judge must not assume one: the TrailRenderer judge's HOLD case reads FROZEN, DRAINED or CHANGED off the facts, and the bake answered FROZEN (a still trail neither adds nor drops a point; points expire only while it moves).

py vfxport/unity_probe/trailrend3_judge.py --selftest      # the plants bite
py vfxport/unity_probe/trailrend3_judge.py                 # the bake: exit 0 READ, 1 refused, 2 no input

When the judge refuses the bake

A refusal is information, never a reason to loosen the judge. The point-light bake is a worked example. Its first judgement refused five of ten cases:

  white_diffuse    worst 55.00 of bound  ratio ['1.3702', '1.5771', '1.9904']   FAIL
  white_specular   worst  0.51 of bound  ratio ['1.0001', '1.0001', '1.0001']   ok
  red_diffuse      worst  2.19 of bound  ratio ['1.0013', '1.0000', '1.0000']   FAIL: a sample is 2.2x its rounding bound (texel 520,272)
  ledger_4         worst  1.01 of bound  ratio ['1.0003', '1.0003', '-']        FAIL: a sample is 1.0x its rounding bound (texel 640,272)

Two different causes, each found in the facts before anything changed:

  • white_diffuse is wrong by a ratio that grows toward blue, while the same light on the next surface fits. Its OFF render was all zero, and every later OFF render held the scene's ambient: the first render after setup came out incomplete, so the ambient was read as light. The probe now throws two renders away first, and the judge refuses a case whose OFF render disagrees with its surface's other OFF renders - by name, as an incomplete render, not as a measurement.
  • Every other failing sample sits on row 272, where the game camera's full-screen pass computes floor(272.5 / 720 x 330.275) = floor(125.0003): on an exact block edge the GPU's float can land either side. The judge now accepts either block on an edge, and counts how many samples it did that for.

Re-judged: nine cases at a ratio of 1.0000 with every sample inside its rounding bound, and white_diffuse refused by name until a clean re-bake. Both fixes went into the judge's selftest as plants. The first version of the consistency check passed its plant and then, on the real bake, refused every case: pooled against everything, one black render made every other case look inconsistent too. The plant was too weak - it only asked that the bad case fail - so it now requires the bad case to be refused alone, and the check compares each case with the per-texel median of its surface's OFF renders.

The window protocol

Scope: one Unity behaviour, measured in the owner's own editor. Precondition: a probe and its judge are written, and a window spec names the probe, its inputs and its outputs. Minimal guarantee: the owner's editor is left as it was - every record and guard file md5-held, the probes removed, nothing replaced. Success guarantee: the fact file is written with the Unity version it was measured on. Trigger: a rule the conversion needs is not measured.

The probe runs in the game owner's own editor, which is in use. A window is built so it cannot cost the owner anything:

  1. Idle gate. Start only after 600 s with no cursor movement and no key or button (wait_quiet.ps1); a launcher whose wait was killed does not start.
  2. Presence watch. A watcher writes one line the moment the owner returns; every later step checks it and stops.
  3. The editor lock. One file (.opus-tools/.locks/unity-editor.lock) names who holds the editor; a window refuses to start while anyone else holds it.
  4. Compile headless first. The probe is type-checked against the project's editor assemblies (typecheck.py --editor --extra) before it is dropped in. A probe that does not compile never enters the project.
  5. Nothing is replaced. A window refuses to start when its fact file or trigger already exists, and records the md5 of every existing fact file before and after: a bake that touched another rule's evidence is visible.
  6. Wait for the real compile. The editor assembly's timestamp must change and isCompiling read false; the probe's name must be in the rebuilt DLL.
  7. Trigger, wait, collect. A trigger file starts the probe; the window waits for the fact file with a timeout.
  8. Play mode only when it must. One short Play, entered and left by the window, with isPlaying checked inside the probe (edit mode never ages a TrailRenderer, so that law needed Play).
  9. Take it out. The probe and its .meta are deleted and the editor recompiles until no trace of its name is left in the DLL.
  10. Read the console. console_check.py --reset before, console_check.py after: new errors stop the work.

A window never answers a dialog it did not open.

The owner comes back. At any step the window leaves Play first, then takes the probes out (step 9); nothing else runs. Branches from step 2.

All of this is one runner, and a window is a data file - the probes, the inputs copied in, the trigger and the outputs expected, never a script cloned from the last window:

py -m u2ue --project <game> window check <spec.json>    # every refusal judged now; nothing touched
py -m u2ue --project <game> window run <spec.json>      # waits for the quiet, then runs steps 1-7 and 9-10 above

{"label": "x6", "probes": ["EffectPhotoProbe"],
 "inputs": [{"from": "<lane>/x6/effect-photo-list-x6.tsv", "to": "effect-photo-list-x6.tsv"}],
 "trigger": {"file": ".RUN_EFFECT_PHOTO", "lines": ["list:effect-photo-list-x6.tsv", "record:effect-photo-unity-x6.json"]},
 "outputs": ["effect-photo-unity-x6.json"], "wait_seconds": 900}

The project names the Editor folder a probe is dropped into (unity.probe_dir) and the files whose md5 must hold (unity.guard). A probe places a real prefab only through ProbeSpawn (the game's own spawn composition, or the prefab as authored, named), which the runner drops in with it; probe_spawn_gate.py refuses a probe that instantiates one itself. The runner's selftest drives the whole flow against a simulated editor - including the owner returning after the compile - and every one of its safety lines is killed by a mutant when removed. (Play mode, step 8, is not in the runner yet: a probe that needs it still has its own script.)

From a bake to the build

A measured rule is not copied into the converter as a constant. At build time the converter re-derives it from the bake through the same judge (for example, the sub-emitter frame rule through vfxport/subframe_rule.py), so a rule that stops holding stops the build instead of drawing wrongly. u2ue check --only facts lists every bake with the Unity version it was measured on, against the project's unity.version:

py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only facts
  163 measured Unity bakes; this project is Unity 2021.3.21f1
       163 measured on Unity 6000.3.16f1    UNVERIFIED for Unity 2021.3 - re-measure where it matters
  163 of 163 rules this project's build uses were measured on another Unity: its report must not call them measured for it

A rule measured on another Unity is still used (the build runs), but the report must not call it measured for that project. Whether to re-measure is the owner's decision; the probes and judges are the means.

The laws measured so far

Every row is in shared/conformance with its judge. A selection, to show the kind of thing that has to be measured:

law what Unity does judge
sub-emitter frame the frame a sub-emitter's particle is born in and the position it inherits vfxport/subframe_rule.py, sub_frame_rule_check.py
node shear the order a turning mesh or billboard particle's rotation and a non-uniform node scale are applied nodeshear_rule_check.py, nodeshear2_rule_check.py
shape scale what the Shape module's own scale does to a particle's birth point and direction shape_scale_judge.py
non-uniform motion a local particle moves unscaled and is drawn through the node's whole transform, scale included nonuniform_motion_judge.py, nonuniform_world_judge.py
ring buffer past its lifetime a ring-buffered particle lives on, its age held, until it is replaced ringbuffer_check.py
mesh alignment a mesh particle's drawn frame under each render alignment, and the frame a view-aligned rotation turns in meshalign_judge.py, alignview_judge.py, alignspin_judge.py
TrailRenderer width, colour and U run on the distance fraction from a head vertex at the transform; on a moving frame the oldest point is dropped while the NEXT point's age exceeds time, then a point is added; a still trail freezes; the tail is drawn at the position time ago, clamped to the oldest segment trailrend_judge.py, trailrend2_judge.py, trailrend3_judge.py; the whole law replayed by U2ue.Runtime.TrailLaw's test (72 / 72 frames, 15 / 15 meshes)
Timeline control a controlled object is off before its clip, simulated at the clip's time less its start delay, off after timeline_judge.py
point light a URP point light's term on a lit surface is URP's formula exactly (the 0.96 diffuse, the sRGB decode, the range window), through the game camera's full-screen pass lights_judge.py (nine cases at a ratio of 1.0000)

Quaternion.Euler turns Z, then X, then Y, about the fixed axes u2ue/transform.py selftest

Writing a new probe

  1. Copy the nearest probe in vfxport/unity_probe/. Keep its shape: an [InitializeOnLoadMethod] that hooks EditorApplication.update to poll for its trigger file, one fact file out, and an error field in that file rather than an exception.
  2. Record what you will judge, not what is convenient: every frame's raw positions rather than a summary.
  3. Write the judge and its plants; run --selftest.
  4. Run the window. Commit the fact file, the probe, the judge and the window script together.
  5. Make the converter re-derive the rule from the bake, and register the judge's selftest (Chapter 12).

The measurement tools

Two kinds of measurement feed the converter: what Unity ACTUALLY draws, baked by probes inside the owner's editor only while the owner is idle, read into fact files under shared/conformance; and what Niagara actually does with a module input, measured in headless Unreal. Every converter rule cites one of them. "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest.

The window plumbing. Before the runner existed, each window was a pair of shell scripts in the lane - the reference port's window_1013ns4.sh and its launcher run_window_1013ns4.sh are kept as the last of them - which waited for ten minutes of quiet and then put the probe in, triggered it, collected the bake, took the probe out and read the console. u2ue window run <spec.json> (above) is the same flow as one runner over a data file; the two wait gates it uses are:

tool part what it does
wait_quiet.ps1 lane waits until nobody has touched the mouse or keyboard for the quiet period: the cursor has not moved and no key or button went down
wait_presence.ps1 lane waits until someone touches the machine - the cursor moves, or a key or button goes down. The Windows idle timer (GetLastInputInfo) cannot answer this where injected input resets it constantly, so the gate polls the cursor position and the key states itself

The Unity-side judges (in vfxport/unity_probe/, beside their probes), each reading a bake:

tool what it reads off its bake check

cube_facts_check.py which texel Unity samples along a direction, on a cube texture -
shapes4_facts_check.py where real emitters' shapes put their particles, and with what velocity, as Unity emits them -
nodeshear_rule_check.py the ORDER Unity applies a turning mesh or billboard particle's rotation and a non-uniform node scale in -
nodeshear2_rule_check.py the second node-shear bakes, holding the rule on more cases yes
viewshear_rule_check.py the view-aligned shear rule, against measured quads -
trailscale_check.py a trail's WIDTH under a uniform Hierarchy node scale: whether the node scale reaches the width yes
sub_frame_rule_check.py a Birth or Death sub-emitter child's emission frame, against every measured case yes
shape_scale_judge.py particle by particle, what Unity does with the Shape module's own scale yes
force_scale_judge.py which rule a force, or a World-space velocity over lifetime, on a LOCAL system follows under scale -
wstretch50_judge.py a World stretched billboard and a Local-scaling child under a scaled root -

The Unreal-side probes - what Niagara does, read before the converter relies on it:

tool part what it measures check
v4_module_inputs.py scene_tools a Niagara module's own input names, types and DEFAULT values, READ off the engine yes
v4_probe2.py scene_tools which write route a colour curve takes -
