A second game supplies nothing here: the probes measure the ENGINES. It re-runs only the windows for features its effects use that the reference port's did not, and the bakes record the Unity version they ran on (above).

10. Verification and gates

A port is only as good as what checks it. This chapter is the toolkit's rules for checking, and the gates that apply them.

Four rules

  1. Read or absent, nothing else. Every value is READ (from a file, with where it came from), MEASURED (Chapter 9), or named ABSENT with the reason. A tool that cannot read a value stops and names it. It does not substitute a default and carry on: a build that silently drops a value is worse than one that fails, because the failure is invisible and later reasoning builds on it.
  2. A gate must be able to fail. Every gate carries planted defects (its --selftest) and must refuse each. A gate that has only ever passed cannot be told apart from one that is switched off. When a gate's scope is widened, its plants are run again.
  3. Verify with both. Numbers and pictures each lie in their own way. On the reference port a render where the whole scene went black scored better on a pixel metric, because dark geometry stopped hiding a bright backdrop. The data must prove itself first; then the metric and the image confirm it. Neither one diagnoses on its own.
  4. A miss is unknown. The toolkit's code readers are lexical. A call through an interface, a delegate, reflection or a UnityEvent is invisible to them, so "no caller found" means unknown, never unused.

The gates

gate what it refuses run by
every tool's own selftest the tool's planted defects u2ue check --only selftests
vfxport/yaml_field_gate.py a Unity field, in a module this project enables, that the reader neither reads nor excuses with the values it may take u2ue check --only gates
vfxport/ir_field_gate.py an IR field the converter neither uses nor lists in DELIBERATELY_UNREAD with its reason u2ue check --only gates
the measured rules' versions a rule measured on another Unity, reported as measured (it is named UNVERIFIED) u2ue check --only facts
layer_gate.py, host_gate.py an engine reference in the model; a platform member outside the hosting folder u2ue check --only model
vfxport/converter_trace_gate.py a converter change that alters what an existing route writes (every engine call recorded against a stub unreal, working copy against a commit) by hand, before a converter change lands
vfxport/whole_trace.py a new route that changes more, or less, than the emitters it names by hand, per route (Chapter 8)
v4_msg_gate.py a write the engine refused: Niagara's SetParameter logs an unknown name or a wrong type as an error and returns false, and the message is saved inside the package per trial, over the built packages
the read-back judges a built system whose particles, per 1/60 s frame, do not match the rule they were built from u2ue read
u2ue parity a model row that differs between runtimes beyond its characterised allowance Chapter 6
scene_fidelity_gate.py a moved hierarchy, material, texture, light or placement in an imported level Chapter 7
u2ue/manual/build.py --check a manual whose generated blocks no longer match the code before a release

Proving a route offline

The converter writes through Unreal's Python API, so a route can be proved without an engine: run the converter against a recording stub, once at a reference commit and once with the change, and compare every call.

py vfxport/whole_trace.py REF.py WORK.py                  # switch off: identical calls on every emitter
py vfxport/whole_trace.py REF.py WORK.py --expect-only K  # switch on: exactly the predicted emitters change

This is what lets a route land behind a switch while other builds are running: it is proved to change nothing until it is turned on.

Conformance over every key, data first

Scope: every effect key of a project at once, Unity's particle state against what the built Niagara systems compute. Precondition: the keys are built in Unreal, and the owner allows a Unity window. Minimal guarantee: an emitter one side does not have is named UNPAIRED, never dropped. Success guarantee: every emitter OK, or its verdict named with its numbers. Trigger: a build is to be held to Unity on numbers before its photos are looked at.

Photos compare one draw at a time. This compares every emitter of every key on numbers, in one pass:

  1. Write the cases: py -m u2ue --project <game> conform cases --name <run> writes, from the project's IR, one probe case per key (its prefab placed by the game's own spawn, the seed pinned, read from a restart at each time), the Unity window that runs them, and the Unreal read of the same keys.
  2. Read Unity: py -m u2ue --project <game> window run <run window spec> runs the one generic probe in the owner's idle editor (Chapter 9).
  3. Read Unreal: py -m u2ue --project <game> trial run <run read spec> reads the keys' built systems at the probe's own step, 0.02 s, with no new build.
  4. Compare: py -m u2ue --project <game> conform diff --unity <record> --unreal <record> --report <file> pairs each emitter by its system's file id and reads BOTH sides at Unity's sample times only - the Unreal read has every frame, Unity only its few samples, and a particle born and gone between two samples is otherwise counted against the port. A first birth is compared by the frame it is first drawn on, Unity's ages are put in real time by the emitter's simulation speed (the converter rescales each emitter to real time), and each emitter reads OK, LATE or EARLY, COUNT, BIRTH UNREAD (no age can be read: an infinite lifetime), UNPAIRED, or NO DATA. The report is stamped with the judge's own id.
  5. Keep the score: py -m u2ue --project <game> conform latest reads the newest stamped report of the run the project names in conform.standing_run, and refuses one that another judge made - re-run the diff. The cycle trends its share of OK emitters, so a converter change that loses some goes red; a denser run is another measurement, made the score only by changing that field.
  6. Name each miss: py -m u2ue --project <game> conform classes --report <file> names a LATE, EARLY or COUNT row only when the converter's own build note on that emitter, joined by file id, or a measured signature agrees with it in direction AND size; every other row is listed as the work, never passed. A class names the WHOLE row: the judge records every sample of a COUNT row, and a class reads them all, never the first difference alone. Some misses are the probe's own: Unity's emission covers the half-open step, so a burst due exactly on a sample time is drawn one step later than the port draws it. The reference port measured that on every such sample of two runs before naming it, and it is a capture artefact, never a game frame. A particle at its exact end on a sample is the same instant from the other side, and is named only when each side's own particles say so (Unity's remaining lifetime, the port's age, both at the end). A probe can be blind. The reference port's case probe, restarting the simulation for each sample, never drew a sub-emitter of a sub-emitter (0 of 284). Stepped at its 0.02 s default it still drew none of some; stepped at the game's own frame step (1/60 s) it drew every one, its counts matching the port's - and stepping uncovered others the PORT does not draw, which the restart read had hidden as no data at all. A class built on a probe's silence is checked against a second way of looking, and the probe steps the way the game steps, before anyone calls the port right or wrong.
  7. Follow the class, not the key. A verdict a whole class of emitters shares is one rule to measure or one route to fix: the reference port's first such read found every non-prewarmed burst born one warm-up tick late, 121 of 121. Its first read of every key also found the judge's own faults before the port's - a first birth taken from every Unreal frame against four Unity samples, and infinite lifetimes passing as OK because an undefined age compared as no difference. Make the judge prove itself with plants before believing what it says about the port.

Looking at the result

Photos are checked by eye, and the toolkit makes that part of the process instead of a courtesy:

  • u2ue photo renders Unreal frames at Unity's sample times; u1e_photo_sheet.py lays each effect's Unity and Unreal frames side by side.
  • A sheet is LOOKED at before a route is called done. A frame where the capture itself failed (a black frame, a missing texture stream) is labelled as a capture artefact and never counted for or against the port.
  • A screenshot route returning ok proves bytes were written. Open the file.

When a gate goes red

  • Check that the thing moved before believing it broke. A port moves code on purpose. The reference port lost hours to gates that walked one folder and reported as ABSENT a symbol that had moved into the model; each was fixed by widening the gate to follow the move, and then re-running its plants.
  • Never re-record a baseline to make a red gate green. A baseline is re-recorded only when the change it records is intended, with the reason committed beside it.
  • Re-run before investigating a test that another worker changed minutes ago. It may already be fixed.

11. Metrics and reports

Every number the toolkit prints is computed from a record on disk, with its denominator and its definition. A number it cannot compute is printed ABSENT with the record it needs. An input older than the newest build is marked STALE, because it describes builds that no longer exist.

The acceptance page: u2ue report

py -m u2ue --project <name> report [--out FILE]

One HTML page per project, built from that project's records: the IR summary, every key's build verdict, the read-back sweep, the photo sheets, the gap roots, and the decisions only the owner can make, each with its evidence. It reads what is there: a key never built reads "never built", and a pass not yet run reads absent. A project's first report, before any build, already lists every key it will have to account for.

The numbers: u2ue metrics

py -m u2ue --project <name> metrics [--json FILE]
number definition
keys the project's effect keys (its IR summary), each with the verdict of the record the page chose for it
drawn an emitter whose build log carries modules: it draws in Unreal
absent, as Unity absent exactly as in Unity, each by a measured or read rule: the game never starts it, Unity never fires it, Unity draws or emits nothing there itself, or Unity has no particle to draw it on
absent, gap every other absent emitter: Unity draws it and Unreal does not. Charged to its root (an absent parent's children to the ancestor absent for its own reason), so a root's count is what porting it brings back
coverage drawn / (drawn + gap): of the emitters Unity draws, the share Unreal draws
measured drawn emitters with no SUBSTITUTED note: drawn by a rule measured against Unity, not a named stand-in
data the read-back sweep: per check, emitters checked and failures, summed
image the photo screen: pairs compared, pairs flagged, and of those how many are labelled capture artefacts
machine the chosen records' own build seconds per key, summed and as a median
routes the converter's switches flipped default ON with their evidence, and those deliberately OFF with what each waits on

The emitter numbers are the acceptance page's, never recounted by the metrics verb. The first draft of the verb recounted them itself and printed a figure that was wrong in both directions. It was caught before anyone quoted it, which is why the definitions are part of the claim: a number quoted without its definition is not one.

The reference port on 2026-10-15 at 13:56, with its acceptance rebuild still running (so data reads STALE and image ABSENT):

keys      674: BUILT 673, IR REFUSED 1; 673 drawn, 197 of them with a named gap; 548 from the acceptance rebuild
emitters  drawn 7810 | absent: gap 642 (Unity draws them, Unreal does not), 374 absent exactly as in Unity
coverage  92.4 % of the emitters Unity draws are drawn in Unreal (7810 / 8452)
measured  86.3 % of the drawn emitters carry no stand-in (6737 of 7810; 1073 drawn with a named SUBSTITUTED note)
machine   31.8 h of build time over 673 keys, median 98 s a key
data      STALE (older than the newest build) - 20378 emitter-checks over 22 checks, 17 FAIL (99.92 % hold)
image     ABSENT: no sheets listing - the photo pass has not run

Porting speed: u2ue tempo

py -m u2ue --project <name> tempo [--json FILE] [--since YYYY-MM-DD]

How long each converter route took from its first line of code to its verified flip, read off git. A route is one switch; first code is the earliest commit whose added lines carry the switch's name; flipped is the earliest commit in which every file that reads it reads it default ON. The reference port, 2026-10-15: 86 routes, median 36.2 h. Routes flipped alone or with fewer than five others took a median of 2.4 h; the 53 flipped together in batch releases took 41.6 h, and that wait was the release's, not the route's.

py -m u2ue --project <game> tempo
u2ue tempo - the toolkit's verified routes, first code -> verified flip, from git (definitions: u2ue/verbs/tempo.py)
  VFXPORT_AMESH                  first code 2026-10-10T17:41 (c369e881)  flipped 2026-10-12T13:47 (70ee5858)     44.1 h
  VFXPORT_BILLMESH               first code 2026-10-10T17:45 (e9e0addb)  flipped 2026-10-12T13:47 (70ee5858)     44.0 h
  ...
  VFXPORT_BUILTINMIPS            first code 2026-10-14T11:30 (83a9ce50)  flipped 2026-10-14T17:30 (74aa80ed)      6.0 h
  86 routes: first code -> flipped, median 36.2 h (quartiles 2.9 / 44.0 h); flipped per day: 2026-10-12 50, 2026-10-13 22, 2026-10-14 14
    flipped alone or with fewer than 5 others: 33 routes, median 2.4 h
    flipped in a batch release (one commit flipping 5+ routes): 53 routes, median 41.6 h - the wait is the release's
  1 switches carry no OFF stage on record (first code already reads them default ON): VFXPORT_CULLFRONT
  NOT FLIPPED / ABSENT VFXPORT_FX35_ORBIT: vfxport/build_niagara.py (reads it default OFF today)

Routes are the toolkit's, so tempo reads the same git history for every project; a switch with an evidence row that still reads OFF is listed, never counted as flipped.

What tempo does not measure, so that it is never implied: the time from finding a defect to its first code, the agent's tokens, and the machine's build hours (those are metrics).

Reading the numbers honestly

  • Quote a number with its denominator and its date. "92.4 % coverage" means 7810 of the 8452 emitters Unity draws, on 2026-10-15.
  • Coverage is not fidelity. An emitter that draws can still draw wrongly; measured, data and image are the numbers that speak to fidelity, and image needs the photos to have been looked at.
  • A gap is a named, owned item, not a failure to hide. The report lists every gap root with the reason the converter gave.
  • A check that ends without a result is UNCOUNTED, never clean. u2ue metrics and the check sweep list such runs apart; on the reference port a crash once went into the sum as zero failures and hid a real one.

What the numbers do not measure yet

"Percent identical" is never one number. It is a family of four, each answering its own question: coverage (does it draw), measured (is it drawn by a measured rule), data (do its particles follow Unity's numbers), image (do the frames agree, capture artefacts excluded and counted). One combined "identical" figure would hide which of the four moved.

Not measured yet, and how it will be:

  • Porting speed on a fresh game. The second game's run, timed from extract to its first report and on to each coverage milestone, with the agent's own wall-clock and token count beside the machine hours. u2ue tempo times routes, not a game, and py -m u2ue --project <name> metrics [--json FILE] sums build hours, not a porter's.
  • What a fix is worth before it is made. The report charges every gap to its root, and the roots are a LONG TAIL. On the reference port on 2026-10-14 (u2ue/PACKAGE.md, mid-rebuild), the biggest root brought back 32 emitters (a non-uniform scale on an enabled shape, over 21 keys), and the next ones 18, 17, 16 and 14: there was no single lever. The same day 368 more absent emitters were absent EXACTLY as in Unity, each by a measured or read rule - Unity never fires it (261), the game never starts it (72), Unity draws or emits nothing there itself (31), a missing material Unity has no particle for (4).

How the definitions were earned: three drafts of the coverage figure were wrong before the one quoted, and each was caught before it was quoted - 99.4 % (a stand-in's "draws nothing" read as Unity's), then 91.3 % and 91.8 % (the verb recounted the records itself, counted skipped logs as drawn, and missed the measured sub-emitter chain rule). Since then the metrics verb takes the acceptance page's own numbers and never recounts.

Read-back and checks: the tools

What a BUILT system really holds - renderers, module inputs, the particles of a simulated frame, mesh properties - read back and held to the IR's prediction, emitter by emitter. Every check names what it could not judge, and every check has a PLANT that must make it FAIL. A plant that depends on a read (--plant on the read-back checks) needs that trial's OWN read pair, never an older one: a check once paired with the newest build FAILED for that reason alone. "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest.

tool part what it does check
u1e_niagara_readback.ps1, u1e_niagara_readback.py effects_tools a built system's particles read back through the engine's simulation cache -
u1e_niagara_readback_check.py effects_tools a built system's per-particle dynamic material parameters, read back and held to the IR -
u1e_color_size_readback.py effects_tools every built system's particles per 1/60 s frame - does it draw Unity's MEASURED start colour and size rules (what u2ue read runs) -
fx17_readback.ps1 effects_tools the read-back of every built system, in parts of about 60 systems -
fx18_parts.py effects_tools the read-back part lists for a whole rebuild, made from the build records themselves -
u1e_meshprops_read.py effects_tools what a built system's mesh renderers hold -
fx17_checks.py effects_tools every read-back check over every read-back part yes
u1e_color_size_check.py effects_tools the colour and size read-back held to Unity's measured rules -
u1e_fin9f_check.py effects_tools before an hour-long build, every NEW engine write that build depends on, each checked first -
u1e_flip_check.py effects_tools every built sprite flip held to Unity's measured rule -
u1e_flipbook_check.py effects_tools every built flipbook emitter's frame held to the measured rule -
u1e_fx37v_check.py effects_tools every built emitter whose build note names one route, read back and held to Unity's rule for it - the pattern every per-route check below follows yes
u1e_mirror_check.py effects_tools every mesh emitter the build drew mirrored plant per trial
u1e_nodeshear_check.py effects_tools every emitter built with the node-shear route plant per trial
u1e_stretchshear_check.py effects_tools every emitter built with the stretched-billboard shear route plant per trial
u1e_viewshear_check.py effects_tools every emitter built with the view-shear route plant per trial
u1e_vmeshnu_check.py effects_tools every mesh emitter drawn with the non-uniform node route plant per trial
u1e_subemit_check.py effects_tools every built sub-emitter child held to Unity's measured rule -
u1e_survivor_child_check.py effects_tools every Collision sub-emitter child of a SURVIVING parent plant per trial
u1e_trail_check.py effects_tools the ported trails held to Unity's measured trail rules plant per trial
u1e_simulates_check.py effects_tools does every built system actually SIMULATE in its read-back yes
v4_msg_gate.py scene_tools the converter's OWN failures read off the SAVED package (Chapter 10) yes
v4_write_gate.py scene_tools every name the converter writes, checked against the module's own input table yes
niagara_read.py scene_tools the renderer and module-input state of a SAVED Niagara system -

v4_write_gate.py is the example of a static check that knows its own reach: it can type only the writes its table covers (92 of the converter's 383 on 2026-10-13, u2ue/README.md), so its selftest passes while the gate itself exits 1 for that coverage. The authority it defers to is v4_msg_gate.py, which reads what the engine actually refused. A second game supplies nothing here beyond its build records.

Photos and contact sheets: the tools

A frame of each built effect beside Unity's, one contact sheet per effect, and a screen for the pairs that differ most - the image half of "verify with both" (Chapter 10), because a metric alone has lied.

tool part what it does
u1e_fx_photo.py effects_tools a FRAME of a built effect without the game: the system spawned alone and drawn at each time (what u2ue photo runs)
u1e_photo_sheet.py effects_tools one contact sheet per effect: Unity's frame (from the photo probe) above Unreal's
u1e_sheet_screen.py effects_tools which photo pairs differ BIG: a screen that says where to LOOK first, never a verdict

A second game supplies its camera framing for a photo.

The acceptance report: the tools

The acceptance sentence is the owner's, and the reference port's was: every effect the game fires draws in the Unreal build as Unity draws it, and every gap is named. One report holds it: per key the verdict, the named gaps, which absences Unity shares (never fires, draws nothing itself), and the decisions only the owner can make.

tool part what it does check
report_build.py lane the acceptance page from the records (what u2ue report runs) -
u1e_gap_census.py effects_tools every NAMED gap in the effect build, from the build records themselves -
u1e_never_fires.py effects_tools every IR emitter Unity NEVER spawns a particle of, by the measured sub-emitter chain rule yes

A second game supplies its own acceptance sentence.

12. Extending the toolkit

The toolkit grows in six ways, and a tool written before the project file existed is converted a seventh. Each has one place to edit and one check that proves the addition works, and each section ends in its recipe, in order.

A game adapter

Scope: one game-specific answer the default adapter gets wrong. Precondition: a project file that info opens. Minimal guarantee: a question the adapter does not override keeps Unity's own answer. Success guarantee: info names the adapter it loaded, and extract holds the key list to the adapter's spawn rules. Trigger: a default answer is wrong for the game.

Most games need none. The default adapter, unity_project, answers the three game-specific questions with Unity's own rules:

question the default answer
effect_keys(p, env, resolve) - which prefabs are the game's effects every prefab under effects.key_source.roots holding a ParticleSystem
spawn_rules - what starts when the game spawns an effect "unity": the play-on-awake systems and their sub-emitters
host_busy(p) - why the Unreal host is not free any Unreal editor process running (one headless Unreal at a time) 
# u2ue/adapters/mygame.py - discovered by name; no edit to the core
from . import UnityProject

class MyGame(UnityProject):
    name = "mygame"
    def effect_keys(self, p, env, resolve):
        ...   # write {"keys": [...]} to `resolve`; return 0, or non-zero with the reason printed

ADAPTER = MyGame
  1. Find the question. Read the default answers above against the game; an adapter overrides only a question whose default answer is wrong for it.
  2. Write the adapter. u2ue/adapters/<game>.py: a subclass of UnityProject that overrides that question alone, and ADAPTER = <the class>. It is discovered by name; nothing in the core is edited.
  3. Name it. Set "adapter": "<game>" in the project file.
  4. See it load. py -m u2ue --project <name> info names the adapter it loaded.
  5. See it hold. py -m u2ue --project <name> extract refuses a key list that contradicts the adapter's spawn_rules (keys read with Unity's rule carry a unity. prefix).

The reference port's adapter is the worked example: its keys are the effects its battles actually fire, resolved the way the game's own code resolves them, and its host is busy while its own build queues run.

A verb

Scope: one command of the facade. Precondition: the work it runs exists as a module or a tool on disk. Minimal guarantee: a verb that wraps a tool which is not on disk stops, by name; it never skips. Success guarantee: the command line, find and Chapter 19 all show the verb, from its one registry row. Trigger: a step of a port has no command.

  1. Write the module. u2ue/verbs/<name>.py: a docstring, which becomes the verb's page in Chapter 19, and run(p, argv), where p is the project, or None for a verb that needs none.
  2. Register it. One row in VERBS in u2ue/verbs/__init__.py, in the order a port runs the verbs. The command line, the verb list, find and this manual all read that registry; a verb added anywhere else is invisible.
  3. Find it. py -m u2ue find <name> lists it under verb, with the file it lives in.
  4. Rebuild the manual. py u2ue/manual/build.py writes its page into Chapter 19; py u2ue/manual/build.py --check exits 1 until it has.

A verb that wraps a tool runs it as a subprocess through u2ue.tools with the project's U2UE_* environment, below normal priority, and stops when the tool is not on disk. It never skips silently.

A converter route

Scope: one Unity behaviour the converter did not port before (Chapter 8). Precondition: the behaviour is measured or read. Minimal guarantee: until the route is flipped, it changes no call the converter makes. Success guarantee: the route is on by default, with its evidence in the flip table. Trigger: the acceptance page names a gap no route ports.

  1. Measure or read the behaviour (Chapter 9).
  2. Write the route behind VFXPORT_<NAME>, read default OFF.
  3. Prove it offline with whole_trace.py: off, identical calls everywhere; on, exactly the predicted emitters change.
  4. Trial it: build, read, judge, photograph and LOOK.
  5. Flip it: one row in vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py's table with its evidence. u2ue tempo and u2ue metrics read that table.

A material family

Scope: one Unity shader and every material that uses it. Precondition: the shader's .shadergraph can be read. Minimal guarantee: every surface the shader exposes is accounted for; none is dropped silently. Success guarantee: every material of the family is an instance of one authored parent, its values read from its .mat. Trigger: an effect material's shader has no Unreal parent.

Unity effect materials use custom shaders, so each distinct shader needs one Unreal parent material, authored once:

  1. Author the parent by a script, never by hand (the reference port's vm1_author.py, for its largest family, a vendor's uber shader graph).
  2. Account for every surface. vm1_account.py reads every property, keyword and node the shader graph exposes from the .shadergraph file, never typed, and marks each APPLIED, INERT with the arithmetic that makes it inert, or ABSENT with the reason. The count of unaccounted surfaces must be 0.
  3. Instance it. Every material of the family becomes an instance of the parent, with its values read from its .mat.

A measured rule

Scope: one rule the converter uses, measured in Unity. Precondition: the rule cannot be read from Unity's data or its source. Minimal guarantee: a bake the judge cannot read the rule from is refused, with its numbers. Success guarantee: the converter re-derives the rule from the fact file at every build. Trigger: the converter needs a rule Unity's files do not state.

  1. Write the judge first, with planted wrong answers it must refuse (Chapter 9).
  2. Write the probe: an Editor script that bakes the behaviour, placing a real prefab only through ProbeSpawn.
  3. Run it in a window: py -m u2ue --project <name> window run <spec.json> waits for the owner's idle editor.
  4. Keep the fact file the judge reads off the bake, with the Unity version it was measured on.
  5. Re-derive it at build time. The converter reads the rule from the fact file when it builds, so the build stops if the rule stops holding.

A selftest

Scope: one tool that can be wrong. Precondition: the tool runs offline, or the reason it cannot is measured. Minimal guarantee: a tool whose selftest cannot run offline is listed with that reason, never skipped silently. Success guarantee: u2ue check runs the selftest and Chapter 20 lists it. Trigger: a tool that can be wrong is written.

  1. Plant the defects. The tool carries --selftest with planted defects, and must refuse each one.
  2. Register it in u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.py (RUNS: the tool, its folder, its exact command). A tool whose selftest cannot run offline goes in NOT_RUN with the measured reason.
  3. Run it with the rest. py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only selftests runs it.
  4. See it listed. py u2ue/manual/build.py writes it into Chapter 20's selftest list.

Where the toolkit's parts live

u2ue/tools.py names each part's folder once (PARTS). Setting U2UE_TOOLKIT_ROOT=<root> resolves every part to <root>/<part>, which is the layout of the release package. A tool never names another part's absolute path; it asks tools.part(name).

Where a tool finds the project

A tool reads the project only through u2ue/env.py. need("U2UE_<NAME>") returns the project's value, or REFUSES by name when it is not set: there is no default, because a default is some other game's folder. part(name) gives the toolkit's own folders. The facade exports the project's values to every tool it runs (Project.env(): the project's folders as U2UE_*, the toolkit's as U2UE_PART_*), and u2ue check hands them to every selftest. To run one tool by hand, run it through the facade:

py -m u2ue --project <name> tool <file> [its own options]

A tool kept in another tree finds the toolkit through U2UE_HOME, or refuses.

Converting a tool

Scope: one tool that still names a game's folders. Precondition: the tool has a selftest, or one is written first. Minimal guarantee: run without the facade, the converted tool refuses by name. Success guarantee: the tool reads the project only through u2ue/env.py, and does what it did before. Trigger: a tool names a game's folder.

Converting a tool is a patch, proven like a route:

  1. Replace each literal with need("U2UE_<NAME>") for a project folder and part(name) for a toolkit folder.
  2. Prove the values. Under the reference project, every literal it replaced resolves to the same value.
  3. Prove the refusal. The converted copy refuses, by name, when it runs without the facade.
  4. Prove the behaviour. Its selftest prints the same output before and after.
  5. Run it through the facade: py -m u2ue --project <name> tool <file>.

The work packages: every tool a port runs

The toolkit began as a survey, read off disk on 2026-10-13 (u2ue/README.md): every tool the reference port actually runs, grouped by work package, each with its entry point, its own selftest's result and its bindings - the paths and names a second game would have to change. The facade was then built over that bag of tools as a project file plus one verb per package, WRAPPING the tools and never rewriting them. Each package's tools are listed in the chapter that uses them:

# package tools where they are described
1 the game model and its seams 26 Chapter 6, "The model's tools"
2 Unity IR extraction (effects) 14 Chapter 7, "The effect readers: the IR extraction tools"
3 the effect converter 5 this chapter, "The converter's tools"
4 materials and shader parents 27 this chapter, "Material parents: the tools"
5 meshes, textures and sprite art 19 Chapter 7, "Meshes, textures and sprite art: the tools"
6 scenes and maps 9 Chapter 7, "The scene tools"
7 UI and HUD 13 Chapter 7, "The UI tools"
8 measurement: the Unity windows and the Niagara probes 25 Chapter 9, "The measurement tools"
9 Unreal runs 12 Chapter 3, "The Unreal-run tools"
10 queues and the pause protocol 4 Chapter 3, "Unattended queues and the pause protocol"
11 read-back and checks 25 Chapter 11, "Read-back and checks: the tools"
12 proofs and flips 8 this chapter, "Proofs and flips: the tools"
13 photos and contact sheets 3 Chapter 11, "Photos and contact sheets: the tools"
14 game integration: the effect ledger 3 Chapter 6, "Game integration: the effect ledger"
15 the acceptance report 3 Chapter 11, "The acceptance report: the tools"

The counts are the survey's (2026-10-13); Chapter 20's generated inventory is today's, by folder.

How the survey was measured

  • Inventory: pt1_inventory.py opened every tool file in the port's tool folders and the model gates, and recorded each one's first docstring line, its usage lines and its bindings.
  • The core: pt1_callgraph.py walked what the live drivers call (the queues, the trial chain, the Unity window and its launcher, the report builder): 143 tools. The packages are that core plus the model gates, the UI converter and the art steps, which the effect drivers do not call.
  • Selftests: pt1_selftests.py ran every core tool's OWN selftest (only the ones its file defines - none invented), offline, at below-normal priority; a selftest whose body writes was read first and writes only to a temporary folder. Two were deliberately not run (below).
  • Bindings: a regular expression per kind over each file's source - a count of the files that NAME a thing, not proof that every use is a dependency.

What the survey found

  • 196 tools placed in 15 packages; the rest on disk are history (finished steps and one-off probes), counted by folder at the end of this section, not deleted.
  • No driver ran any selftest, which is how three sat broken unseen: shuriken_size.py (one case still wanted the size from before the rule was measured), v4_msg_gate.py (two defaults made a bare --selftest compare a package with itself) and ue_adapter_gate.py (below). The facade's answer is u2ue check --only selftests, and a trial runs it first. Of 46 that ran on 2026-10-13, 45 exited 0; the 46th, v4_write_gate.py, exits 1 for its GATE, not its selftest (Chapter 11).
  • The trial machinery lived only in a session's temporary folder (%TEMP%/claude/<session>/scratchpad): 123 of 143 driver-shaped files had no copy in any repository. They were snapshotted into the lane (lane/); a job's orchestration kept in a temporary folder is one clean-up from gone.
  • The tools spanned two repositories, so the facade spans both: u2ue/tools.py names each part's folder once (below).
  • No refused converter write was baked into any saved effect system. v4_msg_gate.py --dir over all 672 saved systems read 0 - and it was not a blind zero: the same reader parsed 1,992,662 exports there (none unreadable) and finds the 80 refusals of a package known to hold them. A zero is believed only when the instrument finds the known positive.
  • A gate could not reach a verdict for eleven days, and nothing said so: one leg of ue_adapter_gate.py held copies another change had removed (so it could only answer BLOCKED), and another leg built a check project missing two references the real project had gained (210 false errors). Both were repaired with plants; the gate then ran, and was red on one real thing.
  • The one command for "what exists" named none of the porting tools. py -m u2ue find <words> is that command for the toolkit now (Chapter 2).

Which tool each verb runs

A project is a JSON file in u2ue/projects/; every tool keeps working by hand, and the facade runs it with the project's U2UE_* variables (project.py, tools.py). The route for a second project, start to finish, is u2ue/GUIDE.md (Chapter 8 is its shape).

  • extract (verbs/extract.py): the guid index (t1_guid_index.py), then the keys - the reference port's own resolver (u1e_resolve.py), or the generic particle_prefabs source in keys.py (every prefab holding a ParticleSystem in its own file or through a nested instance or variant, each keyed unity.prefab.<guid>) - then u1e_ir.py. It strips any inherited U1E_* or VFXPORT_* switch first, and exits 1 unless every READ key came out as an IR file or a NAMED refusal, every IR parses, and every Assets/... path an IR names exists in THAT project's tree. A unity. key is read with Unity's own spawn rules (playOnAwake; a sub-emitter's parent) and no game timing - ABSENT, and named - and its scripts are listed as not read.
  • check (verbs/check.py): what nothing else ran - every tool's own selftest, and the two field gates for the project (yaml_field_gate over its IR, ir_field_gate for the reader against the converter). It exists because both gates were found red on the reference port with no one looking.
  • report (verbs/report.py): report_build.py over the project's records (U2UE_EFFECTS_DIR, U2UE_RECORDS_DIR). Proven on the reference port: the patched tools with no facade give the live page byte for byte (bar its generation time), and through the facade the same page plus its title. The second game's first report, before any build: 60 keys, 56 never built, 4 IR refused - every key it will have to account for.
  • build, read, photo (verbs/build.py, verbs/read.py, verbs/photo.py, sharing verbs/_ue.py): the asset-name table and fx17_build.ps1 (record <records>/u1e-build-<tag>.json); u1e_color_size_readback per frame (<records>/rb_<tag>_<N>.json); u1e_fx_photo then u1e_photo_sheet. Each refuses while the Unreal host is busy (the adapter's host_busy) and refuses a Git Bash launch (UnrealSharp needs Program Files\dotnet\, with its backslash, on the PATH).

The effect tools read the project's paths through one patch, pt23_chain_patch.py in the lane, proven like a route: every binding equals the old literal with no facade variables set and under the reference project, landed only while the build queue was paused, then held to a sample whose facade build equals its records.

What a second project found in the readers

Measured 2026-10-13 (u2ue/README.md):

  • The reference project through the facade is byte-identical: a 21-key sample covering every kind of prefab the reader handles gave 20 IR files equal to a direct run and to the live IR, the summary rows equal, the one refusal the same.
  • The second game (Unity 2021.3.21f1): 3,229 prefabs, 60 keys (52 hold a ParticleSystem, 8 only through nesting), 56 IR files with 189 emitters, 4 refused by name, 0 dropped, 0 foreign paths; 3 more prefabs UNKNOWN (they nest assets the project lacks). It found three reader gaps the reference port never exercised, each fixed with a selftest case and a mutant that must break it: the 2018.1-2018.2 legacy Prefab record (m_SourcePrefab {fileID: 0}, m_IsPrefabAsset), nested MODEL instances (left out and named, refused when a ParticleSystem depends on one) and m_RemovedComponents (applied). Of the 4 refused, 3 are modifications aimed at objects inside a model that was left out (Unity derives a model's object ids internally, which cannot be proven from the files) and 1 is a script field the source's data lacks.
  • Every shader a project's effects use is named. The guid index covers a project's PACKAGES too - its embedded Packages/, then Library/PackageCache, after Assets, a folder starting . or ending ~ pruned as Unity's importer prunes - so URP's particle and lit shaders resolve. Unity's BUILT-IN shaders (guid 0000000000000000f000000000000000, not files) are named off the project's own Editor's Resources/unity_builtin_extra by u1e_builtin_names.py, which walks that SerializedFile by its own type trees. A project opts in with unity.editor.
  • An older format meets no silent default. A census of every field emitter_ir looks for and does not find, over both projects: the new misses were field renames, read from the other name, and Unity 5-era documents whose newer fields ride into the IR as None - ABSENT, which the converter then has to name.
  • yaml_field_gate runs on any project (U2UE_UNITY_ROOT, U2UE_IR_DIR). It found the second game's unread light-module fields, and found the reference port's own whole-game corpus RED: three excuses written on a sample of 51 prefabs ("0 on every fired emitter") were false on 655 - ring buffers, unscaled time, renderer priority. The reader reads all of them now, the gate passes on both projects, and the gap moved down to where it belongs: ir_field_gate names the fields the converter must port or name. An excuse measured on a sample is a claim about the sample.

Not run, and why

  • plugin_sync_gate.py --selftest corrupts and restores the INSTALLED plugin DLL in the owner's live Unity project: a DLL change under an open editor is a domain reload nobody asked for. Run it when that editor is closed.
  • ue_publish_gate.py --selftest launches Unreal, and one headless Unreal runs at a time.
  • Read-dependent plants (--plant* on the read-back checks) need a trial's own read pair; the trial chain runs each in every trial, never against an older read (Chapter 11).

The tools no driver reaches

Counted by folder on 2026-10-13 and kept where they are, because each finished step's tools are its evidence: scenes_tools 185, session_queues 135, effects_tools 79, unity_probe 52, effects_lane 30, vfxport 9. Which of them the facade exposes was decided per folder.

A second game brings nothing project-specific to the rules themselves: only its content root and its IR folder.

Inside the converter

vfxport/build_niagara.py turns one IR emitter into Niagara stack writes through Unreal's FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary. build_emitter is the loop over the twenty stages (Chapter 8 lists them, in the order Unity's own modules run); each stage is a _stage_* function. The state one stage hands to a later one lives on ONE object, _EmitterBuild; everything else is a local of its stage. Each stage calls a family of helpers named for what they write (build_frame_shape, build_frame_mesh_renderer, write_collision, sub_emitter_plan, ...), and a rule measured in Unity is re-derived from its bake at build time by its judge (alignmesh_rule(), ringbuffer_check.rules()), so a rule that stops holding stops the build instead of drawing wrongly.

Until 2026-10-15 this was one 1,430-line function with 221 locals. The split was made by a tool, vfxport/split_build_emitter.py, whose definite-assignment analysis decides which locals cross a stage (only those go on the state object), and proven by whole_trace.py: 0 calls differ, 0 exceptions. A new route therefore lands in one stage, behind its switch, and its offline proof (below) names exactly the emitters it touches.

Material parents: the tools

Unity materials become Unreal material instances over HAND-PORTED parents, one per distinct Unity shader family: the blend read as a NUMBER from the .mat, textures imported with Unity's own alpha and settings, and everything reused only when nothing it was built from changed. The families the reference port carries are vendor asset packs, so the parents are reusable for any game that uses those packs. A second game's real cost is one hand-ported parent per distinct shader its effects use.

The largest family, a vendor's uber shader graph, done in full (scene_tools):

tool what it does check
vm1_read_shadergraph.py reads the .shadergraph (one JSON record per object, no Unity) and emits its complete surface: every property a .mat overrides, every node type the parent must reproduce -
vm1_read_materials.py the REAL numbers off every .mat that uses the shader - the set the game fires, and the superset on disk, both reported, because the difference matters for an INERT claim yes
vm1_hlsl.py the graph's arithmetic as the HLSL of the parent's Custom node: every line names the ShaderGraph node it came from, and every formula is the one Unity's own node source generates -
vm1_hlsl2.py the same arithmetic split across three Custom nodes, so that no texture is sampled inside a Custom node -
vm1_tex3.py the experiment that settled a texture-override blocker: the first of eleven null cases whose control could FAIL -
vm1_author.py builds the parent, and one material instance per Unity .mat with the numbers READ off it -
vm1_account.py every surface the graph exposes marked APPLIED, INERT with the arithmetic that makes it inert, or ABSENT with the reason; exits 1 unless the unaccounted count is 0 (the material-family recipe above) yes

vm1_tex3.py carries the lesson worth copying: ten null cases had ruled out a cause, and all ten had been measured against a control that could not fail. A null result is evidence only when its control could have come out the other way.

Proofs and flips: the tools

A route is turned on only after its proof: the WHOLE engine-call trace of every IR the same with the switch OFF, exactly the predicted set changed with it ON, and a plant refused (and the plant must bite); then a headless trial; then the flip table records the default with its evidence, and an audit checks that no switch is left undecided.

A second game supplies nothing here: the proofs are the converter's.

13. Shuriken to Niagara, in depth

Chapter 8 gives the effects pipeline and the route protocol as steps. This chapter gives the reasons behind each step: what makes a Unity particle effect hard to reproduce in Unreal, what the toolkit reads, what the converter writes for each Shuriken module, how a new behaviour earns its place in the default build, and the traps the reference port paid for. Read Chapter 8 first. Come back here when an effect does not draw as Unity draws it, or before you write a route of your own.

Why a purpose-built converter

When the work began (checked 2026-08-22) no tool converted Unity particle systems to Niagara. The search covered Fab and the Unreal Marketplace, GitHub, Epic's documentation and the Unity Asset Store:

  • Epic's CascadeToNiagaraConverter converts Unreal's own older Cascade systems, not Unity's.
  • ProjectExodus, the one Unity-to-Unreal project converter found, does not convert particles, and targets Unity 2018.3 and UE 4.25.
  • Epic's migration documentation says particle systems are recreated by hand.

Appendix D covers the wider prior art. The toolkit borrows one thing from Epic: the CascadeToNiagaraConverter plugin's Python API, which writes a Niagara stack module by module.

The first pilot asked one question - can a game keep its effects if it moves to Unreal - and its answer still frames the work: the STRUCTURE ports automatically, the LOOK does not. The pilot's chain is still in vfxport/: shuriken_ir.py reads prefab YAML into the engine-neutral IR with no Unity running, gen_ir.py picks the prefabs, build_niagara.py runs inside Unreal and writes the systems, materials and textures, final_render.py takes turntable shots and contact_sheet.py stitches them. The facade's verbs now run that chain for any project ("The verbs, underneath", below). A pilot render is evidence of nothing today: it predates every proof in this chapter.

The rules, before any command

Chapter 10 states the toolkit's rules. Effects give each one a reason of its own:

  1. READ or ABSENT, never a guess. A rule measured at one value is not known at another: a ring-buffered particle is held past its lifetime at 1/60 s and longer, and NOT at 0.005 s or under (window RB3, 2026-10-13). A route that had extrapolated from a 1 s measurement drew a glow Unity never draws.
  2. No fallbacks. log + continue, except: pass and a default substituted on failure are the same lie, made invisible. A refusal names the emitter by its system name (the name the build logs): an IR name does not match an emitter Niagara de-duplicated.
  3. Verify with both. A read-back check can pass while the frame is wrong. LOOK at the pair sheets before calling anything done.
  4. A check that has only ever passed proves nothing. Every check has a plant, a deliberately broken input it must FAIL.
  5. A converter change is proven before it builds anything: vfxport/whole_trace.py over the whole IR, a Niagara probe where the stubbed trace is blind (compile errors, run-time kills), a trial that is read, judged and looked at, then the flip with its evidence row in patch_flip_defaults.py and a clean flip_audit. A new route goes behind a VFXPORT_* switch, default OFF, until its trial.
  6. One headless Unreal at a time, from native PowerShell. UnrealSharp finds dotnet by the PATH entry Program Files\dotnet\ with its trailing backslash, and Git Bash hands PowerShell a PATH without it; the Unreal verbs refuse that shell up front, and refuse while the adapter says the host is busy (any Unreal running, or the game's own build queue).
  7. The owner's Unity editor is the owner's. A measurement window starts after 600 s of idle (wait_quiet.ps1 600), stops the moment the owner returns (wait_presence.ps1), leaves every fact file it did not write untouched (md5 before and after) and never answers a modal. The Unity Test Runner is never used (Chapter 9).

Why it is hard

Two models of one effect

A Shuriken ParticleSystem is one component with a fixed set of modules, each with an enabled flag and a fixed list of fields. Most fields are a MinMaxCurve or MinMaxGradient in one of four modes: a constant, a curve, a random value between two constants, or one between two curves. Unity runs the modules in its own fixed order inside its own particle step.

A Niagara emitter is a set of scripts (emitter spawn and update, particle spawn and update, event handlers), each a stack of modules, plus renderers kept apart. Each module is a graph with declared inputs, and an input can belong to one version of the module and not another, sit behind a static switch or an inline edit condition, or take a dynamic input or a data interface (a curve is one) instead of a value. So one Unity field becomes a module, an input name, a type, a version and sometimes a switch, and the API reports a failure at any of those by returning False rather than raising (see the traps). Niagara runs a stack top to bottom, so the converter writes modules in the order Unity runs its own.

Space, scale and the transform chain

  • Simulation space. A Local system simulates in its node's frame and the transform carries the result into the world; a World system's particles stay where they were born.
  • Scaling mode (scalingMode: Hierarchy 0, Local 1, Shape 2). Under Hierarchy Unity multiplies a particle's size by the node's whole lossy scale, under Local by the system's own scale, under Shape by neither. A Niagara sprite's size is absolute: it is laid along unit tangents and never passes through the component's transform (NiagaraSpriteVertexFactory.ush:993, read in UE 5.7). So the converter folds the scale into the size. Before that fix every sprite of the reference port's first scene drew wrong by exactly one over its lossy scale (3.571 times too large is 1 / 0.28).
  • Motion under a scaled chain. MEASURED (Unity windows 25 and 26, 2026-10-07): a Local system moves in UNSCALED local units (start speed, velocity over lifetime, radial push, limit, drag) and the transform scales the result into the world, but gravity acts in world units. The port's frame carries the chain's turn and place, not its scale, so scaled emitters moved at the unscaled speed (2.5 times too fast at 0.4) until motion_scale in vfxport/build_niagara.py scaled each local-unit input. A World system under a scaled chain takes different factors per part (the WSCALE route).

The transform chain is composed up m_Father to the prefab root, the root's rotation included, and carried into Unreal by one fixed frame: Unreal (X, Y, Z) = (-100 x, 100 z, 100 y) in centimetres. That matrix has determinant +1, so a quaternion maps as (-qx, qz, qy, qw). Unity's Quaternion.Euler turns Z, then X, then Y about the fixed axes.

A NON-uniform node scale shears a facing quad in Unity (window 37: a View-aligned billboard takes the node's lossy scale along the WORLD axes after facing the camera), which no Niagara sprite draws; the VIEWSHEAR route reproduces it in the parent material's World Position Offset. The IR's ownerScale, the axis-aligned product of the local scales, is not Unity's lossy scale diag(R^T M) where a non-uniform scale sits above a turn, so the IR also carries lossyScale and nodeMatrix. And a spawn scale on the Unreal component reaches a Local emitter's positions and a mesh but never a sprite's size (NiagaraSpriteVertexFactory.ush:923-1003): the SPAWNSCALE route writes it into the size every frame, and only a photo at the game's own spawn scale can see the rule.

Two clocks

Unity's particle clock adds each step up in float32 and tests a burst against it half-open. A Unity probe that steps Simulate on the fixed timestep runs at 0.02 s on the reference project while the Unreal read steps 1/60 s: the two share ages only at multiples of 0.1 s, so compare at the particles' own ages and read the step off the data.

With interpolated spawning (the converter's empty template has it), Niagara's spawn script reads every float emitter parameter LERPED between last frame's value and this frame's by the particle's spawn fraction, so Emitter.Age read at spawn is the emission instant; integers and a short list of engine constants are not lerped (read: NiagaraHlslTranslator.cpp:5113-5153). Unity reads a start speed at the emission instant and a start size or lifetime at the END of the emitting step. Pick the clock to match: the lerped parameter as it is, or the frame's end rebuilt from values that are never lerped.

Random draws

The toolkit's Unity probes pin the seed (useAutoRandomSeed = false), so a Unity frame is reproducible. Niagara's VM seeds its randoms per batch off the CPU cycle counter (VectorVMRuntime.cpp:444-446); determinism is a compile-time emitter flag the converter does not set and Python cannot reach. So no random value is compared particle for particle: the port matches the DISTRIBUTION Unity draws, measured. A random-constants start size is uniform and independent of the start rotation, speed and lifetime (KS 0.018, 2026-10-06); a TwoColors start colour draws ONE fraction for all four channels; two RandomRangeFloat inputs in one particle are independent (correlation 0.006); a value Unity holds per particle is a spawn-only random in Niagara.

The IR: reading Shuriken offline

The reader is effects_tools/u1e_ir.py over vfxport/shuriken_ir.py, with effects_tools/u1e_nested.py for nested prefabs. It reads the YAML of a project serialized as text, with no Unity running. Chapter 8 shows an IR excerpt, Chapter 20 its format.

Per effect key it holds: every emitter's modules, each value with its mode and a readAs saying how it was read; the renderer (mode, alignment, rendererEnabled, meshes, pivot, sort); the material, its shader resolved by guid and its blend READ as numbers; the emitter's place in the prefab (prefabPos, prefabRot), ownerScale, lossyScale and nodeMatrix; the system's file id (_psFileID), by which every later record pairs it; the sub-emitter links; and the natural length, or null with the reason.

Reading MinMax values

At serializedVersion 2 the constant modes do not use the curves: minMaxState 0 is scalar, minMaxState 3 the range [minScalar, scalar], and the curves stored beside them are stale. A random-constants range is serialized min > max as often as not, so a reader keeps the pair as serialized and takes max() where it means "the longest". Unity writes a float field holding 0 as 0, which a YAML loader returns as an integer: type a value by the field it replaces.

File ids

  • Signed ids. A header can carry a negative id (--- !u!95 &-745123763528618581); a splitter matching &(\d+) lets the document before it swallow it. The pattern needs -?.
  • Nested prefab instances. An object inside a nested instance has, in the outer file, the id (instance id XOR source object id) AND 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, and references inside the expanded objects re-key the same way (measured 2026-10-07 on every placeholder of 15 expanded prefabs). The outer file's "stripped" placeholders, read as objects, look like extra root transforms. u1e_nested.py expands each instance, applies its modifications, checks every placeholder against the formula and drops it. A prefab variant's root is an instance of its base, so the same expansion reads it.
  • Legacy records. Class 1001 is also a pre-2018.3 prefab's own "Prefab" record (&100100000, m_RootGameObject or m_IsPrefabParent, no source); Unity 2018.1 and 2018.2 wrote it as m_SourcePrefab {fileID: 0} with m_IsPrefabAsset. It is kept, never expanded.
  • Removed and added objects. The effect reader applies m_RemovedComponents and m_RemovedGameObjects (the scene reader is Chapter 7's); added GameObjects and components are refused by name. A nested MODEL instance (an FBX) has no YAML: it is left out and named unless the IR depends on it.
  • Shader Graph shaders are cited with a NEGATIVE file id (a sub-asset of the .shadergraph file). A regex expecting a positive integer reported "no shader" for 1,930 of the reference port's 1,999 effect materials (read 2026-09-29).
  • Built-ins. The guid 0000000000000000f000000000000000 is the Editor's unity_builtin_extra, whose names are read off that file (set unity.editor). The built-in Default-Particle material is file id 10301, its texture 10300 (64 x 64 RGBA32, 7 mips).

What the game decides, not the prefab

What starts when an effect spawns is the game's rule. Unity's own rule plays a system whose Play On Awake is on; a game's pool may do more (the reference port's pool also plays the first system's whole subtree). The adapter names the rule (Chapter 12), the IR records each emitter's spawn start, and an emitter the game never starts is absent in both engines.

The field gates, and what they cannot see

yaml_field_gate holds every key of every ENABLED module (and the ParticleSystem and renderer) to the reader: named by shuriken_ir.py, or excused with the reason and the values it may take, re-checked on every run. ir_field_gate holds every IR field to the converter: named there, or listed in DELIBERATELY_UNREAD with its reason. Both run in u2ue check --only gates.

One hole, READ on 2026-10-17: the reader reads no Color by Speed, Size by Speed or Rotation by Speed module, and yaml_field_gate matches a field by its NAME. Every field those modules serialize (enabled, gradient, curve, range, separateAxes, x, y, z) is a name the reader reads for another module, so the gate passes an enabled by-speed module. (The Trigger module's inside and outside are named nowhere, so an enabled Trigger module fails the gate as it should.) Until the gate keys on the module too, list a project's enabled by-speed modules yourself before trusting a build.

Module by module

"Measured" means a Unity probe baked the rule (Chapter 9) and the converter re-derives it at build time; SUBSTITUTED is a stand-in the acceptance report counts; ABSENT is not drawn, with its reason.

Unity module Niagara state
Main: duration, loop, delay, prewarm, max particles EmitterState (Life Cycle Mode Self), loop delay, system warm-up, a cap route measured; the cap SUBSTITUTED (one frame late)
Emission: rate, bursts, rate over distance SpawnRate (a curve where authored), SpawnBurst_Instantaneous per burst, SpawnPerUnit measured; a random rate over distance ABSENT
Shape SphereLocation V1 / V2, BoxLocation, CylinderLocation, spawn assignments per shape measured per shape; the rest named
Main: start values InitializeParticle, AddVelocity, AddVelocityFromPoint measured, with the instant each is read
Colour / Size / Rotation over Lifetime ScaleColor (RGB and alpha separately), ScaleSpriteSize / ScaleMeshSize, SpriteRotationRate or mesh orientation measured
Colour / Size / Rotation by Speed none not read (see the field gates)
Velocity over Lifetime, Force, Limit, Gravity update assignments, AccelerationForce, VortexForce, Drag, GravityForce, SolveForcesAndVelocity measured where planned; the rest named
Noise CurlNoiseForce SUBSTITUTED: Unity's noise is not measured
Collision its own route on the measured subset, else CollisionQuery measured, else SUBSTITUTED
Renderer sprite renderer (alignment, facing, pivot), mesh renderer, sort hints measured per mode; allowRoll SUBSTITUTED
Texture Sheet Animation SubImageIndex per the measured frame rule Grid, whole sheet, lifetime and FPS modes
Trails a ribbon emitter fed by a location event measured
Sub Emitters event generators on the parent, handlers on the child Birth and Death measured; the rest named
Custom Data Dynamic Material Parameters measured per stream layout
Lights point lights on the effect (Chapter 8) per-particle Lights module ABSENT
External Forces none SUBSTITUTED (wind zones are the scene's)

Emitter state and the loop

EmitterState's "Life Cycle Mode" defaults to System, under which an emitter IGNORES its own loop behaviour, duration and delay while every write reports success: the converter sets Self, and writes the loop delay with its inline edit condition on. Unity prewarms an EMITTER; Niagara warms the whole SYSTEM and floors the warm-up to whole ticks. The port warms the system by the longest prewarmed loop, written half a step over, and delays every other emitter to start where Unity starts it. Unity's run-once window is half-open while Niagara's loop runs one frame long, so 67 of 93 run-once rate emitters grew one extra particle (2026-10-07) until the converter killed a birth at or after the window's end inside the spawn script. Niagara's ParticleState kills a particle a hair before its lifetime where Unity still draws it: the converter kills on Age > Lifetime. A start lifetime of Infinity becomes float32's largest finite value, named.

maxParticles is a cap Unity refills in the step a particle dies. Niagara takes its spawn counts from the count at the frame's START (NiagaraEmitterInstanceImpl.cpp:1300-1313), so the port refills one frame late: exact where nothing is replaced, a named substitute elsewhere. Without the route nothing holds the cap at all (one emitter kept about 50 alive where Unity keeps 1). Its room and frame-start count are INTEGER parameters, because a float one reaches the spawn script lerped. Named, not ported: cullingMode, stopAction (the host decides), useUnscaledTime, and the ring-buffer modes outside their measured range.

Rate, bursts and rate over distance

A rate curve is the scalar times the curve at the loop's normalized time (Chapter 8). Niagara's first tick after activation adds nothing to SpawnRate, so the converter preloads the spawn remainder with rate x DeltaTime at emitter spawn: k / rate at any frame rate. Each burst is its own SpawnBurst_Instantaneous (the duplicate gate must not charge the second, which Niagara names SpawnBurst_Instantaneous001) with an Int32 count. A repeating burst is one module per cycle or a burst train; one that repeats forever is refused; a probability fires the whole burst, one roll per firing. A burst exactly on a step's end in Unity's half-open float32 clock fires on the NEXT step (0.25 s ends step 15 at 1/60 and fires on 16; 0.5 s stays on 30): the BURSTLAG route puts every off-grid burst's first frame on Unity's step. Every non-prewarmed burst under a system warm-up was born one warm-up tick late (WARMBURST's evidence: 178 of 178). Both routes read default ON (2026-10-17).

Rate over distance is particles per unit the SYSTEM travels, one at each crossing (measured). SpawnPerUnit takes the spacing exactly, places each particle up to one frame of travel AHEAD of Unity and at large steps misses the first and last crossings (named). A random rate over distance is ABSENT: Unity draws a new rate every step. A sub-emitter child's distance emission is its PARENT's travel.

Shapes

  • Cone. Unity's Cone emits from its BASE, a disc of radius r (radiusThickness 0 is the rim), along the generator through each point, tilted atan(u tan a) at fraction u of the radius (measured). ConeLocation fills from its apex and has a Cone Length and no radius, so the converter uses CylinderLocation at height 0, at its latest version, turned to the axis, and writes the direction.
  • Sphere and Hemisphere. SphereLocation V1 adds its Offset in simulation space, unturned; V2 with "Offset Coordinate Space" Local turns it with the component. Both sample uniformly in volume (measured).
  • Circle, Donut, Arc. A Random-mode arc spread snaps particles to multiples of spread x 360 degrees; a Loop arc or donut moves at 360 x speed x birth time, wrapped at the arc; a BurstSpread burst of N sits at i / (N - 1) of an arc, i / N of a full 360.
  • Edge. A BurstSpread burst of N lies at i / (N - 1) along [-r, r]; a Loop edge moves at u = Frac(speed t / r), which only a bake at a radius other than 1 could tell.
  • Mesh. Particles start on Unity's own vertices, P = T + R (S . v), the start speed along the turned vertex normal.
  • Rectangle. A moving Rectangle's start velocity is along the shape's turned +Z (measured within 6e-8).

A disabled Shape module's transform does nothing in Unity (measured); an enabled one's rotation turns the emission axis, not the particles, and its position is composed under Hierarchy scaling and refused under the others. Named where unmeasured: randomPositionAmount outside its measured case, a Random radius spread on a shape other than a Circle, animated radius modes.

Start values, colour, size and rotation

InitializeParticle carries the start lifetime, size, colour and rotation ("Sprite Rotation Angle" does nothing unless "Sprite Rotation Mode" is "Direct Angle (Degrees)"); AddVelocity the start speed along the shape's direction; AddVelocityFromPoint a radial push. A start size or lifetime curve is read at the END of the emitting step, a start speed curve at the emission instant (Chapter 8).

Colour over lifetime goes through ScaleColor's "RGB and Alpha Separately" arm, Scale RGB from a VectorFromCurve and Scale Alpha from a FloatFromCurve: the only arm Python can build, and the closer mapping, since Unity authors RGB and alpha as separate gradients. Keys built in Python get automatic tangents unless they go through unreal.InterpCurvePointFloat with CIM_CURVE_BREAK and FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary.keys_from_interp_curve_float; a curve data interface defaults to a 128-sample lookup table, and use_lut False evaluates it exactly. Size over lifetime is ScaleSpriteSize or ScaleMeshSize, each rebuilt from the spawn size so nothing compounds. Rotation is SpriteRotationRate on a sprite; a mesh renderer reads only its mesh orientation, so a mesh's spin goes there.

Motion, collision and noise

Velocity over lifetime (linear, orbital, radial, speed modifier) is written as ordered update assignments where its plan is measured; otherwise the old stand-in (a constant acceleration, one vortex) is SUBSTITUTED and every part it leaves out ABSENT. A pasted module can land BEFORE the solver (Niagara fixes up dependencies on paste), hence the assignments. Gravity falls world-down even in a Local emitter, velocity first, as in Unity; limit and drag use the unscaled size and local speed (measured). The VM's vector length uses an ESTIMATED reciprocal (VectorVMRuntime.cpp:1912: 999.875 for 1000), so a rule that depends on a length uses a dot product and a power of 0.5. Noise is a CurlNoiseForce of the same strength and frequency, SUBSTITUTED.

A Planes collision with every slot unassigned collides with nothing in Unity, so nothing is written. Where the measured subset holds (the touch at radiusScale x size / 2, the bounce, the slide, a lifetime loss of 1, World behaving as Planes, a Collision child's burst on the touching step) the converter writes its own route; any other collision is a CollisionQuery, SUBSTITUTED. GenerateCollisionEvent drops a touch slower than its "Velocity Threshold" (1 cm/s by default) unless the threshold is written -1.

Renderers

  • Billboard. Unity drops the camera's ROLL; Niagara's facing modes keep it, and no stock dynamic input gives the per-particle camera forward that would drop it: allowRoll is SUBSTITUTED.
  • Stretched billboard. The long axis is size x lengthScale. The legacy pivot moves the quad 2 py s forward whatever the length (measured at lengthScale 1 and -1, after a bake at 2 could not tell the rules apart). A negative Niagara sprite size mirrors the IMAGE, never the quad. Velocity alignment zeroes the sprite rotation; custom alignment faces the camera POSITION, not its plane.
  • Horizontal and Vertical. A Horizontal billboard's DIAGONAL is the particle size (side size / sqrt 2) and Niagara's custom facing needs a facing vector written. A Vertical billboard draws the same upright quad under View, World, Local and Facing alignment (measured), side size / sqrt 2.
  • Mesh. The import is REFUSED unless it matches the file per corner: position, UV and winding (an FBX's axis signs turn Unreal's import and not Unity's mesh; a box check cannot see a 180-degree turn). Unity multiplies a mesh's vertex colour into the particle colour (measured); Niagara's VertexColor is the mesh's own colour and 1 on sprites and ribbons, so Particle Color x VertexColor is exact on all three. Niagara corrects culling for the COMPONENT's determinant only: a mirrored mesh is safe only two-sided.
  • Render mode None draws no particle (a trail-only emitter draws its trail); m_Enabled 0 draws nothing. The descending sort is spelled CUSTOM_DECENDING in 5.7's Python.

Texture sheet animation

Measured, re-derived at build time: frame = floor(N x frac(f + s)), N = tilesX x tilesY, f the frame over time (a constant, a random held per particle, scalar x curve(frac(cycles x normalized age)), or fps x age / N in FPS mode) and s the start frame. The converter writes Particles.SubImageIndex itself (SubUVAnimation has no start-frame override). Named where unmeasured: Speed mode, a Sprites-list or single-row sheet, flipped sheets, a partial UV channel mask.

Trails

A trail is a Niagara RIBBON emitter beside its parent, on the route Epic's Cascade converter uses: a location event generator on the parent and a handler on the ribbon spawning one point per event. Measured in Unity: the head vertex IS the particle; each point lives the lifetime fraction x the particle's lifetime; width and colour run from head 0 to tail 1; the trail's colour over lifetime is taken at the particle's CURRENT age and tints the whole trail. A ribbon point cannot read its parent, so each carries its parent's normalized age, lifetime and draws in the event payload, on slots the receive module actually applies. Niagara never scales a ribbon's width (NiagaraRibbonVertexFactory.ush:862) while Unity scales a Hierarchy trail under a scaled parent: the TRAILSPAWN route writes it. A textureScale other than 1 is SUBSTITUTED.

Sub-emitters

The frame a Birth or Death child emits in, MEASURED on 117 cases (vfxport/subframe_rule.py, judged by vfxport/unity_probe/sub_frame_rule_check.py):

R = Cw . LookRotation(u, up = (0, |u.z|, 1 - |u.z|)) . Cl . S     the parent particle moving at the trigger
R = Cl . S  (world-fixed)                                         the parent particle still

Cw is the child system's world rotation, Cl its OWN local rotation (so its local turn counts twice), S its shape rotation, and u the parent particle's total velocity at the trigger in the child's frame (Birth after the parent's first step, Death as it died, Collision after the bounce). A rule fitted on axis-aligned cases alone fitted a WRONG rule exactly; oblique, rotated and grandchild cases broke it. A child's own GameObject position plays no part. In Niagara the child is an event-spawned emitter. A Birth child of a Birth- or Collision-spawned middle NEVER fires in Unity (windows 33 and 34) and is counted apart; an unported child is EMITTER-ABSENT with its reason, never drawn as an ordinary emitter. The event traps are listed below.

Custom data and vertex streams

Custom Data reaches a Unity shader only through the renderer's Custom Vertex Streams. Measured: a Custom1.xyzw list packs uv0.zw = Custom1.xy and uv1.xy = Custom1.zw, default streams give uv0.zw = (0, 1), and Custom Data curves run ONE simulation step behind the particle's age. The converter writes Dynamic Material Parameters above ParticleState, which keeps that lag, and supports a layout only where a control case read it. STREAM_SLOTS_READ names the slots each shader reads, and a read slot on an unmeasured layout is refused; a shader not listed is taken to read none, so each newly ported shader adds its row.

What Niagara has no equivalent for

Each is a named stand-in, an emulation or a refusal: refilling a cap in the step a particle dies; a billboard that drops the camera's roll; a 4-channel colour curve from Python; per-emitter prewarm (emulated); Unity's sheared quad (emulated in the parent material); deterministic random draws from Python; a single-particle event mode (5.7 has Every Particle and Spawned Particles); an event-spawned child whose curves are not applied twice (the console variable that stops it breaks trails); and what an asset pack's custom shader does beyond blending, which needs a hand-authored parent per shader family. Unity's noise field, external forces, culling modes and unscaled time are named for another reason: their Unity rule is not measured yet.

The converter's machinery

vfxport/build_niagara.py writes Niagara stacks through FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary in a real Unreal editor process. build_emitter loops over twenty stages, _EMITTER_STAGES, in the order Unity's modules run: setup, emitter state, spawning, particle spawn, shape, start speed, update, colour, size and rotation over lifetime, gravity, force, noise, velocity over lifetime, collision, renderer, flipbook, sub-emitter roles and trails, inherit velocity, and the unported modules (named per emitter). The split into stages was proven with vfxport/split_build_emitter.py and whole_trace.py: identical engine calls on every emitter. The converter's size is one of the product's pillars, which is why a flip adds no line to it.

Writing one value

  • add_mod refuses a module asset that is not there: create_asset_data on a missing path still returns an asset.
  • setp tries each candidate input name and returns whether one TOOK, honouring set_parameter's boolean, and records every miss in the build report's param_misses.
  • VERSION pins a module's script version per module; some modules answer differently at 1.0 and at their latest graph.
  • Propagated static switches. UNiagaraGraph::FindStaticSwitchInputs (NiagaraGraph.cpp:2143-2166, read 2026-10-17) returns the module graph's own static switch nodes AND every function call node's PropagatedStaticSwitchParameters, renamed to their propagated name when set; SetParameter accepts both. A reader that walks only the switch nodes calls the second kind "not declared" while the engine takes it: ShapeLocation V2's "Rotation Mode" lives on a function call node, and one build wrote it on 57 emitters with 0 refusals. scene_tools/v4_module_inputs.py lists a module's declared inputs off the shipped .uasset, propagated switches included; read it before calling such a write wrong.
  • Module names. find_or_add_module_script finds a module by NAME anywhere in the stack, so every extra instance a route adds gets its own name.
  • One input object, one parent. A script input handed to two parents is lost from one; build a fresh input per use.

Names, rules and notes

Niagara renames a clashing emitter handle, and every event names its source by the REAL handle. vfxport/niagara_names.py reproduces the engine's naming (59 of 59 systems exact against a full build, 2026-10-06), assigns every name before the emitter is added, and avoids the reserved namespace names (an emitter called "Particles" stops the system compiling). Every read-back check recomputes the same table from the IR.

A measured rule is not a constant in the converter. cap_rule, trail_rule, flipbook_rule, sub_emitter_rule and their siblings read the bake (shared/conformance/color-size-facts.json and others) at build time and re-derive the rule from the case's own control; a rule that stops holding makes its route refuse by name.

vfxport/shuriken_size.py holds the size arithmetic with no engine in it, so the converter inside Unreal and a measurement in plain Python import one rule (two copies is how the first scene's size bug survived). It folds the scaling mode in (size_scale returns None to REFUSE when the scale it needs is absent), applies the measured side of a Horizontal or Vertical billboard, the stretch length, the non-uniform arm (a 188 x 1476 cm shaft written as a 200 cm square was the bug it fixed) and the VIEWSHEAR plan. py vfxport/shuriken_size.py runs its selftest.

The acceptance page (lane/report_build.py) counts a stand-in only when its field note contains SUBSTITUTED, so a runtime gap is written "SUBSTITUTED : ...". An absent emitter carries its reason in the record's absentEmitters.

Routes and switches

A route is one Unity behaviour the converter ports, behind a switch named VFXPORT_* (the converter's) or U1E_* (the effect tools'). A new switch is read os.environ.get("VFXPORT_<NAME>", "0") == "1": OFF unless set. extract, build, read and photo remove every VFXPORT_ and U1E_ variable inherited from the shell and name them, so an ordinary build is the defaults and nothing else; a trial sets its route's switches for its build step only.

The evidence table and the flip

vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py holds the evidence once, in TABLE: per row the file that reads the switch, the switch, and the evidence that it may flip (the trial, its read, its judge and plant, the sheets looked at). A flip rewrites the read to os.environ.get("VFXPORT_<NAME>", "1") != "0" (still switchable off with =0) and marks the line with the date and a pointer to its row; it adds no line. A switch read in two files flips in both or not at all: the tool refuses, exit 2, while any read of a flipped switch still defaults OFF anywhere in the code trees.

py vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py --list              every row: its switch, its file, its evidence
py vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py --dry <ROW> ...     what the flip would change; nothing written
py vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py <ROW> ...           the flip: atomic per file, compiled before it replaces the file

Chapter 20's converter switch table is generated from that table and the code, with each switch's state today.

flip_audit and the state of a route

lane/flip_audit.py compares every switch a trial set with its default in the code as it stands, and flags a trial switch read default OFF anywhere (unless DELIBERATE_OFF names why) and a switch whose read sites disagree. DELIBERATE_OFF is evidence too: a route measured SLOWER (a data-processing conversion context made the finalize 1.5 times slower), a route that waits on another (an arc placement exact at the frame's end while every later burst cycle is born a tick late), a route measured DIFFERENT from Unity, a switch for probe builds only.

py -m u2ue --project <game> tool flip_audit.py

u2ue/routes.py reads both files into Route objects: ON when EVERY file that reads the switch reads it default on, DELIBERATELY OFF when flip_audit names what it waits on, OFF otherwise. A table row is evidence that a switch MAY flip, not proof that it did: u2ue metrics counts a route as flipped only when every file reads it on today, and counts switches, not rows.

The route protocol, from evidence to flip

Take the next gap from the acceptance page's absent emitters by root, ordered by what porting each brings back:
