Appendix B carries the related item: the probes and the window driver as the package's Editor assembly, triggered by a file, with no dependency on the reference port's bridge.

The probes

A probe is an editor script that sets up one Unity behaviour, steps it, and writes what it observed to a fact file; its judge states the rule a port relies on and reads it off the facts or refuses it with the numbers (Chapter 9: the judge is written and planted first). Probes live in the toolkit, not the game: vfxport/unity_probe/ held 61 C# files on 2026-10-17 (60 probes and the shared placement helper ProbeSpawn.cs), beside 29 *_judge.py and 10 *_check.py files. A probe is copied into the project's editor folder (unity.probe_dir) for one window and taken out again.

The shape of a probe

  • Triggered by a file. An [InitializeOnLoadMethod] hooks EditorApplication.update (never delayCall) to poll for its trigger in the conformance part. The generic case probe skips every tick while the editor plays or compiles; when its trigger appears it deletes it, reads the lines the window wrote (a spec and a record name), and runs. Nothing has to click.
  • Edit mode, in a preview scene. The case probe and the photo probe place their systems in a preview scene (EditorSceneManager.NewPreviewScene), so the owner's active scene is never touched; its dirty flag is recorded before and after.
  • One record out, never over another. The case probe refuses to write a record that exists (and the runner refuses to start any probe whose output exists); a probe reports an error inside its record rather than throwing.
  • Compiled headless before it enters the project (typecheck.py --editor --extra <probe.cs>).
  • Real prefabs are placed only through ProbeSpawn, which names the placement measured (the game's effect spawn, its projectile spawn, or the prefab as authored). One probe that placed prefabs its own way dropped the root's authored rotation and made 36 reference frames wrong. vfxport/probe_spawn_gate.py refuses a probe that sets an instantiated prefab's transform itself, and the runner drops ProbeSpawn.cs in with any probe that calls it.
  • A query that can crash Unity is guarded. ParticleSystem.Particle.GetMeshIndex on a renderer without meshes kills the editor in native code, which no managed try / catch sees (Chapter 22).

A probe case is data

Hand-written probes grow: ColorSizeFactsProbe.cs reached 5,915 lines of hand-written cases. ParticleCaseProbe.cs is one generic probe for every particle question, the question given as data, and u2ue/probecase.py writes that data:

  • ProbeCase.prefab(name, path, times, spawn=...): a real prefab placed by the game's spawn (effect, projectile, authored), listing the systems the game never starts so they are cleared after every step.
  • ProbeCase.synthetic(name, modules, times): one system whose module properties are set by name ({"main": {...}, "emission": {...}}): a rule question with no new C#.
  • Every case pins the random seed on every system (two runs are identical), lists its read times and per-particle fields, and caps the particles written (the count is always whole).
  • Restart or step. Without a step, each time is simulated from a restart; with one, the probe restarts once and steps the way the game does, so the times must ascend. The restart read is blind to a sub-emitter of a sub-emitter: it drew 0 of 284, and a read stepped at the game's own frame step drew every one (Chapter 10).
  • CaseRun(name, cases, why) writes <name>-cases.json in the conformance part and the window spec <name>.json under the lane part's windows/, refusing to replace either; the window writes <name>-unity.json.
py -m u2ue.probecase --selftest      # a prefab case, a synthetic case, bad cases and runs refused, nothing replaced

u2ue conform cases builds a run of every IR key this way (Chapter 10). The simulation-speed sweep was 24 synthetic cases (simspeed-cases.json), the first Unity rule the reference port measured with no new probe file.

Every rule traced to its probe

A fact file records the format its probe writes, and the probe's source holds that literal. u2ue/survey/rule_probes.py reads both as text and attributes each fact file: ATTRIBUTED when exactly one probe holds its format, AMBIGUOUS when several do, ORPHAN when none does (its probe is gone), UNFORMATTED when the file names no format. Its run on 2026-10-17:

py u2ue/survey/rule_probes.py
RULES ATTRIBUTED 189 of 220 (orphan 0, ambiguous 3, unformatted 28)

An orphan would be a measured rule nobody can re-measure; there are none.

15. The Unreal tools: headless runs, the host, publishing

Every Unreal step of a port runs the same way: headless, from native PowerShell, one engine at a time, through one runner that refuses an unsafe launch, and judged by what the run wrote, never by its exit code. This chapter is each Unreal-side tool, why it is built that way, and the traps it catches; Chapter 22's "Unreal runs" entries are the short form, by symptom.

tool what it is
scene_tools/ue_headless.ps1 the one place an Unreal executable is named: six launch rules, a watchdog, the argument builders
scene_tools/ue_headless_selftest.ps1, ue_headless_gate.py the six rules made to refuse; no other tool may name the executable
u2ue/ue_py.ps1, u2ue/ue_game.ps1 one headless Python script (scene import, readback); one headless game start (host run)
effects_tools/u1e_py.ps1, effects_tools/fx17_build.ps1 one effect instrument; one chunk of effect keys built (build, read, photo, trial)
u2ue/verbs/_ue.py what the Unreal verbs share: the host guard, the PATH check, the runner, the build record
u2ue/hostproject.py, u2ue/verbs/host.py, u2ue/templates/unreal the game's own Unreal project, made from the toolkit's template
u2ue/runtime the engine-free libraries the port links

Headless Unreal runs

Native PowerShell, never a shell that rewrote the PATH

UnrealSharp, the plugin that runs C# in Unreal, finds the .NET SDK by scanning PATH for an existing directory entry that contains Program Files\dotnet\, trailing backslash included (read from the plugin's source). Native PowerShell's PATH has it. A PowerShell started from Git Bash, even indirectly (Bash runs Python, Python runs pwsh), inherits a PATH that MSYS converted, where the entry reads /c/Program Files/dotnet or has lost its backslash. UnrealSharp then reports the SDK missing and raises a modal dialog, which under -unattended is answered and raised again forever: the run never ends and its log never stops growing. The reference port paid twice - 14.5 GB resident and a 3 GB log before anyone looked (2026-09-29), then 265 497 dialogs in a 634 MB log and the run's work never done (2026-10-02).

So it is checked twice before anything starts: every verb that starts Unreal asks native_path_ok (u2ue/verbs/_ue.py) and refuses with "run from native PowerShell", and the runner's rule R6 refuses the launch (since 2026-10-02 asking UnrealSharp's own question, backslash included). Open a PowerShell window and type the facade command there.

One headless Unreal at a time

The Unreal host is one machine-wide resource: two engines contend for memory, the derived-data cache and the project's packages, and an open editor locks packages another process needs to save (below). So every verb that starts Unreal asks the adapter's host_busy and refuses, naming what holds the host, instead of waiting:

  • the default adapter (unity_project) answers busy while any process whose name starts with UnrealEditor runs - an editor the porter has open counts;
  • a game adapter may add its own build queues (Chapter 12).

build, read and photo exit 1 on that refusal, host and scene exit 2. build, read, photo and scene print the host's state with --dry, and run nothing. fx17_build.ps1 also refuses on its own (exit 9 while any UnrealEditor runs), so a tool run by hand keeps the guard. The verbs start Unreal below normal priority, so the person using the machine keeps it.

The runner and its six rules

scene_tools/ue_headless.ps1 is dot-sourced by every launcher, and every launch goes through its Invoke-UeHeadless, which first calls Assert-UeHeadless on the exact argument list. Each rule is a throw that names itself:

rule refuses measured or read
R1 EXE any executable but UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe, or one not on disk the GUI editor puts windows on the desktop
R2 UNATTENDED a launch without -unattended read from the engine source: it changes how a prompt acts, not whether a window is made
R3 OFFSCREEN a launch without -RenderOffScreen 2026-09-28: an -unattended Python run put two visible windows on the desktop, one the "Executing Python Script..." notification; with -RenderOffScreen, none, and a byte-identical answer. The engine then creates its null platform application: there is no OS window to draw into
R4 ABSLOG a launch without -ABSLOG=<file> a run writes its own log, never Saved/Logs, which an open editor also writes
R5 NO GUI PY -ExecutePythonScript together with -game
R6 DOTNET a PATH with no existing entry containing Program Files\dotnet\ above

The watchdog. A plain wait cannot notice a runaway, so the runner polls every 1.5 s and kills the run with a named reason at its time cap ($script:UeHeadlessMaxSeconds, 1800 s unless the launcher sets one: ue_game.ps1 900, ue_py.ps1 3600) or when the log passes $script:UeHeadlessMaxLogMB (600 MB) - almost always one modal or one error repeated: read the log's last lines. A capped run fails; it never passes. ue_game.ps1, ue_py.ps1 and u1e_py.ps1 end with one line, exit=<code> seconds=<s> logMB=<mb> killed=<reason> log=<path>; the second game's host run printed exit=0 seconds=38 logMB=0 killed= log=<work>/host/host-run.log (2026-10-16).

The argument builders. New-UePythonArgs makes an editor Python run (-ExecutePythonScript=<script> -unattended -nosplash -stdout -DeterministicAudio -nocef -RenderOffScreen -AllowCommandletRendering -nosourcecontrol -ABSLOG=<log>); New-UeGameArgs a game run. The command line the second game's host run logged (2026-10-16), its log path shortened:

/Engine/Maps/Entry -game -RenderOffScreen -unattended -nosplash -stdout -DeterministicAudio
  -ini:Engine:[Audio]:UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=1.0 -ResX=1280 -ResY=720 -ForceRes -ABSLOG=<work>/host/host-run.log -ExecCmds=quit

-nocef keeps the editor's embedded Chromium unloaded: an effect build crashed 45 s in with an access violation whose every frame was in that library, which loads because -RenderOffScreen still lets the engine render (2026-10-09).

The gate. ue_headless_gate.py refuses any file under the port's tooling that names an Unreal executable by path outside the runner (one window probe is excepted by name), any launchable reference to UnrealEditor.exe, a file naming an executable without both -unattended and -RenderOffScreen, and a runner that has lost a rule id (exit 0 clean, 1 refused with file and line, 2 could not run). A launcher that named the executable itself would route around every rule above; the gate makes that a failure.

The selftest.

py -m u2ue --project <game> tool ue_headless_selftest.ps1

Nothing launches: Assert-UeHeadless reads only its arguments and the PATH. A clean launch must pass, and R1 to R6 must each throw its own rule (R6 on a Git Bash PATH); each case sets its own PATH, so the result does not depend on the shell that started it.

Audio: no speakers, and no silent mix

A headless game run opens the machine's real audio device unless told otherwise: on the reference port (2026-10-05) a run's sounds played into the owner's headset while they worked, and a recording of the master submix caught 0.77 s of a 23 s run. -DeterministicAudio loads the non-realtime renderer: each tick renders its own delta, nothing reaches a speaker, a recording follows the game clock. The second trap is inside the mixer: the engine's BaseEngine.ini sets [Audio] UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=0.0, a headless run is never focused, so it mixes at volume 0 (the port's voices captured at a peak of 0.000000). -ini:Engine:[Audio]:UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=1.0 fixes it. A third: the engine's own submix recording stops when a silent submix disables itself, so the toolkit's audio plugin captures through a listener that keeps it rendering (below). Add -UseFixedTimeStep -FPS=60 when a capture's timeline must follow the game clock, and leave -DeterministicAudio out of an attended run. A silent run's log says Using Audio Hardware Device Non-realtime Renderer.

Detached launches and the shell's timeout

A shell tool - an agent's, a CI runner's - usually has a timeout, and stopping a task stops its whole process tree. On the reference port (2026-10-06) a full effect build ran about 70 minutes under a tool limit of 60: at 60 minutes the tool stopped the task and its UnrealEditor-Cmd child died with it - 64 of 68 keys rebuilt, the record never finalised, the resave never run. The runner's watchdog was never the limit; the tool's timeout was. So:

  • Compare the two limits before any long launch, and give the shell tool the larger one.
  • Cut long work into chunks that fit. The effect build builds a chunk of keys per run (fx17_build.ps1 -MaxSeconds, 6600 s by default) and keeps each chunk's record. It keeps a key's previous system aside until the new one is saved, and puts back any that a killed run never replaced, so no key is left with no asset.
  • Check that a run finished. A build killed by its own watchdog can still look finished (58 of 68 keys, the resave then saving the ten stale systems as current, 2026-10-06). Compare the record's key count with the keys asked for; u2ue trial names every key not built and calls the trial PARTIAL.

Two PowerShell traps hide a stage that never ran. Select-Object -First N stops every upstream command once it has N objects: a build piped into Select-Object -First 1 printed its result, exit 0, and the resave after it never ran (2026-10-06). And every uncaptured expression in a function is output, so $rec = Build swallows its log lines; print through Write-Host.

What a headless run cannot prove

A script never moves a mouse: every scripted battle on the reference port passed while a click in the attended editor picked nothing. A -game run never stops Play-In-Editor: an object kept alive past a session crashed the editor on Stop while every headless proof was green ("UnrealSharp traps", below). Attended play stays part of acceptance.

Editor scripting limits

The converter and the effect instruments are Python scripts run inside the editor (UnrealEditor-Cmd <project> -ExecutePythonScript=<script>, through the runner). Four limits, each recorded in vfxport/README.md's trap list, shape all of them:

  • -run=pythonscript asserts: the Niagara conversion API needs a real editor process with Slate (Assertion failed: CurrentBaseApplication.IsValid()).
  • -ExecutePythonScript quits when the script returns, so nothing that needs the tick loop ever runs.
  • The editor world does not tick actors. A Niagara component there never simulates - verified with a stock engine system as the control, equally blank. Niagara simulates only in Simulate or Play-In-Editor, or when advanced explicitly.
  • The CascadeToNiagaraConverter plugin must be enabled, or FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary does not exist.

Every instrument writes its answer to a JSON record beside its log, and the verb judges that record.

How the read-back advances a system

effects_tools/u1e_color_size_readback.py (run by u2ue read and a trial's read step) needs no tick loop. For each built system it finishes every pending compile (Editor.AsyncAssetCompilationFinishAll), spawns a fresh component in the editor world (NiagaraFunctionLibrary.spawn_system_at_location, at (0, 0, 100000) unless U1E_RB_XF moves and turns it) and activates it once, the game's path. Then, per frame, it calls NiagaraSimCacheFunctionLibrary.capture_niagara_sim_cache_immediate(cache, params, component, True, dt) - the True advances the simulation by dt (1/60 s, unless U1E_RB_DT names the step Unity's probe took) before the capture - and reads every particle's attributes off the cache: position, velocity, colour, size, age, ids and the converter's own.

Each frame records whether its capture succeeded, because a system can be built and never simulate: on the reference port 19 built systems read 0 of 90 frames in every read-back since the night before ("SimCache Error: No valid simulation data") and no check flagged them - every check judges the emitters that produced data (2026-10-10). Later a read of 0 frames still exited 0, and two judges reported "0 judged" as if they had looked (2026-10-16). So the tool writes a capture summary beside its record, and u2ue read names every system that captured nothing or fewer frames than asked, and exits 1. The record is written one system at a time, because a single json.dump of a 673-key, 181-frame read held 55 GB of a 64 GB machine (2026-10-16); u2ue/readback.py parses it a system at a time.

U1E_RB_SPAWNSCALE is refused by name: fx.NiagaraGlobalSpawnCountScale exists in Unreal 5.7 only as a tooltip string, so setting it was a silent no-op (2026-10-13). Grep for a console variable's registration, never for its name in prose.

Built, compiled, simulating

  • Built: the converter saved the asset and reported no error (the record's BUILT). That says nothing about the Niagara compile, whose status is not reachable from Python.
  • Compiled for a game: finalize() only requests a compile, so run Editor.AsyncAssetCompilationFinishAll before the save. Even then a system built through a conversion context is saved with an EDIT compile, whose id differs from the one any process without an editor on it computes: every fresh process recompiled it on load, and the effect was blank at its first spawn. effects_tools/u1e_resave.py loads and saves each built system again in a fresh process, where the save waits for the non-edit compile, and reports one that still needs a compile after it. u2ue build runs it on what it built.
  • Simulating: only a read-back proves it; effects_tools/u1e_simulates_check.py is the gate.

Other measured limits of editor Python

  • Textures build asynchronously. A draw before a texture's platform data is built samples it as exactly 0; the tell is a size of 32 x 32 whatever the real one. Call Editor.AsyncAssetCompilationFinishAll immediately before every draw.
  • unreal.Rotator(a, b, c) is roll, pitch, yaw, while Vector and Quat are positional as expected. Always write unreal.Rotator(pitch=p, yaw=y, roll=r).
  • Failure by return value. set_parameter returns false for an unknown input or a wrong type (Chapter 10's v4_msg_gate.py), and LevelEditorSubsystem.new_level returns false when the map exists; neither raises. Check every return.
  • Shut down cleanly. A conversion context alive at exit asserts at shutdown (exit 3): call unreal.SystemLibrary.collect_garbage() at the end of the script.
  • An open editor locks existing packages. Re-saving an existing Niagara system returned false and a map could not be opened for writing, while a NEW package saved fine (2026-09-29). Re-test such a constraint per operation: the managed publish, assumed blocked by the same lock, ran with the editor open (below).
  • A preflight before the engine. u1e_py.ps1 runs effects_tools/u1e_preflight.py on the script and its local imports: a syntax error or an undefined name refuses the run (killed=PREFLIGHT) before minutes of Unreal start (2026-10-10).
  • Through the facade only. The effect tools refuse to run without the facade's U2UE_* variables, so a tool never runs with another project's paths. By hand: py -m u2ue --project <game> tool <file>.

The launchers

u2ue/verbs/_ue.py holds host_busy, native_path_ok, run_ps (one effect-tools PowerShell script with the project's environment, below normal priority), build_record and built_systems (the record records/u1e-build-<tag>.json and its BUILT systems), and clean_env: the project's environment with every inherited U1E_* and VFXPORT_* variable removed and named, so a verb runs the project's defaults - the build an acceptance rebuild makes - never a switch left over in the shell.

u2ue/ue_py.ps1 (-ScriptPath -UProject -Log -Headless [-MaxSeconds]) runs one Unreal Python script; u2ue/ue_game.ps1 (-UProject -Map -Log -Headless [-MaxSeconds]) one game start with -ExecCmds=quit, since the host's managed module works at StartupModule. Both print exit=4 with a reason when the runner, the project or the script is missing, and pass their environment on to the engine.

The game's own Unreal project: u2ue host

The reference port's Unreal project was made by hand. u2ue host is that hand work written as steps a stranger can re-run: it makes a game its own .uproject the way a customer would, so the run exercises project creation, the plugin install and the host template, and no other game's project is touched. The class is HostProject (u2ue/hostproject.py); each step is a Step, the command it runs and the line in its output that proves it.

The project file's block

"unreal": {
  "uproject": "<work>/unreal/<Name>/<Name>.uproject",
  "engine": "<Unreal Engine 5.7 install>",
  "content_root": "/Game/U2UE/<Game>",
  "host": {
    "template": "U2ueHost",
    "plugins": [{"name": "UnrealSharp", "source": "<git url or local clone>", "commit": "<sha>"}],
    "toolkit_plugins": ["U2ueAudio"],
    "sdks_root": "<AutoSDK root, or null>",
    "digest": {"entry": "<Ns>.<Class>.<Method>", "cases": ["<model>/<Model>.Core.Tests/DigestCases.cs"]}
  }
}

Every field is named, never defaulted. The .uproject sits in a folder of its own name, as a new Unreal project does. sdks_root is an AutoSDK root for a machine with no Windows SDK installed (below), null otherwise. digest.entry is a static method returning the digest's text (or an object with a Text() method), and cases the files that define it - the entry and cases u2ue digest runs on CoreCLR and on Unity's Mono (Chapter 6).

The template

u2ue/templates/unreal holds host/U2ueHost - the smallest C++ project a plugin builds in: a .uproject for engine 5.7 with the toolkit's audio plugin, one primary game module that does nothing else, the game and editor targets (BuildSettingsVersion.V6: the installed engine was built with those defaults, and a target that shares its build products may not differ), and a Config/DefaultEngine.ini naming /Engine/Maps/Entry as the game's default map and the editor's startup map - plus Plugins/U2ueAudio and the host classes U2ue.Unreal (both below). Once the game has its own level, point EditorStartupMap at it: a project that opens on an engine template map shows an empty world, and the game cannot be started without hunting for its map (the reference port's did).

The steps

py -m u2ue --project <game> host plan prints every step with its command and proof line, host status each step's record (PROVEN, NOT PROVEN, NOT RUN), and host <step> [--dry] runs one.

  1. create - py -m u2ue --project <game> host create writes the project from the template, the template's name replaced by the host's in every path and text file, the block's plugins added to the .uproject. Proves the files are written. Refused when the folder exists: create never overwrites.
  2. install - py -m u2ue --project <game> host install clones each external plugin (git clone --no-checkout, then the pinned commit) and copies each toolkit plugin without build products. Proves each .uplugin on disk and the clone's HEAD at the pin. The source must be a git repository; a local clone downloads nothing.
  3. compile - py -m u2ue --project <game> host compile runs Build.bat <Name>Editor Win64 Development -Project=<uproject> -WaitMutex, with UE_SDKS_ROOT from sdks_root. UnrealSharp's header-tool exporter writes the C# glue on the way, builds the plugin's managed bindings and generates an empty user solution. Proves Result: Succeeded.
  4. generate - py -m u2ue --project <game> host generate runs UnrealSharp's own RunUAT GenerateProject -ScriptDir=<plugin>/Build/Scripts -Project=<uproject> -ProjectFolder=<root>/Script/Managed<Name> -ProjectName=Managed<Name> -CreateModuleClass -GenerateSolution - what the editor's new C# project dialog runs, read off the plugin - with no editor and no dialog. (Without a managed project, a GUI editor raises a "No C# projects were found" modal at start.) Proves AutomationTool exiting with ExitCode=0 (Success).
  5. wire - py -m u2ue --project <game> host wire adds the model's layers and U2ue.Runtime as project references, the digest cases and three settings to Managed<Name>.csproj, copies the host classes in, and rewrites the module class to answer the digest. Proves each is written (the record counts them). Refused before generate, and a second time.
  6. publish - py -m u2ue --project <game> host publish runs RunUAT BuildUserSolution -ScriptsForProject=<uproject> -Project=<uproject> -OutputPath=<out> to Binaries/Managed, then to Binaries/Managed/net10.0 (steps publish, publish2). Proves, per output, the success line AND a log line ending in Managed<Name> -> <that output>/.
  7. run - py -m u2ue --project <game> host run starts the game once, headless, on the host's GameDefaultMap through u2ue/ue_game.ps1, U2UE_DIGEST_OUT naming <parity.dir>/logic-Unreal.txt. Proves U2UE DIGEST WRITTEN in its log AND the digest written after the run started. Then py -m u2ue --project <game> parity --require Unreal compares the runtimes (Chapter 6).

Each step writes <work.effects>/host/host-<step>.json (command, proof line, seconds, ok, evidence, time) with its log beside it. Exit 0 = the step proved itself, 1 = it ran and did not, 2 = refused before it ran. The Unreal steps (compile, generate, publish, run) are refused while the host is busy or the PATH fails the dotnet check; --dry prints the command (for create, every file) and runs nothing.

Judged by a line, never by an exit code

An exit code has lied, so the host's selftest requires a compile with Result: Succeeded to pass though it exited 1, and one that exited 0 without the line to fail. A success line alone can pass the wrong result too: BuildUserSolution's says nothing about where the assembly went (2026-10-16), so a publish also needs Managed<Name> -> <its output>/ to END a log line - a substring test passes Binaries/Managed/ on a publish to Binaries/Managed/net10.0/, which the selftest caught. The run is judged by its line and by the digest's time, so a digest left by an earlier run is never this run's.

What wire writes, and why

  • EnableSourceControlManagerQueries false: an assembly that depends on git's HEAD changes its MVID on every commit (measured on the reference port), and the MVID is what proves a publish (below).
  • ShouldUnsetParentConfigurationAndPlatform false: without it a Release publish builds references from outside the solution in Debug (measured, the same project).
  • Nullable disable: the host classes are written with nullable annotations off and the generated project turns them on - 16 nullable warnings on the second game's host and nothing else (2026-10-16); 0 after.
  • The module class: at StartupModule, only when U2UE_DIGEST_OUT names a file, it calls the digest entry, writes the text and logs U2UE DIGEST WRITTEN <path> (<n> lines); an editor session that names no file is untouched. Pure C# there needs no world, but nothing that spawns may run there: managed classes are registered later (a measured crash on the reference port).

Measured: the second game's host

The second game's host was made with these steps, from nothing, on 2026-10-16. From its records:

step seconds evidence
create 0.0 6 files written
install 0.9 UnrealSharp at its pinned commit; the audio plugin copied
compile 254.6 Result: Succeeded
generate 3.1 AutomationTool exiting with ExitCode=0 (Success)
wire 0.0 2 references (the model's one layer, U2ue.Runtime), 1 case file, 4 host classes, the module class
publish 4.8 the success line and Managed<Name> -> .../Binaries/Managed/
publish2 4.4 the success line and Managed<Name> -> .../Binaries/Managed/net10.0/
run 38.6 U2UE DIGEST WRITTEN .../logic-Unreal.txt (642 lines)

The stamps run from 22:29:49 (create) to 22:38:58 (run): about nine minutes, most of it the C++ compile. parity --require Unreal then exited 0, the Unreal digest byte for byte the headless CoreCLR digest (both runtimes are CoreCLR), and the four host classes had compiled against that host's own UnrealSharp - the template's proof.

py -m u2ue.verbs.host --selftest runs create, install and wire for real in a temporary folder (the real template, a local git plugin with two commits so the pin can be told from the head, the real model's projects) and the Unreal steps through a fake launcher: every judgement and refusal checked, no engine started.

Managed C# in Unreal (UnrealSharp)

UnrealSharp runs the game's model and the host classes as C# inside Unreal. The managed project is Script/Managed<Name>/; the engine loads the published assemblies from Binaries/Managed or Binaries/Managed/net10.0.

Publish to both folders, and prove what runs

Both folders were populated on the reference port and the engine may load either; a publish to one left the other holding the old assemblies (2026-09-29). So every publish runs twice, once per folder. -ScriptsForProject is required, or RunUAT answers "Failed to find command BuildUserSolution", and BuildUserSolution publishes Release (2026-09-30: the published assembly was byte-identical to bin/Release/net10.0 and to no other configuration).

A file's size and time prove nothing about an assembly: both drift between configurations while the code is identical. The witness is the assembly's MVID, from its PE metadata. The reference port's ue_publish_gate.py builds the published configuration fresh and compares, per assembly, the fresh MVID with the published one on each path, requires both paths identical, reads markers from the shipped file itself (an edit never published cannot satisfy it), and checks the run's own witness. Its legs name the reference port's assemblies, so it is the method to copy, and u2ue check does not run it (its selftest launches Unreal).

The run's witness is the lesson that cost most. An artifact with a new time and a hash equal to its headless reference read exactly like a proof arriving - and came from the owner playing their level in an attended editor on the OLD assembly (2026-09-30). A matching hash is not evidence that the run ran your build. So the reference port's run writes a manifest when it arms, naming the assembly it is bound to, and the gate proves an artifact only against that. host run applies the smaller form: the digest must be written by this run.

Then prove it runs, not only that it built - host run, or on the reference port a headless battle (32 s, its logs byte-identical to the headless reference, 2026-09-29). Freeze the managed sources from the publish until that proof passes: the MVID check rebuilds the current source, so an edit made during the proving run fails it, correctly, and costs a whole republish (2026-10-12).

Automatic hot reload OFF

UnrealSharp's editor watches the managed C# and by default (OnScriptSave) recompiles the moment a file changes. A tool that writes managed code continuously - a model extraction, a code generator - lands a reload in a mid-write instant: the compile fails, and the editor can wedge. On the reference port it stopped responding and grew from 14.6 GB to 19.9 GB, and the game could not be started (2026-09-29). The compile errors were a lie about the code: a type reported missing dozens of times sat in its file, and dotnet build reported 0 errors minutes later. Two unrelated tools hit the same window within minutes. The fix, in the host's Config/DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini:

[/Script/UnrealSharpEditor.CSUnrealSharpEditorSettings]
AutomaticHotReloading=Off

Its values are OnScriptSave, OnEditorFocus and Off (the plugin's CSUnrealSharpEditorSettings.h). Tested the same evening: a managed file touched with the editor up, 0 hot reloads in 40 s, the editor responding. Hot reload still works when asked for; a half-written file just cannot take the editor down. With it back on OnScriptSave the rule is absolute: an open editor or a tool writing managed C#, never both. The safe-operation pillar of u2ue cycle reads this file in the project's host and goes red without the line. Since 2026-10-17 the host template writes it (u2ue/templates/unreal/host/U2ueHost/Config/DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini), and host create refuses to make a host whose Config lacks it (u2ue/hostproject.py; the host selftest plants a template without it). A host made before that date has only DefaultEngine.ini: add the file before its editor is opened while any tool writes managed code.

The editor watches only folders holding a .csproj under Script/ (read from the plugin's source), so a model outside Script/ can be edited and tested with the editor open; on save a file is only parsed, and only a SYNTAX error opens the blocking "C# Hot Reload Error" dialog. With hot reload off, three managed files landed and both publishes ran with the editor open (2026-09-30): "Processed dirty file" three times, no reload, no dialog, no assembly locked. The owner then restarts the editor, whose startup builds the solution from the current source; a manual hot reload would compile against the model loaded at start, and fail. The facade is stricter than the engine: host publish refuses while any Unreal runs, an open editor included.

When an editor wedged: the recovery order

In this order and no other:

  1. Stop the writer and close the editor - the tool's own stop (a trial: py -m u2ue --project <game> trial stop). Proves nothing writes any more: no file under Script/ or the model changes time. The editor must close, since the Unreal steps refuse while it runs.
  2. Test - dotnet test on the model's tests. Proves the code the editor will load is green.
  3. Build - dotnet build Script/Managed<Name>/Managed<Name>.csproj. Proves 0 errors, whatever the wedged editor said.
  4. Republish - py -m u2ue --project <game> host publish. Proves both outputs, each by its own line.
  5. Prove it runs - py -m u2ue --project <game> host run. Proves the digest written by this run.
  6. Restart the editor - only now, on the published build.

UnrealSharp traps

  • USTRUCT fields start zeroed from C#. The generated glue is a plain struct, so a C++ default (= -1) is documentation only: built from managed code the field arrives as 0 unless set. On the reference port every UI draw silently changed its colour decode that way (2026-10-02).
  • Glue names. A bool bFoo becomes Foo; when that collides with another property the generator skips one of them, with no error.
  • A missing binding is not proven by a document grep. UnrealSharp.xml lists member names but not return types, and missed whole classes the glue has (347 key names, 0 matches, 2026-09-30). Reflect over copies of the published assemblies (never the live Binaries), or compile a scratch project against the plugin's UnrealSharp.Shared.props - as dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal does for the host classes - and prove the check fails on a planted wrong call.
  • The garbage collector sees only engine-side references. A texture kept in a C# dictionary was purged over several frames and the run crashed reading it; IsValid() does not help in that window (2026-10-01). Hold every asset a managed cache keeps across frames through a strong object pointer (the engine's TStrongObjectPtr); a plain C# property on a managed class is invisible to the collector too. Add -ExecCmds="gc.TimeBetweenPurgingPendingKillObjects 0.5" -LogCmds="LogGarbage Verbose" to a headless run to reproduce such faults on demand: a 6-minute intermittent crash became a 32-second deterministic one.
  • Never root a world object. A widget rooted for the life of the process crashed the editor when Play-In-Editor stopped (the engine asserts on a session object that survives teardown), 2026-10-01. Root only assets; tear views down in EndPlay.
  • Noise. Property generator is not initialized at shutdown is logged when no managed class declares a [UProperty] (the plugin's source). It matters only before the run's verdict, or once a class has a [UProperty].

C++ builds and the SDK root

UnrealBuildTool needs a Windows SDK and a toolchain. A machine with neither fails at once with Platform Win64 is not a valid platform to build (2.5 s on the reference machine, which had no Windows SDK installed at all; 2026-10-03). An AutoSDK folder holds both: set UE_SDKS_ROOT to it in the process that runs Build.bat only - never as a machine or user variable, never by installing an SDK, which needs elevation. host compile sets it from unreal.host.sdks_root. Before reporting an SDK gone, read UnrealBuildTool's backup logs (Log-backup-*.txt, in its folder under the user's local application data) for where the last good build found one.

A project copy of an engine plugin cannot see the engine's Internal headers, which are shown only to modules of their own scope or marked as engine modules (C1083 Cannot open include file, 2026-10-09): add the one Internal folder to the copy's PrivateIncludePaths, checking every include first so one build finds them all.

The runtime libraries the port links

U2ue.Runtime

u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime targets netstandard2.1 (Unity 2021 and later can load it) and net8.0 (the tests and the hosts), and references nothing engine-shaped. Chapter 6 shows a host using it; what each type stands in for:

type in place of
UnityClock Time.deltaTime (the real step clamped to the project's Maximum Allowed Timestep, times TimeScale), unscaledDeltaTime (unclamped), frameCount, Time.time
Coroutines, Handle, Wait StartCoroutine, StopCoroutine, StopAllCoroutines, WaitForSeconds, WaitForSecondsRealtime
UnityFrame the player loop's order: every Update by execution order, the coroutine phase, every LateUpdate
Platform (ILog, ITextAssets, IKeyValueStore, IFileStore, IJsonCodec<T>, IRandomSource, SeededRandom) Debug.Log, Resources.Load<TextAsset>, PlayerPrefs, the save file, JsonUtility, UnityEngine.Random with its bounds
PlaybackQueue<TEvent>, IPresenter<TEvent> no Unity type: an instant model's events shown one per tick, only while the view is idle
Digest, FloatBits no Unity type: one runtime's answers as u2ue parity reads them, floats as bit patterns
TrailLaw TrailRenderer's points and drawn vertices, as measured

UnityClock's maximum step is a constructor argument, never a constant: it is the project's own (py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from ProjectSettings/TimeManager.asset --class 5). PlaybackQueue refuses a history that shrinks, where the code it was extracted from skipped one silently: a shorter history is a different model or a reset.

dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests runs headless: the clock, coroutine, frame, random, bit, digest and queue rules, the trail law replayed against Unity 6000.3's own play-mode bake (a wrong trail time must fail it). It references only the toolkit, so it builds on any machine. The parity test that steps one set of coroutine scripts - a stall past the maximum step, a hit-stop, a waiter, a nested routine, a stop - on the reference port's own measured runner and on the library, and requires identical logs, is u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.OriginTests: it references the reference port's presentation project, so it builds only where that project is on disk, and the release leaves it out (split 2026-10-17; 22 + 2 tests, the same 24 as before).

U2ue.Ui

u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Ui (net10.0) is the generic part of the UI converter, compiled from the ui/ part's sources with no game reference. It stands in for uGUI and TextMesh Pro on a converted screen, ported line for line from the packages' source and held to Unity's captures, so the Unreal side only loads the textures and submits the frame: UiLayout (the anchor solve, the layout groups, ContentSizeFitter; a grid layout or an aspect-ratio fitter refused), UguiMesh (the vertex stream uGUI hands a CanvasRenderer), UiFrameBuilder (one draw per CanvasRenderer, in Unity's order), UiRaycaster and UiSelectables (the hit order, the colour transitions and the click), and TmpLayout (TextMesh Pro's layout, held to TMP's own output at float32 bit equality on every captured text), among others.

py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test runs U2ue.Ui.Tests, the converter's tests that touch no game type, compiled against the library alone. The release plan's N10 record: 398 passed alone, and a planted transform defect failed 264. The same record names a gap: no captured screen holds a rotated node, so a planted rotation defect fails none of them.

U2ue.Unreal and U2ueAudio

u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal holds the host classes AU2ueFrameActor, UnrealPointer, UnrealCameraRig and UnrealPlatform.cs (Chapter 6 says what each does). dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal compiles them against a real UnrealSharp (U2UE_UNREALSHARP); the N8 record: 0 warnings, 0 errors, and a planted wrong binding failed with CS1061.

u2ue/templates/unreal/Plugins/U2ueAudio plays the PCM a port renders at run time (Unity's AudioClip.Create and SetData) as 2D voices, the float samples unconverted (UU2ueAudioBridge.PlayPcm), and captures what the mixer rendered into a float WAV through a listener that keeps the main submix rendering. Its self test is the console command u2ue.audio.selftest <wav> (a 440 Hz tone), judged by selftest_judge.py (correlation, pitch and length on every channel; its own --selftest makes a wrong pitch, silence, a truncated tone and noise each fail). selftest_run.ps1 builds the minimal host with the plugin and runs it headless: the build is recorded (95 s, the N11 record), the headless play not yet (Appendix B).

Build, read, photo

The three Unreal verbs of the effect route (Chapter 8). Each refuses while the host is busy, removes and names inherited U1E_* and VFXPORT_* variables, runs its tools from native PowerShell below normal priority, and is judged by what its run wrote.

u2ue build

py -m u2ue --project <game> build [--keys FILE] [--tag TAG] [--batch N] [--no-resave] [--dry]

The keys are every READ key of the project's resolve that has an IR file, or the list in FILE. Then:

  • effects_tools/fx17_asset_names.py writes the asset-name table (names two different Unity files would share) to records/asset_names.json; a failure stops the build.
  • fx17_build.ps1 builds the keys in one headless run with batched compiles (--batch 12 by default; the cap 450 s a key, at least 2400 s), keeping records/u1e-build-<TAG>.json with each key's verdict. No record is exit 1.
  • Unless --no-resave, the fresh-process resave of only the systems this build made (U1E_RESAVE_ONLY) into <work.effects>/u1e-resave.json - not the build script's own -Resave, which resaves the whole content root (about 70 minutes for the reference port's 672 systems).

Exit 0 only when the build exited 0 and (unless --no-resave) every built system was resaved without error.

u2ue read

py -m u2ue --project <game> read [--tag TAG] [--frames N] [--dry]

Every BUILT system of records/u1e-build-<TAG>.json is read frame by frame (above; 90 frames at 1/60 s by default) into records/rb_<TAG>_<N>.json with its capture summary; a system that captured no frame (a build never resaved reads nothing) or fewer than asked is named, and the verb exits 1. Only the systems and the frame count are passed: a read at another step, moved or repeated, is a trial's (u2ue trial's read step takes dt).

u2ue photo

py -m u2ue --project <game> photo [--tag TAG] [--times 0.1,0.3,0.6,1.0] [--dry]
  • effects_tools/u1e_fx_photo.py draws each BUILT system at each time into photos/unreal/<leaf>_t<ms>.png: spawned in the editor world, advanced by the same sim-cache capture the read uses, photographed by a scene capture that renders only that component from a fixed pose, sky, fog and clouds off. Each system first gets a background frame with nothing in it, which must be black - that is what makes a frame comparable - and warm-up passes come first, because a translucent material still compiling draws nothing.
  • effects_tools/u1e_photo_sheet.py lays each system's Unity frames above its Unreal frames into photos/sheets/<leaf>.png, printing beside each only what the frame is (lit pixel count, the lit area's centre and extent), so an empty or displaced frame is named before anyone opens the sheet.

The run is judged by its capture (u2ue/capture.py), never by the tool's exit: a system with no judgeable frame, or a frame asked for and not written by THIS run, is named, and a system never captured fails the verb. The selftest fakes runs whose exit is 0 every time and requires exit 1 for a system that raised, a frame never written and a run that wrote no result.

The pairing. Unity's frames come from vfxport/unity_probe/EffectPhotoProbe.cs, run in the game's own editor in a measurement window (Chapter 9): the prefab at the origin in a preview scene, every top-level system's automatic random seed off so each draws from its own fixed seed, stepped at 1/60 s (the game's frame) to each time, rendered from (0, 4, -7) looking at (0, 0.5, 0), vertical field of view 50, 512 x 512, on black. u1e_fx_photo.py converts that pose with the port's own axis map. The sheet pairs Unity's float-target frames (photos/unity_hdr) when they exist.

Like for like. Unity's reference camera renders no post-processing, so the Unreal capture leaves the tonemapper off: Unreal's filmic curve sends every display value under about 16/255 to 0, a faint halo's whole outer ring (2026-10-07). The frame must then be encoded as Unity's is: a render target made at run time is linear, so an 8-bit target held linear values as display bytes and every dim pixel read 5 to 13 times too dark. The capture renders to a half-float target, encoded as Unity's target encodes (clamp, sRGB, round).

A photo is one draw. Each frame is one draw of a random process on its own side: compare several frames and the read-back data before calling a route wrong, and label a frame that shows a capture artefact, never counting it (Chapter 10). A frame confirms what the data holds; it decides nothing. Open every sheet: a run that says ok has proved only that bytes were written.

A converter route is tried with py -m u2ue --project <game> trial run <spec.json>: the same steps from a data file, built into the trial's own content root with the route's switch on, one Unreal at a time, stoppable between steps (Chapter 8, Chapter 10).

First time on a new machine

Every item names the check that proves it.

  1. The engine is where the runner looks. $script:UeHeadlessExe at the top of scene_tools/ue_headless.ps1 is the one place an executable is named: point it at your install's Engine/Binaries/Win64/UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe. Check: Test-Path on it is True.
  2. Native PowerShell's PATH carries UnrealSharp's marker. In the PowerShell you will run the facade from, $env:PATH -split ';' | Where-Object { $_.Contains('Program Files\dotnet\') -and (Test-Path $_) } prints one entry.
  3. The .NET SDK. dotnet --list-sdks lists a 10.0 SDK: the managed project targets net10.0 (Chapter 3 lists the rest).
  4. The runner refuses each rule. py -m u2ue --project <game> tool ue_headless_selftest.ps1 prints PASS and exits 0.
  5. The Unreal-side selftests pass with no engine. py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only selftests passes; it runs the host, photo, read-back, capture and trial selftests among the rest (Chapter 20 lists them). The host selftest builds its cases from the second example project in u2ue/projects/, so that project's model must be on disk.
  6. The host is free. After extract (Chapter 4), py -m u2ue --project <game> build --dry prints the Unreal host: free.
  7. A Windows SDK, or an AutoSDK. py -m u2ue --project <game> host compile proves Result: Succeeded, or its log says Platform Win64 is not a valid platform to build: then name an AutoSDK root in unreal.host.sdks_root and run it again.
  8. The host, end to end. host plan, then each step from create to run. Check: py -m u2ue --project <game> host status shows every step PROVEN, and py -m u2ue --project <game> parity --require Unreal exits 0.
  9. The host classes match this UnrealSharp. With U2UE_UNREALSHARP set to the host's Plugins/UnrealSharp, dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal reports 0 errors.
  10. Hot reload is off before the host's editor is opened while any tool writes managed code. Check: the host's Config/DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini holds AutomaticHotReloading=Off under [/Script/UnrealSharpEditor.CSUnrealSharpEditorSettings].
  11. Long launches fit. Check: the shell tool's timeout is at least the launcher's -MaxSeconds.
  12. Runs are silent. Check: a headless game run's log says Using Audio Hardware Device Non-realtime Renderer, never a real device.

16. Test-driven porting

A port has something most software never gets: a finished specification that runs. The Unity game already does everything the port must do, so every test in a port asks one kind of question - does the port do, here, what Unity does here - and every expected value can be READ from the game's files or MEASURED from Unity. This chapter is the discipline that turns that into a method, and ends with the procedure for one newly ported rule.

Chapter 10 holds the verification procedures (the gates, proving a route offline, conformance over every key, looking at photos); this chapter points there instead of repeating them. Chapter 9 is how a Unity rule is measured, Chapter 6 the game-code method these tests serve, Chapter 12 how a selftest is registered.

What makes a test a port's test

  • Its expected value comes from Unity. It is READ (from the game's code or data, with the file and line) or MEASURED (from a Unity run, with the run named). A value typed from memory tests the memory; a value copied from the port's own output tests the port against itself.
  • It can fail. It has been seen to fail on a planted wrong answer. Until then a green result says nothing: a check that has only ever passed cannot be told apart from one that is switched off.
  • It says what it examined. A test that judged nothing reports that it judged nothing, and that report is a failure, not a pass.

The Unity Test Runner is not a layer

Run from outside, Unity's Test Runner launches a second, full Unity Editor that imports assets, takes the foreground window on every assembly reload and throws modal progress dialogs; on the reference port its owner could not use the machine while one ran. A subset run starts the same Editor, so it is not a smaller violation.

So the toolkit's Unity test command (my_unity.py) refuses, exit 3, while .UNITY_TESTS_DISABLED exists at the toolkit root, and pillar 10 of the cycle checks every cycle that the file is still there. A test that truly needs a live Editor - a real scene, AssetDatabase, UnityEditor.* - stays unrun, the report says so, and the owner decides. "Compile-verified headlessly, suite not run" is an honest report; "it works", from a test that did not run, is not.

The layers, cheapest first

flowchart LR
  A["dotnet test: the model's rules"] --> B["headless_nunit: Editor-folder tests"]
  B --> C["typecheck: Unity still compiles"]
  C --> D["parity + digest: the same bits on every runtime"]
  D --> E["conform: every key on numbers"]
  E --> F["photo: LOOKED at, last"]
layer command a pass proves it cannot prove
pure rules dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests a moved rule gives Unity's value on CoreCLR Mono's bits; that Unity still compiles
Editor-folder tests py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test <file> the test passes on the project's freshly compiled code, no Editor anything that needs UnityEditor, AssetDatabase or a scene
typecheck py typecheck.py the Unity project compiles as Unity would compile it that anything behaves
parity py -m u2ue --project <game> parity every runtime agrees by the bit, or differs only where characterised that the rule is right - only that it is the same
Unity's Mono py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run ... Unity's own runtime gave these bits, no Editor that the Editor would, until digest faithful measured it
conformance py -m u2ue --project <game> conform ... each key's built asset computes what Unity's does, per emitter how it looks; what the probe was blind to
photos py -m u2ue --project <game> photo once LOOKED at, the frames confirm the numbers anything, on their own

Pure rules: dotnet test

The game's rules move into an engine-free model (Chapter 6), and a moved rule is first tested in the model's own test project: <Model>.Core.Tests, written by u2ue scaffold, NUnit on net8.0, one test per moved rule, its expected value the one the Unity build gives. Nothing opens, and the model's gates (u2ue check --only model) have already kept the engine out, so the test tests the rule.

The toolkit's runtime library is tested the same way, and its tests show the shape to copy:

dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests

In the reference port's cycle of 2026-10-17 that was 24 tests in 14.5 s, the build included. TrailLawTests replays the TrailRenderer law against Unity's play-mode bake - 72 frames, 15 baked meshes, every point and vertex compared - and the same file carries the replay's plant: A_Wrong_Time_Fails_The_Replay runs the frames with a trail time of 0.45 instead of 0.5 and requires a mismatch. A replay alone would pass a law that ignored its time.

A version trap: the scaffolded tests use NUnit 4 (4.0.1); Unity's NUnit is 3.x, and NUnit 4 moved Assert.IsNotNull and its family to ClassicAssert. A test that must also compile inside Unity is written to NUnit 3, which is why the headless runner pins 3.14.0.

Editor-folder tests: headless_nunit.py

Many Unity projects keep NUnit tests in an Editor folder, and most of them exercise data and logic, not the Editor. headless_nunit.py runs them with no Unity process:

py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test <Assets/.../Editor/XTests.cs>
py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test A.cs --test B.cs --filter "FullyQualifiedName~Resolver"

It compiles the runtime assembly from Unity's own compiler command line (the newest Bee Assembly-CSharp.rsp) with the Roslyn compiler Unity ships, the source list reconciled with the files on disk and nothing under Library/ written. It generates a net10 NUnit 3.14 project that compiles the given tests with UNITY_EDITOR defined, a pure managed shim standing in for UnityEngine.CoreModule (headless_nunit/UnityShimCore; Resources.Load answers null). It runs dotnet test, and HeadlessBoot.cs prints which assembly ran, with its MVID, while the tool checks its md5 against the compile - a stale build cannot pass quietly.

Exit 0 all passed, 1 a test failed, 2 nothing ran or the filter matched nothing, 3 an environment or compile failure. --no-compile reuses the last compile; --typecheck-editor also compiles the Editor assembly. Measured on 2026-09-01, four tests whose setup builds 277 units and the reference port's whole technique table: compile 4 s, run 15 s. A mutation run - the rule reverted, in a scratch copy, to the one it replaced - failed 3 of the 4 with 196 named mismatches.

What it cannot run fails loudly: TypeLoadException, MissingMethodException or FileNotFoundException, naming the member. A pure member is added to headless_nunit/UnityShimCore/Shim.cs; anything else needs a live Editor, and the test is left unrun and said so. "It lives in an Editor folder" is never by itself a reason to reach for the Unity runner. One trap when extending it: the fresh assembly is AC.dll, and the test project's bin keeps that name, so a mutation that swaps bin/Assembly-CSharp.dll swaps a file nothing loads and "passes" - read the printed MVID line every time. The tool names its Unity project and install folder in its own constants (it predates the project file), so another project edits them.

Does it compile: typecheck.py

Unity has already written complete compiler command lines to disk, the Bee .rsp files. typecheck.py reuses them with Unity's bundled Roslyn and compiles both assemblies, the Editor one against the runtime assembly it has just built, so the answer is Unity's own:

py typecheck.py                         # both assemblies (--editor: the Editor one only)
py typecheck.py --as-head [--keep <path>]
py typecheck.py --platform osx          # another editor platform's defines
py typecheck.py --extra <probe.cs>      # a file outside the project, into the Editor assembly
py typecheck.py --model-from-source     # against the model's source, not its installed DLLs

Exit 0 clean, 1 compile errors, 2 could not run the check, and the tool says in as many words that 2 is not a pass. Both assemblies took 42.2 s on the reference port (2026-10-17). --as-head asks whether a fresh checkout would compile: pending edits are swapped for their head revision and uncommitted files dropped (read from Unity Version Control, cm status), --keep keeping named paths as if checked in; the reference port once shipped a reference to four files never checked in, and this is the check for that. --platform compiles the other side of an #if UNITY_EDITOR_WIN block; --extra verifies a probe before it is dropped into an open Editor; --model-from-source refuses a run that did not swap each model DLL exactly once.

It proves the code builds, not that it behaves, and its last line says so. One honest gap, as of 2026-10-17: typecheck.py carries no planted selftest (--selftest-head-has proves only its head listing), and the cycle's pillar 4 row typecheck.py --selftest runs the full typecheck, because the tool reads no --selftest flag. That row proves the project compiled that day, not that the typecheck can fail.

The same bits on every runtime: u2ue parity

A rule that passes on CoreCLR can still answer differently on Unity's Mono. Chapter 6, step 7 is the method, with the reference port's real output. Each runtime writes <parity.dir>/logic-<Engine>.txt - a digestVersion=N line, then one key=value row per case, every float as its float32 bit pattern - and u2ue parity compares every row across every runtime found:

py -m u2ue --project <game> parity                       # exit 0 agree, 1 a row differs, 2 refused
py -m u2ue --project <game> parity --require Unreal      # refuse unless Unreal's digest is there
py -m u2ue --project <game> parity --characterise        # write the allowance from the digests on disk

Bits, not text: Mono prints a float in the old 9-digit round-trip form and .NET the shortest one, so identical bits spell two ways; as text, an early pilot of the reference port reported 230 mismatches that did not exist. The allowance, <parity.dir>/logic-allowance.json, keeps parity a test, not a list of excuses: a differing row is red unless the allowance pins that row to its exact bits and to one ULP, so a new row, a moved value or a wider gap stays red, and --characterise refuses any gap wider than one ULP (logic_diff.py's selftest proves all four refusals). The reference port's 35 characterised rows are all Mono keeping float intermediates wider, which ECMA-334 permits; the fix (explicit float locals) moves Unity's own values by one ULP, so it waits on the owner. Characterising needs a measured cause; it never turns a gate green.

The trap that costs most: the cases' inputs must be exact on every runtime - integer arithmetic, each written to the sheet. On the second game's first slice, inputs made with float maths produced 177 false differences in 321 rows; with exact inputs, the true difference was 2.

Unity's answer with no Unity: u2ue digest

Parity needs Unity's digest, and the Editor is the expensive place to get it. u2ue digest gets it from Unity's own runtime, with nothing opening and nothing taking focus:

py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Cases.Build> --cases <Cases.cs> [--refs X.dll ...] [--dir DIR]
py -m u2ue --project <game> digest faithful

run compiles the cases (a static method returning the digest text or a U2ue.Runtime.Digest) twice: for CoreCLR (logic-Headless.txt, the runtime an Unreal host uses) and with that Unity version's own csc.exe, run on its mono-bdwgc.exe (logic-UnityMono.txt), by default against the model built for netstandard2.1, into parity.dir. logic-UnityMono.provenance.json names the Mono and whether it is MEASURED faithful to the Editor for this Unity.

That label is the point: Unity's Mono is Unity's runtime, not the Editor. digest faithful runs, on standalone Mono, the cases the Editor's own runner compiled and compares them with the digest that Editor wrote (the project's mono.faithful block). On the reference port, Unity 6000.3.16f1, all 383 rows were identical, including the 35 where Mono and CoreCLR differ - measured 2026-10-16 and again 2026-10-17 (shared/conformance/mono-standalone-facts-6000.3.json); on a Unity with no such measurement the provenance reads UNMEASURED. The selftest proves the stand-in both ways: standalone Mono must reproduce the Editor's digest AND must NOT match the CoreCLR one, or the comparison could not tell the runtimes apart.

Every key on numbers: u2ue conform

For assets that simulate - effects, today - this layer compares Unity's state with what the built Unreal asset computes, over every key, on numbers; Chapter 10 has the procedure. It comes after parity because it spends both shared resources (a window in the owner's editor and the one headless Unreal), and its diff over the reference port's 673 keys reads a 1.7 GB read-back, so the cycle reads the newest stamped report instead (conform latest, 0.6 s on 2026-10-17) and refuses, as STALE, one another judge made.

It comes before photos because it sees what a photo cannot: one class-wide read found every non-prewarmed burst born one warm-up tick late, 121 of 121, after nights of per-effect photos had not. Emitters pair by their system's file id, never by name - names repeat inside a prefab, and a pairing by name once produced a finding that did not exist. Its selftest's 28 cases (2026-10-16) include a planted 0.03 s late birth and an emitter missing on one side, which must be named, never dropped. And a data layer can be blind: the first case probe, restarting the simulation for each sample, never drew a sub-emitter of a sub-emitter (0 of 284); stepped the way the game steps (conform cases --step 1/60), it drew them (Chapter 10, step 6).

The picture, last: u2ue photo

py -m u2ue --project <game> photo [--tag TAG] [--times 0.1,0.3,0.6,1.0]

Photos run last, and are never skipped. Last, because a metric over pictures can reward the wrong thing: on the reference port, measured 2026-08-22, a render in which the whole scene went black scored better on a pixel parity metric (a foreground score from 34.0 to 50.0), because dark geometry stopped hiding a bright backdrop; only reading the image caught it. Never skipped, because data can be right about a worthless result: a generated level once passed every file-level check while carrying the same 145 prefab instances as an empty level, where the hand-made level it was meant to match carried 1722.

So the data proves itself first; the metric and the image confirm; neither diagnoses alone. A photo run is judged by its capture (u2ue/capture.py), never its exit - judged by its exit alone, a photo step could read "ok" for a run that drew nothing - and a sheet is evidence only once LOOKED at. A route that returned ok proved bytes were written; open the file.

Why the order matters

  • Cost. The first three layers need only the machine (the second and third read Unity's install and the project's last Unity compile, with no Editor running); conformance needs the owner's editor and the one headless Unreal; photos need the Unreal and a person's eyes. A rule that would have failed dotnet test in seconds must never be what fails a conformance run hours later.
  • Trust. Numbers before pictures: a picture can pass on a metric that rewards the wrong thing, and a look covers one draw. Data that proved itself says what the picture should show. A skipped layer is not a passed layer.

Write the test first

The judge before its trial

A judge (u2ue/judge.py) holds a record - a read-back, a capture, a case record - to a measured rule or to Unity, and must fail on its plant. Chapter 9 gives the order for a measurement: the judge, its plants, then the bake. A converter route's trial keeps the same order, because a judge written after the data is fitted to the data and passes whatever happened.

Judges are read off the trial specs' judge steps (<lane>/trials/**/*.json), never listed by hand, so the list cannot drift from what runs:

py -m u2ue --project <game> judge             # each judge, the trials that run it, how its plant is proven
py -m u2ue --project <game> judge --prove     # runs each judge's --selftest; exit 1 when one fails or has no plant

--prove reads PLANTS (its --selftest refused its planted faults), DECLARED (a trial declares a plant for it), NO PLANT (it has only ever passed) or FAIL. A trial step declares a plant beside its judge:

{"judge": {"argv": ["{lane}/<route>/<route>_check.py", "{dir}/<read>.json"],
           "plant": {"argv": ["{lane}/<route>/<route>_check.py", "{dir}/<route-off read>.json", "--plant"]}}}

u2ue trial runs the judge, then the same judge on the record it must refuse - the route-OFF read, a planted shift - and a plant that passes FAILS the step by name. A plant the judge's own verdict already requires refused is declared with in_run. When this became a cycle check, on 2026-10-16, it found three judges that had only ever passed; each got a plant. On 2026-10-17 judge --prove read 7 judges, 0 without a plant.

A gate that has only ever passed

Every gate carries planted defects in its own --selftest, and the null case: an unperturbed input must PASS, or a gate that refused everything would pass its own plants. The headless NUnit runner's selftest is the pattern: a planted passing test exits 0, a planted failing test 1, a filter that matches nothing 2.

The most expensive failure is a check that passes without examining anything, because it turns "unknown" into "verified". Measured on the reference port: a test command printed None/None passed ... no regressions and exited 0 for a reply it could not parse; a fact-checker that matched only backticked names scored ordinary prose checked=0 and returned CLEAN; a read got 0 of 150 frames for all six systems of a trial, exited 0, and two judges then reported "0 judged" as if they had looked - which is why every read now writes a capture summary (u2ue/readback.py). The repair was never more checking. It was making each check state what it examined, so an empty examination reads as empty. An empty selection is a refusal, never a quiet skip.

Prefer an oracle from what the thing must do over a threshold. An ON/OFF comparison of a light-scattering effect once differed in 315k pixels; but that effect only ever adds light, and the signed difference was brighter in 152,782 pixels and darker in 155,186 - an even split, which is scene motion between two renders.

A plant must move what is judged

A plant proves something only if it changes the input the judge judges. On the reference port plants proved nothing because the check read its default file instead of the planted one (check which file it opened); because the planted value equalled the measured one in every case of the trial (a plant acts on what the judge actually found); because the code refused the plant's input before any engine call, so it tested the refusal, not the route; and because a patch was proven against a stub, while at run time a cache wrapper over the called function kept its old signature (run the selftest of whatever is installed over the callee).

Widening a gate, and proving it still fails

A port moves code on purpose, and a gate that walks one folder stops seeing what moved. When a gate's scope is widened, its plants are re-run and one is added inside the new scope; otherwise the widened gate has only ever passed where it now claims to look.

A selftest on synthetic input proves the matcher, not the aim. The no-toys gate (no_toys_gate.py, which refuses engine primitives standing in for real assets) plants primitives in temporary folders; no_toys_prove_failable.py copies the real adapter tree, plants one offender in the copy and scans it, proving the gate still walks the files that matter. A selftest of a gate is not a run of it, either: while the cycle ran only the manual gate's selftest, three generated chapters went stale unseen, until u2ue/manual/build.py --check joined the cycle (2026-10-16).

A new gate that refuses content also runs offline over the whole existing corpus before a long build relies on it. On the reference port a mesh-import gate proven on two files went into a build of about two hours and refused 3 of 46 meshes it should have passed; 7 emitters vanished from three effects. Checking all 46 offline took about two minutes. A refusal of content that drew correctly yesterday is the gate's bug until shown otherwise.

Mutation: does any test notice?

py -m u2ue --project <game> uml tests <Name> separates called inside a test, merely mentioned in a test file, and not present - and still says only mutation answers whether a test would notice a change. The mutation harness asks it directly:

py mutate/run_mutations.py

It copies the current pure rule files and their tests fresh from the project into an isolated test project on every run, so no open Editor sees a mutant. Each mutation is a row - the file, a label, the exact old text, the new text, and the claim the tests protect. It applies one row at a time, runs dotnet test, restores, and reports each as FAILED (caught), PASSED (survived), COMPILE-BREAK, NO-RESULT or ANCHOR-MISS, ending MUTANTS NOT CAUGHT n of m with each survivor's unchecked claim. The suite runs before any mutation and after restoring; both must pass, or the verdicts between mean nothing.

A rename is not a mutation - it only breaks the build, which every test "catches" for free - so every row changes behaviour and still compiles. An anchor that matches zero times or twice is an ANCHOR-MISS, counted as not caught: the harness refuses to guess. Its last recorded run (mutate/last_run.log, 2026-09-07) caught 13 of 13; the one before said 12 of 13 with an ANCHOR-MISS, because a timeline had grown from 11 beats to 13. The anchor was fixed, not the harness. The harness is the reference port's - its subject list, test list and source folders are written in the file, and a second game edits them. Add a row whenever you add a rule.

The console is the headless test

A compiler proves the code builds. The console proves it ran. On the reference port three faults in one session (2026-09-12) passed every other instrument - typecheck CLEAN, the model's suite 4104 of 4104, the player build with 0 errors - and each was obvious in Unity's console within one frame: a scene with broken prefabs put 79 errors on the tool that opened it; a grid row that lost its tiles threw an exception that emptied the board; a render pass that bound the backbuffer's depth produced 4020 errors and no rendering.

console_check.py reads a running Editor's console through the toolkit's bridge (Chapter 14), in one HTTP call, and reports only what is NEW:

py console_check.py --reset                      # mark everything seen, before the action
py console_check.py --label "what I just did"    # after it: exit 1 when NEW errors appeared
py console_check.py --all                        # ignore the watermark (--quiet: print only news)

A watermark (.console-watermark.json at the toolkit root) means the backlog is never re-read. Identical rows, numbers masked, collapse into one with a count, so 4020 per-frame errors print as one row. Unity's infrastructure noise (search index and LMDB locks, package warnings) is counted apart, so it can neither hide a regression nor trip the exit code; a new warning is reported but is not an error. Exit 0 nothing new, 1 new errors, 2 the bridge unreachable or refused - not a pass.

Use it as a gate: --reset, the action, console_check; new errors stop the work. Pair it with a Play cycle when a change touches rendering. Reading the console starts nothing and takes no focus; it needs an Editor already running.

A fresh record is not a fresh build. On the reference port a Unity-side recording was triggered after a model change, before the Editor's domain reload had settled. Unity re-recorded 17 s later on the OLD assembly: the recompile had failed on one access error (CS0122), so the Editor kept the old code. The record was newer than the DLL, every timestamp check passed, and the tests failed identically. console_check showed the compile error. The order since: typecheck.py before anything that recompiles, wait until the reload has finished, record, console_check, then the tests.

The cycle

Pillars and verdicts

u2ue cycle (u2ue/verbs/cycle.py, over u2ue/pillars.py) holds the toolkit to its promises when a work cycle ends or a report is about to be written. A pillar is one promise the product makes; a check is one command the toolkit already runs, and the rule that reads its output as a verdict.

py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle                 # every pillar; exit 1 when any pillar is FAIL
py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle --pillar 2 3    # only these; a partial run never becomes the baseline
py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle --dry           # list the pillars and checks; nothing runs
pillar the promise
1 AUTO-PORT every asset family that is not logic ports with no human step
2 AI LOGIC PORT Opus, pointed at a game through the skill, ports its logic
3 HUMAN ERGONOMICS every concept a named class; diagrams generated from the code and gated
4 AUTOMATION TOOLS SHIPPED the Unity and Unreal automation a port needs ships in the package
5 PROOF AND CONFORMANCE every judge has a plant that fails; conformance read from data
6 MEASURED KNOWLEDGE every Unity rule measured by a probe case, stored per Unity version
7 GENERIC, NOT ONE GAME adapters and project files, no hard-wired paths in the core
8 PACKAGING AND RELEASE a UPM package that installs into a fresh Unity and a fresh Unreal project
9 SPEED AND PROOF OF VALUE the porting speed and the percent-identical family, from records
10 SAFE OPERATION the toolkit never disturbs the person using the machine
11 RUN INFRASTRUCTURE pinned, resumable runs from data, stoppable between steps
verdict meaning
PASS the check ran and its rule holds
FAIL the check ran and its rule does not hold - red stops the cycle
HELD it fails ONLY in the way a recorded open decision of the owner's says it must; failing any other way is FAIL
ABSENT no check exists yet; never counted as PASS - it names the work that would build it

A pillar is FAIL if any check is FAIL, ABSENT if no check of it ran, otherwise PASS, with HELD checks shown beside it. Red stops the cycle with exit 1, and the record keeps 40 lines of the failing check's output - the lines saying FAIL, REFUSED, ERROR or Traceback first, then the end - so it says why without a re-run.

A plain Check passes on exit 0. A Held check names its decision and the failing lines it explains; every failing line must match them, and one more, or a failure that prints none, is FAIL - a new failure can never hide behind an old decision. A Trend reads a number and a direction it must not move in (the share of conforming emitters must not fall); the first cycle is the baseline, and a number not read is FAIL. An Absent check reads ABSENT with the work that would build it.

The record and the baseline

Each run writes <work.records>/cycle/cycle-<stamp>.json; a full run also writes cycle-latest.json, which the next cycle trends against. A trend that FAILED keeps the previous value as its baseline, marked baseline_held: writing the regressed value would make the regression the new bar. It happened - on 2026-10-16 a red run wrote 154 and 1362 over the 153 and 1361 it had just failed against.

The reference port's cycle of 2026-10-17 read 10 pillars PASS and 1 FAIL - pillar 8, generated blocks of the manual stale. Two checks read HELD on one open decision about an imported level's deliberate lighting: the scene fidelity gate, and its selftest's unperturbed case. Nine read ABSENT, each naming its work - a second game end to end in its own Unreal project among them.

What the cycle does not run

The cycle checks the toolkit against a project; it does not run your game's own tests. dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests and the project's parity are not cycle checks (pillar 2 runs the project's model gates, the runtime library's tests and the parity tool's selftest). Run them yourself; py -m u2ue --project <game> logic reads where the logic port stands, runs check --only model and parity, and names each test run it does not start as NOT RUN, with its command.

The selftest registry and u2ue check

Every tool's selftest is registered once, in u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.py: RUNS holds each tool, its folder and its exact command, read off the tool by hand. It held 107 entries on 2026-10-17; Chapter 20 lists them. A selftest that cannot run safely is in NOT_RUN with its measured reason - two: one corrupts and restores a plugin DLL an owner's open Unity editor loads, one launches the Unreal editor.

py -m u2ue --project <game> check                      # all four parts
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only selftests [--tool console_check.py ...]
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only gates         # the field gates over this project's IR
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only facts         # the measured rules' Unity versions against the project's
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only model         # layer_gate and host_gate on the engine-free model

The selftests run with no U2UE_, U1E_ or VFXPORT_ variable set - on the defaults their plants were written against - below normal priority, launching neither Unity nor Unreal; exit 1 when any fails. The row took 1458 s on the reference port (2026-10-17). py u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.py --project <game> [tool ...] runs the same list and records each exit, time and last lines in u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.json. The verb exists because nothing ran these before: its first survey found three selftests broken unseen and both field gates red.

Rules that keep tests honest

Never re-record a baseline to make a red gate green. A baseline, an allowance or a fingerprint is re-recorded only when the change it records is intended, with the reason committed beside it. The cycle enforces it for trends, parity for allowances; this rule does everywhere else.

A miss is UNKNOWN, never ABSENT. The toolkit's code readers are lexical: a call through an interface, a delegate, reflection or a UnityEvent wired in a prefab is invisible to them, and uml callers and uml tests print UNKNOWN when they find nothing. An ABSENT you write needs the level above: name the search that would prove it, and check the container (a field missing on a record may live on the group holding it), a second rule of the same shape, whether you actually ran the tool, and whether a later pass writes more.

Check whether the code moved before believing a red gate. A gate that walks only the Unity tree reports what the port moved into the model as ABSENT. On the reference port three gates did it in one day (2026-09-29): the class-model gate said a method "does NOT exist in the code (BOTH channels agree)" while it sat in the model - both channels walked one directory; another reported four abilities "NO LONGER CALLED ANYWHERE" whose calls had moved one hop; the requirements checker silently covered less each time an annotation moved. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml where <Name> walks the code roots and the model together.
