Then widen the gate and re-run its plants.

A call site is not coverage. A test can call a method in setup and assert on something else. Say "called from N test files", never "covered".

Re-run a red test in a file another worker just wrote. Compare its modification time with the clock and re-run before investigating. On the reference port a test failed identically three runs in a row while its owner had fixed the line a minute earlier; the next run was green. Never patch a live worker's file: record the finding with its file and line, and let the owner land it.

Snapshot suites when work lands concurrently. A suite that reads expectations from data at run time and compares them with code compiled earlier straddles any landing that changes both, so compare the failing area's sources and data with the compiled assembly's time before diagnosing. On the reference port twelve such failures were diagnosed as drift; an hour later the suite was green with no action taken. A compile break in a file saved a minute ago is the same: poll the build until it settles.

Test an agent, or a skill, by running it. u2ue/survey/skill_gate.py checks that every command a skill names exists and each step has a RUN and one DONE WHEN; it cannot see what a model does with the text. On the reference port a static audit of six generated agent definitions found two defects; running one on a bounded, read-only item found five. Grade the run's report against the definition, fix the generator, run it again.

Requirements and tests

// REQ: annotations

Every feature traces to a requirement through a // REQ: comment on the rule. check_feature_has_req.py scans the files or folders it is given and checks that each citation resolves:

py check_feature_has_req.py <file or folder> [...]      # exit 0 all resolve, 1 one does not
py check_feature_has_req.py <folder> --auto-stub        # a TODO stub per unresolved citation

A citation names a requirements file and line (which must exist and be substantive), a design document, or a spreadsheet tab, resolved against its cached copy. Engineer-owned tags (plumbing, feedback, implementation-only and their kin) pass, and so does an explicit statement that no requirement exists - the ABSENT half of READ-or-ABSENT, written down. An engineer tag citing a line now blank passes marked STALE and counted; --strict-lines fails it. An unresolved citation goes to the designer, and --auto-stub gives them a line to flesh out. --json writes the findings as data; --fix-anchors rewrites drifted line numbers (--dry-run first).

Two warnings. It reads only the paths you hand it, so hand it the model's folders too once annotations move: 259 lived in the reference port's model by 2026-09-29. And it is the reference port's own tool: its requirement sources are named in its constants, and it reads an indexed copy of the requirements before the file, re-synced with req_graph_sync.py after an edit. A second game points those constants at its own documents.

The discipline it serves: every new feature gets a test, linked to the commit that adds it and to its requirement; a feature with no requirement gets a stub, marked for the designer, before it merges.

The use-case model tests the documents

The toolkit's use-case model is read from its manuals, not written beside them, and measured against the code. Both tools are pillar 3 checks:

  • u2ue/survey/req_harvest.py builds the model from the manuals, skills, use cases, verb registry and pillars, each procedure parsed from its source (a skill's ### Step N. with DO, RUN and DONE WHEN; a chapter's numbered steps); a document it cannot read is refused, never guessed around. Its --selftest refuses a step with no DONE WHEN, an epic with no procedure, a procedure with no stated trigger, and a branch naming a step its procedure lacks - which is why this manual's procedures state their Trigger in the text.
  • u2ue/survey/usecase_gaps.py measures against two denominators. Against its own list a model always looks nearly complete. Against the source - every verb, project field, public runtime type, manual page, skill and pillar, READ from the code and files - it lists what no use case owns and prints USECASE COVERAGE n of m, which the cycle trends (130 items owned on 2026-10-17). Its --selftest plants a verb no step runs and a chapter never read; both must come back UNOWNED.

The class model gates

The class model comes first: a new concept gets a named class before code is written around it, and diagrams are generated from the code and gated, never hand-drawn and trusted.

  • The class-model gate, py -m u2ue --project <game> uml check --doc <use case model .md>, looks up every identifier the document names in the class model of the game's code roots and the model; a name the extractor lacks is asked of an independent text scan first. When the channels disagree it ABSTAINS and says where to settle it; it FAILS a name written as a call only when both agree it is absent. It also refuses a document with no PROBLEM STORY, no primary actor or no EPIC, and an epic of fewer than 3 or more than 11 steps. The key case of its selftest is CAN-THE-GATE-FAIL: a fabricated name must be refused.
  • The concept gate, u2ue/survey/concepts_gate.py, holds u2ue/CONCEPTS.md to the code: a row marked EXISTS must name path.py:Class, and that class must be in that file (read with Python's ast, nothing run). It prints CONCEPTS n of m EXIST (18 of 18 on 2026-10-17), which the cycle requires never to go down.
  • The design diagram, py u2ue/survey/design_diagram.py <out.mmd>, draws the toolkit's class diagram from its code alone; the cycle checks that it generates.

Procedure: a test for a newly ported rule

Scope: one rule of the game, moved into the engine-free model. Precondition: the model is scaffolded (u2ue scaffold) and its gates pass. Minimal guarantee: a step that cannot run is reported as not run, never as passed. Success guarantee: the rule has a test that was seen to fail, gives Unity's value by the bit on every runtime, cites its requirement, and the cycle reads PASS or HELD by a named decision. Trigger: a rule is about to move out of the Unity tree.

  1. Find the rule. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml where <Name> names its type, file and line - proof that the name exists. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml callers <Name> lists its candidate call sites; a miss is UNKNOWN.
  2. Read its inputs and Unity's answer. Constants from the code, with file and line; serialized values from the asset, py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from <Assets/...prefab> --script <ClassName>, never the C# initializer. The expected value is the one the Unity build gives, read from a record or measured (Chapter 9); if neither, stop and measure it.
  3. Write the test before the move. One NUnit test in <Model>.Core.Tests, its expected value from step 2, its source in a comment.
  4. Move the rule unchanged, and gate the model. A behaviour change is a separate, named decision. py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only model proves no engine namespace or platform member came with it.
  5. Run the test. dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests - green proves the moved rule gives Unity's value on CoreCLR. Not trusted yet.
  6. Make it fail on purpose. Change the rule's behaviour so it still compiles - a constant off by one, a comparison turned round - and rerun step 5: the test must fail with an assertion naming the value. Restore. For a standing proof, add the change as a mutation harness row and run py mutate/run_mutations.py: MUTANTS NOT CAUGHT 0 of n. A failure that is only a compile error proves nothing.
  7. Prove Unity still compiles. py typecheck.py (with --model-from-source when the Unity project uses the model's built DLLs) - exit 0 proves the Unity project still builds around the moved rule. Exit 2 is not a pass.
  8. Run its Editor-folder test, if it has one. py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test <Editor test.cs> - exit 0 proves it passes on the freshly compiled assembly; exit 2 means nothing ran.
  9. Answer the rule on both runtimes. Add its cases to the digest's case file, inputs exact and written to the sheet, and bump the digest's version. py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Cases.Build> --cases <Cases.cs> writes the CoreCLR and Unity Mono sheets with no Editor; the provenance says whether that Mono is MEASURED faithful.
  10. Compare them by the bit. py -m u2ue --project <game> parity - exit 0 proves every runtime agrees on every row. A one-ULP row is diagnosed and its cause measured; only then, by the owner's decision, parity --characterise pins it.
  11. Check the console, when an editor is running. py console_check.py --reset before the Unity side recompiles, then py console_check.py --label "<rule> moved" - exit 0 proves the Unity build ran with nothing new in its console. With no editor running, the step is reported as not run.
  12. Cite the requirement. A // REQ: comment on the rule, then py check_feature_has_req.py <the model's folder> - exit 0 proves the citation resolves; exit 1 goes to the designer.
  13. Draw the slice. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus <Type> draws it from the code, every member real; py -m u2ue --project <game> uml check --doc <use case model .md> proves every name the use cases use exists.
  14. See where the port stands. py -m u2ue --project <game> logic - each logic skill step DONE, NOT YET, JUDGED or NOT RUN, read from the records now.
  15. Close the cycle. py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle - every pillar PASS, or HELD by a named decision. A FAIL stops the work until it is fixed; it is never re-baselined.

Steps 1 to 8 spend no shared resource, steps 9 and 10 need no Editor, and step 11 only reads one that is already running.

17. Porting with Opus 5.5

u2ue is built to be driven by an AI model. The owner points Opus 5.5 at the game's logic through the toolkit's skills, and every other asset family ports itself. This chapter covers how the reference port was actually run, and the skills that keep a long session working. It covers how to keep the model's tokens down, and what was measured about running several agents at once. It also covers how the work is reviewed: the model is never trusted on its own word.

How the reference port was run

The reference port was done by one model, Opus 5.5, working in Claude Code over many sessions. Four things carried it from session to session. None of them is clever, and each one is there because its absence cost a day.

  • A project rules file, read at the start of every session. It holds the iron law (no guessing, no fallbacks, no toys, verify with both the data and the picture), the safety rules (never the Unity Test Runner, never the owner's live editor, one headless Unreal at a time), "fix the class, not the instance", and the rule that UML class diagrams steer the work.
  • One task list on disk. Every item is a line with an observable a stranger could re-check (DONE WHEN: ...). The session reads it at the start of every item, because a session cannot see its own context being compacted.
  • Memory notes, one fact per file. A trap is written down once, with its fix, so that the next session does not pay for it again. Two examples: a shell that rewrote the PATH so Unreal could not find .NET, and a heredoc that ate backslashes.
  • Skills. A skill is a packaged procedure that the model loads when the task matches it. The port used the owner's own:
  • a long-run skill: finish the list, never stop at a turn boundary, verify before reporting, and when blocked, solve it or ask, never drift sideways - the owner calls it the "don't stop" skill;
  • a senior-dev loop for backlogs: waves of work, one driver for a shared editor, and an assessment after each wave;
  • a use-case skill: use cases from the problem story, and a class model from the source, gated so that a name the code lacks fails. It also used the toolkit's own two skills. For the large fan-outs (the six writers of this manual's new chapters), the work ran as multi-agent workflows that the owner asked for.

The package ships the generic forms of what made this work (below). The owner's personal skills stay the owner's.

The four skills the package ships

skill what it is for read it when
u2ue/skill/u2ue-logic/SKILL.md port a game's C# into an engine-free model behind seams, slice by slice, each step with its command and its DONE WHEN the logic port (Chapter 6)
u2ue/skill/u2ue-port/SKILL.md port an effect gap by the route protocol: census, a switch that starts OFF, proof, trial, LOOK, flip with evidence an effect the converter refuses (Chapter 8, Chapter 13)
u2ue/skill/u2ue-lookup/SKILL.md answer code questions from the index and the class model, read the file last; choose the agent before starting one before reading any file to find something; before fanning out
u2ue/skill/u2ue-long-run/SKILL.md finish a long list: one list on disk, an observable per item, a re-check before any report "finish it all", and any time a session is about to report with items open

The skill gate (u2ue/survey/skill_gate.py, pillar 2 of the cycle) holds all four to the toolkit. A command a skill names must exist. A step written as ### Step N. must carry at least one RUN: line and exactly one DONE WHEN: line. A skill that sends the model hunting for a command that is not there fails the cycle.

Directing the model at a game

A session opens on where the port stands, never on a re-derivation:

py -m u2ue --project <game> logic          each step of the logic skill, judged by its own DONE WHEN; the step to take next
py -m u2ue --project <game> info           every path the project names, opened

What makes a prompt work, as it was learned on the reference port:

  • Name the observable. "Port this slice" ends when the model thinks it looks done. "Port this slice so that py -m u2ue --project <game> parity exits 0 and the slice's diagram resolves" ends when it does.
  • Give it the diagram, not a description. The logic skill's step 2 draws the class model of one slice before anything moves (py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus <TypeA> <TypeB>). The target diagram is the prompt: the model is asked to make it true, and the gate checks every name in it against the code. A prompt that carries a diagram cannot drift into a design the owner never saw.
  • Quote the owner's acceptance sentence at the top of the list. Then every item answers one question: does this move that line? Progress is measured against the owner's words, never against the model's own plan.
  • Forbid the plausible constant. A value that is not read is ABSENT, with the reason. The iron law is in the rules file because a model, when stuck, will otherwise supply a number that looks right.

Saving tokens: ask the index, read the file last

Anthropic's own guidance names the constraint: the context window fills up fast, and performance degrades as it fills (Best practices for Claude Code, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices). Every file the model reads to answer a question is context it cannot use for the port. The toolkit holds three indexes that answer such questions instead:

  • The catalogue: py -m u2ue find <words> searches the verbs, adapters, tools, documents, measured Unity rules, converter stages and routes, and prints each hit as path:line. Its selftest (py -m u2ue find --selftest) checks every source it reads.
  • The game's class model: py -m u2ue --project <game> uml extract, then uml where | ask | callers | tests <Name>. It is built from the game's own code roots, and from its engine-free model once one is scaffolded. A project with no code roots is refused, never pointed at a guessed folder (py -m u2ue.verbs.uml --selftest).
  • The requirements model's triples: every use-case step in Chapter 5 is a set of subject-relation-object facts, each citing the document and the line it was read from. The traceability in Appendix E is a walk over them.

On the reference port, a compiler-grade index of the game's Unity assembly was searched as well, through a local MCP server. It taught the rule that matters most about any index. A fresh rebuild, minutes old, held no rows at all for five symbols that had moved into the engine-free model, because it indexed one assembly and the port had moved code out of it on purpose. A miss is UNKNOWN, never ABSENT. Before you trust a miss, check what the index read and when.

The lookup skill (u2ue-lookup) is the order to ask in: the catalogue, then the class model, then a text search for an exact name, then the file - and only the lines named.

Several agents, or one: measured

A common belief: several agents work faster but spend more tokens. It was tested on this toolkit with an exact answer key (u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py). The task is to find where each named function or class is defined. Python's own parser builds the key, so an answer is right or wrong by construction. The same task ran in each condition below, and every run was judged.

The lookup task (seed 1017): 12 names, each to be found where it is defined, the answer key built by Python's own parser over the toolkit's code, every run judged against it by survey/agent_bench.py. One run per condition.

condition agents right tokens tokens a name wall-clock (slowest agent)
one agent, text search 1 12 of 12 90,998 7,583 16 s
one agent, the toolkit's index 1 12 of 12 92,099 7,674 67 s
three agents in parallel, text search 3 12 of 12 271,002 22,583 14 s
three agents in parallel, the index 3 12 of 12 272,270 22,689 37 s
one lean agent (no project rules file), text search 1 12 of 12 48,228 4,019 9 s

What the runs measured:

  • Every condition was right on every name (12 of 12 each): the task was easy for all of them.
  • Three agents cost 3.0 times the tokens of one (text search: 271,002 against 90,998), and the wall-clock moved from 16 s to 14 s.
  • Most of an agent's cost is its starting context: a lean agent that does not load the project's rules file did the same task for 48,228 tokens against 90,998 - 47 % less - before any work differs.
  • The index did not save tokens on exact names (92,099 against 90,998) and was slower (67 s against 16 s): a single text search per unique name is already cheap.

The manual's writers: six writer agents drafting the u2ue manual's new chapters in parallel (2026-10-17, launched 11:3x), each a general-purpose agent with the project's rules file loaded. Source: the agent platform's usage report for each agent (tokens, wall-clock), copied from each agent's completion notice.

writer tokens minutes words written
a1 Shuriken to Niagara (13) 573,684 26 10,786
a2 the Unity tools (14) 482,178 24 7,992
a3 the Unreal tools (15) 477,652 26 6,971
a4 test-driven porting (16) 433,857 24 7,000
a5 folding eight documents in (01-12) 588,767 39 25,617
a6 prior art (Appendix D) 265,493 12 9,653
  • 2,821,631 tokens for 68,019 words (41 a word); the slowest writer took 39 minutes, the six together 2.5 agent-hours: in parallel the work finished 3.9 times sooner than the same six runs one after another.
  • Not measured: what one agent would have spent doing all six in turn. Its context would have grown with every chapter, so its tokens are not the sum above, and no record says which way that goes.

What this means for a port, read with the caution that each condition ran once:

  • Fan out for big work that splits cleanly, not for small work. The writers' work was large, and each writer owned its own files, so parallel agents bought real time. The lookup task was small, so three agents bought almost none and paid three starting contexts for it.
  • The rules file is a tax every agent pays. The lean agent's saving is the project rules file it did not load. Anthropic's guidance says the same from the other side: keep the rules file short, because a bloated one makes the model ignore the rules that matter. Move what is not needed every time into skills, which load on demand, and give lookups to a lean read-only agent.
  • For exact names, a text search is as good as an index. The index's value lies elsewhere, in the next section.
  • Not measured yet: questions a text search answers badly, such as who calls a function through an interface, which measured rule applies to an emitter, or which use-case step a verb proves. That is the next task family for the benchmark. Until it is run, the toolkit makes no token claim for the index on such questions.

To run the benchmark on your own machine and your own rules file:

py u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py task --seed <S>
py u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py prompt --seed <S> --slice 1/1 --tools grep
py u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py add --seed <S> --condition one-grep --tokens <N> --ms <M> --answers <file>
py u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py report --seed <S>

The index, the triples and the non-hallucination engine: do they fit?

The same author's knowledge engine (the anchor page's "Ask anything" tab) answers questions with no neural weights. Its principle, in its own words: propose from a fixed space, verify by execution, report a measured confidence, refuse rather than invent. u2ue's iron law is the same principle applied to a port:

the engine u2ue
propose from a fixed space every value is READ from the source, with where it came from; a symbol must be one the class model holds
verify by execution every Unity behaviour is MEASURED in Unity by a probe; every change runs a judge, and every judge has a plant it must refuse
report a measured confidence every number names its record and its denominator; a stale input prints STALE
refuse rather than invent a value that cannot be read is ABSENT, with the reason; a miss in an index is UNKNOWN

They fit together as one loop for an AI porter. The model proposes. The index and the triples are the fixed space its proposal must land in. The gates verify by running. A miss is reported, never filled in.

Whether it is beneficial, measured rather than argued:

  • Tokens: no gain was measured on exact-name lookups (above).
  • Correctness: this is where the value shows. Every gate in the loop refuses a planted fabrication. The class-model gate refuses a method name the code lacks (uml.py selftest). The manual's command gate refuses an option the facade does not read. The coverage gate refuses a placement whose identifiers never arrived. The use-case checker refuses a step that cites nothing. The toolkit never relies on the model not to invent. It makes inventions fail, by name, before anyone reads them.

So the honest fit is one principle on three surfaces: the engine's answers, the toolkit's measurements and the model's code. The index earns its place as a refuser of fabrications, not yet as a token saver.

Reviewing AI-written code

Anthropic publishes how it reviews work done by Claude (Best practices for Claude Code, the same page). In short:

  • Give the model a check it can run - a test suite, a build, a script that diffs against a fixture, a screenshot to compare. A model stops when the work looks done, and without a check, "looks done" is the only signal.
  • Have it show evidence rather than assert success: the command it ran, and what that command returned.
  • Explore, plan, then code.
  • Review in a fresh context. A reviewer in a separate subagent sees only the diff and the criteria, not the reasoning that produced the change. One instance can write the tests and another the code.
  • Scope the reviewer. A reviewer asked to find gaps will report some. Tell it to flag only gaps that affect correctness or the stated requirements.
  • Mind the trust-then-verify gap: a plausible implementation that misses its edge cases. If it cannot be verified, do not ship it.

u2ue builds each of these in, and adds UML at both ends: to steer the work, and to review it.

  1. Checks it can run, everywhere. Every step of every skill has a RUN: and a DONE WHEN: (the skill gate). Every pillar of the product has recurring checks (py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle), and red stops the cycle.
  2. Checks that can fail. A judge with no plant proves nothing, so every judge has one (py -m u2ue --project <game> judge --prove), and a gate that is widened is re-proven against its plants (Chapter 16).
  3. Evidence, not claims. Every number names its record (u2ue metrics). Every tile on the hook page names the command that produced it. A task line is ticked with its evidence, never with "done".
  4. Fresh-context reviewers. The writers of this manual's deep chapters were held to gates, not to their own word: the coverage gate, the naming gate and the command gate. While documenting the tools, they read the tools' code with fresh eyes and found defects in the tools themselves: a console check that can miss new errors, a recovery script that acts on every editor on the machine, a field gate blind to a module family. Each finding went to the owner's list with its file, instead of being patched quietly.
  5. UML for the prompt. The target class model is drawn first (u2ue/CONCEPTS.md, Chapter 21), and code is moved under it. A slice's diagram is drawn before its code moves (the logic skill's step 2). The model is asked to make a diagram true, and the diagram is checked against the code.
  6. UML for the review. A reviewer does not read the diff line by line. They read the generated model: the epic and the use cases (Chapter 5), each command as a requirement (Chapter 18), the class model and the facade map (Chapter 21), and the traceability from the owner's words to the selftests (Appendix E). A class the diagram names and the code lacks fails the build, so the model cannot be out of date with the code. Between sessions, the class model's snapshot and diff (uml.py snapshot, uml.py diff) show what changed in structure.
  7. Scoped review. The owner's acceptance sentence sits at the top of the list, and reviews report gaps against it, not style.

A session, start to finish

  1. Find where the port stands. py -m u2ue --project <game> logic names the next step.
  2. Look things up before reading. py -m u2ue find <words>, then py -m u2ue --project <game> uml where <Name>; read only the lines named.
  3. Draw the slice. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus <TypeA> <TypeB>, then the target diagram the slice must become.
  4. Move the slice and prove it. Move it, then run py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Class.Method> --cases <Cases.cs> and py -m u2ue --project <game> parity until they exit 0.
  5. Check the toolkit and the project. py -m u2ue --project <game> check.
  6. Review in a fresh context. Give a separate agent the diff and the slice's diagram, and ask only for gaps against the owner's sentence.
  7. Run the cycle before any report. py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle; red stops the session's report, not the session.
  8. Write the evidence onto the list, take the next item, and report only at the end of the run.

18. The facade: detailed requirements

The facade is the toolkit's one entry point, py -m u2ue. Each verb it answers is one requirement on the toolkit. This chapter states each requirement and everything the code says about it, read from the verb's own source on every build, so the page and the code cannot drift apart.

How each requirement is read

  • Requirement: the verb's row in the registry (u2ue/verbs/__init__.py), the single list the command line, find, the verb list and this manual all read. A verb added anywhere else would be invisible, which is why there is only one list.
  • Implemented by: the verb's module and its public functions. Every verb module exposes run(p, argv), where p is the loaded project (or nothing, for a verb that needs none).
  • Inputs: every option the module's argument parser declares, with its help text, read from the code. A verb that reads its arguments by hand lists the options it compares.
  • Refuses: every refusal message the module can print or raise, with its line. A refusal is the toolkit's answer when an input is missing or wrong: it names the cause and stops, and never substitutes a default. A message that names a machine path or the reference game is shown with that part replaced by <path> or <game>. Those are hard-wired sites the core is shedding (pillar 7, Chapter 16).
  • Exits: the literal exit values in the module. Across the facade, 0 is success, and 2 is a refusal before any work starts (an unknown verb, or a project that does not load). Each verb's own meaning of 1 is in its usage text (Chapter 19).
  • Verified by: the verb's selftest in the selftest registry (u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.py), with the verdict of its last run. ABSENT means the registry runs no selftest for that verb. The gap is listed here instead of being hidden. Each run's date is in u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.json. This page carries only the verdict, so a cycle that re-runs the selftests leaves it current, and a verdict that changes makes it stale.
  • Exercised by: the use-case steps (Chapter 5) whose proof command runs the verb. A verb that no step runs is still a requirement, just one the model does not exercise yet.

28 verbs, each read from its module's own source: 20 with a selftest in the registry, 26 run as the proof of a use-case step. A requirement is numbered FR-<verb>; its inputs, refusals and exits are the code's, line by line.
