22. Troubleshooting

Each entry was hit for real on the reference port. The symptom comes first, then the cause, then what to do. Each section names the step of a procedure it branches from, and an entry that branches elsewhere names its own; the requirements model reads those as the procedures' extensions (Chapter 21).

Finding your problem

Start from what you see. Most problems in a port fall into one of the rows below, and each row names where its answer is.

what you see where the answer is
a command printed REFUSED: ... that verb's refusals, every message with its line, are in Chapter 18; the message names its cause, so fix the input it names and run it again
a command says the project is missing a path or a key py -m u2ue --project <game> info opens every path the project file names; Chapter 3, the project file
a headless Unreal hangs, its log grows without end, or a long build stops half way Unreal runs, below; Chapter 15, headless Unreal runs
Unreal plays sound through the speakers, or records silence Unreal runs, below; Chapter 15, audio
a Niagara system draws nothing in an editor script Unreal runs, below; Chapter 15, editor scripting limits
a managed C# editor wedges, or shows compile errors for code that builds Unreal runs, below; Chapter 15, managed C# in Unreal
the converter writes a value but the effect ignores it Chapter 13, the traps (Unreal's Python API: a failed write returns false)
an emitter is born late, counts differ, or a child never fires Chapter 13, the traps (events, sub-emitters and trails); Chapter 10 for the conformance diff
a texture, a blend or a material looks different though the file is the same Reading Unity files, below; Chapter 13, materials and textures
the YAML reader refuses a prefab or a scene Reading Unity files, below; Chapter 7, prefab YAML
Unity crashes or a probe never runs Measuring in Unity, below; Chapter 14, never disturb the owner
the Unity bridge stops answering, or an editor sits behind a modal dialog Chapter 14, recovery
two agents trample one editor Chapter 14, several agents at once
a float or a printed number differs between Unity and the port Comparing runtimes, below; Chapter 16, the layers
a patch script left a file empty, or two patches fight Writing tools, below
a gate says something is ABSENT that you know exists, or a test is red in a file someone else just wrote Gates and reports, below; Chapter 16, rules that keep tests honest
a photo differs from Unity's but the numbers agree Gates and reports, below; Chapter 13, proof
u2ue metrics prints STALE or ABSENT Gates and reports, below; Chapter 11
the manual will not build it names a game or a path, or shows a command the facade lacks: the build prints each line (About this manual)

Unreal runs

Branches from Chapter 4, step 7.

A headless Unreal never finishes and its log grows to hundreds of megabytes. UnrealSharp finds dotnet by the PATH entry Program Files\dotnet\ with the trailing backslash. Git Bash hands PowerShell a PATH without it, so UnrealSharp reports ".NET SDK can't be found" and, under -unattended, raises the dialog again forever (measured: a 634 MB log, nothing built). Run every Unreal verb from native PowerShell. The verbs refuse the Bash chain up front.

A long build stops at exactly the shell tool's timeout, leaving the content half old and half new. Stopping a background task kills its children, including UnrealEditor-Cmd. Before a long launch, compare the tool's timeout with the script's own watchdog and give the tool the larger one.

Two Unreal runs at once. One headless Unreal at a time. build, read and photo ask the adapter's host_busy and refuse while an Unreal (or the game's own queue) holds the host. build --dry shows the host's state.

Niagara draws nothing in an editor script. -run=pythonscript asserts, and -ExecutePythonScript quits before the tick loop runs. The editor world never ticks actors, so Niagara simulates only inside Simulate or Play-In-Editor unless something advances it. The read-back advances each system itself: NiagaraSimCacheFunctionLibrary's immediate capture with bAdvanceSimulation (_effects/tools/u1e_color_size_readback.py, which u2ue read runs).

A headless run plays sound through the user's speakers, or records silence. Pass -DeterministicAudio (the non-realtime renderer: nothing reaches a device, and each tick renders its own delta) and -ini:Engine:[Audio]:UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=1.0 (an unfocused application otherwise mixes at volume 0).

An UnrealSharp editor wedges while files are being generated. With automatic hot reload on, the editor recompiles a managed file the instant it is written, mid-write, fails, and can stop responding. Set AutomaticHotReloading=Off in the host's DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini, or keep the editor closed while a tool writes managed C#.

Reading Unity files

Branches from Chapter 4, step 5.

The reader refuses a scene with m_RemovedGameObjects. A prefab instance in a scene that deletes one of the prefab's objects is not handled yet (the reader that applies it is proven and lands with the next build; Appendix B). u2ue data --no-expand reads the scene's own components without expanding instances. Branches from Chapter 4, step 4.

A nested prefab's object cannot be found by its fileID. A nested object's id is the instance's id XOR the source object's id.

A material's values look like its shader's defaults. A material variant stores only what it overrides; the rest comes through m_Parent. Read the chain.

An effect's blend mode is wrong. The blend mode is a number in the material (_DstBlend == 1 is additive), never the shader's name.

A texture looks different in Unreal although the file is the same. Unity samples its imported texture (mip chain, alpha fill, size caps), not the source file. The import is in Library/Artifacts and can be read offline (_effects/tools/unity_tex_artifact.py); validate the match against the source, since the artifact index can point at a neighbouring asset. Branches from Chapter 4, step 7.

Measuring in Unity

Branches from Chapter 9, step 7.

Unity crashes in native code during a probe. ParticleSystem.Particle.GetMeshIndex on a renderer that is not a Mesh renderer with meshes kills the editor; a managed try/catch does not see it. Check the renderer before any renderer-dependent query, and write the field ABSENT otherwise.

A probe's work never runs while the editor is in the background. EditorApplication.delayCall does not fire for an unfocused editor. Poll from EditorApplication.update.

The first case a probe renders is wrong, and only that one. The first render after a probe sets up its scene can come out incomplete (measured: without the scene's ambient, so an ON - OFF difference read the ambient as light). Throw one or two renders away before the first case, and have the judge compare every OFF render of a surface against the others, so an incomplete one is refused by name instead of read as data.

A measurement right after a recompile reproduces the old numbers. Entering Play while a compile is pending runs the old assembly. Wait until the editor assembly's timestamp is newer than the source and isCompiling reads false, then Play. Branches from Chapter 9, step 6.

Comparing runtimes

Branches from Chapter 6, step 7.

Text built from floats differs between Unity and .NET. Unity's Mono rounds float text to seven significant digits first, rounds halves away from zero, and prints a value that rounds to zero without a sign. Any number a player reads, or a stream compared against Unity, goes through one formatter that reproduces Mono's rules.

Float results differ by one ULP. Mono may keep a float expression at higher precision. u2ue parity names every such row; an allowance pins the exact row and bits, and the fix (explicit float locals) moves Unity's own value, so it is the owner's call.

System.Text.Json writes {} for a Unity data class. Unity's JsonUtility serializes public fields; System.Text.Json ignores fields unless IncludeFields = true.

Writing tools

Branches from Chapter 12, A converter route, step 2.

A patch that refused left the file it patches empty. open(path, "w").write(patch(text)) opens - and truncates - the file before patch runs, so when patch refuses (an anchor moved, already patched) the file is left at 0 bytes. Build the new text first, then open the file. Every patch script in the toolkit does, and each carries a plant: pointed at a copy that already carries its mark, it must refuse and leave the copy byte-identical.

Two patches to one file, each proven on its own copy. That proves each, not both: an anchor the first one moves would make the second refuse at landing time. Apply them in landing order to one copy and compile it before either lands (the reference port's two converter patches were proven both ways round).

Gates and reports

Branches from Chapter 4, step 6.

A gate reports a symbol ABSENT that you know exists. Check whether the port moved it (into the model, for example) before believing the gate. Widen the gate to follow the move, then re-run its plants.

The photo of an effect differs from Unity's in a way the data does not. A photo is one draw of a random process, and a frame can catch a capture artefact. Labelled frames (RANDDRAW, GRIDTICK) are never counted. Compare several frames and the read-back data before calling a route wrong. Branches from Chapter 4, step 7.

u2ue metrics prints STALE. An input is older than the newest build. Re-run the step that writes it (the sweep, the photo pass); the number is never presented as current until then. Branches from Chapter 4, step 8.

Questions and answers

Every design choice in the toolkit was made for a reason that was measured, usually by something going wrong first. This part answers the questions a reviewer asks on first contact - most of them some form of "why didn't you just..." - and ends with the choices that are still weaknesses, with what is being done about each. It opens with the questions a porter asks before and during a port.

Before you start

What do I need installed? Windows 11 with native PowerShell for the Unreal runs, Python 3.13 with PyYAML, the .NET SDK 8 or later, Unreal Engine 5.7, and the game's own Unity Editor for measurement windows and reference photos. The full table, with what needs each, is in Chapter 3.

Does my Unity project have to be set up in a particular way? One setting: asset serialization must be Force Text, so prefabs, scenes, materials and .meta files are YAML the toolkit can read. The toolkit reads the project and writes nothing into it. Measurement windows are the exception that proves the rule: they run in the owner's editor, wait for the owner to be idle, stop when the owner returns, and never replace a file of the project (Chapter 9).

Does the Unity Editor have to be open? No, for almost everything. Reading prefabs, scenes, materials and data, the inventory, the extraction, the Unreal build, parity and Unity's own Mono runtime all run with no editor. An editor is needed only to measure a behaviour (a window), to take Unity's reference photos, to export a scene and to capture a UI screen (Chapter 14).

Which Unity and Unreal versions does it work with? It was built on Unity 6000.3 with Unreal Engine 5.7, and exercised on a second game on Unity 2021.3. Every measured rule records the Unity version it was measured on. On any other version, u2ue check names the rule as UNVERIFIED and the reports say so instead of calling it measured (Chapter 9).

Do I need an AI model to use it? No. Every verb is a command a person can run. The two skills are written so that an AI model can do the porter's work step by step and have each step checked (Chapter 6, Chapter 16).

What does it not port? Animation and physics are not covered (Chapter 7, Appendix B). On the effects side, VFX Graph assets and particle systems authored directly in scenes are not covered either, and the extraction lists them with their counts (Chapter 4, step 5).

Can I port only the effects? Yes. Part one of the tutorial (Chapter 4) takes a game's effects to a first report with no code port at all. The logic, the scenes and the UI are separate procedures you can run later, or never.

During a port

Where do the results go? Into the work folders your project file names (work.effects, work.records and the rest): the IR, the build records, the read-backs, the photos and the reports. Nothing is written into the Unity project (Chapter 3).

Can I run several things at once? Headless work, yes. Unreal, no: one headless Unreal at a time, and the verbs that need it refuse while it is busy (Chapter 15). A live Unity Editor has one driver at a time, and the other agents work headless or on a second editor instance (Chapter 14).

How do I know the port is right? Four numbers, never one combined figure: coverage (does it draw), measured (drawn by a measured rule), data (do its particles follow Unity's numbers) and image (do the frames agree, with capture artefacts excluded and counted). u2ue metrics prints each with its denominator (Chapter 11). u2ue conform holds every emitter to Unity's own particle state (Chapter 10), and u2ue parity holds the game's rules to every runtime by float bits (Chapter 16).

What happens when the toolkit cannot read or convert something? It says so. A value that cannot be read is ABSENT, with the reason. An effect the reader cannot follow is REFUSED by key. An emitter the converter cannot port carries its named gap on the acceptance page. Nothing is dropped silently, and nothing is replaced by a plausible default (Chapter 1, Chapter 8).

My game chooses its effects in code, not by placing prefabs. What then? Write an adapter. It answers the few questions that depend on a game, and the first of them is which effects the game fires (effect_keys()). Chapter 12 has the recipe.

A gate went red, but I know the code is right. First check whether the code moved. A gate that walks one folder reports a symbol it cannot see as absent. Widen the gate to follow the move, then prove that it can still fail (Chapter 16, Chapter 22). Never re-record a baseline to make a red gate green.

How long does a port take? The toolkit measures this rather than estimating it. u2ue tempo times each converter route from its first code to its verified flip, read off git, and u2ue metrics reports the machine time of the builds (Chapter 11). Appendix A has the reference port's numbers.

Can I review the port without reading the code? Yes - that is what the model is for. Start at the epic in Chapter 5, follow a step to the verb that proves it (Chapter 18), and run that verb. The class model and the facade map in Chapter 21 show where the code sits.

The approach

Why not just translate the MonoBehaviours into Actors? Because then nothing can be compared. Two engines running two hand-translated copies of the rules disagree in ways no one can locate: every difference is an argument. Moving the rules into one engine-free model, run by both engines, turns every difference into a row in a digest that u2ue parity compares bit for bit (Chapter 6). It is also less code: the hosts are thin, and the rules are written once.

Why doesn't the toolkit move the game's code for me? Because where the seams go is a design decision about your game, and a tool that guessed them would produce a model nobody chose. The toolkit does everything around that decision: the inventory says what each type touches, the runtime library gives the moved code Unity's rules, the gates keep the model engine-free, parity proves the result.

Why is there no off-the-shelf Shuriken to Niagara converter in here? There is not one to use. Unreal ships a Cascade to Niagara converter, and the toolkit uses its library (FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary) to write Niagara stacks, but what to write - Shuriken's semantics, module by module - is the toolkit's own work, measured against Unity where Unity does not document it.

Why read Unity's YAML instead of exporting through the Unity editor? Reading text needs no editor, so it runs on any machine, in any order, as often as wanted, and leaves the game owner's editor alone. It is deterministic and diffable. The editor is used only for what cannot be read from files: measuring behaviour, and reference photos. The price is that the project must be serialized as text, and that every corner of the format must be handled - which is why an unhandled case is refused by name rather than half-read.

Why Python for the tools, and C# for the runtime? The converter has to run inside Unreal's editor, whose scripting language is Python, so the readers and the converter share one language and one set of tests. The runtime library is C# because it ships into the game, beside the game's own C#. Whether the readers should move to .NET for packaging is an open decision for the owner (Appendix B).

Measuring Unity

Why measure Unity at all? Read the documentation. The documentation does not say most of what a port must reproduce: the frame a sub-emitter's particle is born in, the order a mesh particle's rotation and a non-uniform scale apply in, how a TrailRenderer drops its points, what a Timeline does before a clip starts. Unity's engine source is not public. Several of these behaved differently from what the documentation implied and what experience predicted; a port built on the guess looked right in a screenshot and wrong in the game.

Why write the judge before the measurement? A judge written after the data is fitted to the data and passes whatever Unity happened to do. Written first, with planted wrong answers it must refuse, it can be wrong in a way the measurement exposes - which is the point (Chapter 9 has a bake the judge refused, and what it taught).

Why run probes in the owner's own editor, and only after ten idle minutes? Because a second Unity editor on the same machine was measured to take the owner's machine away: it steals window focus on every assembly reload and saturates the processor for many minutes. A probe needs a real compile and sometimes Play mode, which interrupts whoever is working. So a window waits for ten minutes without a key or a mouse movement, stops the moment the owner returns, and never answers a dialog it did not open. A dedicated measurement machine is the better setup when there is one; the protocol is the same.

Why are the probes temporary files dropped into the project, not a permanent editor package? So the game's project carries nothing it did not ask for. The release ships them as the package's Editor assembly (Appendix B), which is the same code installed once, by the owner's decision.

Why is a rule measured on Unity 6 called UNVERIFIED for a Unity 2021 game? Because it was not measured there. The build still uses it - most rules hold across versions - but the report must not call a value measured for a version it was not measured on. Re-measuring is the owner's decision; the probes and judges are the means.

Converting and building

Why is every new behaviour behind a switch that defaults to off? Because a converter change that is wrong silently changes hundreds of effects. Behind a switch, the change is proven to alter nothing while off (whole_trace replays the converter over every emitter), then to alter exactly the emitters it names while on, then trialled, read back, photographed and looked at - and only then flipped, with an evidence row. 86 routes went through that. The cost is the number of switches, which is why retiring the permanently-on ones is on the roadmap.

Why are changes written as patch scripts that land "after the queue"? A full rebuild runs for many hours and loads the converter afresh for each chunk of effects. Editing the converter mid-build would make the build two builds, half old and half new, and the acceptance numbers would describe neither. So a change is proven on a copy (--prove) and applied (--land) when the build ends; the landing step refuses if the file moved since the proof, and leaves the file untouched when it refuses.

Why only one Unreal process at a time? Measured: one headless Unreal process holding the effect content reached about 25 GB of memory, and two processes writing one content folder race each other's asset registry. One at a time, with a queue, finishes sooner than two that fail.

Why headless Unreal, and not a running editor? A headless run is reproducible, unattended and owns nothing anyone else is using. The cost is that the editor world does not tick actors, so Niagara does not simulate by itself; the read-back advances each system explicitly (Chapter 22).

Why does the YAML reader refuse a scene that edits an object inside a model? A model (an FBX) is binary, so the scene's YAML holds only the edit, not the object it edits. Reading FBX in Python to rebuild that object's transform would re-derive what Unity has already resolved: the scene's glTF export walks Unity's live hierarchy and writes every node's own transform, model nodes included. So such a scene is refused by name on the YAML route, and u2ue shear --gltf and u2ue scene read the export instead.

Why does the toolkit refuse to run Unreal from Git Bash? UnrealSharp finds dotnet by a PATH entry that Git Bash rewrites; under -unattended it then raises an invisible dialog forever. One such run wrote a 634 MB log and built nothing. Refusing the shell up front costs nothing.

Why one-ULP differences? Surely nobody can see them. Nobody can see them, but a turn-based game can feel them: a damage value one unit in the last place lower can leave a unit alive that should have died. The toolkit pins each such row to its exact bits and reports which runtime is the odd one out, and leaves the fix - which moves the shipped game's own numbers - to the owner.

Rendering, lighting and UI

Why do lit effects compute Unity's lighting inside the Unreal material instead of using Unreal's lights? Because the goal is Unity's look, and URP and Unreal light a surface differently: a different BRDF, a different ambient (URP's spherical harmonics), a different reflection decode. Evaluating URP's own Lit, transcribed from its source, with the scene's measured sun, ambient and reflection cube, reproduces Unity's result. The trade-off is named: those materials follow the lighting that was measured, not lighting that changes at run time, and they draw no fog or shadows (Chapter 8).

Why is a Unity point light of intensity 1 an Unreal light of pi candelas? Read from both engines' source: URP's diffuse term has no 1 / pi and Unreal's Lambert does, and Unreal's candela unit is 1e4 internal units per candela at 100 cm per metre. pi x I candelas makes the two equal. The Unity side was measured on lit pixels to confirm the formula; the remaining 4 % (URP's diffuse carries a 0.96 that Unreal's does not) is measured and named, not hidden.

Why is the UI painted in one widget instead of built as UMG? Two measured reasons. uGUI's layout (anchors, layout groups, TextMeshPro's glyph placement) does not map onto UMG's, so a UMG rebuild lays out differently; a port of uGUI's own solver lays out identically, which its tests hold against Unity's captures. And from C#, UnrealSharp exposes a widget tree's root as read-only, so a UMG tree cannot be assembled from the game's code at all.

Why does Unity's reference photo of an effect have no lights? Most effects are unlit and additive: lights do not change them, and an empty scene makes the frame comparable. For lit materials the photo probe has a lit mode that opens the scene and copies its sun, because a lit material photographed in the dark compares nothing.

Why are the Unreal hosts C# and not Blueprints or C++? The game's code is C#. With UnrealSharp the moved model runs unchanged in Unreal, and the host is a thin C# layer. C++ is used only where the managed bindings do not reach (handing raw PCM to Unreal's mixer).

Numbers and reports

Why does every number come with a denominator and a date? Because a percentage without them cannot be checked or compared, and an old number quoted as current is how a project believes it is further along than it is. "92.4 % coverage" means 7,810 of the 8,452 emitters Unity draws, on 2026-10-15.

Why print STALE or ABSENT instead of the last known value? A last known value describes builds that no longer exist. Printing it would be a substitute, which is the one thing the toolkit does not do anywhere.

Why isn't an effect Unity does not draw counted as a gap? Because porting it would make Unreal draw something Unity does not. The first acceptance pages charged 348 such emitters as gaps; each is now classified by a rule (never fired, never started, draws nothing in Unity), and only what Unity draws and Unreal does not is a gap.

Why look at the pictures if the numbers pass? Numbers and pictures fail differently. One render where the whole scene went black scored better on a pixel metric, because dark geometry stopped hiding a bright backdrop. The data proves itself first; then the numbers and the pictures confirm it, and a picture counts only once someone has opened it.

What is still weak, and what is being done

"Many tools still name one machine's folders." True. The facade and the toolkit's own parts resolve their folders through one module, but many effect, scene and lane tools still default to the reference port's folders. Each is moving onto the project file's variables, proven by its selftest and an unchanged output, after the current build (Appendix B).

"The toolkit lives in two places." True: it grew inside the reference port, in a tools tree and a work tree. u2ue/tools.py names every part's folder once, and U2UE_TOOLKIT_ROOT moves them as a whole; the package plan puts them under one root.

"There are a lot of switches." 99 rows, 87 read on. Each is a proof trail; the permanently-on ones will be retired in one pass that whole_trace proves changes nothing.

"Animation and physics are not covered." True, and said on the first page. No tool is claimed without a game that has them and a measurement behind it.

"The probes need the owner's editor." For now. A dedicated machine running the same window protocol is the obvious next step for a team; nothing in the protocol depends on whose editor it is.

Appendix A. A worked example: the reference port

The toolkit was built while porting one game, and every chapter uses it as the worked example. This appendix puts that port in one place, with the numbers and the dates they were taken.

The game. A turn-based tactics game on Unity 6000.3: painted card units on tiled battle maps, a uGUI battle HUD, and 674 particle effects - of the 673 read, 558 from one asset-store vendor's pack, 64 from a second, 44 from a third and 7 of the game's own. Ported to Unreal Engine 5.7 with UnrealSharp C# hosts.

The effects, in numbers

u2ue metrics and u2ue tempo on 2026-10-15 at 13:56, with the acceptance rebuild part way through its queue:

  • 674 effect keys: 673 built, 1 refused by the IR reader with its reason. 197 of the built keys carry a named gap.
  • 7,810 emitters drawn. 374 more are absent exactly as they are in Unity (267 Unity never fires; 58 the game never starts; the rest draw or emit nothing in Unity itself). 642 are gaps: Unity draws them and Unreal does not, each named and charged to its root.
  • Coverage 92.4 %: of the 8,452 emitters Unity draws, Unreal draws 7,810.
  • 86.3 % measured: 6,737 of the drawn emitters use only rules measured against Unity; 1,073 carry a named stand-in.
  • The read-back: 20,378 emitter-checks over 22 checks, 17 failures (99.92 % hold). STALE until the rebuild finishes.
  • 163 measured Unity bakes behind the converter's rules by the evening of the same day, all on Unity 6000.3.16f1.
  • 31.8 hours of headless build time over 673 keys, a median of 98 s a key.
  • 86 converter routes flipped from off to verified on, median 36.2 h from first code to flip; routes flipped on their own took a median of 2.4 h.

The largest gap roots, which is where the next routes go: an enabled shape under non-uniform scale (31 emitters over 20 keys); sub-emitter children of a few parents whose routes are not ported yet; a gem shader with no Unreal parent yet (17 emitters).

What it taught

  • Move the rules out first. Comparing two engines only became possible once both ran the same model. Before that, every difference was an argument; afterwards each one was a row in a digest.
  • Measure, don't recall. Most of the converter's hard cases (sub-emitter frames, ring buffers, sheared nodes, mesh alignment, trails) behaved differently from what the documentation and intuition said. Each became a probe, a judge and a bake.
  • Count what Unity does not draw. The first acceptance pages charged 348 emitters as gaps that Unity itself never draws.
  • A gate can lie by looking at nothing. Several of the toolkit's own instruments passed while reading an empty set or the wrong folder. Every gate now carries plants, and a check that looked at nothing fails.
  • The look is checked by eye. A metric once improved while the whole scene went black.
  • Fix Unity's own broken assets in Unity first. Two effects drew Unity's magenta error colour in Unity itself (a material whose shader was gone, a trail whose material was gone). Each was fixed in the Unity project by evidence - the first rebuilt from its sibling variants' pattern, the second's renderer turned off because its look is absent from every pack - and only then ported.

Still open

Listed with their plans in Appendix B: the acceptance rebuild finishing (then the read-back sweep and the photo pass re-run); the timeline route and the reader changes landing; the lit-material trial and the point lights' Unreal half; drawing TrailRenderers in Unreal; the gem shader.
