Appendix C. Glossary

ABSENT - a value the toolkit proved does not exist in the source, or could not read, named with the reason. Never replaced by a default.

adapter - the object that answers the three game-specific questions (which prefabs are effects, what starts on spawn, when the host is busy). unity_project is the default (Chapter 12).

aggregate - the one engine-free class that holds an entity's state and rules; the engine's object holds one and forwards to it, so state has one home (Chapter 6).

asset family - one kind of asset that ports itself through the same five steps: extract, build, read, judge, photo (Chapter 2).

bake - one run of a probe in Unity, saved as a fact file.

capability seam - the optional interfaces an engine implements when it draws more of the game than the base view calls say; a view without one gets the base call instead (Chapter 6).

coverage - of the emitters Unity draws, the share Unreal draws: drawn / (drawn + gap).

digest - a runtime's per-case output of the game's model, floats as bit patterns, compared by u2ue parity.

effect key - one effect the game can spawn, usually one prefab; the unit the IR, the build and the report count in.

emitter - one Unity ParticleSystem, and the Niagara emitter built from it.

engine-free model - the game's rules as plain C# that references no engine, run by both engines' hosts.

event stream - the ordered, append-only list of events the model writes as it resolves an action; an engine draws only what it says, so everything a player must see is said once (Chapter 6).

facade - py -m u2ue, the single entry point; every verb is one row of its registry.

fact file - a probe's output in shared/conformance, with the Unity version that produced it.

flip - turning a converter switch's default from OFF to ON, with an evidence row naming the trial.

gap - an emitter Unity draws and Unreal does not, named with the converter's reason.

gap root - the emitter a gap is charged to: an absent parent's children count against the ancestor that is absent for its own reason, so a root's count is what porting it brings back.

host - the engine-side code that runs the model in one engine: Unity's MonoBehaviours, or UnrealSharp actors.

IR - the engine-neutral intermediate representation of an effect: one JSON file per key, read from Unity's YAML.

judge - a script that reads a rule off a fact file or refuses it, with planted defects it must refuse. Written before the bake.

LOOKED - a picture actually opened and examined by a person or agent. A file that was written has not been looked at.

MEASURED - a value or rule taken from Unity itself by a probe, with the run that measured it.

MVID - the module version id in a .NET assembly's metadata; the publish proof compares the loaded model's with the one the source just built, to know which build an engine ran (Chapter 6).

pillar - one promise of the product, checked every cycle by u2ue cycle.

plant - a deliberate defect a selftest feeds a gate or tool; the tool must refuse it.

platform seam - the six services every engine provides and the model never calls directly: the log, text assets, a key-value store, a file store, a JSON codec and a random source (U2ue.Runtime.Platform).

PlaybackQueue - the host's replay of the event stream: one event per frame, only while the views are idle; input waits until it is caught up (Chapter 6).

probe - an Editor C# script that sets up a case in Unity, steps it and writes a fact file.

READ - a value taken from a file, with where it came from.

read-back - the built Niagara systems simulated headless in Unreal, their particles recorded per 1/60 s frame.

route - the converter's handling of one Unity behaviour, behind its own switch.

seam - an interface the model calls instead of an engine API; each host implements it.

selftest - a tool's own check of itself, with plants, run by u2ue check --only selftests.

shear - the skew a rotated child gets under a non-uniformly scaled parent in Unity. Unreal's transform cannot represent it.

slice - one feature's rules, moved into the model at a time, smallest first, and proven by parity before the next is taken (Chapter 6).

stand-in - a value or asset the converter used in place of the real one, marked SUBSTITUTED and never counted as measured.

switch - an environment variable (VFXPORT_<NAME>, U1E_<NAME>) that turns one route on or off.

ULP - unit in the last place: the gap between two neighbouring floats. A one-ULP difference is the smallest a float can differ by.

verb - one command of the facade (extract, build, metrics, ...).

view seam - the interfaces through which the presentation asks an engine to draw; every method is a game verb, never an engine primitive (Chapter 6).

whole_trace - the offline proof of a route: the converter run against a recording stub at two versions, and every engine call compared.

window - a short, guarded session in the game owner's Unity editor that runs one probe and removes it (Chapter 9).

work package - one group of the toolkit's tools that does one part of a port; Chapter 12 indexes the fifteen.

Appendix D. Prior art: other ways to port a Unity game

This appendix is what else exists for moving a Unity game to Unreal, and for the harder question under it: how to keep one game's rules running the same under two engines. It covers Epic's own guidance and tools, the community converter, the plugins that run C# inside Unreal, the engine-free cores that middleware and networking products ship, what studios have published about changing engine, and the strongest arguments against the approach u2ue takes. The last section says where u2ue sits among them.

How to read this appendix

The research behind it was read-only and ran in two passes: a search for effect converters on 2026-08-22 (its record is vfxport/README.md), and a wider pass on 2026-09-30, whose second half read the language standards and the .NET runtime's issues as raw text rather than through a summarising reader. Every claim below was read from the source it names, with its link, or is marked ABSENT with what was searched for.

  • Each finding carries a confidence and the reason for it (VERY HIGH, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, as the research labelled it), because one blog post and the same answer in three shipped systems are not the same evidence.
  • Products move. Star counts, open issues, supported platforms, versions and last-push dates are as measured on the date given. Any of them may have changed since; read the source again before relying on one.
  • Sources were read as data. Their wording is paraphrased here, with the link to the original.

The routes at a glance

route what it moves what it leaves to you read
Epic's migration guidance assets exported from Unity all code (rebuilt in C++ or Blueprints), Shader Graphs, Timeline and Cinemachine, particle systems 2026-08-22, 2026-09-30
ProjectExodus (community) assets all C# game logic, prefabs as Blueprints, custom shaders, particles 2026-08-22, 2026-09-30
Epic's CascadeToNiagaraConverter Unreal's own legacy Cascade effects everything that comes from Unity 2026-08-22
C# inside Unreal (UnrealSharp) lets moved C# run in Unreal the hosts; anything not exposed to reflection needs C++ 2026-09-30
an engine-free core with a layer per engine (the Spine and Quantum shape) the rules, written once every engine-side object, made again in each engine 2026-09-30
a separate process and a protocol (the chess-engine shape) the core, behind a process boundary the boundary becomes serialisation, and state ownership can split 2026-09-30
change engine and rewrite nothing automatically everything 2026-09-30
u2ue effects converted; scenes, UI and transforms by tools; the code by a method with a runtime and gates moving the code, writing the hosts, animation, physics this manual

The 2026-08-22 search covered Fab and the UE Marketplace, the Unity Asset Store, GitHub and Epic's documentation. It found no tool that converts Shuriken effects to Niagara, and named ProjectExodus as the only Unity-to-Unreal project converter. A product may have appeared since.

What Epic and the community converters move

Epic's migration guidance

Epic's page "Migrating assets from Unity to Unreal Engine", read on 2026-09-30, sets the baseline (link):

  • Unity C# scripts and Bolt visual-scripting files cannot be exported from Unity and imported; the functionality is built again in C++ or Blueprints.
  • A Shader Graph cannot be converted to a Material graph. The textures can be exported and the node network rebuilt in the Material Editor.
  • Camera animation and behaviour made with Timeline and Cinemachine cannot be exported; they are recreated with Sequencer.
  • Particle systems are recreated by hand (the 2026-08-22 search, vfxport/README.md).

Confidence VERY HIGH: first-party, read directly.

Read it two ways, because both are true. Epic's baseline assumes the code does not come across at all, and a route that moves the rules into plain C# and runs that C# inside Unreal beats it; that is a real result and can be claimed. But it makes a community plugin the load-bearing beam of the code half of the port, and that plugin's limits are in "C# inside Unreal" below.

ProjectExodus

The leading community migration tool works on assets only and ignores all of the game's C#. It does not turn prefabs into Blueprints and does not support custom shaders (its README, read 2026-09-30, link). The 2026-08-22 search found that it targets Unity 2018.3 and UE 4.25 and does not convert particles. It agrees with Epic about where the work is.

Epic's Cascade converter

CascadeToNiagaraConverter is Epic's plugin for converting Unreal's own older Cascade particle systems to Niagara; it does not read Unity. Its library is still useful to a Unity port: FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary is a Python API that writes Niagara emitter stacks, and it exists only while the plugin is enabled in the project (vfxport/README.md). u2ue's converter writes through it (Chapter 8).

Why engine independence is not paranoia

EA acquired Criterion in October 2004 and later withdrew RenderWare from the commercial market, stranding its licensees (link). An engine can be taken away. That is a named precedent for keeping a game's rules free of any one engine.

Keeping one game core under two engines

The shipped shape is almost never one core under two engines. It is one core, one engine and one headless server; and where a product really does span engines, it keeps a separate layer per engine, often over a separate core per language, not one binary.

One core, one engine, one headless server

Photon Quantum is the closest commercial product to the engine-free-core architecture. Its documentation credits the split between the simulation (Quantum) and the view (Unity) for the product's modularity. The simulation is a pure C# assembly with no Unity types, Unity is the view, and the same assembly runs on the server as a Quantum plugin. Its events even carry client and server keywords to scope which side raises them, which only exists because one build runs on both. Confidence HIGH: the vendor's current documentation for a product with paying customers, read directly (events, DSL, frames).

SharedMeta (CoreGameIO) does the same for another server stack: one C# game-logic assembly that runs on Microsoft Orleans grains and replays on a Unity or .NET client, with optimistic execution, rollback and desync detection; 25 stars, version 0.12.x (link). Confidence LOW as proof that anything works (a tiny project, no shipped title, its README read but not its code), MEDIUM as evidence that the same shape keeps being arrived at.

Middleware keeps two cores, not one binary

Spine (Esoteric Software) is animation middleware shipped in many games on both Unity and Unreal; open source, 5,305 stars on 2026-09-30. Its per-runtime READMEs on the 4.2 branch say:

  • spine-cpp loads and manipulates skeletal animation data in C++ and does no rendering: the engine-free core.
  • spine-ue is built on spine-cpp.
  • spine-unity is built on spine-csharp.

So the Unity path and the Unreal path share neither a binary nor a language. They are two hand-maintained implementations of one documented model, held together by a version rule the repository states: freeze the Spine editor version to the runtime source in use and update the two in lock step.

The presentation layers do not reach parity either. spine-unity claims every Spine feature; spine-ue lists what it lacks: multiply and screen blending, pre-multiplied alpha atlases and two-colour tinting.

Measured from the repository tree on the 4.2 branch, counting only .cs, .cpp, .h, .c and .hpp files and leaving out example, sample, test and demo paths:

part files bytes
spine-csharp (core) 48 599,469
spine-unity (engine layer) 132 1,527,046
spine-cpp (core) 160 1,131,900
spine-ue (engine layer) 39 180,585

On the Unity side the engine layer is about two and a half times the size of the engine-free core. Confidence HIGH: four READMEs read, sizes computed from the tree, not estimated (repository, spine-ue, spine-unity, spine-cpp).

What it means for a port: moving the core is the part the field agrees works. A presentation layer that lags on the second engine is the documented, normal outcome for a mature example of exactly this pattern, and its maintainers' answer was to write the gap down in the README rather than close it.

Plain data and systems, not interfaces

Quantum declares its game state in a DSL (.qtn files) that generates plain C# structs: components are structs attached to entities and used to filter them. The documented reason is memory layout and generated serialisation and checksums, not polymorphism. There are no per-rule interfaces anywhere in its state model. Confidence HIGH, vendor documentation read directly (link).

Overwatch arrived at the same place independently: strict ECS, server-authoritative, prediction on top (Tim Ford, GDC 2017, "Overwatch Gameplay Architecture and Netcode", video, vault). Confidence MEDIUM: the talk's existence and subject are known from several secondary descriptions; it was not watched, so it is not quoted.

A separate process and a text protocol

Chess has run one simulation core behind many unrelated front ends since November 2000 through UCI, which puts the GUI and the engine in separate processes talking over stdin and stdout (link).

The caveat cuts against a naive reading: under UCI the GUI keeps the board state and decides who wins, and the engine only picks moves. Even the canonical decades-old example splits state ownership, and that split is exactly what makes engine and GUI disagreements a known class of bug there. Confidence MEDIUM-HIGH: the Chessprogramming wiki is a reliable community reference, not a vendor's primary source.

One aggregate interface and a cue stream

Forge (gamesmiths-guild) is an engine-agnostic C# gameplay framework modelled on Unreal's Gameplay Ability System, built for netstandard2.1 and .NET 8, and claiming Unity, Godot and other C# engines. Its integration point is ONE interface, IForgeEntity, which exposes attributes, tags, effects, abilities, events and shared variables. Presentation goes through a "Cues" event system. The framework owns the state; the engine reads it (link).

Confidence LOW as proof (32 stars, a README that calls it a work in progress not ready for production, no multiplayer), HIGH as a data point about shape: someone else, solving the same problem, independently arrived at one aggregate interface and a cue event stream.

What was not found

No shipped game was found that runs one shared gameplay core inside both Unity and Unreal. Searched: "shared game simulation core across Unity and Unreal engine-agnostic postmortem", "game logic library separate from engine Unity Unreal same C# core adapter interfaces open source", "github engine agnostic game logic C# dll Unity Unreal both adapters netstandard shared simulation", and "we abandoned/we stopped engine abstraction layer game shared core two engines postmortem". The results were patents for simulation-industry middleware, generic engine comparisons and machine-written blogs; nothing primary.

The nearest real thing is Photon itself: Fusion ships for Unity, Unreal and Godot over a shared Photon Realtime C++ core, with a separate SDK per engine (Fusion, Realtime core). That is the Spine shape again: a shared core and separate per-engine layers, not one binary everywhere.

The absence is itself a finding. One artifact under two engines is something the field mostly does not attempt, and where it does (middleware), it maintains parallel code per engine rather than one artifact.

What published engine changes say

  • Slay the Spire 2. Mega Crit built it in Unity for over two years, moved it to Godot after the runtime-fee episode, and stayed moved after Unity backed down. No shared core is reported as extracted; the work was a move, not a bridge. Confidence MEDIUM: press reporting of the developer's statements, not an engineering write-up (link).
  • Caves of Qud. It began as a raw C# application with its own component-based architecture and later moved into Unity for cross-platform deployment, keeping its C# game logic; its lead has said the original architecture was close to how Unity works underneath, which made that feasible (press kit). Confidence LOW-MEDIUM: interview and press-kit sourcing, no engineering post-mortem. A later report points the other way about the same game ("Caves of Qud, both ways", below), so it should not be cited as evidence in either direction.

The line for a port: moving the core matches what Quantum, Spine and Forge all do. One artifact running inside both Unity and Unreal has no published precedent, so treat a shared binary as a convenience you happen to get, not as the thing the architecture depends on.

Who owns the state

The simulation owns it

The field's answer is not split.

  • Photon Quantum. The Frame is the game state. The Unity view holds none of it, and the documentation tells it to use the Frame API only to read, because writing from Unity would be non-deterministic. State lives in generated structs inside the frame, and the view polls them (link).
  • Forge. The framework owns attributes, tags, effect lifecycles, ability grants and cooldowns; engines keep no parallel state.
  • Unity's own guidance. Unity's testing articles and its ScriptableObject guidance both push logic out of MonoBehaviour into plain C# for testability, for the blunt reason that a MonoBehaviour cannot be created with new, so it cannot be constructed or mocked in a test (unit testing, data and logic).

Confidence HIGH: three independent sources, one of them the engine vendor a port leaves, agreeing on the direction. None of them has the model reading state back out of the engine object. Chapter 6's method starts from the same rule: the model owns the state and the host shows it.

Role interfaces and header interfaces

Cutting a model out of engine classes tends to leave many narrow interfaces, each naming exactly the members one collaboration needs, all implemented by the one engine-side class. That has a name, and Martin Fowler recommends it: it is his RoleInterface, which he argues for against the HeaderInterface (one big interface that mirrors the class). The only cost he names is the effort of studying each collaboration to form its role interface, and he does not treat many small interfaces as a problem in themselves (RoleInterface). Confidence HIGH on what the page says.

So the argument for collapsing them cannot be "role interfaces are bad"; that loses to Fowler. The argument that survives is a measurement: with one production implementor nothing is actually segregated, and every forwarding member and generic parameter is a cost paid for a substitutability nobody uses. The reference port's first extraction, as recorded on 2026-09-30, had 130 interfaces, 128 of them with one implementor, and 141 members whose only job was to forward.

The sharper name comes from putting the two definitions together. Each interface cut per collaboration is a role interface, and Fowler says he much prefers those. But when dozens of them together enumerate the class's entire public surface, member for member, with no transformation at any step, the aggregate is a header interface split many ways, and Fowler defines the header interface as an explicit interface mimicking the class's implicit public one and recommends against it (HeaderInterface). Role interfaces in construction, one header interface in aggregate: that explains why each individual decision looked right and the whole did not, and it is a better argument than either "role interfaces are fine" or "too many interfaces".

Names for the fix

Three traditions point the same way:

  • Aggregate (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design): one object owns a consistency boundary, and outside code holds a reference to it, not to its parts.
  • Humble Object: the hard-to-test environment object becomes a thin shell over a testable core. Its primary page, xunitpatterns.com, refused the connection on 2026-09-30, so it is named here, not quoted.
  • Plain-data components (Quantum's DSL, Overwatch's ECS, data-oriented design generally): the state is a struct, there is no interface at all, and systems run over filtered sets of structs.

The third is the one the field actually ships: Quantum did not solve the problem of many facets with a better interface; it removed interfaces from the state model. When moving a model's runtime state into one sealed aggregate, justify it with the measured cost (generic parameters and forwarding members that only ever serve one class), not with the interface count, because on interface count alone the literature is against you.

How the core tells the view what happened

"The simulation emits events and the view interprets them" is the standard answer, but the field never uses events alone. Two independent shipped systems - one commercial middleware, the other Epic's own framework inside the engine a port moves to - describe the same three-part split. Their agreement is the strongest single result of this research.

Poll, events, commands

Poll for anything continuous. Quantum's guidance is that polling the simulation from Unity is generally preferable for ongoing visuals, and events are for one-off occurrences where the simulation triggers a reaction in the view. Polling code is simpler, suits visual data that changes very often, and makes late joiners automatic: everything needed to build the view is already in the game state.

Events for one-off occurrences, with their unreliability documented. Quantum events are fire-and-forget, carry information from the simulation to the view, and must never be used to change game state. A late joiner does not receive events raised before it joined, so anything visual built from events has to be re-created by hand; and by the time an event arrives, the entity view it targets may already be destroyed.

Epic says the same in Unreal's vocabulary. Gameplay Cues (the Gameplay Ability System documentation for UE 5.8, read 2026-09-30) are the Actors and UObjects that run visual and sound effects, and the preferred way to replicate cosmetic feedback in a multiplayer game. They do not use reliable replication, so a client may never receive one; tying gameplay code to them causes desyncs, so they are for cosmetic feedback only (link).

Address effects by tag, not by call. This is the part worth copying. A Gameplay Cue is not called: it is associated with Gameplay Tags, and any Gameplay Effect that matches those tags applies it, which Epic presents as a way to build a universal library of visual effects without triggering them from code. The simulation applies an effect carrying a tag; the presentation registers handlers against tags; no simulation code names a presentation function.

Commands for the direction that needs an answer, and never synchronous. Quantum Commands carry input from the view into the simulation. They are DeterministicCommand objects, serialised, sent and consumed by the simulation on a later tick, and a remote client cannot predict which tick (link). The view asks; the simulation answers by acting on a later frame; nothing blocks.

Confidence HIGH: two independent vendors, both primary documentation, read verbatim, saying the same three things.

Where events break

  • Rollback duplicates events. A frame can be simulated more than once (prediction, rollback), so its events can be raised more than once. Quantum's mitigations are a hash over the event's data to drop duplicates (nothashed marks the members left out of the hash) and a synced keyword that holds an event until the server confirms the frame, trading latency for never raising a false event or missing a true one. Both exist because the naive version is wrong.
  • Anything built from events cannot be rebuilt on a late join, a reconnect, a save and load, or a replay scrub. Quantum's polling advice and its late-joiner warning both exist for this.
  • The general form. Fowler, on Event Sourcing: if events cause update messages to external systems, things go wrong on replay, because those systems cannot tell real processing from a replay; and queries and updates to external systems are where Event Sourcing gets most complicated, worst of all when one interaction does both. His fix is a Gateway that holds a reference to the event processor and checks for replay mode before passing a call out (link).

Confidence HIGH on Fowler (primary, read directly) and on Quantum (vendor documentation, read verbatim). A callback from the model into the engine is this general form: each is a call to an external system that a replay will repeat.

What really needs a synchronous answer

As far as the research could find evidence, fewer things than it seems, and they split two ways:

  • "Can this move?" is a QUERY on the model, not a call into the view. The model can answer it at once, because the model owns the state; it is a callback only while the state still lives in the engine object, and moving the state dissolves it. Keeping queries apart from state-changing commands is CQRS (link), cited as a name and not as game-specific evidence.
  • "Did the player confirm?" is a COMMAND that arrives later, as Quantum's do. The simulation does not wait for it; it processes it on a later tick. A playback queue between the model and the host is the mechanism that makes this possible.

The line for a port: everything shaped "something happened, show it" becomes a tagged event, and each engine's layer registers handlers by tag, which is Epic's own answer inside Unreal. Everything continuous is polled off the model instead. The residue that truly needs an answer is checked again once the state has moved into the model, because "can this move" becomes a query the model can answer itself.

Determinism across runtimes

A port that runs the same C# on Unity's Mono and on CoreCLR (an UnrealSharp host, a headless test run) meets this directly: Chapter 6 compares the runtimes' answers by float bits. Most of this section was read as raw text from the standards and from the .NET runtime's GitHub issues.

What the standards allow

ECMA-334, the C# language standard, section 8.3.7 "Floating-point types", says floating-point operations may be performed with higher precision than the operation's result type, and that an explicit cast forces a value to its type's exact precision. Its own illustration: some hardware has an extended floating-point type and does all arithmetic in it, and C# allows that rather than make such hardware give up speed and precision. Usually this has no measurable effect, but in an expression of the form x * y / z, where the multiplication leaves the double range and the division brings it back, the wider evaluation can give a finite result instead of an infinity (standard, Microsoft's copy).

ECMA-335, the CLI standard, Partition I section 12.1.3, says the size of the internal floating-point representation is implementation-dependent and may vary, as long as it is at least as precise as the value it represents; that freedom ends at an explicit conversion (conv.r4 or conv.r8), after which the value must be exactly representable in its type (PDF).

Confidence VERY HIGH: both read as raw text from the standards' own sources.

What it means: a one-ULP difference between runtimes is not a bug. Both specifications explicitly license it, and the C# standard chose a multiply-divide to show it. Byte identity across Mono, CoreCLR and a headless run is an observed property of today's builds, not a guarantee; it can break on a Unity or .NET upgrade with no change to the game's code.

Fused multiply-add, and Mono's float32

A natural first diagnosis of cross-runtime float drift is the JIT fusing a multiply and an add. The .NET team went the other way, deliberately:

  • dotnet/runtime#64591 proposed emitting fmadd for x * y + z. Tanner Gooding, who owns System.Numerics, closed it: not a safe or legal default optimisation, because a fused operation returns a different result for many inputs. He noted that Clang and MSVC allow it only under ffast-math and fp:fast, while GCC defaults to -ffp-contract=fast, and that it is a value-changing optimisation, not IEEE 754 compliant.
  • dotnet/runtime#64604 then set -ffp-contract=off for GCC builds of the runtime itself.
  • dotnet/runtime#12753, "Configurable floating-point behavior (Fast Math)", was closed unimplemented, with no long-term plans. .NET has no fast-math mode.

Confidence VERY HIGH: maintainer comments read raw from the GitHub API.

The better suspect is Mono. Miguel de Icaza wrote (2018-04-11) that Mono, decades earlier, made the mistake of performing all 32-bit float computation as 64-bit while storing the data in 32-bit locations, and later added a runtime feature, "float32", enabled with --O=float32, to do 32-bit float operations in 32 bits like everyone else (link). The Mono man page lists float32 as an opt-in optimisation.

That is exactly a one-ULP generator on a float multiply-divide: Mono computing a*b/c at double precision and rounding once at the store, CoreCLR rounding to float32 after each operation. ECMA-335 section 12.1.3 is the clause that makes Mono's behaviour legal. Confidence HIGH on the mechanism and the sources; MEDIUM that it is the cause in a given game, because which Mono build and which float32 setting a Unity version ships was not verified.

The one-line experiment that settles it. ECMA-335 says extra precision must be discarded at an explicit conversion, so compare (float)((float)(a * b) / c) against a * b / c in a differential harness. If the casts close the gap, the cause is intermediate precision and the fused-multiply-add hypothesis is dead. The reference port ran this as two rule groups: written as one expression, Unity's Mono was the odd one out on every differing row; written with explicit float locals, the same expression agreed on every runtime (Chapter 6).

Two divergences that are not rounding

Float-to-int casts are a known, open, unfixed difference between Mono and CoreCLR. dotnet/runtime#119821, filed 2025-09-17, shows (int)(float)int.MaxValue giving 7fffffff on CoreCLR and 80000000 on Mono. Jan Kotas, a .NET architect, replied that since .NET 9 float-to-integer conversions saturate on CoreCLR on every architecture, that this was not fixed on Mono, and that these conversions are undefined behaviour there. It is tracked by dotnet/runtime#100368, not fixed (the .NET 9 change).

System.Math transcendentals call into the platform's C runtime (FCALLs), and the same .NET build was measured to differ between operating systems. From dotnet/runtime#12753, on one .NET 3.0 preview:

call Windows macOS
MathF.Asinh(0.48549962f) 0.46820483 0.46820486
MathF.Acos(0.57316583f) 0.96043230 0.96043223
MathF.Log2(1/3.0f) -1.5849625 -1.5849624

dotnet/runtime#9001, which asks for System.Math and System.MathF to be implemented in managed code rather than as FCALLs to the C runtime, is still open. Only Math.Sqrt is IEEE-guaranteed.

An independent Unity measurement agrees on the shape. IronWarrior's harness, run on Windows (Intel and AMD), Mac, Android, iOS and WebGL, reported non-deterministic results only in the trigonometric functions; arithmetic, comparisons and int / float casts matched (link). Confidence MEDIUM-HIGH: one author's harness, but a real cross-device measurement, and it matches the theory.

Confidence on the two divergences themselves: VERY HIGH (a maintainer's statement with an open tracking issue; numbers in the issue, with an open design issue explaining the cause). Both are likelier, larger and cheaper to find than a ULP.

Fixed point

For bit identity across arbitrary hardware, fixed point is the standard answer. Four independent projects say so in their own documentation:

  • Photon Quantum replaces every float and double with its FP struct to ensure cross-platform determinism: Q48.16, one long, lookup tables for trigonometry and square root. Its documentation warns that converting from a float inside the simulation is not deterministic and desyncs every time (link).
  • mas-bandwidth/fixed (Q48.16): its README says deterministic lockstep and client / server simulations need every machine to compute the same numbers from the same inputs, that fused multiply-add, libm transcendentals and -ffp-contract differ across compilers and architectures, and that fixed point removes the whole class (link).
  • Klotho (deterministic C# for Unity and Godot): 32.32 fixed point and Xorshift128+, explicitly targeting Mono and IL2CPP (link).
  • Factorio does not store positions as floats: MapPosition is a 32-bit integer with 8 fraction bits, a smallest step of 1/256 (link).

The reversal that carries the most weight. Glenn Fiedler's canonical 2010 article "Floating Point Determinism" concluded, conditionally, that floating-point results can be deterministic across computers given an executable built with the same compiler, machines of the same architecture and some platform-specific tricks (link). Sixteen years later the same author's company ships the fixed-point library above and names fused multiply-add and fp-contract as the reason floats cannot do it. Note his 2010 condition: the same compiler. Two JITs are two compilers, so by the field's own rule byte identity across Mono and CoreCLR is outside what anyone claims to be able to rely on. Confidence VERY HIGH: vendor and author documentation, read raw.

What fixed point costs

Quantum's own documentation names the costs:

  • the representable fraction is limited and never as accurate as a double;
  • two parsing routes can give different values on the same machine: FP.FromFloat_UNSAFE(1.1f).RawValue != FP.FromString("1.1").RawValue;
  • an overflow ceiling: FP.UseableMax, 32767.9999847412, is the largest value that can be squared without overflowing;
  • precision is decent while numbers stay in about 0.01 to 1000; multiplying very large or very small numbers and dividing back to the original range loses precision;
  • FP is a struct, so it cannot be a C# constant: a constant is written as its raw long, with the decimal value in a comment.

BOID, a shipped cross-platform RTS that moved entirely to 64-bit fixed point with a 12-bit fraction, adds that no third-party library can be used and that float cannot simply be replaced globally with a fixed-point type (link).

The irony worth naming: Quantum's own stated worst case for fixed point is multiply-then-divide, the same expression shape the C# standard uses for the float hazard. Moving to fixed point would not make that expression's problem vanish; it would turn a one-ULP disagreement into a bounded precision loss that both runtimes agree on. That is a real improvement, and a different thing from the problem going away. Confidence VERY HIGH on Quantum's list (its documentation, read raw), MEDIUM-HIGH on BOID (one studio's article).

What desynced shipped games

Every shipped lockstep success in this literature is one binary on one architecture.

  • Supreme Commander and Demigod (Gas Powered Games, quoted in Fiedler's article) set the FPU's precision and rounding at start-up, _controlfp(_PC_24, _MCW_PC) and _controlfp(_RC_NEAR, _MCW_RC), and then asserted both every tick, because some Microsoft API functions change the FPU mode behind the program's back. Over a million customers, with no reported FPU mismatch. Forrest Smith, on the same engine: setting the CPU to follow IEEE 754 strictly does the job, at a performance cost (link).
  • MotoGP (Shawn Hargreaves, quoted in Fiedler's article): replays stored as controller inputs could not be played back on machines with different CPU architectures, compilers or optimisation settings, so saved replays could not be shared between Xbox and PC, and any patch had to be built with exactly the original compiler.

And the published desync causes are overwhelmingly not floating point:

  • Forrest Smith's narrated Supreme Commander desyncs were memory bugs: uninitialised variables, dangling pointers to deleted components, the allocator reusing an address.
  • Factorio FFF #52: the team had feared float discrepancies between computers, and they turned out not to be a big problem. The bug was an ambiguous sort comparator, which different compilers' standard-library sorts order differently for equal elements (link).
  • Factorio FFF #108: a cross-platform desync from printf formatting, gcc printing 1e-05 where VS2013 printed 1e-005 (link).
  • Factorio FFF #340: Lua serialisation used nil as a placeholder for a cyclic reference, which deletes the key and changes the iteration order; and a cached maximum speed was recomputed instead of saved (link).
  • Age of Empires ("1500 Archers on a 28.8"): however thoroughly the team checksummed the world, its objects, pathfinding and targeting, one more thing always slipped under the radar, and out-of-sync was the stubborn bug that went to the wire. The coding discipline it cost: programmers had to learn to make the same number of random calls inside the simulation (link).

Confidence HIGH: four independent primary sources, agreeing on where the bugs come from - iteration order, sort stability, serialisation, string formatting, random-call counts, caching. Not ULPs.

Not needing bit identity at all

The modern alternative is not to need cross-platform determinism.

  • Valorant (Riot's own write-up): a server-authoritative model, in which some divergence between the server's simulation and a client's prediction is accepted as unavoidable; the server's result is the truth and the client adjusts. Its fixed 128 Hz step exists so the comparison is like for like, not so the bits match (link).
  • Rocket League (Jared Cone, GDC 2018, 182 slides): networked rigid-body physics shipping on PC and consoles, fully server-authoritative - inputs up, the full physics state down. The server's physics is compared with recorded history, and a large difference is corrected by reverting and re-simulating, at a stated cost of 24 correction frames at 200 ms ping and 120 Hz. The words determinism, float, double, precision and bitwise appear nowhere in the 182 slides (link). That is the tell: the comparison is a tolerance test, not an equality test.

Confidence HIGH on both (Riot's own article; the slide text read directly and searched for the absent words).

The line for a port: a byte-identical event log across runtimes is a stronger oracle than any shipped game in this literature attempted, and it is worth keeping as an instrument, but no specification backs it. The cheap moves, in order: run the explicit-cast experiment; audit for float-to-int casts and for System.Math calls other than Sqrt; then decide deliberately whether the contract is byte identity or logical parity with an ordering-and-tolerance comparison, because the first will one day break on a toolchain upgrade that the second would survive.

C# inside Unreal

A game whose rules are C# can keep them only if C# runs inside Unreal. All figures here were measured on 2026-09-30 from the GitHub API and the projects' own sites; any of them may have changed since.

UnrealSharp

  • UnrealSharp/UnrealSharp: MIT licence, 1,942 stars, 33 open issues, last push 2026-09-29. Active.
  • It requires Unreal Engine 5.6 to 5.8 and .NET 10.0.5 or newer, and strongly recommends a C++ project (repository, site).
  • It ships games and disclaims production readiness at the same time, and both statements are current. Its homepage lists three Steam titles made with it (Ballistic Brews, Forged: Reconquest, Prompt Crisis); its FAQ still says the plugin is not production ready yet, though the plan is that it will be (FAQ). The FAQ also says up-to-date binary builds are not released consistently, because of the pace of change, so it is compiled from source.

Read that as: it works well enough for small PC titles, its maintainers will not promise more, and its API is still moving. u2ue's Unreal hosts are UnrealSharp C# (Chapter 6), so this is the toolkit's dependency too.

Platforms

From the site's supported-platforms section: Windows and macOS are supported; Linux, iOS and Android are planned; no console appears at all, neither as supported nor as planned. Console and mobile builds are an open feature request, "NativeAOT (Console, mobile)" (issues). A community fork for native C++ transpilation and AOT builds exists, takuma-komatsu/UnrealSharp-dn2cpp, pushed 2026-09-23 with 0 stars: an experiment, not a route. Confidence HIGH: the project's own platform table and the open issue, both read on the day.

If consoles are in scope, the arrangement that runs the model's assembly inside Unreal through this plugin has an expiry date, and the model's boundary should stay serialisable, so that a separate process or a reimplementation could drive it one day. If they are not in scope, this costs nothing.

The trap class

The recent open issues are almost all interop lifetime and marshalling - what you would predict of a managed layer over UObject memory, and a class of bug a logic-parity test does not see:

  • TArrayReadOnly<T> is a live view into native memory with no lifetime tracking. If the owning native object is garbage collected while managed code holds the view, a later access reads freed memory, which surfaces as a NullReferenceException or as silently wrong data (#740).
  • TextMarshaller.ToNative writes a null TSharedRef for a null managed FText, which corrupts a C#-defined struct's cached defaults and crashes FText::IsEmpty() (#738).
  • An exception escaping an async void method in game code aborts the whole editor.
  • A crash in UCancellableAsyncAction's "Disregard for GC" object class.
  • "Missing dependency / Create Export" errors in a packaged game: a bug on the shipping path.
  • [UFunction] on a C# local function is silently inert.

From the FAQ: UnrealSharp reaches only what is exposed to reflection, the same restriction Blueprint has, so anything else needs C++ written by you; and a UObject class is made with NewObject<T>(), never new T(). The traps the reference port met with it are in Chapter 22.

The alternatives

option its state on 2026-09-30
UnrealCLR (nxrighthere) 3,305 stars, last push 2023-06-07: over three years dormant. Asked about this exact use, "all game logic in C#, Unreal used as UI only", its maintainer said the plugin accepts compiled assemblies whatever the project's structure, but that interop with managed code from widgets is the biggest problem, that only desktop is supported, and that the project depends on Microsoft and Epic (discussion)
USharp (pixeltris) archived, last push 2020-05-16; its own README said it was not usable for most use cases
Mono-UE a personal side project of several Microsoft employees, supported by neither Microsoft nor Epic (link)
a native core plus a layer per engine the Spine shape: proven, expensive, two implementations kept in lock step
a separate process plus a protocol the UCI shape: proven for decades, but the boundary moves out to serialisation and, in the chess case, state ownership splits between the two sides
reimplement the presentation per engine, keep only the model portable what Spine actually does

Confidence HIGH on the repository facts (measured through the API on the day), MEDIUM on the maintainer's words (read through summaries of the linked discussion, not the raw thread).

The line for a port: UnrealSharp is the only live option, and it is good enough to prove logic parity today. With no console path and no production promise from its maintainers, treat its CoreCLR run as a very good test instrument rather than a shipping commitment. The engine-free model is what keeps the options open if the plugin stalls; callbacks from the model into the engine are what close them.

The case against an engine-free core

This part of the research was told to find the case against. It found one, and not the one expected: it is not "do not separate the core". It is about the motive, and about where the seam is drawn.

Test the motive

Fowler's YAGNI page names four costs of a presumptive feature: building it, the delay, carrying it, and repairing it. Then it exempts the case that decides this one: YAGNI applies only to capabilities built for a presumptive feature, not to effort that makes the software easier to modify (link).

Run that over the work. Determinism, replay, save-game integrity and tests that need no editor all make the software easier to modify, and they pay this month, on the engine the game already runs on: exempt. A set of adapters for a second engine is a presumptive feature, and it pays build, delay, carry and repair every week until the second engine is real.

So the test: if taking the second engine off the roadmap would kill the appetite for extracting the model, the extraction was never about testability, and the literature will not back it. If it survives that question, it is exempt and the argument is closed. Confidence HIGH on Fowler's text; the test is the research's own framing of it.

The one measured study

BinSubaih and Maddock, "G-factor Portability in Game Development Using Game Engines", CyberGames 2007, University of Sheffield (PDF), built a "Game Space Architecture" - an engine-free game state with an adapter per engine - and ported it between Torque and a second engine. They measured:

  • a CPU overhead of 1.51 % and a memory overhead of 16.49 MB;
  • frames per second down 11.6 % at 55.49 messages per second, with the warning that the game space becomes the bottleneck;
  • data integrity across the different game states at risk: initial tests found no problems, but more were needed;
  • that the approach plainly requires extra work;
  • and, from their own port checklist, the finding that matters most: the game logic is not affected, but while the game objects in the game space stay intact, the ones in the engine have to be created again, and so does the object model.

Confidence MEDIUM-HIGH: peer-reviewed and actually measured, which is rare here, but on a small Torque demo, not a shipped commercial game, so the numbers are indicative rather than transferable.

What it says: the shared core saves the logic, and every engine-side object still has to be created again. The part the architecture protects is not the part the port costs.

How many ports

Alistair Cockburn, on the hexagonal architecture, writes that what is and is not a port is largely a matter of taste: one port per use case would give hundreds, merging them all would give only two, and neither extreme seems best. His own choice tends to a small number, two, three or four. In the same paragraph he adds that there seems to be no particular damage in choosing the "wrong" number (link). So he does not say a high port count is harmful; he says his taste runs low.

The correction that makes the charge useful: count ports properly. A port in Cockburn's sense is a boundary to an external technology. A model's view seams and platform services (Chapter 6) are ports; interfaces the model uses internally to read its own state are a coupling problem, not a port count. Counted that way, a presentation seam of a few interfaces sits inside his range, and the overshoot is the callbacks from the model into the engine. Confidence VERY HIGH on Cockburn's words, read on the day; the recount is the research's analysis of what a port is.

The rule of three

Robert Glass, Facts and Fallacies of Software Engineering: Fact 16, reuse-in-the-large (components) remains a mostly unsolved problem, though everyone agrees it matters; Fact 18 restates Biggerstaff's rules of three - a reusable component is three times as hard to build as a single-use one, and should be tried in three different applications before it is general enough to accept into a reuse library (link, restated independently at Coding Horror).

A model extracted from one game has been exercised in one application. By this rule it is two short of known-general, and the three-fold cost is being paid now. Confidence HIGH: a published book, a named researcher, cited independently.

One implementor per interface

  • The Reused Abstractions Principle (Jason Gorman): an interface with only one implementation is a code smell. Gorman's own posts returned HTTP 500 on every attempt and were not read. The verified anchor is Mark Seemann, "Interfaces are not abstractions" (2010-12-02), which credits the principle and separately describes header interfaces as stating the same thing twice without apparent benefit (link).
  • The honest counter: Ted Kaminski defends single-implementation interfaces because an intermediate interface cuts off transitive dependencies; his own caveat is that the benefit disappears when the interface and its only implementation live in the same module (link).

So look at where they live. When the interfaces live in the model's assembly and their one implementor - the engine's unit class, a MonoBehaviour - lives in the Unity assembly, they cut a real assembly boundary, and that is exactly why the model need not reference UnityEngine. They are doing genuine work. The case for one aggregate is then not that they do nothing; it is that one interface cuts the same boundary for a fraction of the price. Confidence HIGH on Seemann and Kaminski (both read directly), MEDIUM on the principle itself (its primary text was not reachable).

Pass-through layers

  • Architecture Sinkhole antipattern (Mark Richards and Neal Ford, Fundamentals of Software Architecture): requests that pass through layers with no business logic applied. Richards' rule of thumb is 80-20: up to about 20 % pass-through traffic is healthy. The O'Reilly chapter returned 403 and was not read; this is a secondary restatement that cites them (link). A layer that is 100 % pass-through (the reference port's 141 of 141 forwarding members) is five times the tolerated ratio: a number rather than a taste.
  • Middle Man, and its fix Remove Middle Man (Fowler), are the class-level names (link). The catalogue's own caveat: a middle man created on purpose to avoid dependencies between classes, or implementing Proxy or Decorator, is legitimate. That is Kaminski's point again, and it is why forwarding is not a mistake to begin with.
  • Speculative Generality (Fowler and Beck) is the name for the motive.
  • The sharpest operational test is Aleksey Kladov's "Concrete Abstraction" (2020-08-15): if every call site uses a concrete type and never a generic one, you do not need the abstraction; his case study deleted 124 lines by replacing traits with named functions (link). It is directly measurable: count how many of a model's generic type parameters are ever instantiated, outside test doubles, with anything but the one engine-side class. If the answer is zero, that number is the whole argument.

Abstraction as speculation

Robert Nystrom, Game Programming Patterns, is the strongest game-specific voice: every layer of abstraction or point of extensibility is a bet that the flexibility will be needed later; interfaces and abstractions everywhere make it slow to trace through the scaffolding to code that does something; and because predicting the future is hard, modularity that does not turn out useful quickly becomes actively harmful (link).

Sandi Metz, "The Wrong Abstraction" (2016): duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction, and the fastest way forward is back (link).

Confidence HIGH that these are the arguments and their sources; both are qualitative, with no measurements.

The performance argument does not apply

The performance case against abstraction is real and beside the point here. Casey Muratori's "Clean Code, Horrible Performance" measures roughly 1.5x from dropping polymorphism and up to about 15x with table-driven rewrites (link), and Mike Acton's CppCon 2014 keynote (video) is a console-engine performance argument. A turn-based rules core that resolves a whole turn at once is not a hot loop. Offered as the reason to collapse a model's interfaces, these are bad arguments, and the right response is to say so rather than to accept a free win on a bad premise.

Caves of Qud, both ways

Caves of Qud is reported to have completed a Unity-to-Godot port in a little over 24 hours (GameFromScratch), and then to have shipped its 1.0 on Unity anyway (Wikipedia). Confidence LOW on the 24 hours (one secondary source citing a post that could not be fetched), HIGH that 1.0 shipped on Unity. It partly contradicts the account of the game's earlier move into Unity under "What published engine changes say"; both could be true at different times, and neither is well sourced. Do not build an argument on Caves of Qud in either direction.

Why studios separate a core

  • BIT.GAMES. Pavel Schevaev, its CTO, on a shipped match-3 with a deterministic C# core split out of Unity, gives five motives: replays, determinism, testing, scripted logic and bot validation. Engine portability is not among them, and he says the overhead may not make sense in small projects (link).
  • Hearthstone runs its rules engine on the server, off the Unity client, for server authority, not portability.
  • Age of Empires separated simulation from rendering because 28.8 kbit bandwidth forced it, and got replays and anti-cheat free as a side effect.
  • Factorio's separation exists for lockstep.

The pattern across every real case in this research: people separate the core for determinism, testing and server authority. In the sources reached, nobody separated it in order to change engines. Confidence MEDIUM-HIGH: four independent cases, but "nobody" is bounded by what was found, not by what exists.

What nobody has published

  • No published case was found of an engine-agnostic core making a real engine port cheap. Searched across Unity to Godot, Unity to Unreal, Unreal to Unity, studio engineering blogs and the academic literature. The one measured study found the port still recreates every engine-side object. That is the hole in the justification for an engine-free core as a porting strategy, and it is stated here rather than papered over.
  • No published breakdown was found of a real engine port's work by part - game code against assets, effects, UI and tools. Epic's documentation answers it qualitatively (code does not transfer; everything visual is rebuilt), but nobody published percentages.
  • Not read, flagged rather than asserted: Gorman's posts on the Reused Abstractions Principle (HTTP 500 every time), Casey Yano's Godot evaluation (Medium, 403), Brian Bucklew's post on the Qud port (X, 402), the Road to Vostok devlogs (Patreon, 403), the O'Reilly Architecture Sinkhole chapter (403), xunitpatterns.com for Humble Object (connection refused), and Reddit (unreachable by the search tool). The research spent its search budget part way through and fetched sources directly after that, which is why a few are cited through a secondary restatement rather than their primary.

What the prior art says to do in a port

The lessons above, as one list, in the order the research would act on them:

  • Settle the motive in writing first ("Test the motive"). It is the only finding that can invalidate a plan rather than adjust it. If the second engine came off the roadmap tomorrow, would the extraction still be worth finishing? If yes, name the reasons that pay now; if no, the plan is a port strategy resting on one community plugin, tried in one application, with no published case of an engine-free core making a real port cheap.
  • Make byte identity a tripwire, and name the real contract. Neither ECMA-334 nor ECMA-335 promises it, and Fiedler's condition for float determinism is the same compiler, which two JITs are not. Make the contract the same ordered events with the same identities and values, floats compared to a stated tolerance, and keep the bit-for-bit checksum as the cheap, strict thing that fires first. Rocket League's comparison is a tolerance test; a port's can be stricter and still not be equality.
  • Run the explicit-cast experiment before spending anything else on drift: (float)((float)(a * b) / c) against a * b / c, since conv.r4 must discard extra precision. Expect it to rule out fused multiply-add: RyuJIT deliberately refuses to contract a*b+c (dotnet/runtime#64591), and .NET has no fast-math mode (#12753, closed unimplemented); Mono's historical float32-as-double arithmetic is the better suspect.
  • Audit the model for the two known non-rounding divergences: any float-to-int cast (undefined on Mono, dotnet/runtime#119821 and #100368), and any System.Math or MathF call other than Sqrt (FCALLs into the platform's C runtime, measured to differ between Windows and macOS on one .NET build). Both are likelier, larger and cheaper to find than a ULP.
  • Guard against what actually desynced shipped games: ambiguous sort comparators (Factorio FFF #52), iteration order over hash containers (FFF #340), random-call-count discipline (Age of Empires), and number-to-string formatting inside the model (FFF #108, 1e-05 against 1e-005). A checksum catches these after the fact; a guard names them.
  • Address presentation events by tag, not by method name. Epic's Gameplay Cues are not called: an effect carries a tag and the presentation registers handlers against tags. If events carry an identifier instead of naming a host method, a third engine gets a registry to fill rather than a list of members to implement. Converting N callbacks into N named event types moves the problem without solving it.
  • Give those events the three properties the field says they need: cosmetic only (Epic), droppable (Quantum: missed, duplicated, or arriving after the target view is gone), and rebuildable from state. Quantum's late-joiner rule and Fowler's replay rule are the same rule, and it bites on save and load and on scrubbing a replay even in a game with no multiplayer.
  • Sort the callbacks by shape before converting any, into three buckets: punctual (an event), continuous (the view reads it off the model every frame), and needs-an-answer (a query on the model, or a command answered on a later tick).
  • Count the "genuinely needs a synchronous answer" residue after the state has moved into the model, not before. "Can this move" is a query on state; once the model owns the state, that callback disappears, and counting earlier makes callbacks look more necessary than they are.
  • Argue an interface collapse with the sharper names: a header interface in aggregate, the sinkhole ratio, and Kladov's count of generic instantiations - and keep Kaminski's defence in view, so the refactor does not throw away interfaces that cut a real assembly boundary.
  • Write the presentation gaps on the second engine down as a feature matrix, as Spine's READMEs do, not as a to-do list. That is not a confession; it is how the pattern is operated.
  • Decide whether consoles are in scope, because it has an architectural consequence today (see "Platforms").

How u2ue differs

Measured against the routes above, using only this appendix's sources and the manual's own measured claims:

  • The shape is not new, and that is the point. An engine-free simulation that resolves a step and hands the view an ordered list of events is what Photon Quantum sells and what Epic's Gameplay Ability System does inside Unreal. u2ue's runtime library ships that split as PlaybackQueue<TEvent>: the model resolves an action at once and appends ordered events, and the host shows one per frame and takes input only when it has caught up (Chapter 6). As with Quantum's commands, nothing in the model waits on the view.
  • The model owns the state, the unanimous answer of every source here, and u2ue holds it with gates rather than advice: u2ue check --only model refuses an engine reference in the model and a platform member outside the hosting folder (Chapter 6, Chapter 10).
  • Logic parity is the contract for the code, and it is measured. On the reference port, three scripted battles write event logs that are byte-identical between the headless run and the Unreal host, and u2ue parity compares 383 rows across three runtimes (Unity on Mono, the Unreal host on CoreCLR, a headless test run): all agree except 35 one-ULP rows, each characterised and pinned to its exact bits (Chapter 6, Appendix A). No source in this research had a byte-comparable log across three runtimes; the Age of Empires post-mortem is an account of not having one. Because the standards do not promise bit identity, u2ue does not assume it: a difference is red unless that exact row is characterised, pinned to its bits and to one ULP.
  • It beats Epic's baseline for the code, and does not automate it. Epic's guidance assumes the code does not come across, and ProjectExodus ignores it. u2ue gives the code a method instead - an inventory, an engine-free model, Unity's frame, clock and coroutine rules in a runtime library, gates and parity - and thin UnrealSharp C# hosts. It does not move the code or write the hosts for you (Chapter 1, Chapter 6).
  • It converts the part an engine-free core does not protect. The one measured study found that every engine-side object has to be created again, and that is where u2ue's content tools are. No off-the-shelf Shuriken converter was found on 2026-08-22; u2ue converts Shuriken effects to Niagara through Epic's own FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary, and on the reference port (2026-10-15, its acceptance rebuild part way through) Unreal draws 7,810 of the 8,452 emitters Unity draws, 92.4 % (Chapter 8, Appendix A). Scenes are imported and graded by a fidelity gate (the reference port's first map: 45 checks, PASS), and uGUI screens are laid out by a port of uGUI's own solver (Chapter 7).
  • Gaps are written down, as Spine writes its gaps down. Every emitter Unity draws and the port does not is a gap, named and charged to its root, and an emitter one side lacks is named UNPAIRED, never dropped (Chapter 8, Chapter 10, Chapter 11).
  • Its gates can fail. mas-bandwidth/fixed hashes every result against a constant frozen into its source and ships deliberately broken targets, so that a suite which goes blind says so instead of passing quietly. Every u2ue gate carries planted defects it must refuse, because a gate that has only ever passed cannot be told apart from one that is switched off (Chapter 10).

And what the prior art says u2ue has not answered:

  • UnrealSharp is load-bearing for the Unreal hosts. On 2026-09-30 it had no console path, supported or planned, and its maintainers did not call it production ready.
  • Two games are one short of the rule of three. u2ue has run on the reference port and on a second, unrelated game, whose own Unreal host went from nothing to parity --require Unreal passing in 9 minutes (Chapter 3).
  • There is still no independent published case of an engine-free core making a real port cheap. The reference port is one case, documented in this manual (Appendix A), not an independent one.
  • Animation and physics are not covered (Chapter 1).
